abdominal aorta.name: Abdominal aorta
abdominal aorta.desc: The part of the aorta below the diaphragm, entering through the aortic hiatus at T12 and running down the front of the lumbar vertebrae, just left of the inferior vena cava. It gives the celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, renal, suprarenal, lumbar and inferior phrenic arteries, then splits into the two common iliac arteries at about L4.
clinical: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a widening, usually below the renal arteries, that can rupture and is screened for with ultrasound.
The aortic bifurcation sits roughly at the level of the umbilicus.

arch of aorta.name: Arch of aorta
arch of aorta.desc: The curved segment between the ascending and descending aorta, arching backward and to the left over the root of the left lung; it starts and ends at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5). Its three branches are the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum.
clinical: An aneurysm of the arch can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness.
Coarctation of the aorta usually narrows the vessel just past the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum.

ascending aorta.name: Ascending aorta
ascending aorta.desc: The first part of the aorta, about 5 cm long, rising from the left ventricle at the aortic valve inside the pericardial sac. Its only branches are the right and left coronary arteries, which leave from the aortic sinuses just above the valve cusps. It becomes the arch of the aorta at the level of the sternal angle.
clinical: Aortic dissection most often starts in the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) and is a surgical emergency.
Dilation of the aortic root can stretch the valve and cause aortic regurgitation.

descending aorta.name: Descending aorta
descending aorta.region: Thorax and abdomen, along the vertebral column
descending aorta.desc: The long segment of the aorta that continues from the arch at T4 down to the aortic bifurcation at L4. It has a thoracic part in the posterior mediastinum and an abdominal part below the diaphragm. Along the way it supplies the chest wall, esophagus, bronchi, spinal cord, gut, kidneys and posterior abdominal wall before dividing into the common iliac arteries.
clinical: Stanford type B dissections involve only the descending aorta and are often managed with blood pressure control or stent grafts.

descending thoracic aorta.name: Descending thoracic aorta
descending thoracic aorta.desc: The thoracic part of the descending aorta, running from T4 down the left side of the vertebral bodies, behind the left lung root and next to the esophagus. It gives the posterior intercostal and subcostal arteries, bronchial, esophageal and pericardial branches. It passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12 to become the abdominal aorta.
clinical: Its posterior intercostal arteries help feed the spinal cord, so surgery here risks spinal cord ischemia.
It lies right behind the esophagus, which is why transesophageal echo views it so well.

anterior cusp of aortic valve.name: Anterior cusp of aortic valve
anterior cusp of aortic valve.desc: One of the three semilunar cusps of the aortic valve, also called the right coronary cusp because the right coronary artery opens from the aortic sinus just above it. Its pocket-shaped cusp closes against the other two during diastole to stop blood flowing back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
clinical: Right coronary cusp prolapse can occur with a ventricular septal defect just below the valve.

{S} posterior cusp of aortic valve.name: Posterior cusp of aortic valve
{S} posterior cusp of aortic valve.desc: One of the two posterior semilunar cusps of the aortic valve in the older naming. The left posterior cusp is the left coronary cusp, with the left coronary artery opening from the sinus above it; the right posterior cusp is the non-coronary cusp, which sits next to the interatrial septum. Both seal the valve during diastole.
clinical: The non-coronary cusp lies close to the conduction system, so aortic valve surgery can cause heart block.
Calcification of the cusps causes aortic stenosis, common in older adults.

middle collateral branch of {S} deep bra.name: Middle collateral branch of the {S} deep brachial artery
middle collateral branch of {S} deep bra.desc: The posterior terminal branch of the deep brachial artery (profunda brachii). It runs down behind the humerus within or beside the medial head of triceps toward the elbow, supplying triceps along the way. It ends in the anastomosis around the elbow, joining the interosseous recurrent artery behind the lateral epicondyle.
clinical: The elbow anastomosis it joins keeps the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is slowly blocked or tied off below the deep brachial origin.

radial collateral branch of {S} deep bra.name: Radial collateral branch of the {S} deep brachial artery
radial collateral branch of {S} deep bra.region: Upper limb: lateral arm and elbow
radial collateral branch of {S} deep bra.desc: The anterior terminal branch of the deep brachial artery. It travels with the radial nerve through the lateral intermuscular septum to the front of the lateral epicondyle, running between brachialis and brachioradialis. It anastomoses with the radial recurrent artery, forming part of the collateral circulation around the elbow.
clinical: Because it accompanies the radial nerve, humeral shaft fractures that injure the nerve can also damage this vessel.

{S} brachial artery.name: Brachial artery
{S} brachial artery.region: Upper limb: medial arm and cubital fossa
{S} brachial artery.desc: The main artery of the arm, continuing from the axillary artery at the lower border of teres major. It runs down the medial arm with the median nerve, then lies in the cubital fossa medial to the biceps tendon and under the bicipital aponeurosis. It gives the deep brachial and ulnar collateral arteries and divides near the neck of the radius into the radial and ulnar arteries.
clinical: Blood pressure cuffs compress it, and the stethoscope listens over it in the cubital fossa.
Supracondylar humerus fractures in children can injure it, threatening the forearm's blood supply.

{S} deep brachial artery.name: Deep brachial artery
{S} deep brachial artery.desc: Also called the profunda brachii, it is the largest branch of the brachial artery, arising just below teres major. It spirals with the radial nerve in the radial groove behind the humerus, supplying triceps and the humerus. It ends by dividing into the middle collateral and radial collateral arteries, which join the elbow anastomosis.
clinical: A midshaft humeral fracture can damage both this artery and the radial nerve lying with it in the radial groove.

{S} common carotid artery.name: Common carotid artery
{S} common carotid artery.desc: The main artery to the head and neck. The right one arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left directly from the arch of the aorta. It climbs in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve, has no branches in the neck, and divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (about C3/C4) into the internal and external carotid arteries.
clinical: The carotid pulse is felt just beside the larynx, in front of sternocleidomastoid.
Plaque at the bifurcation is a major cause of stroke and can be removed by carotid endarterectomy.

{S} internal carotid artery.name: Internal carotid artery
{S} internal carotid artery.region: Neck and skull base into brain
{S} internal carotid artery.desc: The branch of the common carotid that supplies the brain and eye. It has no branches in the neck, enters the skull through the carotid canal, runs through the cavernous sinus, then gives the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries. It ends by splitting into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, forming part of the circle of Willis.
clinical: Narrowing of the ICA can cause transient ischemic attacks, including brief one-eye vision loss (amaurosis fugax).
Aneurysms at its posterior communicating junction can compress the oculomotor nerve and cause a droopy eyelid and dilated pupil.

circumflex branch of {S} coronary artery.name: Circumflex branch of the {S} coronary artery
circumflex branch of {S} coronary artery.desc: One of the two main branches of the left main coronary artery. It curves left and back in the atrioventricular groove under the left auricle, giving obtuse marginal branches to the lateral wall of the left ventricle and branches to the left atrium. In about 40% of people it supplies the sinoatrial node, and in left-dominant hearts it gives the posterior interventricular artery.
clinical: Blockage of the circumflex causes lateral wall heart attacks, which can be easy to miss on a standard ECG.

conus branch of anterior interventricula.name: Conus branch of the anterior interventricular branch of the {S} coronary artery
conus branch of anterior interventricula.desc: A small branch from the start of the left anterior descending artery that runs to the conus arteriosus (infundibulum), the outflow part of the right ventricle below the pulmonary valve. It often meets the conus artery from the right coronary to form an arterial ring around the outflow tract (the circle of Vieussens).
clinical: The circle of Vieussens can act as a collateral route between the left and right coronary systems when one is blocked.

diagonal branch of anterior descending b.name: Diagonal branch of the anterior descending branch of the {S} coronary artery
diagonal branch of anterior descending b.desc: A branch of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) that runs diagonally down and to the left over the anterior surface of the left ventricle. Diagonal branches supply the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle and help feed the anterolateral papillary muscle. Most people have one to three, numbered D1, D2 and so on.
clinical: A large diagonal branch counts as a major vessel, so its blockage can cause a significant anterolateral heart attack.

first anterior ventricular branch of {S}.name: First anterior ventricular branch of the {S} coronary artery
first anterior ventricular branch of {S}.desc: An early branch of the right coronary artery that leaves it in the atrioventricular groove and runs onto the front (sternocostal) surface of the right ventricle. Anterior ventricular branches supply the free wall of the right ventricle.
clinical: Proximal right coronary blockage takes out these branches and can cause right ventricular infarction with low blood pressure.

first posterior ventricular branch of {S.name: First posterior ventricular branch of the {S} coronary artery
first posterior ventricular branch of {S.desc: A branch of the right coronary artery given off near the crux of the heart, on the inferior surface. Posterior ventricular branches supply the diaphragmatic wall of the left ventricle in right-dominant hearts, extending the right coronary's territory beyond the posterior interventricular groove.
clinical: These branches are part of why right coronary blockage usually causes an inferior wall heart attack.

first septal branch of {S} posterior int.name: First septal branch of the {S} posterior interventricular artery
first septal branch of {S} posterior int.desc: The first of the small perforating branches that the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery sends up into the interventricular septum. Together these posterior septal branches supply roughly the back third of the septum, the rest being supplied by septal branches of the LAD.
clinical: Loss of posterior septal perfusion in an inferior heart attack can contribute to conduction problems or rarely a septal rupture.

first {S} anterior branch of anterior in.name: First {S} anterior branch of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery
first {S} anterior branch of anterior in.region: Heart: anterior right ventricle near the septum
first {S} anterior branch of anterior in.desc: The first of several small branches that the left anterior descending artery (LAD) gives off toward the right, onto the anterior wall of the right ventricle next to the anterior interventricular groove. These right ventricular branches supplement the right coronary's supply to the right ventricle.
clinical: These small branches can carry collateral flow to the right ventricle when the right coronary artery is blocked.

marginal branch of {S} coronary artery.name: Marginal branch of the {S} coronary artery
marginal branch of {S} coronary artery.region: Heart: acute (inferior) margin of right ventricle
marginal branch of {S} coronary artery.desc: Also called the acute marginal artery, this branch of the right coronary artery runs along the sharp lower (acute) margin of the heart toward the apex. It supplies the free wall of the right ventricle.
clinical: Its territory is part of what is lost in right ventricular infarction, which can cause low blood pressure with clear lungs.

posterior interventricular branch of {S}.name: Posterior interventricular branch of the {S} coronary artery
posterior interventricular branch of {S}.desc: Also called the posterior descending artery. It runs in the posterior interventricular groove toward the apex, supplying the inferior walls of both ventricles and the back third of the interventricular septum through septal branches. It comes from the right coronary in most people (right-dominant circulation); whichever artery gives it defines coronary dominance.
clinical: The atrioventricular nodal artery usually arises near its origin, so inferior heart attacks can cause heart block.

second septal branch of {S} posterior in.name: Second septal branch of the {S} posterior interventricular artery
second septal branch of {S} posterior in.desc: One of the small perforating branches the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery sends into the back part of the interventricular septum. With the other posterior septal branches it supplies roughly the posterior third of the septum.
clinical: Septal branches from the front and back can link up, giving collateral flow when either the LAD or the posterior descending artery is blocked.

second {S} anterior branch of anterior i.name: Second {S} anterior branch of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery
second {S} anterior branch of anterior i.region: Heart: anterior right ventricle near the septum
second {S} anterior branch of anterior i.desc: One of the small branches that the left anterior descending artery gives off toward the right, crossing onto the anterior wall of the right ventricle beside the interventricular groove. These branches add to the right ventricle's blood supply.
clinical: Like the other right ventricular branches of the LAD, it can carry collateral flow when the right coronary artery is blocked.

septal branch of anterior interventricul.name: Septal branch of the anterior interventricular artery
septal branch of anterior interventricul.desc: A perforating branch that the left anterior descending artery sends straight down into the interventricular septum. Septal branches supply about the front two-thirds of the septum, including the bundle of His and the bundle branches of the conduction system. The first septal perforator is usually the largest.
clinical: Blockage of septal branches can cause bundle branch block.
In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a septal branch can be deliberately blocked to thin an overgrown septum (septal ablation).

third {S} anterior branch of anterior in.name: Third {S} anterior branch of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery
third {S} anterior branch of anterior in.region: Heart: anterior right ventricle near the septum
third {S} anterior branch of anterior in.desc: A small branch that the left anterior descending artery sends to the right, onto the anterior wall of the right ventricle near the anterior interventricular groove. With the first and second branches it supplements the right ventricle's supply from the right coronary artery.
clinical: These branches are small, but they are a route for collateral blood flow between the left and right coronary systems.

trunk of anterior interventricular branc.name: Trunk of the anterior interventricular branch of the {S} coronary artery
trunk of anterior interventricular branc.desc: The main stem of the left anterior descending artery (LAD), which runs down the anterior interventricular groove from the left main coronary to the apex, often wrapping around it. It gives diagonal branches to the anterior left ventricle and septal branches to the front two-thirds of the septum, supplying the largest share of left ventricular muscle.
clinical: A blockage near the start of the LAD is nicknamed the widowmaker because it can stop blood to a huge area of heart muscle.
LAD blockage typically shows ST elevation in the anterior chest leads V1 to V4.

trunk of {S} coronary artery.name: Trunk of the {S} coronary artery
trunk of {S} coronary artery.region: Heart: coronary sulcus at the aortic root
trunk of {S} coronary artery.desc: The first stretch of a coronary artery after it leaves its aortic sinus. On the left it is the short left main coronary artery, which passes behind the pulmonary trunk and splits into the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex arteries. On the right it is the proximal right coronary artery, which runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving the conus and sinoatrial nodal branches in most people.
clinical: A significant left main blockage endangers most of the left ventricle and is often treated with bypass surgery.
Proximal right coronary blockage can cause inferior and right ventricular infarction with slow heart rhythms.

{S} conus artery.name: Conus artery
{S} conus artery.desc: Usually the first branch of the right coronary artery, though in many people it has its own opening in the aortic sinus (a third coronary artery). It runs to the conus arteriosus, the outflow part of the right ventricle, and joins the conus branch of the LAD to form the circle of Vieussens.
clinical: When it arises separately, it can be missed during coronary angiography.
It can provide collateral flow to the LAD territory if the LAD is blocked.

{S} femoral artery.name: Femoral artery
{S} femoral artery.region: Lower limb: femoral triangle and adductor canal
{S} femoral artery.desc: The main artery of the lower limb. It continues from the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, runs through the femoral triangle lateral to the femoral vein, then through the adductor canal under sartorius. Its biggest branch is the deep femoral artery, which supplies the thigh. It becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus.
clinical: The femoral pulse is felt just below the inguinal ligament, halfway between the pubic symphysis and the hip bone's anterior superior spine.
It is the most common access point for cardiac catheterization and angiography.

inferior vena cava.name: Inferior vena cava
inferior vena cava.region: Abdomen: retroperitoneum, right of the aorta
inferior vena cava.desc: The largest vein in the body, returning blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen to the heart. It forms at about L5 where the two common iliac veins join, ascends to the right of the aorta, and receives the lumbar, renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic and hepatic veins. It passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium.
clinical: An IVC filter can be placed to catch clots from leg veins before they reach the lungs.
Ultrasound of how much the IVC collapses with breathing helps estimate a patient's fluid status.

{S} internal jugular vein.name: Internal jugular vein
{S} internal jugular vein.desc: The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus, descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery with the vagus nerve, and joins the subclavian vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein. Tributaries include the facial, lingual and superior and middle thyroid veins.
clinical: The right IJV is a common site for central venous catheters because it runs straight down into the superior vena cava.
Its pulsation in the neck (jugular venous pressure) reflects pressure in the right atrium.

cavity of {S} atrium.name: Cavity of the {S} atrium
cavity of {S} atrium.desc: The inside chamber of an atrium, which collects blood before it passes to the ventricle. The right atrial cavity receives the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus and empties through the tricuspid valve; its septal wall shows the fossa ovalis. The left atrial cavity receives the four pulmonary veins and empties through the mitral valve, and its auricle forms a small pouch.
clinical: In atrial fibrillation, clots most often form in the left atrial appendage and can travel to the brain.
A patent foramen ovale lets blood or clots cross from the right atrium to the left.

wall of {S} atrium.name: Wall of the {S} atrium
wall of {S} atrium.desc: The thin muscular wall of an atrium. The right atrial wall has a smooth part where the venae cavae enter and a rough part with pectinate muscles, separated by the crista terminalis; it holds the sinoatrial node near the superior vena cava. The left atrial wall is mostly smooth, with pectinate muscles only in its auricle, and forms most of the back of the heart.
clinical: An enlarged left atrium can press on the esophagus, which is why transesophageal echo gives clear views of it.
Atrial fibrillation often starts from muscle sleeves where the pulmonary veins join the left atrial wall, the target of catheter ablation.

anterolateral head of lateral papillary.name: Anterolateral head of the lateral papillary muscle of the {S} ventricle
anterolateral head of lateral papillary.desc: One head of the anterolateral (lateral) papillary muscle of the left ventricle, a finger-like muscle rising from the anterolateral wall. Its chordae tendineae attach to both mitral leaflets and pull them taut during systole so they do not flip back into the left atrium.
clinical: The anterolateral papillary muscle usually has a dual blood supply (LAD and circumflex), so it ruptures less often than the posteromedial one.

cavity of {S} ventricle.name: Cavity of the {S} ventricle
cavity of {S} ventricle.desc: The inner chamber of a ventricle, which pumps blood out of the heart. The right ventricular cavity is crescent-shaped around the septum, lined with coarse trabeculae carneae and the moderator band, and flows from the tricuspid valve to the pulmonary valve through the smooth infundibulum. The left ventricular cavity is cone-shaped with a thick wall, filling through the mitral valve and ejecting through the aortic valve.
clinical: After a large heart attack, a clot can form in the left ventricular cavity over the damaged wall and travel to the brain.
In pulmonary hypertension the right ventricular cavity dilates and pushes the septum toward the left.

lateral papillary muscle of {S} ventricl.name: Lateral papillary muscle of the {S} ventricle
lateral papillary muscle of {S} ventricl.desc: Usually called the anterolateral papillary muscle, it is one of the two papillary muscles of the left ventricle, rising from the anterolateral wall. Its chordae tendineae anchor the anterolateral halves of both mitral leaflets, keeping the valve shut against high pressure during systole.
clinical: It usually gets blood from both the LAD (diagonals) and circumflex, making it more resistant to rupture after a heart attack than the posteromedial papillary muscle.

posterior vein of {S} ventricle.name: Posterior vein of the {S} ventricle
posterior vein of {S} ventricle.region: Heart: inferior surface of left ventricle
posterior vein of {S} ventricle.desc: A cardiac vein that runs on the diaphragmatic (inferior) surface of the left ventricle, between the left marginal vein and the middle cardiac vein. It drains that part of the left ventricle and empties into the coronary sinus, which returns the blood to the right atrium.
clinical: Leads for cardiac resynchronization pacemakers are passed through the coronary sinus into lateral and posterior cardiac veins like this one to pace the left ventricle.

anterolateral central branch of {S} midd.name: Anterolateral central branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery
anterolateral central branch of {S} midd.region: Brain: deep, through the anterior perforated substance
anterolateral central branch of {S} midd.desc: One of the lenticulostriate arteries, thin perforating branches that leave the first (M1) segment of the middle cerebral artery and climb through the anterior perforated substance. They supply deep structures, including the putamen, much of the caudate and globus pallidus, and the internal capsule. They are end arteries with little backup supply.
clinical: Rupture of these vessels, often from long-term high blood pressure, is a classic cause of deep brain hemorrhage.
Blockage causes small lacunar strokes in the internal capsule, such as pure motor weakness of one side of the body.

branch of {S} middle cerebral artery to.name: Branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery to the {S} angular gyrus
branch of {S} middle cerebral artery to.desc: A cortical (M4) branch of the middle cerebral artery, often regarded as its terminal continuation, that emerges from the back end of the lateral sulcus to supply the angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule, where the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes meet. This region links reading, writing, calculation and spatial attention.
clinical: Damage to the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus can cause Gerstmann syndrome: trouble writing, calculating, naming fingers and telling left from right.

insular part of {S} middle cerebral arte.name: Insular part of the {S} middle cerebral artery
insular part of {S} middle cerebral arte.region: Brain: insula, deep in the lateral sulcus
insular part of {S} middle cerebral arte.desc: The M2 segment of the middle cerebral artery. After turning at the genu over the limen insulae, its divisions run back and up across the surface of the insula, giving small insular branches. It ends at the top of the insula's circular sulcus, where the branches turn out of the lateral sulcus as the opercular (M3) segment.
clinical: A blockage here (an M2 occlusion) can cause a stroke affecting either the upper or lower division territory, and is sometimes treated by clot retrieval.

middle temporal branch of {S} middle cer.name: Middle temporal branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery
middle temporal branch of {S} middle cer.desc: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery, usually from its inferior division, that leaves the lateral sulcus and runs down across the middle of the lateral temporal lobe. It supplies the superior and middle temporal gyri, which include auditory association cortex.
clinical: In the dominant hemisphere, strokes in the inferior division's temporal branches can cause Wernicke aphasia: fluent speech with poor comprehension.

posterior temporal branch of {S} middle.name: Posterior temporal branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery
posterior temporal branch of {S} middle.desc: A cortical branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery that runs back and down over the posterior part of the lateral temporal lobe. It supplies the back parts of the superior and middle temporal gyri, including Wernicke's area in the dominant hemisphere.
clinical: Blockage on the dominant side can cause Wernicke aphasia, often with a visual field cut from involvement of the optic radiation beneath.

sphenoid part of {S} middle cerebral art.name: Sphenoid part of the {S} middle cerebral artery
sphenoid part of {S} middle cerebral art.region: Brain base: lateral sulcus near the sphenoid ridge
sphenoid part of {S} middle cerebral art.desc: The M1 or horizontal segment of the middle cerebral artery, running from its origin at the end of the internal carotid laterally along the sphenoid ridge to the limen insulae, where it usually splits into superior and inferior divisions. It gives the lenticulostriate (anterolateral central) arteries to the deep brain and the anterior temporal artery.
clinical: An M1 blockage causes a large stroke with face and arm weakness, sensory loss and gaze deviation, and is a key target for emergency clot retrieval.
Aneurysms commonly form at the MCA bifurcation at the end of M1.

temporo-occipital branch of {S} middle c.name: Temporo-occipital branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery
temporo-occipital branch of {S} middle c.region: Brain: junction of posterior temporal and occipital lobes
temporo-occipital branch of {S} middle c.desc: A cortical branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery that runs back over the posterior temporal lobe toward the occipital lobe. It supplies the back of the lateral temporal lobe and nearby lateral occipital cortex, overlapping at its edges with the posterior cerebral artery's territory.
clinical: Strokes here can damage the optic radiation beneath the cortex and cause a loss of the upper quarter of the visual field on the opposite side.

trunk of inferior terminal branch of {S}.name: Trunk of the inferior terminal branch of the {S} middle cerebral artery
trunk of inferior terminal branch of {S}.region: Brain: lateral sulcus and temporal lobe
trunk of inferior terminal branch of {S}.desc: The stem of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery, formed where M1 splits at the limen insulae. It runs over the lower insula and gives the temporal cortical branches (anterior, middle and posterior temporal and temporo-occipital), and often the angular branch, supplying the lateral temporal lobe and parts of the inferior parietal lobe.
clinical: An inferior division stroke in the dominant hemisphere typically causes Wernicke aphasia without much weakness.

anterior leaflet of mitral valve.name: Anterior leaflet of mitral valve
anterior leaflet of mitral valve.region: Heart: between left atrium and left ventricle
anterior leaflet of mitral valve.desc: The larger, roughly semicircular leaflet of the mitral valve, also called the aortic leaflet. It hangs between the inflow and outflow of the left ventricle and is continuous with the aortic valve through fibrous tissue (aortomitral continuity). Chordae tendineae from both papillary muscles attach to it, holding it shut during systole.
clinical: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the anterior leaflet can be pulled toward the septum in systole and block outflow (systolic anterior motion).
Rheumatic heart disease thickens and fuses the leaflets, causing mitral stenosis.

posterior leaflet of mitral valve.name: Posterior leaflet of mitral valve
posterior leaflet of mitral valve.region: Heart: between left atrium and left ventricle
posterior leaflet of mitral valve.desc: The smaller, crescent-shaped leaflet of the mitral valve, attached along a longer stretch of the valve ring. It is usually divided into three scallops (P1, P2 and P3). Chordae from both papillary muscles anchor it, and it seals against the anterior leaflet during systole.
clinical: Mitral valve prolapse most often involves the middle scallop (P2), which is a common target of surgical valve repair.

anterior inferior segmental branch of {S.name: Anterior inferior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
anterior inferior segmental branch of {S.desc: A branch of the anterior sectoral division of the right portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment V, the lower part of the right anterior liver near the gallbladder bed. It brings nutrient-rich gut blood into that segment's sinusoids, running alongside the matching hepatic artery and bile duct branches.
clinical: Because each segment has its own portal branch, surgeons can remove a single segment such as V along these vascular boundaries.

anterior superior segmental branch of {S.name: Anterior superior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
anterior superior segmental branch of {S.region: Liver: right anterior section, upper part
anterior superior segmental branch of {S.desc: A branch of the anterior sectoral division of the right portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment VIII, the upper part of the right anterior liver under the diaphragm. It travels with the segment's hepatic artery and bile duct branches as a portal triad.
clinical: Tumors in segment VIII sit close to the hepatic veins and diaphragm, which makes their resection technically demanding.

caudate lobe branch of {S} portal vein.name: Caudate lobe branch of the {S} portal vein
caudate lobe branch of {S} portal vein.desc: Small branches from the right and left portal veins (and sometimes the bifurcation) that supply the caudate lobe, Couinaud segment I, which sits behind the porta hepatis against the inferior vena cava. The caudate lobe gets blood from both sides and drains straight into the IVC through its own small veins.
clinical: In Budd-Chiari syndrome (blocked hepatic veins), the caudate lobe often enlarges because its veins drain directly into the IVC and are spared.

hepatic portal vein.name: Hepatic portal vein
hepatic portal vein.desc: The vein carrying blood from the digestive tract, spleen and pancreas to the liver, supplying about three quarters of the liver's blood flow. It forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament behind the bile duct and hepatic artery, and divides at the porta hepatis into right and left portal veins.
clinical: Cirrhosis raises pressure in it (portal hypertension), causing varices in the esophagus, an enlarged spleen and fluid in the abdomen.
A portal vein clot can cause portal hypertension even with a healthy liver.

lateral inferior segmental branch of {S}.name: Lateral inferior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
lateral inferior segmental branch of {S}.region: Liver: left lateral section, lower part
lateral inferior segmental branch of {S}.desc: A branch arising from the umbilical part of the left portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment III, the lower part of the left lateral section of the liver. It runs with the matching hepatic artery and bile duct branches.
clinical: Segments II and III together (the left lateral section) are the part most often used in living liver donation for small children.

lateral superior segmental branch of {S}.name: Lateral superior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
lateral superior segmental branch of {S}.region: Liver: left lateral section, upper part
lateral superior segmental branch of {S}.desc: A branch of the left portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment II, the upper, back part of the left lateral section of the liver. It travels with the segment's arterial and biliary branches.
clinical: Removing segments II and III (left lateral sectionectomy) is one of the most common and straightforward liver resections.

medial inferior segmental branch of {S}.name: Medial inferior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
medial inferior segmental branch of {S}.region: Liver: left medial section, lower part
medial inferior segmental branch of {S}.desc: A branch from the umbilical part of the left portal vein that supplies the lower part of Couinaud segment IV (IVb), the area between the gallbladder bed and the falciform ligament, including the quadrate lobe.
clinical: Segment IVb lies next to the gallbladder, so gallbladder cancer often spreads into it and it may be removed along with the gallbladder.

medial superior segmental branch of {S}.name: Medial superior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
medial superior segmental branch of {S}.region: Liver: left medial section, upper part
medial superior segmental branch of {S}.desc: A branch of the left portal vein that supplies the upper part of Couinaud segment IV (IVa), the part of the left medial section that lies under the diaphragm near the middle hepatic vein.
clinical: Segment IV's portal branches come from the umbilical part of the left portal vein, which surgeons must protect when removing the left lateral section.

posterior inferior segmental branch of {.name: Posterior inferior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
posterior inferior segmental branch of {.region: Liver: right posterior section, lower part
posterior inferior segmental branch of {.desc: A branch of the posterior sectoral division of the right portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment VI, the lower, back part of the right lobe that rests near the right kidney.
clinical: Segment VI is a common site for ultrasound-guided liver biopsy because it is easy to reach between the lower ribs.

posterior superior segmental branch of {.name: Posterior superior segmental branch of the {S} portal vein
posterior superior segmental branch of {.region: Liver: right posterior section, upper part
posterior superior segmental branch of {.desc: A branch of the posterior sectoral division of the right portal vein that supplies Couinaud segment VII, the upper, back part of the right lobe beneath the diaphragm and next to the right hepatic vein.
clinical: Segment VII lesions are hard to reach laparoscopically because they sit high and far back under the ribs and diaphragm.

pre-hepatic portal vein.name: Pre-hepatic portal vein
pre-hepatic portal vein.desc: The main trunk of the portal vein before it enters the liver, about 7 to 8 cm long. It forms behind the neck of the pancreas, runs up in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) behind the common bile duct and hepatic artery, and reaches the porta hepatis. Along the way it receives the left gastric and other small veins.
clinical: Pressure on the hepatoduodenal ligament with finger and thumb (the Pringle maneuver) stops portal and arterial inflow during liver surgery.
A clot in this trunk causes pre-hepatic portal hypertension even when the liver itself is normal.

trunk of {S} portal vein.name: Trunk of the {S} portal vein
trunk of {S} portal vein.desc: The stem of the right or left portal vein just after the main portal vein divides at the porta hepatis. The right trunk is short and soon splits into anterior and posterior sectoral branches. The left trunk has a longer transverse part running left along the porta hepatis, then turns forward as the umbilical part that feeds segments II, III and IV.
clinical: Surgeons can block one side's portal flow (portal vein embolization) so the other side of the liver grows before a large resection.

{S} portal vein.name: Portal vein
{S} portal vein.desc: One of the two main branches of the hepatic portal vein, formed at the porta hepatis. The right portal vein supplies the right liver, segments V to VIII, through anterior and posterior divisions. The left portal vein supplies segments II, III and IV through its transverse and umbilical parts. Both give branches to the caudate lobe (segment I).
clinical: Portal vein anatomy has frequent variations, so it is mapped by CT before liver surgery or living donation.

accessory subsuperior branch of {S} post.name: Accessory subsuperior branch of the {S} posterior basal segmental artery
accessory subsuperior branch of {S} post.desc: An inconstant small branch of the posterior basal segmental artery of the right lower lobe that supplies the subsuperior area, an extra region between the superior segment and the basal segments present in some lungs. Like all pulmonary artery branches it carries deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and follows its matching bronchus.
clinical: Variant branches like this are mapped on CT before segment-level lung surgery so the right vessels are divided.

anterior branch of lateral segmental art.name: Anterior branch of the lateral segmental artery
anterior branch of lateral segmental art.region: Lung: right middle lobe, lateral segment
anterior branch of lateral segmental art.desc: A subsegmental branch of the lateral segmental artery of the right middle lobe, supplying the front part of the lateral segment. It runs beside the matching subsegmental bronchus and carries deoxygenated blood from the right pulmonary artery to the alveoli for gas exchange.
clinical: Small subsegmental emboli in branches like this are increasingly found on CT, and whether every one needs treatment is debated.

anterior branch of {S} anterior segmenta.name: Anterior branch of the {S} anterior segmental artery
anterior branch of {S} anterior segmenta.region: Lung: right upper lobe, anterior segment
anterior branch of {S} anterior segmenta.desc: A subsegmental branch of the anterior segmental artery of the right upper lobe, supplying the front part of the anterior segment. It follows the matching bronchus and delivers deoxygenated blood for gas exchange.
clinical: Pulmonary arteries track the bronchi closely, so surgeons use the bronchial tree as a map when dividing vessels in segmentectomy.

anterior part of {S} apical segmental ar.name: Anterior part of the {S} apical segmental artery
anterior part of {S} apical segmental ar.desc: The front subsegmental branch of the apical segmental artery of the right upper lobe, a branch of the truncus anterior. It supplies the anterior part of the apical segment at the very top of the lung, carrying deoxygenated blood to the alveoli.
clinical: The apical segments are a classic site of reactivated tuberculosis because they are well ventilated relative to their blood flow.

apical part of {S} apical segmental arte.name: Apical part of the {S} apical segmental artery
apical part of {S} apical segmental arte.desc: The upper subsegmental branch of the apical segmental artery of the right upper lobe, supplying the tip of the apical segment that rises above the clavicle into the root of the neck. It runs with its matching bronchus.
clinical: Tumors at the lung apex (Pancoast tumors) can invade nearby nerves and cause shoulder pain and a droopy eyelid with a small pupil.

apical part of {S} posterior segmental a.name: Apical part of the {S} posterior segmental artery
apical part of {S} posterior segmental a.region: Lung: right upper lobe, posterior segment
apical part of {S} posterior segmental a.desc: The upper subsegmental branch of the posterior segmental artery of the right upper lobe, supplying the upper back part of the posterior segment near the apex. It carries deoxygenated blood to the alveoli alongside its matching bronchus.
clinical: The posterior segment of the right upper lobe is a common spot for aspiration pneumonia in someone lying down.

basal branch of {S} anterior basal segme.name: Basal branch of the {S} anterior basal segmental artery
basal branch of {S} anterior basal segme.region: Lung: right lower lobe, anterior basal segment
basal branch of {S} anterior basal segme.desc: A subsegmental branch of the anterior basal segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the lower, diaphragmatic part of the anterior basal segment. It follows its matching subsegmental bronchus.
clinical: The basal segments get the most blood flow when upright, so emboli and infarcts often show up in the lung bases.

inferior branch of medial segmental arte.name: Inferior branch of the medial segmental artery
inferior branch of medial segmental arte.region: Lung: right middle lobe, medial segment
inferior branch of medial segmental arte.desc: A subsegmental branch of the medial segmental artery of the right middle lobe, supplying the lower part of the medial segment, which lies against the heart. It carries deoxygenated blood to the alveoli beside its matching bronchus.
clinical: Disease in the middle lobe's medial segment blurs the right heart border on a chest X-ray (the silhouette sign).

inferior lingular artery.name: Inferior lingular artery
inferior lingular artery.desc: A segmental branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the inferior lingular segment, the lower part of the lingula, the tongue-shaped part of the left upper lobe that corresponds to the right middle lobe. It follows the inferior lingular bronchus.
clinical: Lingular pneumonia or collapse can blur the left heart border on a chest X-ray.

lateral branch of {S} anterior basal seg.name: Lateral branch of the {S} anterior basal segmental artery
lateral branch of {S} anterior basal seg.region: Lung: right lower lobe, anterior basal segment
lateral branch of {S} anterior basal seg.desc: A subsegmental branch of the anterior basal segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the lateral part of the anterior basal segment. It runs alongside the matching subsegmental bronchus.
clinical: Segmental and subsegmental arteries are the usual places where CT pulmonary angiography finds emboli.

lateral branch of {S} superior segmental.name: Lateral branch of the {S} superior segmental artery
lateral branch of {S} superior segmental.region: Lung: right lower lobe, superior segment
lateral branch of {S} superior segmental.desc: A subsegmental branch of the superior segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the lateral part of the superior segment, the top of the lower lobe behind the oblique fissure.
clinical: The superior segment of the lower lobe is a common site of aspiration pneumonia in people lying on their back.

laterobasal branch of {S} posterior basa.name: Laterobasal branch of the {S} posterior basal segmental artery
laterobasal branch of {S} posterior basa.region: Lung: right lower lobe, posterior basal segment
laterobasal branch of {S} posterior basa.desc: A subsegmental branch of the posterior basal segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the lateral part of the posterior basal segment near the costodiaphragmatic recess. It follows its matching bronchus.
clinical: Pulmonary infarcts from emboli are often wedge-shaped and touch the pleura in the posterior bases.

medial branch of {S} superior segmental.name: Medial branch of the {S} superior segmental artery
medial branch of {S} superior segmental.region: Lung: right lower lobe, superior segment
medial branch of {S} superior segmental.desc: A subsegmental branch of the superior segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the medial part of the superior segment near the vertebral column. It runs with its matching bronchus.
clinical: Knowing which subsegmental branches feed an area lets surgeons remove a small tumor while sparing healthy lung.

mediobasal branch of {S} posterior basal.name: Mediobasal branch of the {S} posterior basal segmental artery
mediobasal branch of {S} posterior basal.region: Lung: right lower lobe, posterior basal segment
mediobasal branch of {S} posterior basal.desc: A subsegmental branch of the posterior basal segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the medial part of the posterior basal segment, near the spine and the diaphragm. It runs beside its matching subsegmental bronchus.
clinical: The posterior basal segments are where fluid and aspirated material collect most in a person lying flat.

posterior branch of lateral segmental ar.name: Posterior branch of the lateral segmental artery
posterior branch of lateral segmental ar.region: Lung: right middle lobe, lateral segment
posterior branch of lateral segmental ar.desc: A subsegmental branch of the lateral segmental artery of the right middle lobe, supplying the back part of the lateral segment next to the oblique fissure. It carries deoxygenated blood to the alveoli alongside its matching bronchus.
clinical: Middle lobe collapse can result from enlarged lymph nodes squeezing the narrow middle lobe bronchus and its vessels.

posterior branch of {S} anterior segment.name: Posterior branch of the {S} anterior segmental artery
posterior branch of {S} anterior segment.region: Lung: right upper lobe, anterior segment
posterior branch of {S} anterior segment.desc: A subsegmental branch of the anterior segmental artery of the right upper lobe, supplying the back part of the anterior segment. It follows its matching subsegmental bronchus.
clinical: Segment-level anatomy like this guides video-assisted lung surgery for small early cancers.

posterior part of {S} posterior segmenta.name: Posterior part of the {S} posterior segmental artery
posterior part of {S} posterior segmenta.region: Lung: right upper lobe, posterior segment
posterior part of {S} posterior segmenta.desc: The back subsegmental branch of the posterior segmental artery of the right upper lobe, supplying the lower back part of the posterior segment. In the right lung the posterior segment can receive supply from both the truncus anterior and a separate ascending branch.
clinical: The variable origin of the posterior segment's artery is a known trap during right upper lobectomy.

pulmonary trunk.name: Pulmonary trunk
pulmonary trunk.desc: The large artery that leaves the right ventricle at the pulmonary valve and carries deoxygenated blood toward the lungs. About 5 cm long, it runs up and back, wrapping around the left side of the ascending aorta, and divides under the aortic arch at about T4/T5 into the right and left pulmonary arteries. The ligamentum arteriosum links its bifurcation to the aortic arch.
clinical: A large clot lodged at its bifurcation (a saddle embolus) can cause sudden collapse.
Before birth, the ductus arteriosus here shunts blood into the aorta, bypassing the lungs.

superior branch of medial segmental arte.name: Superior branch of the medial segmental artery
superior branch of medial segmental arte.region: Lung: right middle lobe, medial segment
superior branch of medial segmental arte.desc: A subsegmental branch of the medial segmental artery of the right middle lobe, supplying the upper part of the medial segment, which lies against the right side of the heart. It follows its matching subsegmental bronchus.
clinical: Because the middle lobe touches the right heart border, its disease is often spotted as a blurred border on a frontal chest X-ray.

superior branch of {S} superior segmenta.name: Superior branch of the {S} superior segmental artery
superior branch of {S} superior segmenta.region: Lung: right lower lobe, superior segment
superior branch of {S} superior segmenta.desc: A subsegmental branch of the superior segmental artery of the right lower lobe, supplying the uppermost part of the superior segment, which sits behind the oblique fissure at about the level of the scapula. It runs with its matching bronchus.
clinical: The superior segment is a favored site for aspiration because its bronchus points straight backward.

superior lingular artery.name: Superior lingular artery
superior lingular artery.desc: A segmental branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the superior lingular segment, the upper part of the lingula of the left upper lobe. It may arise alone or from a common lingular trunk with the inferior lingular artery, and follows the superior lingular bronchus.
clinical: Lingulectomy, removing just the lingula, is a common lung-sparing operation for small tumors in this area.

{S} anterior basal segmental artery.name: Anterior basal segmental artery
{S} anterior basal segmental artery.region: Lung: lower lobe, anterior basal segment
{S} anterior basal segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the lower lobe pulmonary artery that supplies the anterior basal segment, the front part of the lower lobe resting on the diaphragm. In the left lung it often shares a trunk with the medial basal artery (anteromedial basal). It runs with the anterior basal bronchus.
clinical: Emboli from leg veins often lodge in the lower lobe basal arteries, which receive the most blood flow.

{S} anterior segmental artery.name: Anterior segmental artery
{S} anterior segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the pulmonary artery that supplies the anterior segment of the upper lobe. On the right it usually comes from the truncus anterior (upper lobar artery); on the left it comes from the arching left pulmonary artery. It runs with the anterior segmental bronchus and divides into anterior and posterior subsegmental branches.
clinical: During upper lobectomy, each segmental artery must be found and divided separately, as their origins vary a lot between people.

{S} apical segmental artery.name: Apical segmental artery
{S} apical segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the pulmonary artery to the apical segment at the top of the upper lobe. On the left, the apical and posterior segments are often combined (apicoposterior), and the artery is among the first branches of the left pulmonary artery as it arches over the left main bronchus. It runs with the apical bronchus.
clinical: The left apical branches are short and arise from the top of the left pulmonary artery, making them vulnerable to tearing during surgery.

{S} lateral basal segmental artery.name: Lateral basal segmental artery
{S} lateral basal segmental artery.region: Lung: lower lobe, lateral basal segment
{S} lateral basal segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the lower lobe pulmonary artery supplying the lateral basal segment, the outer part of the lower lobe base near the costodiaphragmatic recess. It runs with the lateral basal bronchus in both lungs.
clinical: Pleural fluid first collects in the costodiaphragmatic recess next to the lateral and posterior basal segments.

{S} medial basal segmental artery.name: Medial basal segmental artery
{S} medial basal segmental artery.region: Lung: lower lobe, medial basal segment
{S} medial basal segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the lower lobe pulmonary artery supplying the medial basal segment, the part of the lower lobe base next to the heart and inferior vena cava. In the left lung this segment is small and often combined with the anterior basal segment.
clinical: Disease in the medial basal segment can blur the outline of the diaphragm next to the heart on a chest X-ray.

{S} posterior basal segmental artery.name: Posterior basal segmental artery
{S} posterior basal segmental artery.region: Lung: lower lobe, posterior basal segment
{S} posterior basal segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the lower lobe pulmonary artery, usually its largest terminal branch, supplying the posterior basal segment, the lowest back part of the lung beside the spine. It runs with the posterior basal bronchus and divides into subsegmental branches.
clinical: The posterior basal segments are the most dependent part of the lungs when lying down, so aspiration and fluid often collect there.

{S} posterior segmental artery.name: Posterior segmental artery
{S} posterior segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the pulmonary artery supplying the posterior segment of the upper lobe. On the left it arises from the arch of the left pulmonary artery, often sharing a trunk with the apical artery, and runs with the posterior (or apicoposterior) bronchus.
clinical: Reactivated tuberculosis typically affects the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes.

{S} pulmonary artery.name: Pulmonary artery
{S} pulmonary artery.desc: One of the two branches of the pulmonary trunk carrying deoxygenated blood to a lung. The right pulmonary artery is longer and runs horizontally behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the right hilum. The left pulmonary artery is shorter, arches over the left main bronchus and is attached to the aortic arch by the ligamentum arteriosum. Each divides into lobar and segmental branches.
clinical: Pulmonary emboli often lodge in these arteries or their branches, straining the right ventricle.
Enlarged pulmonary arteries on a chest X-ray can be a sign of pulmonary hypertension.

{S} superior segmental artery.name: Superior segmental artery
{S} superior segmental artery.desc: A segmental branch of the lower lobe pulmonary artery supplying the superior segment of the lower lobe, its upper back part just behind the oblique fissure. It is usually the first branch of the lower lobe artery after it passes the fissure, and runs with the superior segmental bronchus.
clinical: Superior segmentectomy is a common lung-sparing operation because this segment has a clear, single artery and bronchus.

{S} upper lobar artery.name: Upper lobar artery
{S} upper lobar artery.desc: The first branch of the right pulmonary artery, also called the truncus anterior, arising inside the pericardium or near the hilum before the artery reaches the oblique fissure. It supplies most of the right upper lobe, usually giving the apical and anterior segmental arteries and often part of the posterior segment's supply.
clinical: It is short and arises early, so it is the first vessel the surgeon divides in a right upper lobectomy and a major bleeding risk.

posterior cusp of pulmonary valve.name: Posterior cusp of pulmonary valve
posterior cusp of pulmonary valve.desc: One of the three thin, pocket-shaped semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, named here by an older scheme (cusp names differ between naming systems). It sits on the side of the valve nearest the aortic root. Together with the two anterior cusps it closes during diastole, stopping blood in the pulmonary trunk from leaking back into the right ventricle.
clinical: In the Ross procedure, the patient's own pulmonary valve is moved to replace a diseased aortic valve.

{S} anterior cusp of pulmonary valve.name: Anterior cusp of pulmonary valve
{S} anterior cusp of pulmonary valve.desc: One of the two anterior semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, named here by an older scheme (cusp names differ between naming systems). The thin, pocket-shaped cusps fill with blood and press together in diastole, stopping backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle, and lie flat against the wall when the ventricle ejects.
clinical: Pulmonary valve stenosis, often present from birth, is usually treated by stretching the valve with a balloon catheter.

anterior division of {S} renal artery.name: Anterior division of the {S} renal artery
anterior division of {S} renal artery.region: Kidney: renal hilum, in front of the pelvis
anterior division of {S} renal artery.desc: The larger of the two main divisions of the renal artery, passing in front of the renal pelvis at the hilum. It typically gives four segmental arteries: superior (apical), anterior superior, anterior inferior and inferior, supplying most of the kidney. Segmental arteries are end arteries with no overlap between them.
clinical: Because segmental arteries do not connect, blocking one causes a wedge-shaped infarct of the matching kidney segment.

inferior segmental branch of {S} renal a.name: Inferior segmental branch of the {S} renal artery
inferior segmental branch of {S} renal a.desc: A segmental artery, usually from the anterior division of the renal artery, that supplies the inferior segment, the lower pole of the kidney on both its front and back surfaces. Like other segmental arteries it is an end artery.
clinical: A lower pole artery can cross in front of the ureter and press on it, a recognized cause of obstruction where the renal pelvis meets the ureter.

posterior division of {S} renal artery.name: Posterior division of the {S} renal artery
posterior division of {S} renal artery.region: Kidney: renal hilum, behind the pelvis
posterior division of {S} renal artery.desc: The smaller of the two main divisions of the renal artery, passing behind the renal pelvis. It continues as the posterior segmental artery, supplying the posterior segment of the kidney. The boundary between anterior and posterior territories forms a relatively bloodless plane (Brodel's line) on the kidney's back-lateral surface.
clinical: Surgeons cut along the bloodless plane between the anterior and posterior territories to open the kidney with less bleeding.

posterior segmental branch of {S} renal.name: Posterior segmental branch of the {S} renal artery
posterior segmental branch of {S} renal.desc: The segmental artery formed by the posterior division of the renal artery. It runs behind the renal pelvis and supplies the posterior segment of the kidney, the middle of its back surface. It is an end artery, branching into lobar and interlobar arteries.
clinical: It passes close behind the upper renal pelvis, so procedures through the back of the kidney must avoid it to prevent major bleeding.

superior segmental branch of {S} renal a.name: Superior segmental branch of the {S} renal artery
superior segmental branch of {S} renal a.desc: Also called the apical segmental artery, it supplies the superior (apical) segment, the tip of the upper pole of the kidney. It usually comes from the anterior division but may arise from the main renal artery or even the aorta as an accessory upper pole artery.
clinical: Accessory polar arteries are common and must be identified before kidney donation or surgery.

trunk of {S} renal artery.name: Trunk of the {S} renal artery
trunk of {S} renal artery.region: Abdomen: between aorta and renal hilum
trunk of {S} renal artery.desc: The main stem of the renal artery from its origin on the side of the abdominal aorta (about L1/L2) to where it divides near the hilum. The right trunk is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava; the left is shorter. Before dividing it gives the inferior suprarenal artery and small branches to the ureter and renal capsule.
clinical: Narrowing of the trunk (renal artery stenosis) can cause hard-to-control high blood pressure.
In young people, fibromuscular dysplasia gives the artery a beaded look on imaging.

ureteric segment of {S} renal artery.name: Ureteric segment of the {S} renal artery
ureteric segment of {S} renal artery.desc: The part of the renal artery's supply that serves the renal pelvis and upper ureter through small ureteric branches. The ureter has a chain of small arterial supplies along its length, and the renal artery provides the top link, joining with branches from lower vessels in the ureter's outer coat.
clinical: Stripping the tissue around the ureter during surgery or transplant can cut off these small vessels and cause narrowing of the ureter.

{S} inferior suprarenal artery.name: Inferior suprarenal artery
{S} inferior suprarenal artery.region: Abdomen: adrenal gland and upper kidney
{S} inferior suprarenal artery.desc: A small artery arising from the renal artery that runs up to the lower part of the adrenal gland. It is one of three arterial supplies to each adrenal gland, along with the superior (from the inferior phrenic artery) and middle (from the aorta) suprarenal arteries.
clinical: The adrenal glands' many small arteries feed a rich capsular network, making them very vascular and prone to bleeding in severe sepsis.

{S} middle suprarenal artery.name: Middle suprarenal artery
{S} middle suprarenal artery.desc: A small paired artery arising directly from the side of the abdominal aorta near the level of the superior mesenteric artery (about L1). It runs laterally over the crura of the diaphragm to the adrenal gland, where it joins the superior and inferior suprarenal arteries in a network around the gland.
clinical: During adrenal removal, the many small arteries matter less than the single adrenal vein, which is tied first to limit hormone release.

{S} renal artery.name: Renal artery
{S} renal artery.desc: Each kidney's main artery, arising from the side of the abdominal aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery at about L1/L2. The right renal artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava. Near the hilum it divides into anterior and posterior divisions and segmental arteries. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output.
clinical: About a quarter to a third of people have an accessory renal artery, important in kidney transplant planning.
Renal artery stenosis lowers kidney blood flow and activates renin, raising blood pressure.

anterior papillary muscle of {S} ventric.name: Anterior papillary muscle of the {S} ventricle
anterior papillary muscle of {S} ventric.desc: The largest papillary muscle of the right ventricle, rising from the anterior wall, often linked to the septum by the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula). Its chordae tendineae attach to the anterior and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve, holding them closed during systole.
clinical: The moderator band attached near it carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle so it contracts in time to brace the valve.

posterior papillary muscle of {S} ventri.name: Posterior papillary muscle of the {S} ventricle
posterior papillary muscle of {S} ventri.desc: A conical muscle rising from the inferior (diaphragmatic) wall of the right ventricle. Its chordae tendineae attach to the posterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve. It contracts during systole to tense the chordae, stopping the leaflets from everting into the right atrium so blood is not pushed backward.
clinical: Rupture or dysfunction, for example after an inferior wall infarction involving the right ventricle, can cause acute tricuspid regurgitation.

septal papillary muscle of {S} ventricle.name: Septal papillary muscle of the {S} ventricle
septal papillary muscle of {S} ventricle.desc: The smallest and most variable right ventricular papillary muscle, often just a few muscular nubs arising from the interventricular septum near the conus. Its chordae tendineae anchor the anterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve. One constant septal papillary muscle (the medial papillary muscle of Lancisi) is a surgical landmark near the right bundle branch.
clinical: Its position near the right bundle branch means septal surgery or ventricular septal defect repair in this area can cause conduction block.

{S} great saphenous vein.name: Great saphenous vein
{S} great saphenous vein.region: Lower limb: medial leg and thigh
{S} great saphenous vein.desc: The longest vein in the body. It begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes anterior to the medial malleolus, climbs the medial leg with the saphenous nerve, runs behind the medial femoral condyle and up the medial thigh, then pierces the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament. It drains superficial tissue of the medial foot, leg and thigh.
clinical: It is the most commonly harvested vessel for coronary artery bypass grafting.
Incompetent valves, especially at the saphenofemoral junction, cause varicose veins.

{S} subclavian artery.name: Subclavian artery
{S} subclavian artery.region: Root of neck and thoracic outlet
{S} subclavian artery.desc: On the right it arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; on the left directly from the aortic arch. It arches over the cervical pleura and is divided into three parts by scalenus anterior. Branches include the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery, thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk and dorsal scapular artery. At the lateral border of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery and supplies the upper limb.
clinical: Subclavian steal: a stenosis proximal to the vertebral artery lets the arm draw blood backward down the vertebral artery, causing dizziness with arm exercise.
It can be compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome, for example by a cervical rib.

superior vena cava.name: Superior vena cava
superior vena cava.region: Thorax: superior and middle mediastinum, right side
superior vena cava.desc: A large valveless vein formed behind the first right costal cartilage by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins. It descends along the right side of the ascending aorta, receives the azygos vein just before entering the pericardium, and opens into the upper right atrium at the level of the third right costal cartilage. It returns blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and upper thorax.
clinical: SVC syndrome, often from lung cancer or lymphoma, causes facial swelling and distended neck veins.
The tip of a central venous catheter is usually placed in the lower SVC.

anterior leaflet of tricuspid valve.name: Anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve
anterior leaflet of tricuspid valve.desc: The largest leaflet of the tricuspid valve, extending from the infundibulum toward the inferolateral wall of the right ventricle. Its chordae tendineae come mainly from the anterior papillary muscle, which is tied to the septum by the moderator band. Together with the posterior and septal leaflets it closes in systole to prevent backflow into the right atrium.
clinical: Right ventricular dilation stretches the annulus mostly along the anterior and posterior leaflets, causing functional tricuspid regurgitation.

posterior leaflet of tricuspid valve.name: Posterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve
posterior leaflet of tricuspid valve.region: Heart: right atrioventricular orifice, inferior part
posterior leaflet of tricuspid valve.desc: Usually the smallest tricuspid leaflet, lying along the inferior (diaphragmatic) margin of the valve ring. Its chordae tendineae come from the posterior papillary muscle and, toward the septal side, from small septal muscles. It coapts with the anterior and septal leaflets during ventricular systole.
clinical: In Ebstein anomaly the posterior and septal leaflets are displaced toward the apex, making part of the right ventricle behave like atrium.
Surgical annuloplasty often plicates the posterior leaflet region to shrink a dilated annulus.

septal leaflet of tricuspid valve.name: Septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve
septal leaflet of tricuspid valve.region: Heart: right atrioventricular orifice, septal side
septal leaflet of tricuspid valve.desc: The leaflet attached along the interventricular septum, including the region of the membranous septum. Its chordae tendineae come from the septal papillary muscles and directly from the septal wall. Its hinge line lies close to the atrioventricular node and the penetrating bundle of His, at the apex of the triangle of Koch.
clinical: Sutures placed near the septal leaflet during valve repair can injure the conduction system and cause heart block.
Pacemaker leads crossing the valve can impinge on this leaflet and cause regurgitation.

basilar artery.name: Basilar artery
basilar artery.region: Posterior cranial fossa: anterior to the pons
basilar artery.desc: Formed at the pontomedullary junction by the union of the two vertebral arteries, it runs up the basilar groove of the pons on the clivus. It gives the anterior inferior cerebellar arteries, many pontine perforators, often the labyrinthine arteries, and the superior cerebellar arteries, then ends in the interpeduncular cistern by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It supplies the brainstem, cerebellum, inner ear and, through the PCAs, the occipital lobes and thalamus.
clinical: Basilar occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome: quadriplegia and loss of speech with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.
The basilar tip is a classic site for aneurysms, which are difficult to reach surgically.

{S} vertebral artery.name: Vertebral artery
{S} vertebral artery.desc: Usually the first branch of the subclavian artery. It enters the transverse foramen of C6, ascends through the foramina to C1, curves behind the lateral mass of the atlas over its posterior arch, pierces the dura and passes through the foramen magnum. Intracranially it gives the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and contributes to the anterior spinal artery, then joins its partner to form the basilar artery.
clinical: Vertebral artery dissection, sometimes after neck trauma or sudden neck movement, is an important cause of stroke in young people.
Occlusion of the vertebral artery or PICA causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

anterior cecal artery.name: Anterior cecal artery
anterior cecal artery.region: Abdomen: ileocecal junction, front of cecum
anterior cecal artery.desc: A small branch of the ileocolic artery (from its inferior division) that runs in the vascular fold of the cecum across the front of the ileocecal junction. It supplies the anterior wall of the cecum and anastomoses with the posterior cecal artery.
clinical: It must be identified and ligated during right hemicolectomy and ileocecal resection.

posterior cecal artery.name: Posterior cecal artery
posterior cecal artery.region: Abdomen: ileocecal junction, back of cecum
posterior cecal artery.desc: A branch of the ileocolic artery, usually larger than the anterior cecal artery, that passes behind the ileocecal junction to supply the posterior wall of the cecum. The appendicular artery often arises from it or alongside it.
clinical: Because the appendicular artery frequently comes off this vessel, it is a reference point when tracing the appendix blood supply in surgery.

anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal ar.name: Anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal ar.region: Abdomen: front of the pancreatic head
anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal ar.desc: A branch of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which comes from the superior mesenteric artery or the first jejunal artery. It runs to the right on the anterior surface of the pancreatic head and joins the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery to form the anterior arcade, supplying the pancreatic head and the second and third parts of the duodenum.
clinical: The pancreaticoduodenal arcades link the celiac and superior mesenteric territories, so they enlarge as a collateral path when the celiac trunk is narrowed.

posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal a.name: Posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal a.region: Abdomen: back of the pancreatic head
posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal a.desc: A branch of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery that runs on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head. It anastomoses with the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery to form the posterior arcade, supplying the head of the pancreas and the adjacent duodenum.
clinical: Aneurysms of the pancreaticoduodenal arcades are rare but are associated with celiac trunk stenosis and can rupture.

anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal ar.name: Anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal ar.region: Abdomen: front of the pancreatic head
anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal ar.desc: A terminal branch of the gastroduodenal artery (with the right gastro-omental artery) that descends on the anterior surface of the pancreatic head, near the curve of the duodenum. It supplies the pancreatic head and duodenum and joins the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery to complete the anterior arcade.
clinical: It is divided during a pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).

posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal a.name: Posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal a.region: Abdomen: back of the pancreatic head
posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal a.desc: Usually the first branch of the gastroduodenal artery, given off above the duodenum. It spirals behind the pancreatic head, crossing the common bile duct, and joins the posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery to form the posterior arcade. It supplies the pancreatic head, the duodenum and the lower bile duct.
clinical: Its close relation to the distal common bile duct makes it a bleeding risk during biliary and pancreatic surgery.

inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.name: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.region: Abdomen: between the pancreatic head and duodenum
inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.desc: Usually the first branch of the superior mesenteric artery, arising near the lower border of the pancreas, though it often shares a trunk with the first jejunal artery. It divides into anterior and posterior branches that ascend to meet the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal artery, forming the arcades that supply the pancreatic head and duodenum.
clinical: It is a key collateral route between the superior mesenteric artery and celiac territory, for example in median arcuate ligament compression.

pancreaticoduodenal vein.name: Pancreaticoduodenal vein
pancreaticoduodenal vein.desc: Veins that accompany the pancreaticoduodenal arteries in arcades around the pancreatic head. The posterior superior vein typically drains directly into the portal vein, while the others drain into the superior mesenteric vein, often via the gastrocolic trunk. They carry blood from the pancreatic head and duodenum to the portal system.
clinical: These small veins must be carefully ligated when freeing the pancreatic head from the portal vein during a Whipple procedure.

anterior inferior segmental hepatic arte.name: Anterior inferior segmental hepatic artery
anterior inferior segmental hepatic arte.desc: A segmental branch of the anterior division of the right hepatic artery. It supplies the anterior inferior segment of the right liver (Couinaud segment V), which lies next to the gallbladder bed.
clinical: Because segment V borders the gallbladder bed, injury to its artery is possible during cholecystectomy.

anterior superior segmental hepatic arte.name: Anterior superior segmental hepatic artery
anterior superior segmental hepatic arte.desc: A segmental branch of the anterior division of the right hepatic artery that supplies the anterior superior segment of the right liver (Couinaud segment VIII), high under the diaphragm. Its territory lies between the middle and right hepatic veins.
clinical: Segmental hepatic arteries are targeted in selective chemoembolization to treat liver tumors confined to one segment.

posterior inferior segmental hepatic art.name: Posterior inferior segmental hepatic artery
posterior inferior segmental hepatic art.desc: A segmental branch of the posterior division of the right hepatic artery. It supplies the posterior inferior segment of the right liver (Couinaud segment VI), the lowest and most lateral part of the right lobe.
clinical: Segment-based anatomy lets surgeons remove one segment (segmentectomy) while preserving the rest of the liver.

posterior superior segmental hepatic art.name: Posterior superior segmental hepatic artery
posterior superior segmental hepatic art.desc: A segmental branch of the posterior division of the right hepatic artery that supplies the posterior superior segment of the right liver (Couinaud segment VII), lying high and posteriorly against the diaphragm.
clinical: Tumors in segment VII are among the hardest to reach surgically because of its high posterior position.

medial inferior segmental hepatic artery.name: Medial inferior segmental hepatic artery
medial inferior segmental hepatic artery.desc: A segmental branch from the medial division of the left hepatic artery (sometimes from a separate middle hepatic artery). It supplies the inferior part of the medial segment of the left liver (Couinaud segment IVb), next to the gallbladder fossa.
clinical: Segment IVb is often resected along with the gallbladder bed in surgery for gallbladder cancer.

medial superior segmental hepatic artery.name: Medial superior segmental hepatic artery
medial superior segmental hepatic artery.desc: A segmental branch from the medial division of the left hepatic artery (or a middle hepatic artery). It supplies the superior part of the medial segment of the left liver (Couinaud segment IVa), lying between the middle hepatic vein and the falciform ligament.
clinical: The variable origin of segment IV arteries matters when planning split-liver or living-donor transplantation.

lateral inferior segmental hepatic arter.name: Lateral inferior segmental hepatic artery
