lateral inferior segmental hepatic arter.desc: A segmental branch from the lateral division of the left hepatic artery. It supplies the lateral inferior segment of the left liver (Couinaud segment III), to the left of the falciform ligament.
clinical: Segments II and III form the left lateral section, the part most often used in living-donor liver transplants for children.

lateral superior segmental hepatic arter.name: Lateral superior segmental hepatic artery
lateral superior segmental hepatic arter.desc: A segmental branch from the lateral division of the left hepatic artery that supplies the lateral superior segment of the left liver (Couinaud segment II), the upper tip of the left lobe.
clinical: A replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric artery can supply this segment, which surgeons must recognize before gastric surgery.

appendicular artery.name: Appendicular artery
appendicular artery.desc: A branch of the ileocolic artery, often arising from its inferior division or the posterior cecal artery. It passes behind the terminal ileum and runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix to supply the appendix. It is an end artery with little collateral supply.
clinical: Because it is an end artery, thrombosis in appendicitis leads quickly to gangrene and perforation.
It is ligated during appendectomy.

ascending branch of inferior branch of i.name: Ascending branch of the inferior branch of the ileocolic artery
ascending branch of inferior branch of i.region: Abdomen: right lower quadrant, ascending colon
ascending branch of inferior branch of i.desc: A colic branch from the inferior division of the ileocolic artery that runs up along the beginning of the ascending colon. It supplies the cecum and lower ascending colon and joins the marginal artery, anastomosing with branches of the right colic artery.
clinical: It is ligated with the ileocolic pedicle during right hemicolectomy.

ileal branch of inferior branch of ileoc.name: Ileal branch of the inferior branch of the ileocolic artery
ileal branch of inferior branch of ileoc.region: Abdomen: right lower quadrant, terminal ileum
ileal branch of inferior branch of ileoc.desc: A branch of the inferior division of the ileocolic artery that runs to the left along the terminal ileum. It supplies the last part of the ileum and anastomoses with the terminal ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
clinical: The terminal ileum is where vitamin B12 and bile salts are absorbed, so its blood supply is preserved where possible in ileocecal resections.

ascending branch of {S} colic artery.name: Ascending branch of the {S} colic artery
ascending branch of {S} colic artery.region: Abdomen: left upper quadrant, splenic flexure
ascending branch of {S} colic artery.desc: One of the two terminal divisions of the left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery). It ascends toward the splenic flexure, supplying the upper descending colon and distal transverse colon, and anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery to help form the marginal artery.
clinical: The splenic flexure, where this branch meets the middle colic territory (Griffiths' point), is a watershed area prone to ischemic colitis.

descending branch of {S} colic artery.name: Descending branch of the {S} colic artery
descending branch of {S} colic artery.desc: The lower terminal division of the left colic artery. It descends along the descending colon, supplying it, and anastomoses with the uppermost sigmoid artery to continue the marginal artery. It runs behind the peritoneum on the left posterior abdominal wall.
clinical: Preserving the left colic artery and its branches can improve blood flow to the bowel join after sigmoid or rectal resection.

caudal pancreatic artery.name: Caudal pancreatic artery
caudal pancreatic artery.region: Abdomen: tail of pancreas near the splenic hilum
caudal pancreatic artery.desc: Small branches from the distal splenic artery, its terminal branches or the left gastro-omental artery that supply the tail of the pancreas. They anastomose with branches of the great and inferior pancreatic arteries.
clinical: The tail of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament close to the splenic hilum, so these vessels are at risk during splenectomy.

dorsal pancreatic artery.name: Dorsal pancreatic artery
dorsal pancreatic artery.region: Abdomen: behind the neck of the pancreas
dorsal pancreatic artery.desc: A variable branch, most often from the proximal splenic artery but sometimes from the celiac trunk, common hepatic artery or superior mesenteric artery. It descends behind the pancreatic neck and divides into a right branch to the head and a left branch that becomes the inferior pancreatic artery along the body and tail.
clinical: Its variable origin matters in pancreatic surgery and in planning embolization of pancreatic bleeding.

great pancreatic artery.name: Great pancreatic artery
great pancreatic artery.region: Abdomen: junction of pancreatic body and tail
great pancreatic artery.desc: Also called the arteria pancreatica magna, it is the largest pancreatic branch of the splenic artery. It enters the pancreas near the junction of the body and tail and branches along the pancreatic duct, anastomosing with the inferior and caudal pancreatic arteries.
clinical: It is a frequent source of bleeding into pseudocysts or the duct after severe pancreatitis.

inferior pancreatic artery.name: Inferior pancreatic artery
inferior pancreatic artery.region: Abdomen: lower border of pancreatic body and tail
inferior pancreatic artery.desc: Also called the transverse pancreatic artery, it usually continues from the left branch of the dorsal pancreatic artery. It runs along the lower posterior border of the pancreatic body and tail, supplying them and anastomosing with the great and caudal pancreatic arteries.
clinical: It must be controlled when the pancreatic body and tail are removed in distal pancreatectomy.

caudate lobe branch of {S} hepatic arter.name: Caudate lobe branch of the {S} hepatic artery
caudate lobe branch of {S} hepatic arter.desc: A small branch from the right or left hepatic artery that supplies the caudate lobe (Couinaud segment I), which lies against the inferior vena cava. The caudate lobe receives arteries, portal branches and bile ducts from both sides.
clinical: Because the caudate lobe drains straight into the IVC by its own short veins, it is often spared and enlarges in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

celiac artery.name: Celiac artery
celiac artery.desc: Another name for the celiac trunk: the first unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, arising just below the aortic hiatus at about T12. After about 1 to 2 cm it divides into the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries. It supplies the foregut: the lower esophagus, stomach, upper duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
clinical: In median arcuate ligament syndrome the diaphragm's ligament compresses its origin, causing pain after eating.

celiac trunk.name: Celiac trunk
celiac trunk.desc: A short, wide artery leaving the front of the abdominal aorta at about T12, surrounded by the celiac nerve plexus and lymph nodes. It splits into three branches: left gastric, common hepatic and splenic. Together these supply the foregut organs: stomach, abdominal esophagus, first half of the duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
clinical: A celiac plexus block near this vessel is used to relieve severe pain from pancreatic cancer.

common hepatic artery.name: Common hepatic artery
common hepatic artery.region: Abdomen: upper border of pancreatic head
common hepatic artery.desc: One of the three branches of the celiac trunk. It runs to the right along the upper border of the pancreas, then divides into the gastroduodenal artery and the hepatic artery proper. Its territory includes the liver, gallbladder, pylorus, duodenum and pancreatic head.
clinical: If the common hepatic artery is blocked, the liver can still be supplied backward through the gastroduodenal artery from the pancreaticoduodenal arcades.

hepatic artery proper.name: Hepatic artery proper
hepatic artery proper.desc: The continuation of the common hepatic artery after the gastroduodenal branch. It ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, to the left of the common bile duct and in front of the portal vein (the portal triad), and divides into right and left hepatic arteries. It often gives the right gastric artery and supplies about a quarter of the liver's blood flow but much of its oxygen.
clinical: The Pringle maneuver clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament to control liver bleeding.
Hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplant can destroy the bile ducts, which depend on arterial blood.

trunk of {S} hepatic artery.name: Trunk of the {S} hepatic artery
trunk of {S} hepatic artery.desc: The main stem of the right or left hepatic artery before it divides. The right hepatic artery usually passes behind the common hepatic duct, often through the cystohepatic (Calot's) triangle where it gives the cystic artery, then enters the right liver. The left hepatic artery ascends toward the umbilical fissure to supply the left liver.
clinical: The right hepatic artery can be mistaken for the cystic artery and injured during gallbladder removal.
Replaced right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery occur in roughly 10 to 15 percent of people.

{S} lobe branch of {S} hepatic artery.name: Lobe branch of the hepatic artery
{S} lobe branch of {S} hepatic artery.desc: On the right, the right lobe branch of the right hepatic artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions for segments V to VIII. On the left, the left lobe branch of the left hepatic artery supplies the left lobe, giving branches to the medial (IV) and lateral (II and III) segments. Each follows the matching portal vein branch and bile duct.
clinical: Selective blockage of one lobar artery is used to treat liver tumors while sparing the other lobe.

gastroduodenal artery.name: Gastroduodenal artery
gastroduodenal artery.region: Abdomen: behind the first part of the duodenum
gastroduodenal artery.desc: A branch of the common hepatic artery that descends behind the first part of the duodenum, between it and the pancreatic head. It gives the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery and supraduodenal branches, then ends as the right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery and the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery. It supplies the pylorus, duodenum, pancreatic head and greater curvature.
clinical: A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it and cause life-threatening bleeding.

esophageal artery.name: Esophageal artery
esophageal artery.desc: Small unpaired arteries arising from the front of the descending thoracic aorta, usually four or five in number. They run forward to the thoracic esophagus and form a longitudinal network in its wall, anastomosing above with esophageal branches of the inferior thyroid arteries and below with those of the left gastric and left inferior phrenic arteries.
clinical: The esophagus's segmental, delicate blood supply is one reason leaks are a risk after esophagectomy.

set of oesophageal branches of thoracic.name: Esophageal branches of the thoracic aorta
set of oesophageal branches of thoracic.desc: The group of small arteries that leave the anterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta to supply the middle and lower thoracic esophagus. Within the esophageal wall they form a continuous plexus linked to the inferior thyroid arteries above and the left gastric artery below.
clinical: Bleeding from these branches can complicate tears of the esophagus, and they are ligated during esophagectomy.

ileal artery.name: Ileal artery
ileal artery.region: Abdomen: small bowel mesentery, lower abdomen
ileal artery.desc: Several arteries arising from the left side of the superior mesenteric artery and running in the mesentery to the ileum. They form several tiers of arterial arcades, more than the jejunal arteries, and end in short straight vessels (vasa recta) that enter the bowel wall. They supply the ileum.
clinical: An embolus lodging in the superior mesenteric artery can cut off these vessels, causing acute mesenteric ischemia with pain out of proportion to the exam.

ileal vein.name: Ileal vein
ileal vein.desc: Veins that follow the ileal arteries through the mesentery, collecting blood from the ileum and draining into the superior mesenteric vein. Their blood, rich in absorbed nutrients, passes on to the liver via the portal vein.
clinical: Mesenteric venous thrombosis can involve these veins and cause bowel ischemia, often in people with clotting disorders.

ileocolic artery.name: Ileocolic artery
ileocolic artery.desc: The last branch from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery. It runs down and right toward the ileocecal junction and divides into a superior branch, which anastomoses with the right colic artery, and an inferior branch giving the anterior and posterior cecal arteries, the appendicular artery, an ileal branch and a colic branch. It supplies the terminal ileum, cecum, appendix and lower ascending colon.
clinical: It is divided at its origin during a right hemicolectomy for cecal cancer, along with its lymph nodes.

ileocolic vein.name: Ileocolic vein
ileocolic vein.desc: The vein that accompanies the ileocolic artery, draining the terminal ileum, cecum, appendix and lower ascending colon into the superior mesenteric vein. It runs in the mesentery with the ileocolic artery and lymph nodes, ending on the right side of the superior mesenteric vein near the root of the mesentery.
clinical: Infection spreading from appendicitis can cause clots in this vein (pylephlebitis) that travel into the portal vein.

inferior mesenteric artery.name: Inferior mesenteric artery
inferior mesenteric artery.desc: The smallest of the three unpaired gut arteries, arising from the front of the aorta at about L3, behind the horizontal part of the duodenum. It runs down and to the left, giving the left colic and sigmoid arteries, then crosses the left common iliac vessels as the superior rectal artery. It supplies the hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon and upper rectum.
clinical: A horseshoe kidney gets caught under the IMA during its development.
It is often covered or tied off during aortic aneurysm repair, usually without harm thanks to collaterals.

inferior mesenteric vein.name: Inferior mesenteric vein
inferior mesenteric vein.region: Abdomen: left of the duodenojejunal flexure
inferior mesenteric vein.desc: Begins as the continuation of the superior rectal vein and ascends on the left posterior abdominal wall, lateral to the inferior mesenteric artery and beside the duodenojejunal flexure. It usually ends in the splenic vein behind the pancreas, though it may join the superior mesenteric vein or their junction. It drains the hindgut from the rectum up to the splenic flexure.
clinical: Its lower tributaries connect with systemic rectal veins, one of the portosystemic anastomoses that open up in portal hypertension.

marginal artery of colon.name: Marginal artery of the colon
marginal artery of colon.region: Abdomen: along the mesenteric border of the colon
marginal artery of colon.desc: Also called the marginal artery of Drummond, it is a continuous arterial channel running along the inner (mesenteric) border of the colon. It is formed by linked branches of the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, left colic and sigmoid arteries, and gives short vasa recta to the colon wall. It lets the superior and inferior mesenteric territories back each other up.
clinical: It keeps the left colon alive when the inferior mesenteric artery is tied off.
It can be thin or interrupted at the splenic flexure, a watershed zone for ischemic colitis.

marginal colic artery.name: Marginal colic artery
marginal colic artery.region: Abdomen: along the mesenteric border of the colon
marginal colic artery.desc: Another name for the marginal artery of the colon (of Drummond). It forms an arterial loop close to the colon wall from the cecum to the rectosigmoid junction, built from end-to-end connections between all the colic and sigmoid arteries, and sends straight vessels into the bowel.
clinical: Surgeons check flow in this artery to decide where to divide the colon so the remaining ends have good blood supply.

middle colic artery.name: Middle colic artery
middle colic artery.desc: A branch of the superior mesenteric artery arising at the lower border of the pancreas. It enters the transverse mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that anastomose with the right colic and left colic arteries. It supplies most of the transverse colon.
clinical: It can be injured during surgery on the stomach or pancreas because it runs in the transverse mesocolon just below them.

middle colic vein.name: Middle colic vein
middle colic vein.desc: Accompanies the middle colic artery and drains the transverse colon into the superior mesenteric vein, often via the gastrocolic trunk (of Henle) at the lower border of the pancreas. It runs in the transverse mesocolon beside the artery.
clinical: Tearing of the gastrocolic trunk or its colic tributaries is a cause of troublesome bleeding during pancreatic or colon surgery.

{S} callosomarginal artery.name: Callosomarginal artery
{S} callosomarginal artery.desc: A major cortical branch of the anterior cerebral artery (A2 segment) that runs back in or near the cingulate sulcus, parallel to the pericallosal artery. Its branches (anterior, middle and posterior internal frontal and paracentral) supply the medial superior frontal gyrus, much of the cingulate gyrus and the paracentral lobule, curling over the top of the hemisphere onto the lateral surface.
clinical: Its occlusion causes weakness and numbness of the opposite leg more than the arm, because it supplies the leg area of motor and sensory cortex.
It is absent in a minority of people, with its territory taken over by pericallosal branches.

intermediomedial branch of {S} callosoma.name: Intermediomedial frontal branch of the {S} callosomarginal artery
intermediomedial branch of {S} callosoma.desc: Also called the middle internal frontal artery, it is a cortical branch of the callosomarginal artery. It supplies the middle part of the medial superior frontal gyrus and continues over the convexity to the upper lateral frontal lobe.
clinical: Damage in this medial frontal territory can reduce motivation and spontaneous movement (abulia).

posteromedial branch of {S} callosomargi.name: Posteromedial frontal branch of the {S} callosomarginal artery
posteromedial branch of {S} callosomargi.desc: Also called the posterior internal frontal artery, it is a cortical branch of the callosomarginal artery. It supplies the posterior part of the medial superior frontal gyrus, including the supplementary motor area, and part of the cingulate gyrus, reaching the upper convexity.
clinical: Injury to the supplementary motor area, for example during tumor surgery, can cause temporary loss of speech and movement on the opposite side (SMA syndrome), which usually recovers.

paracentral branch of {S} callosomargina.name: Paracentral branch of the {S} callosomarginal artery
paracentral branch of {S} callosomargina.desc: A cortical branch of the callosomarginal artery (or of the pericallosal artery) that supplies the paracentral lobule. This lobule contains the medial continuation of the primary motor and sensory cortex for the opposite leg and foot, and areas involved in voluntary bladder control.
clinical: Occlusion causes weakness and sensory loss of the opposite leg and foot, sometimes with urinary incontinence.

sigmoid artery.name: Sigmoid artery
sigmoid artery.region: Abdomen: sigmoid mesocolon, left lower quadrant
sigmoid artery.desc: Usually two to four branches of the inferior mesenteric artery that run down and left in the sigmoid mesocolon. They supply the lower descending colon and sigmoid colon, linking with each other, with the left colic artery above and with the superior rectal artery below to form the marginal artery.
clinical: The junction between the lowest sigmoid artery and the superior rectal artery (Sudeck's point) is a classic watershed for ischemia.

splenic artery.name: Splenic artery
splenic artery.region: Abdomen: upper border of pancreas, left upper quadrant
splenic artery.desc: The largest branch of the celiac trunk. It winds tortuously to the left along the upper border of the pancreas, behind the stomach, and through the splenorenal ligament to the splenic hilum. It gives pancreatic branches (including the dorsal and great pancreatic arteries), short gastric arteries, the left gastro-omental artery, then splenic branches. It supplies the spleen, pancreatic body and tail, and part of the stomach.
clinical: It is the most common site of visceral artery aneurysms.
It may be embolized to control bleeding after spleen trauma.

splenic vein.name: Splenic vein
splenic vein.desc: Drains the spleen from its hilum and runs to the right in a groove on the back of the pancreatic body, receiving short gastric, pancreatic and usually the inferior mesenteric vein. Behind the neck of the pancreas it joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
clinical: Pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer can cause splenic vein thrombosis, leading to isolated gastric varices.
It is used in a distal splenorenal shunt to lower portal pressure.

superior mesenteric artery.name: Superior mesenteric artery
superior mesenteric artery.desc: Arises from the front of the aorta at about L1, roughly 1 cm below the celiac trunk, behind the pancreatic neck and splenic vein. It passes in front of the left renal vein and the third part of the duodenum into the root of the mesentery. Branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, middle colic, right colic and ileocolic arteries. It supplies the midgut, from the second part of the duodenum to the distal transverse colon.
clinical: An embolus here causes acute mesenteric ischemia, a surgical emergency.
A narrow aortomesenteric angle can squeeze the duodenum (SMA syndrome) or the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome).

trunk of superior mesenteric artery.name: Trunk of the superior mesenteric artery
trunk of superior mesenteric artery.desc: The main stem of the superior mesenteric artery from its aortic origin at L1 to its terminal branches in the mesentery. It curves down and to the right, giving jejunal and ileal arteries from its left side and the middle colic, right colic and ileocolic arteries from its right side, with the superior mesenteric vein lying on its right.
clinical: In intestinal malrotation the normal position of the superior mesenteric vein to the right of the artery is lost, a sign seen on imaging.

superior mesenteric vein.name: Superior mesenteric vein
superior mesenteric vein.region: Abdomen: root of the mesentery, right of the SMA
superior mesenteric vein.desc: Ascends in the root of the mesentery to the right of the superior mesenteric artery, crossing the third part of the duodenum and the uncinate process of the pancreas. It collects jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, colic and pancreaticoduodenal veins and the gastrocolic trunk, then joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
clinical: Tumor involvement of the SMV is a key factor in deciding whether a pancreatic cancer can be removed.
Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis can cause venous bowel ischemia.

superior rectal artery.name: Superior rectal artery
superior rectal artery.region: Pelvis: sigmoid mesocolon and upper rectum
superior rectal artery.desc: The continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it crosses the left common iliac vessels into the pelvis. It descends in the sigmoid mesocolon, then divides at about S3 into right and left branches that supply the upper rectum, anastomosing with the middle and inferior rectal arteries.
clinical: In rectal cancer surgery the IMA or superior rectal artery is tied high to remove the lymph nodes along it.

{S} colic artery.name: Colic artery
{S} colic artery.region: Abdomen: posterior abdominal wall beside the colon
{S} colic artery.desc: The right colic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery (or ileocolic artery), runs to the right behind the peritoneum and supplies the ascending colon and hepatic flexure; it is absent in a fair number of people. The left colic artery is the first branch of the inferior mesenteric artery, running left to divide into ascending and descending branches that supply the distal transverse and descending colon. Both feed the marginal artery.
clinical: The right colic artery is divided in right hemicolectomy, the left colic in left-sided colon resections.

{S} colic vein.name: Colic vein
{S} colic vein.region: Abdomen: posterior abdominal wall beside the colon
{S} colic vein.desc: The right colic vein drains the ascending colon into the superior mesenteric vein, often via the gastrocolic trunk of Henle. The left colic vein drains the descending colon and splenic flexure into the inferior mesenteric vein. Both carry colonic blood toward the portal vein and liver.
clinical: Colon cancer spreads through these veins to the liver first, which is why the liver is the most common site of colorectal metastases.

{S} gastric artery.name: Gastric artery
{S} gastric artery.region: Abdomen: lesser curvature of the stomach
{S} gastric artery.desc: The left gastric artery is the smallest branch of the celiac trunk; it rises to the cardia, gives esophageal branches, then runs down the lesser curvature. The right gastric artery usually arises from the hepatic artery proper and runs left along the lesser curvature from the pylorus. The two anastomose to supply the lesser curvature of the stomach.
clinical: A lesser-curvature gastric ulcer can erode the left gastric artery and cause major bleeding.
A replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery.

{S} gastric vein.name: Gastric vein
{S} gastric vein.region: Abdomen: lesser curvature of the stomach
{S} gastric vein.desc: The left gastric (coronary) vein runs up the lesser curvature to the esophageal opening, receives esophageal veins, then turns down to drain into the portal vein. The right gastric vein runs along the lesser curvature near the pylorus, receives the prepyloric vein, and drains directly into the portal vein.
clinical: In portal hypertension, back-flow through the left gastric vein into esophageal veins creates esophageal varices that can bleed massively.

{S} inferior epigastric artery.name: Inferior epigastric artery
{S} inferior epigastric artery.desc: Arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament. It runs up and medially, medial to the deep inguinal ring, pierces the transversalis fascia and ascends behind rectus abdominis inside the rectus sheath, where it anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery. It supplies the lower anterior abdominal wall and rectus abdominis.
clinical: It marks the lateral border of Hesselbach's triangle: direct hernias pass medial to it, indirect hernias lateral.
It can be injured by laparoscopic port placement, causing a hematoma in the abdominal wall.

{S} inferior epigastric vein.name: Inferior epigastric vein
{S} inferior epigastric vein.desc: Usually paired veins accompanying the inferior epigastric artery behind rectus abdominis. They drain the lower anterior abdominal wall into the external iliac vein and connect above with the superior epigastric veins, linking the inferior and superior vena cava territories.
clinical: When the IVC is blocked, these veins enlarge as a collateral route for blood to reach the superior vena cava.

{S} superficial epigastric artery.name: Superficial epigastric artery
{S} superficial epigastric artery.desc: A small branch of the femoral artery just below the inguinal ligament. It passes through the saphenous opening, crosses over the inguinal ligament and ascends in the superficial fascia toward the umbilicus. It supplies the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the lower abdominal wall.
clinical: It is the basis of skin flaps from the lower abdomen used in reconstructive surgery.

{S} superficial epigastric vein.name: Superficial epigastric vein
{S} superficial epigastric vein.desc: A superficial vein draining the lower abdominal wall skin. It descends toward the groin and ends in the great saphenous vein near the saphenofemoral junction. Above, it connects with the thoracoepigastric vein and around the umbilicus with the small paraumbilical veins.
clinical: In portal hypertension, enlarged paraumbilical veins fill these veins and create caput medusae around the umbilicus.

{S} superior epigastric artery.name: Superior epigastric artery
{S} superior epigastric artery.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery, beginning at the sixth intercostal space. It descends through the gap between the sternal and costal parts of the diaphragm into the rectus sheath, behind rectus abdominis, and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery. It supplies the upper rectus abdominis, upper abdominal wall and part of the diaphragm.
clinical: In coarctation of the aorta, the internal thoracic to epigastric pathway becomes an enlarged bypass carrying blood to the lower body.

{S} superior epigastric vein.name: Superior epigastric vein
{S} superior epigastric vein.desc: Paired veins accompanying the superior epigastric artery behind rectus abdominis. They drain the upper abdominal wall into the internal thoracic vein and connect below with the inferior epigastric veins. They also receive small veins from the upper rectus abdominis muscle.
clinical: This channel is one route blood can use to bypass a blocked inferior or superior vena cava.

lateral proper palmar digital artery of.name: Lateral proper palmar digital artery of the {S} little finger
lateral proper palmar digital artery of.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the radial (lateral) side of the little finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the ring and little fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: After a finger is cut off, these digital arteries must be rejoined under a microscope for the finger to survive replantation.

lateral proper palmar digital artery of.name: Lateral proper palmar digital artery of the {S} middle finger
lateral proper palmar digital artery of.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the radial (lateral) side of the middle finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the index and middle fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: Digital artery and nerve injuries often happen together in palm-side finger cuts because they run side by side.

lateral proper palmar digital artery of.name: Lateral proper palmar digital artery of the {S} ring finger
lateral proper palmar digital artery of.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the radial (lateral) side of the ring finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the middle and ring fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: Ring avulsion injuries can tear these arteries and may need microsurgical repair.

medial proper palmar digital artery of m.name: Medial proper palmar digital artery of the middle finger
medial proper palmar digital artery of m.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the ulnar (medial) side of the middle finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the middle and ring fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: A digital nerve block at the finger base numbs the area these arteries supply; the arteries lie right next to the injected nerves.

medial proper palmar digital artery of r.name: Medial proper palmar digital artery of the ring finger
medial proper palmar digital artery of r.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the ulnar (medial) side of the ring finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the ring and little fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: Damage to both digital arteries of a finger threatens its survival, while one intact artery is usually enough.

medial proper palmar digital artery of {.name: Medial proper palmar digital artery of the {S} index finger
medial proper palmar digital artery of {.desc: A proper palmar digital artery running along the ulnar (medial) side of the index finger, beside the proper palmar digital nerve. It arises from the common palmar digital artery of the web between the index and middle fingers and supplies the skin, flexor tendon sheath, joints and pulp of the finger, anastomosing with its partner on the other side of the finger at the fingertip.
clinical: In cold-triggered Raynaud phenomenon, spasm of the digital arteries turns the fingers white, then blue, then red.

proper palmar digital vein of {S} index.name: Proper palmar digital vein of the {S} index finger
proper palmar digital vein of {S} index.desc: Small veins on the palmar side of the index finger, along each border beside the digital arteries. They drain the palmar skin and pulp, mostly passing back between the knuckles (via intercapitular veins) to the dorsal venous network of the hand, with some flow to the common palmar digital veins.
clinical: Repairing at least one vein, often a dorsal one, is needed in finger replantation to prevent congestion.

proper palmar digital vein of {S} little.name: Proper palmar digital vein of the {S} little finger
proper palmar digital vein of {S} little.desc: Small veins on the palmar side of the little finger, along each border beside the digital arteries. They drain the palmar skin and pulp, mostly passing back between the knuckles (via intercapitular veins) to the dorsal venous network of the hand, with some flow to the common palmar digital veins.
clinical: Repairing at least one vein, often a dorsal one, is needed in finger replantation to prevent congestion.

proper palmar digital vein of {S} middle.name: Proper palmar digital vein of the {S} middle finger
proper palmar digital vein of {S} middle.desc: Small veins on the palmar side of the middle finger, along each border beside the digital arteries. They drain the palmar skin and pulp, mostly passing back between the knuckles (via intercapitular veins) to the dorsal venous network of the hand, with some flow to the common palmar digital veins.
clinical: Repairing at least one vein, often a dorsal one, is needed in finger replantation to prevent congestion.

proper palmar digital vein of {S} ring f.name: Proper palmar digital vein of the {S} ring finger
proper palmar digital vein of {S} ring f.desc: Small veins on the palmar side of the ring finger, along each border beside the digital arteries. They drain the palmar skin and pulp, mostly passing back between the knuckles (via intercapitular veins) to the dorsal venous network of the hand, with some flow to the common palmar digital veins.
clinical: Repairing at least one vein, often a dorsal one, is needed in finger replantation to prevent congestion.

common palmar digital vein.name: Common palmar digital vein
common palmar digital vein.region: Hand: palm, between the metacarpal heads
common palmar digital vein.desc: Veins in the distal palm formed by the union of proper palmar digital veins from adjacent finger sides. They drain into the superficial palmar venous arch and, through intercapitular veins between the knuckles, into the dorsal venous network of the hand.
clinical: Most blood from the palm drains to the back of the hand, which is why hand swelling shows up mostly on the dorsum.

dorsal metacarpal vein.name: Dorsal metacarpal vein
dorsal metacarpal vein.desc: Veins on the back of the hand formed by dorsal digital veins from adjacent fingers. They join to form the dorsal venous network, which drains laterally into the cephalic vein and medially into the basilic vein.
clinical: The dorsal hand veins are common sites for IV cannulas.

dorsal carpal branch of {S} radial arter.name: Dorsal carpal branch of the {S} radial artery
dorsal carpal branch of {S} radial arter.desc: A small branch of the radial artery given off as it winds around the lateral wrist, deep to the thumb extensor tendons in the anatomical snuffbox. It runs medially across the back of the carpus and joins the dorsal carpal branch of the ulnar artery to form the dorsal carpal arch, which gives the second to fourth dorsal metacarpal arteries.
clinical: The dorsal carpal network supplies the scaphoid in part; scaphoid blood enters from distal to proximal, so waist fractures risk avascular necrosis.

{S} dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.name: Dorsal carpal branch of the ulnar artery
{S} dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.desc: A branch of the ulnar artery arising just above the pisiform. It winds around the medial side of the wrist deep to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon and passes across the back of the carpus to join the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery in the dorsal carpal arch.
clinical: It contributes collateral flow that keeps the hand perfused if the radial artery is used for a graft or catheter.

set of dorsal metacarpal arteries.name: Dorsal metacarpal arteries
set of dorsal metacarpal arteries.desc: Arteries running distally on the dorsal interosseous muscles. The first usually arises directly from the radial artery before it enters the palm; the second to fourth arise from the dorsal carpal arch. Each receives perforating branches from the deep palmar arch and divides at the web into dorsal digital arteries for adjacent fingers.
clinical: The first dorsal metacarpal artery supplies the kite flap, used to cover defects on the thumb.

set of dorsal digital arteries.name: Dorsal digital arteries
set of dorsal digital arteries.region: Hand and foot: dorsum of the digits
set of dorsal digital arteries.desc: Small arteries running along the dorsal borders of the fingers (from the dorsal metacarpal arteries) and toes (from the dorsal metatarsal arteries). They supply the skin over the back of the digits, usually reaching only as far as the middle phalanx, beyond which palmar or plantar digital arteries take over.
clinical: Dorsal digital arteries are the basis of small local flaps used to cover fingertip injuries.

set of dorsal digital veins.name: Dorsal digital veins
set of dorsal digital veins.region: Hand and foot: dorsum of the digits
set of dorsal digital veins.desc: Veins along the dorsal sides of the fingers and toes that receive blood from the palmar or plantar digital veins via communicating veins. In the hand they join to form dorsal metacarpal veins and the dorsal venous network; in the foot they form dorsal metatarsal veins and the dorsal venous arch.
clinical: Dorsal digital veins are often the veins repaired in finger replantation because they are larger and easier to reach than palmar ones.

dorsal digital artery of foot.name: Dorsal digital artery of the foot
dorsal digital artery of foot.desc: Small arteries running along the dorsal borders of the toes. Each dorsal metatarsal artery (the first from the dorsalis pedis, the others from the arcuate artery) splits near the web into two dorsal digital arteries for the adjacent sides of neighboring toes. They supply the skin of the dorsal toes.
clinical: In peripheral arterial disease, poor flow in these small toe arteries contributes to toe ulcers and gangrene.

set of common plantar digital arteries.name: Common plantar digital arteries
set of common plantar digital arteries.desc: Also called plantar metatarsal arteries, they arise from the deep plantar arch, formed by the lateral plantar artery and the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis. They run forward between the metatarsals and split near the webs into proper plantar digital arteries for adjacent toe sides, also sending perforating branches to the dorsal arteries.
clinical: Diabetic foot disease often affects these small arteries, which affects healing after toe amputations.

set of plantar digital arteries proper.name: Proper plantar digital arteries
set of plantar digital arteries proper.region: Foot: plantar side of the toes
set of plantar digital arteries proper.desc: Arteries running along each side of the plantar surface of the toes, formed by division of the common plantar digital arteries; the medial side of the great toe and lateral side of the little toe are supplied by separate branches. They supply the skin, joints and pads of the toes.
clinical: Toe pressure measurements, which reflect flow in these vessels, help assess blood supply in diabetic patients whose ankle readings are unreliable.

set of plantar digital veins.name: Plantar digital veins
set of plantar digital veins.region: Foot: plantar side of the toes
set of plantar digital veins.desc: Small veins along the plantar sides of the toes that join to form plantar metatarsal veins draining into the deep plantar venous arch. Many connect through intercapitular veins between the metatarsal heads to the dorsal venous arch, so much toe blood drains to the top of the foot.
clinical: Pressure from standing squeezes the plantar veins, acting as a foot pump that pushes blood up the leg.

{S} common interosseous artery.name: Common interosseous artery
{S} common interosseous artery.region: Forearm: proximal anterior, at the interosseous membrane
{S} common interosseous artery.desc: A short trunk arising from the ulnar artery just below the radial tuberosity in the cubital region. It passes back to the upper border of the interosseous membrane and divides into the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries, which supply the deep muscles of both compartments of the forearm and the radius and ulna.
clinical: It can be injured in proximal forearm fractures, contributing to compartment syndrome.

{S} anterior interosseous artery.name: Anterior interosseous artery
{S} anterior interosseous artery.region: Forearm: anterior, on the interosseous membrane
{S} anterior interosseous artery.desc: A branch of the common interosseous artery that descends on the front of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous nerve, between flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus. It supplies these deep flexors, the radius and ulna, and gives the median artery. At the upper border of pronator quadratus it pierces the membrane to reach the dorsal carpal network.
clinical: Its companion nerve, the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, can be compressed, causing loss of the OK sign pinch.

{S} anterior ulnar recurrent artery.name: Anterior ulnar recurrent artery
{S} anterior ulnar recurrent artery.region: Elbow: anterior to the medial epicondyle
{S} anterior ulnar recurrent artery.desc: A small branch of the ulnar artery just below the elbow. It ascends between brachialis and pronator teres, in front of the medial epicondyle, and anastomoses with the inferior ulnar collateral artery as part of the elbow's arterial network.
clinical: The elbow anastomosis keeps the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is blocked or tied off above the elbow.

{S} anterior tibial recurrent artery.name: Anterior tibial recurrent artery
{S} anterior tibial recurrent artery.desc: A branch of the anterior tibial artery given off just after it passes forward through the interosseous membrane. It ascends through tibialis anterior to the front of the lateral tibial condyle and joins the genicular anastomosis around the knee, supplying the knee joint and nearby muscles.
clinical: It can be torn in fractures of the upper tibia, contributing to anterior compartment syndrome.

{S} arteria radialis indicis.name: Radialis indicis artery
{S} arteria radialis indicis.desc: A branch of the radial artery in the palm, often arising with or from the princeps pollicis artery near the first web space. It runs along the radial (lateral) side of the index finger, supplying it, and connects with the superficial palmar arch.
clinical: It is a source of collateral flow to the index finger and can be used in local flaps for thumb reconstruction.

{S} deep palmar arch.name: Deep palmar arch
{S} deep palmar arch.region: Hand: deep palm, on the metacarpal bases
{S} deep palmar arch.desc: An arterial arch formed mainly by the end of the radial artery, which enters the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous, completed by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies on the bases of the metacarpals and interossei, deep to the long flexor tendons, about a finger-width above the superficial arch. It gives palmar metacarpal arteries, perforating branches and recurrent branches to the wrist.
clinical: The modified Allen test checks whether the palmar arches let the ulnar artery supply the hand before radial artery cannulation or harvest.

{S} deep palmar venous arch.name: Deep palmar venous arch
{S} deep palmar venous arch.desc: Paired veins (venae comitantes) accompanying the deep palmar arterial arch. They receive the palmar metacarpal veins and drain into the radial and ulnar deep veins of the forearm. They lie deep to the long flexor tendons on the metacarpal bases and interossei.
clinical: Deep hand infections can spread along the tissue planes around the deep arch and require surgical drainage.

{S} first common palmar digital artery.name: First common palmar digital artery
{S} first common palmar digital artery.desc: The most radial of the common palmar digital arteries arising from the superficial palmar arch. It runs distally over the lumbrical and flexor tendons, receives a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch, and divides near the web into proper palmar digital arteries for the adjacent sides of neighboring fingers.
clinical: Palmar cuts near the finger bases can injure the common digital artery and the digital nerves together.

{S} fourth common palmar digital artery.name: Fourth common palmar digital artery
{S} fourth common palmar digital artery.desc: The most ulnar of the common palmar digital arteries from the superficial palmar arch, which is mainly formed by the ulnar artery. It runs toward the ring and little finger web, joins a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch, and divides into proper palmar digital arteries for the adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers.
clinical: Repeated pounding with the heel of the hand can damage the ulnar artery and this territory (hypothenar hammer syndrome), causing cold, painful fingers.

{S} inferior ulnar collateral artery.name: Inferior ulnar collateral artery
{S} inferior ulnar collateral artery.region: Upper limb: distal arm, medial elbow
{S} inferior ulnar collateral artery.desc: Arises from the brachial artery a few centimetres above the elbow and runs medially, anterior to the medial epicondyle region. It joins the anastomosis around the elbow, linking with the anterior ulnar recurrent artery and, behind the epicondyle, with the posterior ulnar recurrent and superior ulnar collateral arteries.
clinical: Its anastomoses help keep the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is ligated below the profunda brachii origin.

{S} medial brachial vein.name: Medial brachial vein
{S} medial brachial vein.desc: One of the paired venae comitantes that run alongside the brachial artery, on its medial side. It drains deep tissues of the arm and forearm and joins the lateral brachial vein and basilic vein near the lower border of teres major to form the axillary vein.
clinical: Deep vein thrombosis can occur in the brachial veins, often linked to central lines or catheters.

{S} median antebrachial vein.name: Median antebrachial vein
{S} median antebrachial vein.desc: A variable superficial vein that runs up the middle of the front of the forearm in the subcutaneous tissue. It begins from the superficial palmar venous network and usually ends in the basilic vein, the median cubital vein, or splits to join both basilic and cephalic veins near the elbow.
clinical: Its course is highly variable, which is why phlebotomists palpate rather than rely on a fixed map of forearm veins.

{S} palmar metacarpal artery.name: Palmar metacarpal artery
{S} palmar metacarpal artery.desc: Small arteries arising from the deep palmar arch that run distally on the interosseous muscles between the metacarpal bones. Near the finger webs they join the common palmar digital arteries from the superficial arch, and they send perforating branches to the dorsal metacarpal arteries.
clinical: These links between deep and superficial arches keep the fingers perfused when one arch is injured.

{S} palmar metacarpal vein.name: Palmar metacarpal vein
{S} palmar metacarpal vein.desc: Deep veins that accompany the palmar metacarpal arteries between the metacarpal bones. They drain the interosseous muscles and deep palm into the deep palmar venous arch, which continues into the radial and ulnar venae comitantes.
clinical: Most hand venous return travels superficially on the dorsum, so deep palmar veins are rarely accessed clinically.

{S} posterior ulnar recurrent artery.name: Posterior ulnar recurrent artery
{S} posterior ulnar recurrent artery.desc: A branch of the ulnar artery just below the elbow (sometimes sharing a trunk with the anterior ulnar recurrent). It ascends behind the medial epicondyle alongside the ulnar nerve, between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, to anastomose with the superior ulnar collateral artery around the elbow.
clinical: It travels with the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel region, where surgical decompression of the nerve takes place.

{S} radial artery.name: Radial artery
{S} radial artery.region: Upper limb: lateral forearm and wrist
{S} radial artery.desc: The smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery, beginning in the cubital fossa. It runs down the lateral forearm under brachioradialis, is palpable at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis, then crosses the anatomical snuffbox and pierces the first dorsal interosseous to form the deep palmar arch. It supplies lateral forearm muscles and the thumb side of the hand.
clinical: The radial pulse at the wrist is the most commonly checked pulse.
It is the preferred access route for coronary angiography and for arterial blood gas sampling; the Allen test checks ulnar backup first.

{S} radial recurrent artery.name: Radial recurrent artery
{S} radial recurrent artery.desc: The first branch of the radial artery, arising just below the elbow. It ascends between brachioradialis and brachialis, near the radial nerve, to anastomose with the radial collateral branch of the profunda brachii artery, forming part of the lateral elbow anastomosis.
clinical: It is a landmark in surgical exposure of the radial nerve and the proximal radius.

{S} radial vein.name: Radial vein
{S} radial vein.desc: Paired deep veins (venae comitantes) that accompany the radial artery. They arise from the deep palmar venous arch and the dorsal hand veins, run up the lateral forearm, and join the ulnar veins near the elbow to form the brachial veins.
clinical: Arteriovenous fistulas for dialysis are often created at the wrist between the radial artery and a nearby superficial vein.

{S} recurrent interosseous artery.name: Recurrent interosseous artery
{S} recurrent interosseous artery.desc: A branch of the posterior interosseous artery (from the common interosseous branch of the ulnar artery). It ascends deep to anconeus and supinator toward the lateral epicondyle, where it joins the middle collateral branch of the profunda brachii in the posterior elbow anastomosis.
clinical: It contributes to the collateral network that can sustain forearm blood flow after proximal arterial injury.

{S} second common palmar digital artery.name: Second common palmar digital artery
{S} second common palmar digital artery.desc: A branch of the superficial palmar arch that runs distally on the lumbricals toward the web between the index and middle fingers. It receives a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch, then divides into proper palmar digital arteries supplying the adjacent sides of those two fingers.
clinical: Injury to digital arteries in palm lacerations can threaten finger blood supply and may need microsurgical repair.

{S} superficial palmar arterial arch.name: Superficial palmar arch
{S} superficial palmar arterial arch.desc: An arterial arcade lying just deep to the palmar aponeurosis, formed mainly by the terminal ulnar artery and usually completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. Its convexity sits roughly level with the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives the common palmar digital arteries to the fingers.
clinical: The arch is incomplete in a meaningful share of people, which matters for hand surgery and radial artery harvesting.
Deep palm lacerations near its surface marking can cause brisk bleeding.

{S} superficial palmar venous arch.name: Superficial palmar venous arch
{S} superficial palmar venous arch.desc: A venous arcade accompanying the superficial palmar arterial arch. It receives the common palmar digital veins and drains into the ulnar and radial venae comitantes and into the superficial veins of the forearm.
clinical: Pressure on the palm during gripping pushes blood toward the dorsal hand veins, which carry most of the hand's return.

{S} superior ulnar collateral artery.name: Superior ulnar collateral artery
{S} superior ulnar collateral artery.desc: Arises from the brachial artery near the middle of the arm and accompanies the ulnar nerve, piercing the medial intermuscular septum. It descends behind the medial epicondyle to anastomose with the posterior ulnar recurrent and inferior ulnar collateral arteries.
clinical: Because it runs with the ulnar nerve, it is encountered during ulnar nerve transposition at the elbow.

{S} third common palmar digital artery.name: Third common palmar digital artery
{S} third common palmar digital artery.desc: A branch of the superficial palmar arch that runs toward the web between the middle and ring fingers. It joins a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch and divides into proper palmar digital arteries for the adjacent sides of those fingers.
clinical: Digital arteries are vulnerable in Dupuytren's surgery, where diseased cords can displace them.

{S} ulnar artery.name: Ulnar artery
{S} ulnar artery.region: Upper limb: medial forearm and wrist
{S} ulnar artery.desc: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, starting in the cubital fossa. It passes deep to pronator teres, gives the common interosseous artery, then runs down the medial forearm with the ulnar nerve on its medial side. It enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal and forms most of the superficial palmar arch.
clinical: Repetitive hammering with the hypothenar eminence can damage it, causing hypothenar hammer syndrome and finger ischemia.
The Allen test checks that it alone can perfuse the hand before radial artery procedures.

{S} ulnar vein.name: Ulnar vein
{S} ulnar vein.desc: Paired deep veins accompanying the ulnar artery. They begin from the deep and superficial palmar venous arches, receive interosseous veins, and unite with the radial veins near the elbow to form the brachial veins.
clinical: Deep forearm veins are rarely used for access; superficial veins are chosen instead.

brachiocephalic artery.name: Brachiocephalic trunk
brachiocephalic artery.desc: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch, arising behind the manubrium. It ascends to the right in front of the trachea and, behind the right sternoclavicular joint, divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. It normally has no other branches, though a small thyroid ima artery sometimes arises from it.
clinical: It crosses in front of the trachea, so a low tracheostomy can erode into it, causing life-threatening bleeding.
Stenosis here can cause right arm and brain symptoms, including subclavian steal.

{S} basilic vein.name: Basilic vein
{S} basilic vein.region: Upper limb: medial forearm and arm
{S} basilic vein.desc: A large superficial vein arising from the ulnar side of the dorsal venous network of the hand. It ascends on the medial forearm, receives the median cubital vein at the elbow, then pierces the deep fascia in the mid-arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
clinical: It is a common route for peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC lines).
It can be surgically moved to create a dialysis fistula.

{S} brachiocephalic vein.name: Brachiocephalic vein
{S} brachiocephalic vein.region: Root of the neck and superior mediastinum
{S} brachiocephalic vein.desc: Formed behind the sternoclavicular joint by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The right vein is short and nearly vertical; the left is longer and crosses obliquely in front of the arch branches. The two join behind the right first costal cartilage to form the superior vena cava. They receive vertebral, internal thoracic and inferior thyroid veins, and the thoracic duct enters at the left venous angle.
clinical: The left brachiocephalic vein can be compressed by an aortic aneurysm or tumor.
Central venous catheters often pass through it on the way to the SVC.

{S} cephalic vein.name: Cephalic vein
{S} cephalic vein.region: Upper limb: lateral forearm, arm and deltopectoral groove
{S} cephalic vein.desc: A superficial vein arising from the radial side of the dorsal venous network of the hand. It ascends on the lateral forearm and arm, runs in the deltopectoral groove, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein.
clinical: It is used for pacemaker lead insertion via the deltopectoral groove.
The wrist cephalic vein is the classic partner for a radiocephalic dialysis fistula.

{S} median cubital vein.name: Median cubital vein
{S} median cubital vein.desc: A superficial vein crossing the front of the elbow obliquely, linking the cephalic vein to the basilic vein. It lies on the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve below.
clinical: It is the most common site for drawing blood because it is large, superficial and fairly fixed.
The bicipital aponeurosis protects the brachial artery beneath it during venipuncture.

anterior communicating artery.name: Anterior communicating artery
anterior communicating artery.desc: A short vessel joining the two anterior cerebral arteries in front of the optic chiasm, closing the front of the circle of Willis. Its small perforating branches supply the lamina terminalis, fornix columns, anterior hypothalamus and parts of the cingulate region.
clinical: It is the single most common site of saccular (berry) aneurysms, which can rupture to cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Surgery here risks perforators to the fornix and hypothalamus, causing memory and personality changes.

anterior inferior cerebellar artery.name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
anterior inferior cerebellar artery.desc: Usually arises from the lower basilar artery and runs back across the pons toward the cerebellopontine angle, often looping near the internal acoustic meatus with the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. It supplies the lateral pons, middle cerebellar peduncle, anterior-inferior cerebellum, and usually gives the labyrinthine artery.
clinical: AICA stroke causes lateral pontine syndrome: facial weakness, ipsilateral hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia and crossed sensory loss.
Its loop can compress the facial nerve, a cause of hemifacial spasm.

branch of {S} anterior choroidal artery.name: Branch of the {S} anterior choroidal artery to the posterior limb of the {S} internal capsule
branch of {S} anterior choroidal artery.desc: A small perforating branch of the anterior choroidal artery that enters the brain to supply the lower (ventral) part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule. This region carries descending corticospinal fibres and thalamocortical sensory and optic radiation fibres.
clinical: Occlusion can cause contralateral hemiplegia, hemisensory loss and sometimes hemianopia from a small deep infarct.

hypothalamic branch of {S} posterior com.name: Hypothalamic branch of the {S} posterior communicating artery
hypothalamic branch of {S} posterior com.desc: A small perforating branch from the posterior communicating artery that enters the base of the brain to supply part of the hypothalamus, including the region of the tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies.
clinical: Damage to these perforators during aneurysm surgery can disturb hypothalamic functions such as temperature, thirst and memory circuits.

lateral branch of {S} pontine artery.name: Lateral branch of the {S} pontine artery
lateral branch of {S} pontine artery.desc: One of the pontine branches of the basilar artery that runs around the side of the pons (a short circumferential branch). It supplies the lateral pontine tegmentum and basis, including fibres heading into the middle cerebellar peduncle.
clinical: Small vessel occlusions in pontine branches cause lacunar strokes, such as dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome.

lateral branch of {S} superior cerebella.name: Lateral branch of the {S} superior cerebellar artery
lateral branch of {S} superior cerebella.desc: One of the two main divisions of the superior cerebellar artery. It supplies the upper surface of the cerebellar hemisphere and, through deeper branches, contributes to the dentate nucleus region.
clinical: Infarcts in its territory cause ipsilateral limb ataxia, often with dizziness and slurred speech.

medial branch of {S} pontine artery.name: Medial branch of the {S} pontine artery
medial branch of {S} pontine artery.desc: One of the paramedian pontine branches of the basilar artery that penetrates the pons near the midline. It supplies the basis pontis, including descending corticospinal tracts, pontine nuclei and medial lemniscus.
clinical: Paramedian pontine infarcts cause contralateral weakness; bilateral basis pontis damage causes locked-in syndrome.

medial branch of {S} superior cerebellar.name: Medial branch of the {S} superior cerebellar artery
medial branch of {S} superior cerebellar.desc: One of the two main divisions of the superior cerebellar artery. It supplies the superior vermis and medial upper cerebellar hemisphere and gives the superior vermian branches. It anastomoses with branches of the inferior cerebellar arteries.
clinical: Vermis infarcts cause truncal and gait ataxia more than limb clumsiness.

postcommunicating part of {S} posterior.name: Postcommunicating part of the {S} posterior cerebral artery
postcommunicating part of {S} posterior.region: Brain: around the midbrain, medial temporal and occipital lobes
postcommunicating part of {S} posterior.desc: The segment of the posterior cerebral artery beyond its junction with the posterior communicating artery. It curves around the midbrain in the ambient cistern above the tentorium, giving thalamogeniculate, posterior choroidal and temporal branches, then ends as the medial and lateral occipital arteries.
clinical: Uncal herniation can compress it against the tentorium, causing occipital infarction.
Occlusion beyond here typically causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

posteromedial central branch of {S} post.name: Posteromedial central branches of the {S} posterior cerebral artery
posteromedial central branch of {S} post.desc: Perforating branches from the proximal posterior cerebral artery (and posterior communicating artery) that enter the posterior perforated substance. They supply the anterior and medial thalamus, subthalamic region, hypothalamus and medial midbrain, including the oculomotor nucleus region.
clinical: The artery of Percheron, a single variant perforator, can supply both medial thalami; its occlusion causes sudden coma or hypersomnolence.

precommunicating part of {S} posterior c.name: Precommunicating part of the {S} posterior cerebral artery
precommunicating part of {S} posterior c.desc: The first segment of the posterior cerebral artery, from the basilar bifurcation to where the posterior communicating artery joins. It lies near the oculomotor nerve, which passes between it and the superior cerebellar artery, and gives thalamoperforating and other perforators to the midbrain and thalamus.
clinical: When P1 is small, the PCA is mainly fed from the internal carotid (fetal PCA), changing stroke patterns.
Aneurysms nearby can compress the oculomotor nerve.

superior vermian branch of medial branch.name: Superior vermian branch of the medial branch of the {S} superior cerebellar artery
superior vermian branch of medial branch.desc: A small branch of the medial division of the superior cerebellar artery that runs over the upper surface of the vermis, supplying it and anastomosing with branches from the opposite side and from the inferior cerebellar arteries.
clinical: Vermian ischemia causes truncal ataxia and unsteady gait.

{S} anterior cerebral artery.name: Anterior cerebral artery
{S} anterior cerebral artery.region: Brain: medial frontal and parietal lobes
{S} anterior cerebral artery.desc: A terminal branch of the internal carotid artery. It runs forward above the optic nerve, connects with its partner via the anterior communicating artery, then curves around the genu of the corpus callosum in the interhemispheric fissure. It supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex, and most of the corpus callosum.
clinical: ACA stroke causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss more than arm or face.
Bilateral ACA damage can cause abulia and urinary incontinence.

{S} anterior choroidal artery.name: Anterior choroidal artery
{S} anterior choroidal artery.region: Brain: deep, temporal horn and internal capsule
{S} anterior choroidal artery.desc: A slender branch of the internal carotid artery just above the posterior communicating artery. It runs back along the optic tract, enters the temporal horn to supply the choroid plexus, and supplies the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, posterior limb of the internal capsule, globus pallidus, uncus and parts of the hippocampus and midbrain.
clinical: AChA syndrome is contralateral hemiplegia, hemisensory loss and hemianopia.
It is at risk during temporal lobe and carotid aneurysm surgery.

{S} ophthalmic artery.name: Ophthalmic artery
{S} ophthalmic artery.desc: The first intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery, arising just after it leaves the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal below the optic nerve. Its branches include the central retinal artery, ciliary arteries, lacrimal, supraorbital, supratrochlear and ethmoidal arteries, supplying the eye, orbit and parts of the forehead and nasal cavity.
clinical: Occlusion of its central retinal branch causes sudden painless monocular blindness.
It forms anastomoses with external carotid branches, a collateral route in carotid occlusion.

{S} posterior choroidal artery.name: Posterior choroidal artery
{S} posterior choroidal artery.desc: Usually several branches (medial and lateral) of the postcommunicating posterior cerebral artery. The medial branches supply the choroid plexus of the third ventricle and the pineal and medial thalamic region; the lateral branches supply the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle, pulvinar and fornix.
clinical: Occlusion is uncommon but can cause visual field defects from lateral geniculate involvement.

{S} posterior communicating artery.name: Posterior communicating artery
{S} posterior communicating artery.desc: A branch of the internal carotid artery that runs back to join the posterior cerebral artery, linking the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems in the circle of Willis. It runs above and close to the oculomotor nerve and gives perforators to the thalamus, hypothalamus and internal capsule.
clinical: A PComm aneurysm classically compresses the oculomotor nerve, causing a dilated pupil and drooping eyelid.
Its size varies a lot, affecting collateral flow in carotid disease.

{S} posterior inferior cerebellar artery.name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
{S} posterior inferior cerebellar artery.region: Brain: lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum
{S} posterior inferior cerebellar artery.desc: Usually the largest branch of the vertebral artery. It winds around the medulla between the lower cranial nerve rootlets, loops near the cerebellar tonsil, and supplies the lateral medulla, the inferior cerebellar vermis and the underside of the cerebellar hemisphere, plus choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle.
clinical: Occlusion (often from vertebral artery disease) causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: vertigo, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, hoarseness, Horner syndrome.

{S} superior cerebellar artery.name: Superior cerebellar artery
{S} superior cerebellar artery.desc: Arises near the top of the basilar artery just below the posterior cerebral artery, with the oculomotor nerve passing between them. It winds around the midbrain and divides into medial and lateral branches supplying the upper surface of the cerebellum, the superior vermis, the deep cerebellar nuclei and parts of the upper pons and midbrain.
clinical: It commonly contacts the trigeminal nerve root, a cause of trigeminal neuralgia treated by microvascular decompression.

{S} thalamogeniculate artery.name: Thalamogeniculate artery
{S} thalamogeniculate artery.desc: Small perforating branches from the postcommunicating posterior cerebral artery that enter near the geniculate bodies. They supply the posterolateral thalamus, including the ventral posterior sensory nuclei and pulvinar, and part of the lateral geniculate body.
clinical: Occlusion can cause thalamic (Dejerine-Roussy) syndrome: contralateral sensory loss followed by severe burning pain.

{S} thalamoperforating artery.name: Thalamoperforating artery
{S} thalamoperforating artery.desc: Perforating arteries from the precommunicating posterior cerebral artery near the basilar tip. They pass through the posterior perforated substance to supply the medial and anterior thalamus and adjacent midbrain. Their exact pattern varies from person to person.
clinical: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts cause sleepiness, memory loss and vertical gaze problems.

anterior cardiac vein.name: Anterior cardiac veins
anterior cardiac vein.desc: Several small veins on the front of the right ventricle that cross the right coronary sulcus and open directly into the right atrium rather than the coronary sinus. They drain much of the anterior right ventricular wall.
clinical: Because they bypass the coronary sinus, coronary sinus catheter studies do not capture all of the heart's venous return.

anterior interventricular vein.name: Anterior interventricular vein
anterior interventricular vein.desc: Begins near the cardiac apex and ascends in the anterior interventricular groove beside the left anterior descending artery. At the top of the groove it turns left into the coronary sulcus, where it continues as the great cardiac vein. It drains the anterior ventricles and interventricular septum.
clinical: It is a route for placing left ventricular pacing leads and for mapping certain ventricular arrhythmias.

coronary sinus.name: Coronary sinus
coronary sinus.desc: A wide venous channel about 2-3 cm long in the posterior part of the coronary groove between left atrium and ventricle. It receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the posterior left ventricular vein, and opens into the right atrium between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve, guarded by a thin valve.
clinical: Leads for cardiac resynchronization therapy are threaded through it into a lateral vein of the left ventricle.
A persistent left SVC often drains into a dilated coronary sinus.

great cardiac vein.name: Great cardiac vein
great cardiac vein.desc: The continuation of the anterior interventricular vein, running leftward in the coronary groove around the left side of the heart with the circumflex artery. It receives the left marginal vein and becomes the coronary sinus where the oblique vein of the left atrium joins it.
clinical: It runs near the mitral annulus, which allows some catheter-based mitral and arrhythmia procedures from inside it.

middle cardiac vein.name: Middle cardiac vein
middle cardiac vein.desc: Begins near the apex and ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior descending artery. It drains the posterior parts of both ventricles and the septum and empties into the coronary sinus near its right atrial opening.
clinical: Some accessory pathways in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are reached and ablated from within it.

small cardiac vein.name: Small cardiac vein
small cardiac vein.desc: Runs in the right part of the coronary groove with the right coronary artery, draining the back of the right atrium and right ventricle, often receiving the right marginal vein. It empties into the coronary sinus or directly into the right atrium.
clinical: It is small and variably present, so it is rarely used for device leads.

{S} marginal vein.name: Marginal vein
{S} marginal vein.desc: Runs along the margin of the heart beside the corresponding marginal artery. The left marginal vein ascends along the left border of the left ventricle into the great cardiac vein; the right marginal vein runs along the acute margin of the right ventricle into the small cardiac vein or directly into the right atrium.
clinical: The left marginal vein is a common target branch for left ventricular pacing leads.

accessory hemiazygos vein.name: Accessory hemiazygos vein
accessory hemiazygos vein.desc: Descends on the left side of the vertebral bodies, receiving the left 4th to 8th posterior intercostal veins and sometimes left bronchial veins. It crosses behind the aorta and esophagus around T7-T8 to join the azygos vein, often also connecting with the hemiazygos vein.
clinical: The azygos system provides a collateral path back to the heart if the SVC or IVC is blocked.

azygos vein.name: Azygos vein
azygos vein.desc: Begins in the abdomen, often from the right ascending lumbar and subcostal veins, and enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus. It ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies, receiving right posterior intercostal, esophageal, bronchial and the hemiazygos veins, then arches over the right main bronchus at about T4 to enter the superior vena cava.
clinical: It becomes a major bypass route when the IVC or SVC is obstructed.
A visible azygos lobe on chest X-ray is a normal variant from an aberrant arch.

bronchial artery.name: Bronchial arteries
bronchial artery.desc: Small arteries supplying oxygenated systemic blood to the bronchi, lung connective tissue and visceral pleura. The left ones (usually two) arise from the thoracic aorta; the right usually comes from the third right posterior intercostal artery or a shared aortic trunk. They follow the bronchial tree into the lungs.
clinical: Most serious coughing up of blood (massive hemoptysis) comes from bronchial arteries and is treated by embolizing them.
They anastomose with spinal arteries, a risk during embolization.

hemiazygos vein.name: Hemiazygos vein
hemiazygos vein.desc: Arises on the left from the left ascending lumbar and subcostal veins, enters the thorax through the left crus of the diaphragm, and ascends on the left of the vertebral bodies receiving the lower left posterior intercostal veins. Around T9 it crosses behind the aorta, esophagus and thoracic duct to join the azygos vein.
clinical: With the azygos it forms a collateral route if the inferior vena cava is blocked.

inferior phrenic vein.name: Inferior phrenic veins
inferior phrenic vein.desc: Accompany the inferior phrenic arteries on the abdominal surface of the diaphragm. The right drains into the inferior vena cava; the left usually drains into the left suprarenal or left renal vein, sometimes directly into the IVC.
clinical: They can open as collaterals in portal hypertension and are relevant in adrenal vein sampling.

posterior intercostal arteries.name: Posterior intercostal arteries
posterior intercostal arteries.desc: Arteries running in each intercostal space in the costal groove with the intercostal vein above and nerve below (VAN). The first two arise from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk); the 3rd to 11th come from the thoracic aorta. They supply intercostal muscles, ribs, skin, back muscles and give spinal branches to the vertebral column and spinal cord.
clinical: Chest drains and needles are placed just above a rib to avoid the vessels in the costal groove.
A large lower intercostal branch often gives the artery of Adamkiewicz, which supplies the lower spinal cord.

set of anterior intercostal veins.name: Anterior intercostal veins
set of anterior intercostal veins.desc: Small veins draining the front of the intercostal spaces. The upper ones drain into the internal thoracic vein and the lower ones into the musculophrenic vein; they anastomose with the posterior intercostal veins.
clinical: They are part of collateral pathways that open when the superior vena cava is obstructed.

superior phrenic vein.name: Superior phrenic veins
superior phrenic vein.region: Thorax: upper surface of the diaphragm
superior phrenic vein.desc: Small veins draining the posterior thoracic (upper) surface of the diaphragm, accompanying the small superior phrenic arteries from the thoracic aorta. They empty into the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left.
clinical: They are small and seldom of direct clinical importance, but contribute to azygos collateral flow.

{S} first posterior intercostal artery.name: First posterior intercostal artery
{S} first posterior intercostal artery.desc: A branch of the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk, not the aorta. It runs in the first intercostal space, supplying the intercostal muscles, rib and adjacent back structures, and gives a dorsal branch.
clinical: Its origin from the subclavian system rather than the aorta matters when planning embolization or aortic surgery.

{S} inferior phrenic artery.name: Inferior phrenic artery
{S} inferior phrenic artery.desc: Usually the first branch of the abdominal aorta (sometimes from the celiac trunk), arising just below the aortic hiatus. It runs up and outward across the crus to supply the abdominal surface of the diaphragm and gives superior suprarenal arteries to the adrenal gland.
clinical: It can feed liver tumors that reach the bare area, and may need embolizing during liver cancer treatment.

{S} internal thoracic vein.name: Internal thoracic vein
