{S} internal thoracic vein.desc: Accompanies the internal thoracic artery behind the costal cartilages, just lateral to the sternum. It is formed by the musculophrenic and superior epigastric veins, receives the anterior intercostal veins, and ends in the brachiocephalic vein.
clinical: It forms a collateral pathway between the SVC and IVC systems via the epigastric veins.
Its artery partner is the vessel most used for coronary bypass grafting.

{S} lateral thoracic vein.name: Lateral thoracic vein
{S} lateral thoracic vein.desc: Runs down the lateral chest wall with the lateral thoracic artery on serratus anterior, draining the lateral thoracic wall. It ends in the axillary vein and connects below with the superficial epigastric vein through the thoracoepigastric vein.
clinical: When the IVC is blocked, these connections enlarge and appear as visible veins on the side of the trunk.

{S} musculophrenic artery.name: Musculophrenic artery
{S} musculophrenic artery.region: Anterior chest wall and costal margin
{S} musculophrenic artery.desc: A terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, arising around the sixth intercostal space. It runs along the costal margin behind the costal cartilages, supplying the anterior intercostal spaces 7 to 9, the diaphragm and upper abdominal wall muscles.
clinical: It can be injured by drains or needles placed close to the costal margin.

{S} musculophrenic vein.name: Musculophrenic vein
{S} musculophrenic vein.region: Anterior chest wall and costal margin
{S} musculophrenic vein.desc: Accompanies the musculophrenic artery along the costal margin, draining the lower anterior intercostal spaces and the diaphragm. It joins the superior epigastric vein to form the internal thoracic vein. It also receives small veins from the diaphragm.
clinical: It is part of the anterior collateral route between superior and inferior venae cavae.

{S} second posterior intercostal artery.name: Second posterior intercostal artery
{S} second posterior intercostal artery.desc: Arises from the superior intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk and runs in the second intercostal space in the costal groove. It supplies intercostal muscles, the rib, skin and back muscles and gives a spinal branch.
clinical: Like the first, its subclavian-system origin matters in thoracic vascular procedures.

{S} subcostal artery.name: Subcostal artery
{S} subcostal artery.region: Posterior abdominal wall, below the 12th rib
{S} subcostal artery.desc: The last paired branch of the thoracic aorta, running below the twelfth rib with the subcostal vein and nerve. It passes behind the kidney region and supplies the upper abdominal wall muscles and skin, with a dorsal branch to the back.
clinical: It and the subcostal nerve lie in the path of flank incisions to the kidney.

{S} subcostal vein.name: Subcostal vein
{S} subcostal vein.region: Posterior abdominal wall, below the 12th rib
{S} subcostal vein.desc: Runs below the twelfth rib with the subcostal artery and nerve. On the right it joins the ascending lumbar vein to help form the azygos vein; on the left it helps form the hemiazygos vein.
clinical: It is part of the azygos-lumbar collateral network around a blocked IVC.

{S} superior intercostal artery.name: Superior intercostal artery
{S} superior intercostal artery.region: Thoracic inlet, first two intercostal spaces
{S} superior intercostal artery.desc: A branch of the costocervical trunk that descends in front of the necks of the first and second ribs. It gives the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. It also gives small branches to the deep back muscles and spinal canal.
clinical: It explains why the top two intercostal arteries do not arise from the aorta, a frequent exam point.

{S} superior intercostal vein.name: Superior intercostal vein
{S} superior intercostal vein.desc: Drains the second and third (sometimes fourth) intercostal spaces. The right vein ends in the azygos vein. The left crosses the aortic arch, passing between the phrenic and vagus nerves, to end in the left brachiocephalic vein.
clinical: On a frontal chest X-ray the left vein can appear as a small normal bump beside the aortic knob.

anterior temporal branch of {S} lateral.name: Anterior temporal branch of the {S} lateral occipital artery
anterior temporal branch of {S} lateral.desc: A cortical branch of the lateral occipital artery, itself a terminal division of the posterior cerebral artery. It runs forward on the underside of the temporal lobe, supplying the anterior inferior temporal surface including parts of the parahippocampal and fusiform gyri.
clinical: Ischemia of inferior temporal cortex can contribute to memory problems when bilateral.

middle temporal branch of {S} lateral oc.name: Middle temporal branch of the {S} lateral occipital artery
middle temporal branch of {S} lateral oc.desc: A cortical branch of the lateral occipital artery (posterior cerebral artery territory) supplying the middle part of the inferior temporal surface, including the fusiform region. It lies between the anterior and posterior temporal branches of the same artery.
clinical: Inferior temporal-occipital infarcts can impair face or object recognition.

set of posterior temporal branches of la.name: Posterior temporal branches of the lateral occipital artery
set of posterior temporal branches of la.desc: Cortical branches of the lateral occipital artery, from the posterior cerebral artery, that supply the posterior inferior temporal lobe and adjoining occipitotemporal (fusiform) cortex. They anastomose with temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery on the lateral surface.
clinical: Damage to the fusiform region, especially on the right, can cause prosopagnosia, an inability to recognize faces.

{S} anterior temporal artery.name: Anterior temporal artery
{S} anterior temporal artery.desc: An early cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs out of the lateral sulcus over the front of the lateral temporal lobe, supplying the anterior superior, middle and inferior temporal gyri.
clinical: Anterior temporal cortex is often involved in temporal lobe epilepsy surgery, where these vessels are preserved or divided deliberately.

{S} costocervical trunk.name: Costocervical trunk
{S} costocervical trunk.desc: A short branch of the subclavian artery, usually from its second part behind anterior scalene (or first part on the left). It arches back over the dome of the pleura and divides into the deep cervical artery and the superior intercostal artery.
clinical: It sits over the lung apex, so apical tumors and procedures in this area can involve it.

{S} deep cervical artery.name: Deep cervical artery
{S} deep cervical artery.desc: A branch of the costocervical trunk that passes back between the transverse process of C7 and the neck of the first rib, then ascends between semispinalis capitis and cervicis. It supplies deep posterior neck muscles and anastomoses with the occipital and vertebral arteries.
clinical: It is a collateral route to the vertebral artery territory when the vertebral artery is blocked.

{S} inferior thyroid artery.name: Inferior thyroid artery
{S} inferior thyroid artery.desc: The main branch of the thyrocervical trunk. It ascends along the medial border of anterior scalene, arches medially behind the carotid sheath, and reaches the back of the thyroid gland, supplying the lower thyroid, the parathyroid glands, larynx, trachea and esophagus. It is closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: The recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses close to it, so it is at risk during thyroidectomy, causing hoarseness.
It is usually the main blood supply of the parathyroid glands.

{S} lateral occipital artery.name: Lateral occipital artery
{S} lateral occipital artery.region: Brain: inferior temporal and occipital lobes
{S} lateral occipital artery.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the posterior cerebral artery. It runs laterally on the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes, giving anterior, middle and posterior temporal branches that supply the inferior temporal and occipitotemporal cortex.
clinical: Its territory includes face- and color-processing cortex; infarcts can cause prosopagnosia or achromatopsia.

{S} medial occipital artery.name: Medial occipital artery
{S} medial occipital artery.desc: The other terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It runs on the medial occipital surface and gives the calcarine artery to the primary visual cortex, the parieto-occipital branch, and a dorsal branch to the corpus callosum splenium.
clinical: Occlusion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often sparing the macula thanks to MCA collaterals.

{S} polar temporal artery.name: Polar temporal artery
{S} polar temporal artery.desc: A cortical branch, usually of the early middle cerebral artery, that supplies the temporal pole at the front tip of the temporal lobe. It may also arise from the anterior temporal artery, and it anastomoses with neighbouring temporal branches.
clinical: The temporal pole is removed in standard anterior temporal lobectomy for epilepsy.

{S} superficial cervical artery.name: Superficial cervical artery
{S} superficial cervical artery.desc: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk (or the superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery, depending on the description). It crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius and nearby muscles, running with the accessory nerve region.
clinical: The pattern of these neck branches varies a lot between people, so surgeons identify them individually.

{S} thyrocervical trunk.name: Thyrocervical trunk
{S} thyrocervical trunk.desc: A short branch from the first part of the subclavian artery, at the medial border of anterior scalene. It gives the inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries (or superficial cervical and dorsal scapular, depending on pattern), and the ascending cervical artery via the inferior thyroid.
clinical: Its branches form collaterals around the scapula that help perfuse the arm if the subclavian or axillary artery narrows.

{S} transverse cervical artery.name: Transverse cervical artery
{S} transverse cervical artery.desc: Usually a branch of the thyrocervical trunk that runs laterally across the anterior scalene and phrenic nerve, then through the posterior triangle. It supplies trapezius and, through a deep branch (often the dorsal scapular artery), levator scapulae and the rhomboids.
clinical: It is a useful recipient vessel for free flaps in head and neck reconstruction.

anterior inferior segmental tributary of.name: Anterior inferior segmental tributary of the middle hepatic vein
anterior inferior segmental tributary of.desc: A segmental vein draining the right anterior inferior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment V, into the middle hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Preserving this drainage is important in living-donor liver transplant, where the middle hepatic vein's fate is a key surgical decision.

anterior superior segmental tributary of.name: Anterior superior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
anterior superior segmental tributary of.desc: A segmental vein draining the right anterior superior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment VIII, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Segment VIII lies high under the diaphragm, making its veins important landmarks in resections near the hepatic vein confluence.

lateral inferior segmental tributary of.name: Lateral inferior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
lateral inferior segmental tributary of.desc: A segmental vein draining the left lateral inferior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment III, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Segments II and III are the left lateral section used in pediatric living-donor liver transplantation.

lateral superior segmental tributary of.name: Lateral superior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
lateral superior segmental tributary of.desc: A segmental vein draining the left lateral superior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment II, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Its outflow must be kept intact when the left lateral section is used as a graft.

medial inferior segmental tributary of m.name: Medial inferior segmental tributary of the middle hepatic vein
medial inferior segmental tributary of m.desc: A segmental vein draining the left medial inferior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment IVb, into the middle hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Segment IVb lies next to the gallbladder bed and can be involved in extended resections for gallbladder cancer.

medial superior segmental tributary of {.name: Medial superior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
medial superior segmental tributary of {.desc: A segmental vein draining the left medial superior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment IVa, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Drainage of segment IV varies between left and middle hepatic veins, so surgeons map it on imaging before resection.

posterior inferior segmental tributary o.name: Posterior inferior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
posterior inferior segmental tributary o.desc: A segmental vein draining the right posterior inferior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment VI, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: An accessory inferior right hepatic vein draining segment VI directly into the IVC is common and must be ligated or preserved in surgery.

posterior superior segmental tributary o.name: Posterior superior segmental tributary of the {S} hepatic vein
posterior superior segmental tributary o.desc: A segmental vein draining the right posterior superior part of the liver, roughly corresponding to Couinaud segment VII, into the hepatic vein. Hepatic venous tributaries run between the portal segments rather than with the portal triads, so they mark segment boundaries rather than segment centres.
clinical: Segment VII sits deep under the right diaphragm, making its veins hard to reach in laparoscopic resection.

tributary of middle hepatic vein.name: Tributary of the middle hepatic vein
tributary of middle hepatic vein.desc: A smaller vein draining liver tissue on either side of the main portal fissure (Cantlie's line) into the middle hepatic vein, which runs in the plane dividing the functional right and left halves of the liver.
clinical: Tributaries of the middle hepatic vein are carefully handled when splitting a liver for transplantation.

middle hepatic vein.name: Middle hepatic vein
middle hepatic vein.desc: Runs in the main portal fissure (Cantlie's line) between the functional right and left liver, draining segment IV and segments V and VIII. It usually joins the left hepatic vein in a common trunk before entering the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
clinical: It marks the plane of a standard right or left hemihepatectomy.
Hepatic vein blockage (Budd-Chiari syndrome) causes painful liver enlargement and ascites.

{S} hepatic vein.name: Hepatic vein
{S} hepatic vein.desc: The hepatic veins drain all the liver's blood into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. The right hepatic vein runs in the right portal fissure between the anterior and posterior right sections, draining segments V to VIII. The left hepatic vein runs in the left fissure and drains segments II and III, often joining the middle hepatic vein.
clinical: Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, causing liver enlargement and ascites.
The veins have no valves and short extrahepatic course, making them dangerous to injure in trauma.

{S} renal vein.name: Renal vein
{S} renal vein.desc: Drains each kidney into the inferior vena cava, lying in front of the renal artery at the hilum. The left renal vein is longer, crossing in front of the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery origin, and receives the left suprarenal and left inferior phrenic veins; the right is short and receives few tributaries.
clinical: The left renal vein can be squeezed between the aorta and SMA (nutcracker syndrome), causing blood in the urine.
Kidney cancer can grow into the renal vein and up the IVC.

{S} suprarenal vein.name: Suprarenal vein
{S} suprarenal vein.desc: A single main vein leaving the hilum of each adrenal gland. The right is very short and drains directly into the back of the inferior vena cava; the left is longer and drains into the left renal vein, often joined by the left inferior phrenic vein.
clinical: Adrenal vein sampling, used to locate aldosterone-producing tumors, is technically hardest on the right because the vein is so short.
The short right vein is easily torn during adrenalectomy.

plantar metatarsal vein.name: Plantar metatarsal veins
plantar metatarsal vein.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
plantar metatarsal vein.desc: Deep veins running between the metatarsal bones on the sole, accompanying the plantar metatarsal arteries. They drain the deep sole and toes into the deep plantar venous arch and connect with dorsal veins through perforating veins.
clinical: Compression of plantar veins with each step helps pump blood up the leg, part of the foot venous pump.

plantar venous arch of {S} foot.name: Plantar venous arch of the {S} foot
plantar venous arch of {S} foot.desc: A deep venous arch accompanying the plantar arterial arch across the bases of the metatarsals. It receives the plantar metatarsal veins and drains into the medial and lateral plantar veins, which form the posterior tibial veins behind the medial malleolus.
clinical: The plantar venous plexus acts as a foot pump; intermittent foot compression devices exploit it to prevent DVT.

set of calcaneal branches of posterior t.name: Calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery
set of calcaneal branches of posterior t.desc: Small branches of the posterior tibial artery arising near the medial malleolus. They pierce the flexor retinaculum to supply the skin, fat pad and periosteum on the medial and plantar heel, anastomosing with calcaneal branches of the fibular artery.
clinical: Heel blood supply matters for healing of heel pressure ulcers and surgical incisions around the calcaneus.

tributary of plantar venous arch.name: Tributary of the plantar venous arch
tributary of plantar venous arch.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
tributary of plantar venous arch.desc: A small vein from the deep tissues of the sole and toes that drains into the plantar venous arch, from which blood passes to the plantar and then posterior tibial veins.
clinical: These veins fill and empty with each step, contributing to venous return from the foot.

{S} anterior tibial artery.name: Anterior tibial artery
{S} anterior tibial artery.desc: A terminal branch of the popliteal artery at the lower border of popliteus. It passes forward above the interosseous membrane and descends on it with the deep fibular nerve, between tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus. It supplies the anterior compartment and, at the ankle, continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.
clinical: It is compressed in anterior compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency.
It may be injured in tibial fractures or high fibular surgery.

{S} anterior tibial vein.name: Anterior tibial vein
{S} anterior tibial vein.desc: Paired deep veins accompanying the anterior tibial artery. They continue up from the dorsalis pedis veins, pass back through the top of the interosseous membrane, and join the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.
clinical: Calf deep vein thrombosis can involve the tibial veins and may extend upward.

{S} arcuate artery.name: Arcuate artery
{S} arcuate artery.region: Lower limb: dorsum of the foot
{S} arcuate artery.desc: A branch of the dorsalis pedis artery that arches laterally across the bases of the metatarsals beneath the extensor tendons. It gives the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries, which supply the toes.
clinical: It is inconsistent and often small, so dorsal foot perfusion frequently relies on other branches.

{S} deep plantar artery.name: Deep plantar artery
{S} deep plantar artery.region: Lower limb: foot, first intermetatarsal space
{S} deep plantar artery.desc: A terminal branch of the dorsalis pedis artery that dives down between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle into the sole. There it joins the lateral plantar artery to complete the deep plantar arch.
clinical: It links the dorsal and plantar circulations, so the foot may stay perfused if one tibial artery is blocked.

{S} descending genicular artery.name: Descending genicular artery
{S} descending genicular artery.region: Lower limb: medial thigh and knee
{S} descending genicular artery.desc: The last branch of the femoral artery, arising in the adductor canal just before the adductor hiatus. It gives a saphenous branch that travels with the saphenous nerve and articular branches that join the genicular anastomosis around the knee.
clinical: It is the pedicle of the medial femoral condyle flap, used to graft bone in nonunions.
Its saphenous branch can be injured during medial knee approaches.

{S} dorsalis pedis artery.name: Dorsalis pedis artery
{S} dorsalis pedis artery.region: Lower limb: dorsum of the foot
{S} dorsalis pedis artery.desc: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery in front of the ankle, between the tendons of extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus. It runs to the first intermetatarsal space, giving tarsal and arcuate branches, and ends as the first dorsal metatarsal and deep plantar arteries.
clinical: Its pulse, felt lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, is checked to assess foot circulation in peripheral arterial disease.
It is absent or very small in a few percent of healthy people.

{S} fibular vein.name: Fibular vein
{S} fibular vein.desc: Paired deep veins (venae comitantes) that run alongside the fibular (peroneal) artery close to the fibula, deep to flexor hallucis longus. They drain the lateral and deep posterior compartments of the leg and join the posterior tibial veins just below the knee to help form the popliteal vein.
clinical: Fibular veins are a common site of calf deep vein thrombosis, best seen on compression ultrasound.

{S} genicular vein.name: Genicular vein
{S} genicular vein.desc: Small veins that accompany the genicular arteries around the knee joint. They drain the joint capsule, the ends of the femur and tibia and the surrounding soft tissue, emptying into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
clinical: Genicular veins are part of the rich vascular network that makes the knee bleed readily after trauma or surgery.

{S} inferior lateral genicular artery.name: Inferior lateral genicular artery
{S} inferior lateral genicular artery.desc: A branch of the popliteal artery that runs laterally above the head of the fibula, deep to the lateral collateral ligament. It supplies the lateral side of the knee joint and joins the genicular anastomosis around the patella.
clinical: It lies close to the lateral meniscus and can be injured during lateral meniscus repair or arthroscopic lateral release.

{S} inferior medial genicular artery.name: Inferior medial genicular artery
{S} inferior medial genicular artery.desc: A branch of the popliteal artery that passes medially below the medial tibial condyle, deep to the medial collateral ligament. It supplies the medial knee joint and upper tibia and contributes to the genicular anastomosis.
clinical: The genicular arteries can be targeted by embolization to treat recurrent bleeding into the knee joint after knee replacement.

{S} lateral plantar artery.name: Lateral plantar artery
{S} lateral plantar artery.desc: The larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery, arising deep to the flexor retinaculum. It runs laterally across the sole between flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae, then curves medially to form the deep plantar arch with the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. It supplies most of the sole and toes.
clinical: Injury to the lateral plantar artery, such as from a puncture wound, can bleed heavily because of its connection to the plantar arch.

{S} lateral superior genicular artery.name: Superior lateral genicular artery
{S} lateral superior genicular artery.desc: A branch of the popliteal artery that winds around the femur just above the lateral femoral condyle, deep to biceps femoris tendon. It supplies the lower femur, the lateral knee joint and the vastus lateralis region, and joins the genicular anastomosis.
clinical: It is often cut during lateral retinacular release, a known cause of bleeding into the knee afterward.

{S} lateral tarsal artery.name: Lateral tarsal artery
{S} lateral tarsal artery.desc: A branch of the dorsalis pedis artery that arises over the navicular bone and runs laterally deep to extensor digitorum brevis. It supplies that muscle and the tarsal bones and joints, and anastomoses with the arcuate artery and branches of the fibular artery.
clinical: It is part of the dorsal foot anastomosis that keeps the foot perfused when one artery is blocked.

{S} medial plantar artery.name: Medial plantar artery
{S} medial plantar artery.desc: The smaller terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery, arising under the flexor retinaculum. It runs forward along the medial sole between abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis, supplying those muscles and the skin of the medial sole and big toe.
clinical: The medial plantar artery supplies the medial plantar flap, used by surgeons to rebuild weight-bearing heel skin.

{S} medial superior genicular artery.name: Superior medial genicular artery
{S} medial superior genicular artery.desc: A branch of the popliteal artery that curves around the femur above the medial femoral condyle, deep to the hamstring tendons. It supplies the lower femur, medial knee joint and vastus medialis, and joins the genicular anastomosis.
clinical: It is a target of genicular artery embolization, an emerging treatment for knee osteoarthritis pain.

{S} middle genicular artery.name: Middle genicular artery
{S} middle genicular artery.desc: A small branch from the front of the popliteal artery that pierces the oblique popliteal ligament to enter the knee joint. It supplies the cruciate ligaments, the synovial membrane and the posterior joint capsule.
clinical: It is the main blood supply of the cruciate ligaments, relevant to how ACL grafts revascularize after reconstruction.

{S} plantar arch.name: Deep plantar arch
{S} plantar arch.desc: An arterial arch in the deep sole, formed mainly by the lateral plantar artery and completed by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. It lies across the bases of the metatarsals and gives off plantar metatarsal arteries that supply the toes.
clinical: Because it links the anterior and posterior tibial circulations, the foot can survive blockage of one of them.

{S} popliteal artery.name: Popliteal artery
{S} popliteal artery.region: Lower limb: popliteal fossa (back of knee)
{S} popliteal artery.desc: The continuation of the femoral artery after it passes through the adductor hiatus. It is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, lying on the femur and knee capsule, and gives the genicular arteries before dividing at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
clinical: Knee dislocation can tear the popliteal artery, so pulses and ankle-brachial index must always be checked.
Popliteal artery aneurysm is the commonest peripheral aneurysm and can clot and threaten the leg.

{S} popliteal vein.name: Popliteal vein
{S} popliteal vein.region: Lower limb: popliteal fossa (back of knee)
{S} popliteal vein.desc: Formed at the lower border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It ascends through the popliteal fossa between the popliteal artery and tibial nerve, receives the small saphenous vein, and becomes the femoral vein at the adductor hiatus.
clinical: Popliteal vein thrombosis is a proximal DVT with a higher risk of pulmonary embolism than isolated calf clots.

{S} posterior tibial artery.name: Posterior tibial artery
{S} posterior tibial artery.region: Lower limb: posterior leg and medial ankle
{S} posterior tibial artery.desc: A terminal branch of the popliteal artery that descends in the deep posterior compartment of the leg with the tibial nerve. It gives off the fibular artery, passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, and divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
clinical: Its pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus and is a key check in peripheral arterial disease.

{S} posterior tibial vein.name: Posterior tibial vein
{S} posterior tibial vein.desc: Paired venae comitantes of the posterior tibial artery, formed behind the medial malleolus from the plantar veins. They drain the sole and deep posterior compartment, receive the fibular veins, and join the anterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.
clinical: Calf deep vein thrombosis often starts in the posterior tibial veins or soleal sinuses.

{S} superficial medial plantar artery.name: Superficial branch of the medial plantar artery
{S} superficial medial plantar artery.desc: The superficial branch of the medial plantar artery that runs along the medial side of the sole and big toe. It supplies the skin and abductor hallucis region along the medial border of the foot.
clinical: It helps perfuse the skin of the medial arch, often used for small local flaps in foot reconstruction.

artery of central sulcus.name: Artery of the central sulcus
artery of central sulcus.desc: A cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) that climbs out of the lateral sulcus and runs in the central sulcus. It supplies the adjacent precentral (primary motor) and postcentral (primary sensory) gyri, mainly the face and arm areas.
clinical: Occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness and numbness, sparing the leg, which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

artery of {S} postcentral sulcus.name: Artery of the {S} postcentral sulcus
artery of {S} postcentral sulcus.desc: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs up the postcentral sulcus. It supplies the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) and the adjacent anterior parietal lobe on the lateral surface.
clinical: Infarction in its territory causes contralateral loss of touch and position sense, mostly in the face and arm.

artery of {S} precentral sulcus.name: Artery of the {S} precentral sulcus
artery of {S} precentral sulcus.desc: A cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery that runs in the precentral sulcus. It supplies the posterior middle and inferior frontal gyri, including premotor cortex and the frontal eye field, and the front of the precentral gyrus.
clinical: Ischemia here can cause contralateral weakness and gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion.

distal perforating artery.name: Distal perforating artery
distal perforating artery.desc: The lowest of the perforating arteries of the thigh, usually regarded as the terminal branch of the deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery. It pierces adductor magnus near the femur to reach the posterior compartment, supplying the hamstrings and anastomosing with branches of the popliteal artery.
clinical: Perforating arteries hug the back of the femur and can bleed significantly in femoral shaft fractures or femoral surgery.

dorsal venous arch of {S} foot.name: Dorsal venous arch of the {S} foot
dorsal venous arch of {S} foot.desc: A superficial venous arch across the top of the foot over the metatarsal heads, formed by the dorsal digital and metatarsal veins. Its medial end continues as the great saphenous vein and its lateral end as the small saphenous vein.
clinical: These veins are visible through the skin and are a backup site for intravenous access when arm veins are unusable.

dorsal venous network of {S} hand.name: Dorsal venous network of the {S} hand
dorsal venous network of {S} hand.desc: A superficial network of veins on the back of the hand formed by the dorsal metacarpal veins. Its radial (thumb) side drains into the cephalic vein and its ulnar side into the basilic vein, collecting blood from the fingers and hand.
clinical: It is one of the most common sites for inserting intravenous cannulas.

precuneal branch of {S} pericallosal art.name: Precuneal branch of the {S} pericallosal artery
precuneal branch of {S} pericallosal art.desc: A cortical branch from the distal pericallosal artery (anterior cerebral artery territory) that runs onto the medial surface of the parietal lobe. It supplies the precuneus, a region involved in visuospatial processing, self-referential thought and the default mode network.
clinical: Distal anterior cerebral artery infarcts involving this branch can affect medial parietal functions alongside contralateral leg weakness.

set of perforating arteries.name: Perforating arteries of the thigh
set of perforating arteries.desc: Usually three or four branches of the deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery that wind around the back of the femur, piercing adductor magnus close to the bone. They supply the adductors, hamstrings and vastus lateralis, give nutrient arteries to the femur, and link into an anastomotic chain down the thigh.
clinical: They are a major source of bleeding in femoral shaft fractures and posterior thigh surgery.

set of perforating veins.name: Perforating veins
set of perforating veins.desc: Short veins that pierce the deep fascia to connect the superficial veins (great and small saphenous systems) with the deep veins of the limb. Their valves normally let blood flow only from superficial to deep, so the calf muscle pump can push it back toward the heart.
clinical: Incompetent perforator valves let blood reflux outward, contributing to varicose veins and venous leg ulcers near the ankle.

sigmoid vein.name: Sigmoid vein
sigmoid vein.desc: Several veins that drain the sigmoid colon and run in the sigmoid mesocolon alongside the sigmoid arteries. They empty into the inferior mesenteric vein, which carries blood toward the splenic vein and then the hepatic portal vein.
clinical: Blood from the sigmoid colon passes through the liver first, so colon cancer often spreads to the liver via this portal route.

superior rectal vein.name: Superior rectal vein
superior rectal vein.desc: The vein draining the upper rectum, running in the mesorectum with the superior rectal artery and continuing upward as the inferior mesenteric vein, part of the portal system. Its tributaries anastomose with the middle and inferior rectal veins, which drain to the systemic (caval) circulation.
clinical: This portal-to-systemic link can form rectal varices in portal hypertension.

tendinous arch of levator ani.name: Tendinous arch of levator ani
tendinous arch of levator ani.desc: A thickened band of the obturator internus fascia that runs along the side wall of the pelvis from the back of the pubic bone to the ischial spine. It is a fascial structure, not a vessel, and serves as the origin of the iliococcygeus part of levator ani, anchoring the pelvic floor to the pelvic wall.
clinical: Detachment or weakening of this attachment reduces pelvic floor support and can contribute to bladder descent and incontinence.

{S} anterior parietal artery.name: Anterior parietal artery
{S} anterior parietal artery.desc: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs near the postcentral sulcus. It supplies the postcentral gyrus and anterior part of the parietal lobe, including somatosensory cortex for the face and arm.
clinical: Its occlusion causes contralateral sensory loss of the face and arm, and on the nondominant side can contribute to neglect.

{S} anterior spinal artery.name: Anterior spinal artery (vertebral root)
{S} anterior spinal artery.desc: A small branch from each vertebral artery near the medulla; the two join to form a single anterior spinal artery in the anterior median fissure of the cord. It supplies the medial medulla and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, reinforced lower down by segmental radicular arteries such as the artery of Adamkiewicz.
clinical: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causes paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, with vibration and position sense spared.

{S} arteria princeps pollicis.name: Princeps pollicis artery
{S} arteria princeps pollicis.desc: A branch of the radial artery that arises deep in the palm as the radial artery turns medially to form the deep palmar arch. It runs along the first metacarpal under flexor pollicis longus tendon and splits into two branches supplying both sides of the thumb.
clinical: It is at risk during thumb base surgery and is important when replanting an amputated thumb.

{S} gastro-epiploic artery.name: Gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery
{S} gastro-epiploic artery.desc: The right gastroepiploic artery comes from the gastroduodenal artery and the left from the splenic artery; they run along the greater curvature of the stomach within the greater omentum and join each other. They supply the greater curvature of the stomach and the greater omentum.
clinical: The right gastroepiploic artery can be used as an arterial graft in coronary artery bypass surgery.

{S} gastroepiploic vein.name: Gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) vein
{S} gastroepiploic vein.desc: Veins running along the greater curvature of the stomach with the gastroepiploic arteries. The right gastroepiploic vein drains into the superior mesenteric vein and the left into the splenic vein, both part of the hepatic portal system.
clinical: In portal hypertension these veins can enlarge as collaterals around the stomach.

{S} pericallosal artery.name: Pericallosal artery
{S} pericallosal artery.region: Brain: medial hemisphere, above the corpus callosum
{S} pericallosal artery.desc: The continuation of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) that runs backward in the callosal sulcus over the corpus callosum. It supplies the corpus callosum and, with the callosomarginal artery, the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex.
clinical: Distal ACA aneurysms classically occur where the pericallosal artery curves around the genu of the corpus callosum.
Its occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss.

{S} posterior parietal artery.name: Posterior parietal artery
{S} posterior parietal artery.desc: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery, usually from its inferior division, that supplies the posterior parietal lobe, including the supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule. These areas integrate sensory and spatial information.
clinical: Infarction on the dominant side can cause problems with language and calculation; on the nondominant side, hemispatial neglect.

{S} prefrontal artery.name: Prefrontal artery
{S} prefrontal artery.desc: A cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery that fans out over the lateral frontal lobe. It supplies the middle and inferior frontal gyri, including parts of Broca area on the dominant side.
clinical: Occlusion on the dominant side can cause expressive (Broca) aphasia with relatively preserved comprehension.

{S} splenial artery.name: Splenial artery
{S} splenial artery.region: Brain: medial hemisphere, posterior corpus callosum
{S} splenial artery.desc: A small artery, usually from the posterior cerebral artery or its parieto-occipital branch, that curves over the splenium of the corpus callosum. It supplies the splenium and anastomoses with the pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral artery.
clinical: This ACA-PCA anastomosis can provide collateral flow over the corpus callosum when one territory is blocked.

{S} subclavian vein.name: Subclavian vein
{S} subclavian vein.region: Root of neck and upper thorax
{S} subclavian vein.desc: The continuation of the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib. It arches over the first rib in front of anterior scalene, separated from the subclavian artery by that muscle, then joins the internal jugular vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein.
clinical: It is a standard site for central venous catheters; pneumothorax is a key complication.
Effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome) is clotting caused by compression at the thoracic outlet.

{S} thoracodorsal artery.name: Thoracodorsal artery
{S} thoracodorsal artery.region: Upper limb: posterior axilla and lateral chest wall
{S} thoracodorsal artery.desc: The continuation of the subscapular artery after it gives off the circumflex scapular artery. It runs down the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal nerve and supplies latissimus dorsi and nearby serratus anterior.
clinical: It is the pedicle of the latissimus dorsi flap, widely used in reconstructive surgery.

{S} thoracodorsal vein.name: Thoracodorsal vein
{S} thoracodorsal vein.region: Upper limb: posterior axilla and lateral chest wall
{S} thoracodorsal vein.desc: The vein accompanying the thoracodorsal artery and nerve on the posterior wall of the axilla. It drains latissimus dorsi and adjacent chest wall and empties into the subscapular vein, a tributary of the axillary vein.
clinical: It is preserved with the artery as the drainage of latissimus dorsi flaps and is a landmark in axillary surgery.

ascending lumbar vein.name: Ascending lumbar vein
ascending lumbar vein.desc: A longitudinal vein running up the posterior abdominal wall, behind psoas major and in front of the lumbar transverse processes. It links the common iliac vein with the lumbar veins and continues up as the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left.
clinical: It forms a key collateral route back to the heart when the inferior vena cava is blocked.

common iliac artery.name: Common iliac artery
common iliac artery.desc: The two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, formed at the aortic bifurcation at about L4. Each runs down and laterally along psoas major and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint into the external iliac artery (to the lower limb) and the internal iliac artery (to the pelvis and buttock).
clinical: Aortic aneurysms often extend into the common iliac arteries, affecting endovascular repair planning.

descending branch of {S} lateral circumf.name: Descending branch of the {S} lateral circumflex femoral artery
descending branch of {S} lateral circumf.desc: A long branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery that runs down the thigh deep to rectus femoris, along the anterior border of vastus lateralis with the nerve to that muscle. It supplies vastus lateralis and the overlying skin and joins the genicular anastomosis at the knee.
clinical: It is the pedicle of the anterolateral thigh (ALT) flap, a workhorse flap in reconstructive surgery.

lumbar artery.name: Lumbar artery
lumbar artery.desc: Usually four pairs of arteries that arise from the back of the abdominal aorta opposite the upper four lumbar vertebrae. They wind around the vertebral bodies deep to psoas and supply the posterior abdominal wall, back muscles, lumbar vertebrae and, through spinal branches, the cauda equina and meninges.
clinical: They can bleed during lumbar spine surgery and can feed a type II endoleak after aortic aneurysm stenting.

lumbar vein.name: Lumbar vein
lumbar vein.desc: Paired segmental veins that accompany the lumbar arteries and drain the posterior abdominal wall, back muscles and vertebral venous plexuses. They drain into the inferior vena cava and are connected vertically by the ascending lumbar veins.
clinical: Through links with the vertebral venous plexus, they offer a route for cancer spread to the spine.

median sacral vein.name: Median sacral vein
median sacral vein.desc: A single vein running up the midline on the front of the sacrum and coccyx, accompanying the median sacral artery. It drains the sacrum and joins the presacral venous plexus, usually emptying into the left common iliac vein.
clinical: Presacral veins can bleed heavily and are hard to control during rectal or anterior spine surgery.

{S} ascending lumbar vein.name: Ascending lumbar vein
{S} ascending lumbar vein.desc: A vertical vein on each side behind psoas major that connects the common iliac vein and the lumbar veins. The right one continues upward as the azygos vein and the left as the hemiazygos vein, linking the inferior and superior vena cava systems.
clinical: When the inferior vena cava is obstructed, the ascending lumbar veins enlarge to carry blood to the azygos system.

{S} common iliac artery.name: Common iliac artery
{S} common iliac artery.desc: A terminal branch of the abdominal aorta, beginning at the aortic bifurcation at about L4. It runs inferolaterally along psoas major and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint into the external and internal iliac arteries. The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein.
clinical: Atherosclerotic narrowing here causes buttock and thigh claudication.

{S} common iliac vein.name: Common iliac vein
{S} common iliac vein.desc: Formed in front of the sacroiliac joint by the union of the external and internal iliac veins. The two common iliac veins ascend and join at about L5, to the right of the midline, to form the inferior vena cava. The left vein is longer and passes behind the right common iliac artery.
clinical: In May-Thurner syndrome, the right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein, predisposing to left leg DVT.

{S} deep femoral vein.name: Deep femoral vein
{S} deep femoral vein.desc: The vein accompanying the deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery, lying in front of it. It receives the perforating and circumflex femoral veins draining the thigh muscles and joins the femoral vein just below the inguinal ligament to form the common femoral vein.
clinical: Deep vein thrombosis can involve the deep femoral vein, extending into the common femoral vein.

{S} external iliac artery.name: External iliac artery
{S} external iliac artery.region: Pelvis: pelvic brim and iliac fossa
{S} external iliac artery.desc: Arising from the common iliac artery in front of the sacroiliac joint, it runs along the medial border of psoas major. Just above the inguinal ligament it gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, then passes under the ligament at the mid-inguinal point to become the femoral artery.
clinical: It is used as an access route for large catheters and as the inflow vessel for kidney transplants.

{S} external iliac vein.name: External iliac vein
{S} external iliac vein.region: Pelvis: pelvic brim and iliac fossa
{S} external iliac vein.desc: The upward continuation of the femoral vein behind the inguinal ligament. It runs along the pelvic brim medial to the external iliac artery, receives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins, and joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.
clinical: A transplanted kidney's vein is usually joined to the external iliac vein.

{S} femoral vein.name: Femoral vein
{S} femoral vein.region: Lower limb: thigh and femoral triangle
{S} femoral vein.desc: The continuation of the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus. It ascends through the adductor canal and femoral triangle, lying medial to the femoral artery in the femoral sheath, receives the deep femoral vein and great saphenous vein, and becomes the external iliac vein at the inguinal ligament.
clinical: It is a common site for central venous access, found just medial to the femoral pulse.
Femoral vein DVT carries a high risk of pulmonary embolism.

{S} iliolumbar vein.name: Iliolumbar vein
{S} iliolumbar vein.region: Posterior abdominal wall and iliac fossa
{S} iliolumbar vein.desc: A vein accompanying the iliolumbar artery that drains the iliacus, psoas and quadratus lumborum region and the lower lumbar vertebrae. It usually drains into the common iliac vein, sometimes into the internal iliac vein.
clinical: It must be identified and tied during anterior approaches to the L4-L5 disc to avoid major bleeding.

{S} inferior gluteal vein.name: Inferior gluteal vein
{S} inferior gluteal vein.desc: Paired veins accompanying the inferior gluteal artery. They drain gluteus maximus and the upper back of the thigh, enter the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, and empty into the internal iliac vein.
clinical: They connect thigh veins with pelvic veins, offering a collateral route in iliofemoral venous obstruction.

{S} internal iliac artery.name: Internal iliac artery
{S} internal iliac artery.desc: Arising from the common iliac artery in front of the sacroiliac joint, it descends into the pelvis and splits into anterior and posterior divisions. Its branches supply the pelvic organs, pelvic walls and floor, gluteal region and medial thigh.
clinical: Embolization of internal iliac branches is used to stop life-threatening bleeding from pelvic fractures.

{S} internal iliac vein.name: Internal iliac vein
{S} internal iliac vein.desc: Formed near the greater sciatic foramen by veins that accompany the internal iliac artery branches. It drains the pelvic organs, pelvic walls, gluteal region and medial thigh, and joins the external iliac vein in front of the sacroiliac joint to form the common iliac vein.
clinical: Its tributaries form thin-walled pelvic venous plexuses that bleed heavily in pelvic fractures and are hard to control.

{S} lateral circumflex femoral artery.name: Lateral circumflex femoral artery
{S} lateral circumflex femoral artery.desc: Usually a branch of the deep femoral artery that passes laterally between branches of the femoral nerve, deep to sartorius and rectus femoris. It divides into ascending, transverse and descending branches supplying the hip region, greater trochanter and the quadriceps.
clinical: Its descending branch is the pedicle of the anterolateral thigh flap.

{S} lateral circumflex femoral vein.name: Lateral circumflex femoral vein
{S} lateral circumflex femoral vein.desc: Veins accompanying the lateral circumflex femoral artery and its branches. They drain the quadriceps and lateral hip region and empty into the deep femoral vein or the femoral vein. Like most deep veins of the limbs, they are often paired.
clinical: Its veins drain anterolateral thigh flaps and are joined to recipient veins during flap transfer.

{S} lateral sacral vein.name: Lateral sacral vein
{S} lateral sacral vein.desc: Veins accompanying the lateral sacral arteries on the front of the sacrum, beside the anterior sacral foramina. They form part of the presacral venous plexus, connect with the vertebral venous plexus through the sacral foramina, and drain into the internal iliac vein.
clinical: Presacral plexus bleeding during rectal surgery can be torrential because these veins retract into the sacral foramina.

{S} medial circumflex femoral vein.name: Medial circumflex femoral vein
{S} medial circumflex femoral vein.region: Lower limb: hip and upper medial thigh
{S} medial circumflex femoral vein.desc: Veins accompanying the medial circumflex femoral artery around the back of the femoral neck. They drain the adductor muscles and the hip region and empty into the deep femoral or femoral vein.
clinical: The neighbouring medial circumflex femoral artery is the main blood supply of the femoral head, at risk in displaced hip fractures.

{S} obturator vein.name: Obturator vein
{S} obturator vein.desc: A vein that drains the hip joint region and the adductor muscles of the medial thigh. It enters the pelvis through the obturator canal, runs along the lateral pelvic wall below the obturator nerve and artery, and empties into the internal iliac vein.
clinical: Obturator vessels lie in the dissection field for pelvic lymph node removal and can bleed during it.

{S} small saphenous vein.name: Small saphenous vein
{S} small saphenous vein.desc: A superficial vein that begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot and passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve. It runs up the middle of the back of the calf, pierces the deep fascia and usually drains into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
clinical: Reflux at the saphenopopliteal junction causes varicose veins in the back of the calf.
The sural nerve beside it can be injured during vein treatment.

{S} superior gluteal vein.name: Superior gluteal vein
{S} superior gluteal vein.desc: Paired veins accompanying the superior gluteal artery. They drain gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and the upper buttock, enter the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis, and join the internal iliac vein.
clinical: Superior gluteal vessels can be injured by fractures through the greater sciatic notch or during posterior pelvic surgery.

{S} lateral frontobasal artery.name: Lateral frontobasal (lateral orbitofrontal) artery
{S} lateral frontobasal artery.region: Brain: orbital surface of frontal lobe
{S} lateral frontobasal artery.desc: Usually the first cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery. It runs forward over the lateral orbital surface of the frontal lobe and supplies the lateral orbital gyri and the pars orbitalis of the inferior frontal gyrus.
clinical: Orbitofrontal damage can change personality, impulse control and decision-making while leaving movement intact.

{S} medial frontobasal artery.name: Medial frontobasal (medial orbitofrontal) artery
{S} medial frontobasal artery.region: Brain: orbital surface of frontal lobe
{S} medial frontobasal artery.desc: Usually the first cortical branch of the A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery, just beyond the anterior communicating artery. It runs forward on the underside of the frontal lobe, supplying the gyrus rectus, medial orbital gyri and the olfactory bulb and tract.
clinical: It is a landmark in surgery for anterior communicating artery aneurysms, where the gyrus rectus is sometimes partly removed for access.

anterior part of lateral segmental vein.name: Anterior part of the lateral segmental vein
anterior part of lateral segmental vein.desc: One of the two parts of the lateral segmental vein of the right middle lobe (segment 4). It drains the anterior portion of the lateral segment and joins the posterior part to form the lateral segmental vein, which empties into the middle lobe vein and then the right superior pulmonary vein. It carries oxygenated blood toward the left atrium.
clinical: Like other pulmonary veins it runs between segments, so surgeons use it to find planes during segment resection.

anterior part of {S} apical segmental ve.name: Anterior part of the {S} apical segmental vein
anterior part of {S} apical segmental ve.desc: A tributary of the apical segmental vein of the right upper lobe (segment 1) that drains the front of the apical segment. It joins the other parts of the apical vein, which drains into the upper lobe trunk of the right superior pulmonary vein, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Pulmonary vein branches vary a lot between people, so CT mapping is routine before segmentectomy.

apical part of {S} apical segmental vein.name: Apical part of the {S} apical segmental vein
apical part of {S} apical segmental vein.desc: A tributary of the apical segmental vein of the right upper lobe that drains the very top of the lung (segment 1). It joins the anterior part to form the trunk of the apical vein, which feeds the right superior pulmonary vein and carries oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Tumours at the lung apex (Pancoast tumours) lie in the territory this vein drains.

inferior lingular vein.name: Inferior lingular vein
inferior lingular vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the inferior lingular segment (segment 5) of the left upper lobe. It joins the superior lingular vein to form the lingular vein, which empties into the left superior pulmonary vein and returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: The lingular veins are identified and divided during lingulectomy, a lung-sparing segment resection.

inferior part of medial segmental vein.name: Inferior part of the medial segmental vein
inferior part of medial segmental vein.desc: A tributary draining the lower portion of the medial segment (segment 5) of the right middle lobe. It joins the superior part to form the medial segmental vein, which drains via the middle lobe vein into the right superior pulmonary vein and on to the left atrium.
clinical: The middle lobe vein usually joins the right superior pulmonary vein, which must be preserved when only the upper lobe is removed.

inferior part of {S} anterior segmental.name: Inferior part of the {S} anterior segmental vein
inferior part of {S} anterior segmental.desc: A tributary draining the lower portion of the anterior segment (segment 3) of the right upper lobe. It joins the superior part to form the anterior segmental vein, which empties into the right superior pulmonary vein, carrying oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Segmental veins run in the intersegmental planes, guiding surgeons during anatomical segmentectomy.

posterior part of lateral segmental vein.name: Posterior part of the lateral segmental vein
posterior part of lateral segmental vein.desc: A tributary draining the posterior portion of the lateral segment (segment 4) of the right middle lobe. It joins the anterior part to form the lateral segmental vein, which drains via the middle lobe vein into the right superior pulmonary vein and then the left atrium.
clinical: It lies close to the horizontal and oblique fissures, a relation surgeons use when separating the middle lobe.

superior lingular vein.name: Superior lingular vein
superior lingular vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the superior lingular segment (segment 4) of the left upper lobe. It joins the inferior lingular vein to form the lingular vein, a tributary of the left superior pulmonary vein that returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: The lingula is the left lung equivalent of the right middle lobe, and its veins are mapped before lingula-sparing or lingula resection.

superior part of medial segmental vein.name: Superior part of the medial segmental vein
superior part of medial segmental vein.desc: A tributary draining the upper portion of the medial segment (segment 5) of the right middle lobe. It joins the inferior part to form the medial segmental vein, which flows via the middle lobe vein into the right superior pulmonary vein and on to the left atrium.
clinical: Right middle lobe veins sit beside the right heart border, where middle lobe pneumonia blurs the heart outline on X-ray.

superior part of {S} anterior segmental.name: Superior part of the {S} anterior segmental vein
superior part of {S} anterior segmental.desc: A tributary draining the upper portion of the anterior segment (segment 3) of the right upper lobe. It joins the inferior part to form the anterior segmental vein, a tributary of the right superior pulmonary vein that carries oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Accidental ligation of the wrong pulmonary vein branch can cause congestion of the lung tissue left behind.

trunk of {S} apical segmental vein.name: Trunk of the {S} apical segmental vein
trunk of {S} apical segmental vein.desc: The main stem of the apical segmental vein of the right upper lobe, formed by the union of its apical and anterior parts. It drains the apical segment (segment 1) and empties into the upper lobe trunk of the right superior pulmonary vein, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: It is one of the first veins met at the front of the hilum during right upper lobectomy.

{S} anterior basal segmental vein.name: Anterior basal segmental vein
{S} anterior basal segmental vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the anterior basal segment (segment 8) of the lower lobe. It usually joins other basal veins to form the superior basal vein, which feeds the common basal vein and then the inferior pulmonary vein, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Lower lobe basal veins are mapped on CT before basal segmentectomy for small lung cancers.

{S} anterior segmental vein.name: Anterior segmental vein
{S} anterior segmental vein.desc: A vein draining the anterior segment (segment 3) of the upper lobe, running in the planes between segments. It empties into the superior pulmonary vein, which carries oxygenated blood from the upper lung into the left atrium.
clinical: It is a key landmark when dissecting the front of the hilum during upper lobectomy.

{S} apical segmental vein.name: Apical segmental vein
{S} apical segmental vein.desc: A vein draining the apical segment (segment 1) of the upper lobe; on the left it is usually combined with the posterior segmental vein as the apicoposterior vein. It empties into the superior pulmonary vein and returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Apical lung segments are classic sites for reactivation tuberculosis, which can distort these vessels.

{S} inferior basal vein.name: Inferior basal vein
{S} inferior basal vein.desc: A vein draining the lower and posterior basal parts of the lower lobe, including much of the posterior basal segment. It joins the superior basal vein to form the common basal vein, which empties into the inferior pulmonary vein and on to the left atrium.
clinical: The inferior pulmonary ligament leads surgeons to the inferior pulmonary vein and its basal tributaries during lower lobectomy.

{S} inferior pulmonary vein.name: Inferior pulmonary vein
{S} inferior pulmonary vein.region: Thorax: lung hilum and left atrium
{S} inferior pulmonary vein.desc: The lower of the two pulmonary veins on each side, the lowest structure at the lung hilum, lying in the upper end of the pulmonary ligament. It drains the lower lobe through the superior segmental vein and common basal vein, carrying oxygenated blood into the back of the left atrium.
clinical: Electrical triggers for atrial fibrillation often come from muscle sleeves in pulmonary veins, which ablation isolates.

{S} lateral basal segmental vein.name: Lateral basal segmental vein
{S} lateral basal segmental vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the lateral basal segment (segment 9) of the lower lobe. It joins neighbouring basal veins and drains through the common basal vein into the inferior pulmonary vein, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: Aspiration while upright tends to reach the basal segments of the lower lobes, especially on the right.

{S} medial basal segmental vein.name: Medial basal segmental vein
{S} medial basal segmental vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the medial basal segment (segment 7) of the lower lobe, beside the heart. On the left this segment is usually combined with the anterior basal segment. It drains through the basal veins into the inferior pulmonary vein and on to the left atrium.
clinical: The medial basal segment lies against the heart and inferior vena cava, a relation seen on chest CT.

{S} posterior basal segmental vein.name: Posterior basal segmental vein
{S} posterior basal segmental vein.desc: A segmental vein draining the posterior basal segment (segment 10), the lowest and most posterior part of the lower lobe. It drains mainly through the inferior basal vein and common basal vein into the inferior pulmonary vein.
clinical: In upright patients, pleural fluid and aspirated material tend to settle at the lung bases, including this segment.

{S} posterior segmental vein.name: Posterior segmental vein
{S} posterior segmental vein.desc: A vein draining the posterior segment (segment 2) of the upper lobe; on the left it is usually fused with the apical vein as the apicoposterior vein. It runs behind the upper lobe bronchus and empties into the superior pulmonary vein, then the left atrium.
clinical: The posterior segment of the upper lobe is a classic site for aspiration pneumonia in someone lying on their back and for tuberculosis.

{S} superior pulmonary vein.name: Superior pulmonary vein
{S} superior pulmonary vein.region: Thorax: lung hilum and left atrium
{S} superior pulmonary vein.desc: The upper of the two pulmonary veins on each side, lying in front of and below the pulmonary artery at the hilum. The right one drains the upper and middle lobes and the left drains the upper lobe including the lingula. It carries oxygenated blood into the left atrium.
clinical: Pulmonary vein isolation for atrial fibrillation encircles the superior and inferior pulmonary veins at the left atrium.
A rare narrowing of these veins can follow ablation.

{S} superior segmental vein.name: Superior segmental vein
{S} superior segmental vein.desc: A vein draining the superior segment (segment 6) at the top of the lower lobe. It usually empties directly into the inferior pulmonary vein, separately from the common basal vein, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
clinical: The superior segment of the lower lobe is where aspirated material often goes when someone lies on their back.

acromial branch of {S} thoraco-acromial.name: Acromial branch of the {S} thoraco-acromial artery
acromial branch of {S} thoraco-acromial.desc: A branch of the thoraco-acromial trunk that runs laterally over the coracoid process, deep to deltoid, toward the acromion. It supplies deltoid and joins the acromial network with branches of the suprascapular and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
clinical: It is often cauterized during subacromial decompression, a common shoulder arthroscopy procedure.

deltoid branch of {S} thoraco-acromial a.name: Deltoid branch of the {S} thoraco-acromial artery
deltoid branch of {S} thoraco-acromial a.desc: A branch of the thoraco-acromial trunk that runs in the deltopectoral groove alongside the cephalic vein. It supplies the adjoining parts of deltoid and pectoralis major. It anastomoses with branches of the circumflex humeral arteries around the shoulder.
clinical: It is met in the deltopectoral approach to the shoulder, the standard route for shoulder replacement.

pectoral branch of {S} thoraco-acromial.name: Pectoral branch of the {S} thoraco-acromial artery
pectoral branch of {S} thoraco-acromial.desc: A branch of the thoraco-acromial trunk that descends between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor. It runs with the lateral pectoral nerve and supplies both pectoral muscles and anastomoses with the intercostal and lateral thoracic arteries.
clinical: It is the main pedicle of the pectoralis major flap, used to reconstruct defects in the head and neck.

trunk of {S} thoraco-acromial artery.name: Trunk of the {S} thoraco-acromial artery
trunk of {S} thoraco-acromial artery.region: Upper limb: infraclavicular region and axilla
trunk of {S} thoraco-acromial artery.desc: A short wide branch from the second part of the axillary artery, behind pectoralis minor. It curves around the upper border of pectoralis minor, pierces the clavipectoral fascia and divides into pectoral, acromial, clavicular and deltoid branches.
clinical: It is a landmark in the infraclavicular region, near where the cephalic vein and lateral pectoral nerve pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

{S} anterior circumflex humeral artery.name: Anterior circumflex humeral artery
{S} anterior circumflex humeral artery.desc: A small branch of the third part of the axillary artery that passes laterally in front of the surgical neck of the humerus, deep to coracobrachialis and biceps. An ascending branch runs up the intertubercular groove to the humeral head, and it anastomoses with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
clinical: Damage to its ascending branch in proximal humerus fractures raises the risk of humeral head avascular necrosis.

{S} anterior circumflex humeral vein.name: Anterior circumflex humeral vein
{S} anterior circumflex humeral vein.desc: The vein accompanying the anterior circumflex humeral artery in front of the surgical neck of the humerus. It drains the front of the shoulder joint, the humeral head and nearby muscles into the axillary vein.
clinical: These vessels are a bleeding source in the deltopectoral approach and are often tied at the lower edge of subscapularis.

{S} axillary artery.name: Axillary artery
{S} axillary artery.desc: The continuation of the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. Pectoralis minor divides it into three parts, and it is surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus. Its six branches supply the shoulder, chest wall and scapular region.
clinical: Anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humerus fractures can injure it along with the brachial plexus.
It is used as an access site for cardiac support devices.

{S} axillary vein.name: Axillary vein
{S} axillary vein.desc: Formed at the lower border of teres major as the continuation of the basilic vein, joined by the brachial veins. It runs medial to the axillary artery, receives the cephalic vein and other tributaries, and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
clinical: It is used for ultrasound-guided central venous access and pacemaker lead placement.

{S} circumflex scapular artery.name: Circumflex scapular artery
{S} circumflex scapular artery.region: Upper limb: posterior axilla and scapula
{S} circumflex scapular artery.desc: A branch of the subscapular artery that passes through the triangular space (bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps) to reach the infraspinous fossa. It supplies the muscles on the back of the scapula and joins the scapular anastomosis.
clinical: It is the pedicle of the scapular and parascapular skin flaps.
The scapular anastomosis can keep the arm perfused if the axillary artery is slowly blocked.

{S} circumflex scapular vein.name: Circumflex scapular vein
{S} circumflex scapular vein.region: Upper limb: posterior axilla and scapula
{S} circumflex scapular vein.desc: Veins accompanying the circumflex scapular artery through the triangular space. They drain the infraspinous fossa muscles and overlying skin of the back into the subscapular vein and then the axillary vein.
clinical: They provide venous drainage for scapular and parascapular flaps.

{S} dorsal scapular artery.name: Dorsal scapular artery
{S} dorsal scapular artery.desc: Usually a branch of the subclavian artery (sometimes the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery) that passes through the brachial plexus and runs down the medial border of the scapula with the dorsal scapular nerve, deep to the rhomboids. It supplies rhomboids, levator scapulae and trapezius and joins the scapular anastomosis.
clinical: Its course through the brachial plexus matters in neck surgery and in plexus nerve blocks.

{S} internal thoracic artery.name: Internal thoracic artery
{S} internal thoracic artery.desc: A branch of the first part of the subclavian artery that descends behind the upper six costal cartilages about a finger width lateral to the sternum. It gives anterior intercostal, perforating and pericardiacophrenic branches, then divides at the sixth intercostal space into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
clinical: The left internal thoracic artery grafted to the LAD is the gold standard coronary bypass, with excellent long-term patency.

{S} lateral thoracic artery.name: Lateral thoracic artery
{S} lateral thoracic artery.desc: A branch of the second part of the axillary artery that runs down along the lower border of pectoralis minor onto the side of the chest wall. It supplies serratus anterior, the pectoral muscles, the axillary lymph nodes and the skin of the lateral chest wall.
clinical: It is encountered during axillary lymph node dissection along with the long thoracic nerve.

{S} posterior circumflex humeral artery.name: Posterior circumflex humeral artery
{S} posterior circumflex humeral artery.desc: A branch of the third part of the axillary artery that passes through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. It supplies deltoid, teres minor, the shoulder joint and much of the humeral head, and anastomoses with the anterior circumflex humeral artery.
clinical: Surgical neck fractures can injure it together with the axillary nerve.
Overhead athletes can develop compression of it in the quadrangular space.

{S} subscapular artery.name: Subscapular artery
{S} subscapular artery.desc: The largest branch of the axillary artery, arising from its third part. It runs down along the lower border of subscapularis and divides into the circumflex scapular artery and the thoracodorsal artery.
clinical: Its branching system supplies several flaps (scapular, latissimus, serratus) from one pedicle, valuable in reconstruction.

{S} subscapular vein.name: Subscapular vein
{S} subscapular vein.desc: The vein accompanying the subscapular artery, formed by the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal veins. It drains the scapular muscles and lateral chest wall into the axillary vein. It runs along the lower border of subscapularis.
clinical: It is a landmark during axillary lymph node dissection and drains flaps based on the subscapular system.

{S} suprascapular artery.name: Suprascapular artery
{S} suprascapular artery.region: Shoulder: posterior scapula and root of neck
{S} suprascapular artery.desc: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk that crosses anterior scalene and the brachial plexus, then passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament while the suprascapular nerve passes beneath it. It supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and joins the scapular anastomosis.
clinical: A memory aid: the artery goes over the ligament (the bridge) and the nerve goes under it.

{S} suprascapular vein.name: Suprascapular vein
{S} suprascapular vein.region: Shoulder: posterior scapula and root of neck
{S} suprascapular vein.desc: The vein accompanying the suprascapular artery. It drains supraspinatus and infraspinatus and runs forward across the root of the neck, usually into the external jugular vein. Near its end it lies close to the transverse cervical vein above the clavicle.
clinical: It lies in the field of supraclavicular nerve blocks and neck dissection.

atlas.name: Atlas (first cervical vertebra)
atlas.desc: A ring-shaped vertebra with no body and no spinous process, made of anterior and posterior arches joined by two lateral masses. Its superior facets cradle the occipital condyles (atlanto-occipital joint, the 'yes' nodding movement) and its inferior facets sit on the axis (atlanto-axial joint, the 'no' rotation). The transverse ligament holds the dens against the back of its anterior arch, and the vertebral artery grooves the top of its posterior arch.
clinical: A Jefferson fracture is a burst of the ring from axial loading, such as diving into shallow water.
Atlanto-axial instability is a concern in rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome.

axis.name: Axis (second cervical vertebra)
axis.desc: The second cervical vertebra, defined by the dens (odontoid process), a peg that projects up through the ring of the atlas and acts as the pivot for head rotation. The alar ligaments run from the dens to the occipital condyles and the apical ligament to the foramen magnum. It has a large, strong bifid spinous process, a key palpable landmark below the occiput, and articulates with C3 through the first intervertebral disc.
clinical: Dens fractures are classified I to III; type II, through the base of the dens, is the most common and often fails to unite.
A hangman's fracture is a bilateral fracture of the C2 pars interarticularis from hyperextension.

third cervical vertebra.name: Third cervical vertebra
third cervical vertebra.desc: A typical cervical vertebra with a small oval body, uncinate processes on the upper body rim, bifid spinous process and transverse foramina carrying the vertebral artery and vein. It articulates with C2 above and C4 below, with facet joints angled about 45 degrees that allow wide flexion, extension and rotation. It lies roughly at the level of the hyoid bone, and the C3 spinal nerve exits above it.
clinical: The C3 to C5 segments give rise to the phrenic nerve, so cord injury at or above this level can stop breathing.
Its uncovertebral joints can grow osteophytes that narrow the foramen and irritate exiting roots.

fourth cervical vertebra.name: Fourth cervical vertebra
fourth cervical vertebra.desc: A typical cervical vertebra lying around the level of the upper thyroid cartilage, near where the common carotid artery divides (C3 to C4). It has transverse foramina for the vertebral vessels, a bifid spinous process and uncinate processes forming uncovertebral joints with C3. Deep neck muscles such as longus colli and the scalenes attach to its transverse processes, and the C4 spinal nerve exits above it.
clinical: A complete cord injury at C4 typically causes quadriplegia and often needs breathing support because phrenic output from C3 to C5 is impaired.
C4 radiculopathy causes pain over the shoulder top without a classic reflex change.

fifth cervical vertebra.name: Fifth cervical vertebra
fifth cervical vertebra.desc: A typical cervical vertebra in the middle of the cervical lordosis, with transverse foramina for the vertebral artery, a bifid spinous process and uncinate processes. Its transverse processes give attachment to the scalene and longus colli muscles, and the C5 root, which supplies the deltoid and biceps, exits above it. The C5 to C6 segment is one of the most mobile and most stressed in the neck.
clinical: The C5 to C6 level is a common site of cervical spondylosis and degenerative stenosis.
Cord injuries at C5 preserve shoulder abduction and elbow flexion but lose wrist and hand function.

sixth cervical vertebra.name: Sixth cervical vertebra
sixth cervical vertebra.desc: A typical cervical vertebra whose transverse process carries a large anterior tubercle, the carotid (Chassaignac) tubercle, against which the common carotid artery can be pressed. The vertebral artery usually enters the transverse foramina here. C6 marks the level of the cricoid cartilage, where the larynx becomes the trachea and the pharynx becomes the esophagus.
clinical: The carotid tubercle is a landmark for stellate ganglion and other anterior neck blocks.
The C5 to C6 and C6 to C7 discs are the most frequently herniated in the neck.
