seventh cervical vertebra.name: Seventh cervical vertebra (vertebra prominens)
seventh cervical vertebra.desc: The transitional vertebra at the base of the neck, called the vertebra prominens because its long, non-bifid spinous process is the first easily felt bump when running a finger down the back of the neck. Its transverse foramina are small and usually carry only vertebral veins, not the artery. It articulates with C6 above and T1 below; the ligamentum nuchae and trapezius attach to its spinous process.
clinical: It is the standard landmark for counting spinous processes down the back.
An extra cervical rib can arise from C7 and compress the brachial plexus or subclavian artery (thoracic outlet syndrome).

intervertebral disk of third cervical ve.name: Intervertebral disc between C3 and C4
intervertebral disk of third cervical ve.desc: The fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of C3 and C4, made of an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus). It absorbs load and allows motion, and its back edge faces the spinal canal and the intervertebral foramina. Because cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, a posterolateral herniation here usually compresses the C4 nerve root.
clinical: Herniation at C3–C4 typically produces a C4 radiculopathy.
It is a less common herniation level than the lower cervical discs.

intervertebral disk of fourth cervical v.name: Intervertebral disc between C4 and C5
intervertebral disk of fourth cervical v.desc: The fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of C4 and C5, made of an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus). It absorbs load and allows motion, and its back edge faces the spinal canal and the intervertebral foramina. Because cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, a posterolateral herniation here usually compresses the C5 nerve root.
clinical: Herniation at C4–C5 typically produces a C5 radiculopathy.
A C5 root lesion weakens shoulder abduction and the biceps and reduces the biceps reflex.

intervertebral disk of fifth cervical ve.name: Intervertebral disc between C5 and C6
intervertebral disk of fifth cervical ve.desc: The fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of C5 and C6, made of an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus). It absorbs load and allows motion, and its back edge faces the spinal canal and the intervertebral foramina. Because cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, a posterolateral herniation here usually compresses the C6 nerve root.
clinical: Herniation at C5–C6 typically produces a C6 radiculopathy.
A C6 root lesion causes thumb-side forearm numbness and a weak biceps and brachioradialis reflex.

intervertebral disk of sixth cervical ve.name: Intervertebral disc between C6 and C7
intervertebral disk of sixth cervical ve.desc: The fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of C6 and C7, made of an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus). It absorbs load and allows motion, and its back edge faces the spinal canal and the intervertebral foramina. Because cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, a posterolateral herniation here usually compresses the C7 nerve root.
clinical: Herniation at C6–C7 typically produces a C7 radiculopathy.
This is the most commonly herniated cervical disc; C7 compression weakens the triceps and reduces the triceps reflex.

intervertebral disk of seventh cervical.name: Intervertebral disc between C7 and T1
intervertebral disk of seventh cervical.desc: The fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of C7 and T1, made of an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus). It absorbs load and allows motion, and its back edge faces the spinal canal and the intervertebral foramina. Because cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, a posterolateral herniation here usually compresses the C8 nerve root.
clinical: Herniation at C7–T1 typically produces a C8 radiculopathy.
A C8 lesion weakens finger flexion and numbs the little-finger side of the hand.

first lumbar vertebra.name: First lumbar vertebra
first lumbar vertebra.desc: A lumbar vertebra with a large kidney-shaped body built for weight bearing, no transverse foramina or rib facets, a short hatchet-shaped spinous process and facet joints oriented near the sagittal plane, which allow flexion and extension but limit rotation. L1 lies at the transpyloric plane, the right diaphragmatic crus attaches to its body, and the spinal cord's tip (conus medullaris) usually ends near the L1 to L2 level.
clinical: The thoracolumbar junction (T11 to L2) is the most common site of spinal fractures from falls and crashes.
An L1 burst fracture can injure the conus medullaris, mixing cord and nerve root signs.

second lumbar vertebra.name: Second lumbar vertebra
second lumbar vertebra.desc: A lumbar vertebra with a large kidney-shaped body built for weight bearing, no transverse foramina or rib facets, a short hatchet-shaped spinous process and facet joints oriented near the sagittal plane, which allow flexion and extension but limit rotation. Both diaphragmatic crura attach to its body, and psoas major arises from its body and transverse processes. In adults the cauda equina, not the cord, usually fills the canal from L2 down.
clinical: Lumbar puncture is done below L2, at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, to avoid the spinal cord.
L2 root compression weakens hip flexion and numbs the upper front thigh.

third lumbar vertebra.name: Third lumbar vertebra
third lumbar vertebra.desc: A lumbar vertebra with a large kidney-shaped body built for weight bearing, no transverse foramina or rib facets, a short hatchet-shaped spinous process and facet joints oriented near the sagittal plane, which allow flexion and extension but limit rotation. It usually has the longest transverse processes in the lumbar spine, giving attachment to psoas major, quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia. The umbilicus lies roughly at the L3 to L4 level.
clinical: The L3 to L4 interspace is a standard lumbar puncture site.
L3 root problems weaken knee extension and numb the front of the thigh.

fourth lumbar vertebra.name: Fourth lumbar vertebra
fourth lumbar vertebra.desc: A lumbar vertebra with a large kidney-shaped body built for weight bearing, no transverse foramina or rib facets, a short hatchet-shaped spinous process and facet joints oriented near the sagittal plane, which allow flexion and extension but limit rotation. A line joining the tops of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses its spinous process or the L4 to L5 interspace, and the abdominal aorta divides into the common iliac arteries in front of its body.
clinical: Tuffier's line is the bedside landmark for finding a safe lumbar puncture level.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis, a forward slip of L4 on L5, is common in older adults.

fifth lumbar vertebra.name: Fifth lumbar vertebra
fifth lumbar vertebra.desc: The largest vertebra, with a wedge-shaped body taller in front that creates the lumbosacral angle where it sits on the sacrum. Its thick transverse processes anchor the iliolumbar ligaments to the iliac crests. It articulates with L4 above and the sacrum below, and the inferior vena cava forms in front of it from the two common iliac veins.
clinical: Spondylolysis, a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis, is most common at L5 and is a frequent cause of back pain in teenage athletes.
Bilateral pars defects can let L5 slip forward on S1 (isthmic spondylolisthesis).

intervertebral disk of first lumbar vert.name: Intervertebral disc between L1 and L2
intervertebral disk of first lumbar vert.desc: The thick fibrocartilage pad joining L1 and L2, with a tough annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus that spreads compressive load. It is the thinnest of the lumbar discs and lies near the end of the spinal cord. A typical posterolateral herniation here spares the root exiting at this level and compresses the root traveling down to the next one, the L2 root.
clinical: Herniation at L1–L2 classically causes L2 sciatica-type leg pain.
Large central herniations here can compress the conus medullaris.

intervertebral disk of second lumbar ver.name: Intervertebral disc between L2 and L3
intervertebral disk of second lumbar ver.desc: The thick fibrocartilage pad joining L2 and L3, with a tough annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus that spreads compressive load. A typical posterolateral herniation here spares the root exiting at this level and compresses the root traveling down to the next one, the L3 root.
clinical: Herniation at L2–L3 classically causes L3 sciatica-type leg pain.
Upper lumbar herniations are uncommon and can weaken hip flexion or knee extension.

intervertebral disk of third lumbar vert.name: Intervertebral disc between L3 and L4
intervertebral disk of third lumbar vert.desc: The thick fibrocartilage pad joining L3 and L4, with a tough annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus that spreads compressive load. A typical posterolateral herniation here spares the root exiting at this level and compresses the root traveling down to the next one, the L4 root.
clinical: Herniation at L3–L4 classically causes L4 sciatica-type leg pain.
An L4 lesion weakens knee extension and reduces the knee-jerk reflex.

intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar ver.name: Intervertebral disc between L4 and L5
intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar ver.desc: The thick fibrocartilage pad joining L4 and L5, with a tough annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus that spreads compressive load. With L5 to S1 it carries the highest loads in the spine and is one of the two most commonly herniated discs. A typical posterolateral herniation here spares the root exiting at this level and compresses the root traveling down to the next one, the L5 root.
clinical: Herniation at L4–L5 classically causes L5 sciatica-type leg pain.
An L5 lesion weakens big-toe and ankle dorsiflexion and can cause foot drop.

intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vert.name: Lumbosacral intervertebral disc (L5 to S1)
intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vert.desc: The thick fibrocartilage pad joining L5 and S1, with a tough annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus that spreads compressive load. It is wedge-shaped, thicker in front, and with L4 to L5 is one of the two most commonly herniated discs. A typical posterolateral herniation here spares the root exiting at this level and compresses the root traveling down to the next one, the S1 root.
clinical: Herniation at L5–S1 classically causes S1 sciatica-type leg pain.
An S1 lesion weakens plantarflexion and reduces the ankle-jerk reflex.

first thoracic vertebra.name: First thoracic vertebra
first thoracic vertebra.desc: The first thoracic vertebra has a full costal facet on its body for the head of rib 1 and a demifacet below for rib 2, plus transverse costal facets for the rib tubercle. Its body still looks somewhat cervical, and its prominent spinous process lies just below C7. The T1 root contributes to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and carries sympathetic fibers headed for the head and eye.
clinical: Damage to T1 sympathetic outflow, for example by an apical lung (Pancoast) tumor, causes Horner syndrome.
A T1 root lesion weakens the small muscles of the hand.

second thoracic vertebra.name: Second thoracic vertebra
second thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T2 carries superior and inferior demifacets for the heads of ribs 2 and 3. The jugular notch of the sternum lies roughly at the T2 to T3 level, and rhomboid minor and major attach near its spinous process.
clinical: Upper thoracic sympathetic chain surgery (sympathectomy) near T2 to T3 is used for severe sweating of the hands.
The T2 dermatome covers the inner upper arm and armpit region.

third thoracic vertebra.name: Third thoracic vertebra
third thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T3 articulates with the heads of ribs 3 and 4 through demifacets and with their tubercles at its transverse processes. Rhomboid major and the trapezius attach to its spinous process, and the spine of the scapula sits roughly at its level.
clinical: The scapular spine at about T3 is a quick surface landmark for counting thoracic levels.
Thoracic vertebral fractures without major trauma raise concern for osteoporosis or a tumor.

fourth thoracic vertebra.name: Fourth thoracic vertebra
fourth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T4 articulates with ribs 4 and 5. The sternal angle projects back to the T4 to T5 disc, marking where the aortic arch begins and ends and where the trachea divides into the main bronchi.
clinical: The T4 dermatome lies at chest level and is a common landmark when testing a sensory level in spinal cord injury.
Cord injuries at or above T6 risk autonomic dysreflexia, a dangerous blood pressure surge.

fifth thoracic vertebra.name: Fifth thoracic vertebra
fifth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T5 articulates with the heads of ribs 5 and 6 and lies just below the tracheal bifurcation. The descending thoracic aorta runs along the left side of the bodies at this level, with the esophagus just to its right and in front.
clinical: The upper and middle thoracic cord has a narrow canal and a thin blood supply, making it vulnerable to ischemia.
Metastatic cancer most often lands in the thoracic spine and can compress the cord.

sixth thoracic vertebra.name: Sixth thoracic vertebra
sixth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T6 articulates with ribs 6 and 7 and sits in the middle of the thoracic kyphosis. The greater splanchnic nerve begins to gather from sympathetic ganglia near T5 to T9 alongside these bodies.
clinical: Cord injury at or above T6 carries a risk of autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder or bowel distension.
Wedge compression fractures are common in the mid thoracic spine and increase kyphosis.

seventh thoracic vertebra.name: Seventh thoracic vertebra
seventh thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T7 articulates with ribs 7 and 8; rib 7 is the last true rib. The inferior angle of the scapula lies near the T7 spinous process when the arms hang at the sides, and the T7 dermatome lies over the xiphoid region.
clinical: The scapular inferior angle at about T7 is a classic surface landmark for counting levels.
Scheuermann kyphosis, wedging of several mid-thoracic vertebrae, appears in adolescents.

eighth thoracic vertebra.name: Eighth thoracic vertebra
eighth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T8 articulates with ribs 8 and 9. The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm at about the T8 level.
clinical: The 'I ate 10 eggs at 12' rule: vena cava at T8, esophagus at T10, aorta at T12.
Lower thoracic disc herniations (T8 to T12) account for most of the uncommon thoracic disc cases.

ninth thoracic vertebra.name: Ninth thoracic vertebra
ninth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T9 has superior demifacets for the head of rib 9 and often lacks inferior ones, since rib 10 usually articulates with T10 alone. The xiphisternal joint lies roughly at the T9 level.
clinical: Lower thoracic spinous processes are less steep, which makes thoracic epidural access easier here than mid-thorax.
Vertebral osteomyelitis and tuberculosis (Pott disease) favor the lower thoracic spine.

tenth thoracic vertebra.name: Tenth thoracic vertebra
tenth thoracic vertebra.desc: A thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and costal facets for the ribs, with facet joints set in the coronal plane that favor rotation while the rib cage limits flexion. T10 usually has a single full costal facet on its body for the head of rib 10, often with a transverse costal facet. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at about this level, and the T10 dermatome surrounds the umbilicus.
clinical: The T10 dermatome at the umbilicus is a key landmark for sensory level testing.
Early appendicitis pain is felt around the umbilicus because the appendix shares T10 visceral afferents.

eleventh thoracic vertebra.name: Eleventh thoracic vertebra
eleventh thoracic vertebra.desc: A transitional thoracic vertebra whose body resembles a lumbar one. It has a single full facet for the head of rib 11 and usually no transverse costal facet, since rib 11 is a floating rib that does not articulate with the transverse process. It lies in the stiff-to-mobile thoracolumbar transition zone.
clinical: The T11 to L2 region is the most common site of traumatic spinal fractures.
Its location near the cord's lumbar enlargement means injury can affect leg function.

twelfth thoracic vertebra.name: Twelfth thoracic vertebra
twelfth thoracic vertebra.desc: The last thoracic vertebra, transitional in shape: its superior articular processes face like a thoracic vertebra's while its inferior ones face like a lumbar vertebra's. It has a single full facet for rib 12 and no transverse costal facet. The aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm at this level, and the celiac trunk arises near it.
clinical: T12 is among the most commonly fractured vertebrae, especially in osteoporotic compression fractures.
The aortic hiatus lies at T12.

intervertebral disk of first thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T1 and T2
intervertebral disk of first thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T1 and T2, with an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 2 articulates across its side with demifacets on both vertebrae. Upper thoracic discs are thin, and the rib cage and sternum make this segment one of the least mobile in the spine.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of second thoracic v.name: Intervertebral disc between T2 and T3
intervertebral disk of second thoracic v.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T2 and T3, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 3 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of third thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T3 and T4
intervertebral disk of third thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T3 and T4, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 4 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of fourth thoracic v.name: Intervertebral disc between T4 and T5
intervertebral disk of fourth thoracic v.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T4 and T5, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 5 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
The T4 to T5 disc lies at the level of the sternal angle and the tracheal bifurcation.

intervertebral disk of fifth thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T5 and T6
intervertebral disk of fifth thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T5 and T6, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 6 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of sixth thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T6 and T7
intervertebral disk of sixth thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T6 and T7, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 7 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of seventh thoracic.name: Intervertebral disc between T7 and T8
intervertebral disk of seventh thoracic.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T7 and T8, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 8 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Surgery for a thoracic disc often needs a lateral or transthoracic approach because the cord cannot be retracted.

intervertebral disk of eighth thoracic v.name: Intervertebral disc between T8 and T9
intervertebral disk of eighth thoracic v.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T8 and T9, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 9 articulates across its side, with demifacets on both vertebrae and an intra-articular ligament anchored to the disc itself. Thoracic discs are thin relative to their vertebrae, and the rib cage keeps this segment stiff.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Most symptomatic thoracic herniations occur between T8 and T12, where the spine is more mobile.

intervertebral disk of ninth thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T9 and T10
intervertebral disk of ninth thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T9 and T10, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. The head of rib 10 sometimes touches its side, though it usually articulates with T10 alone. Thoracic discs grow thicker toward the lumbar spine, and this lower segment is more mobile than those above as it nears the thoracolumbar junction.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Most symptomatic thoracic herniations occur between T8 and T12, where the spine is more mobile.

intervertebral disk of tenth thoracic ve.name: Intervertebral disc between T10 and T11
intervertebral disk of tenth thoracic ve.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T10 and T11, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. Unlike the discs above, it lies at a level where the ribs no longer cross the disc, because the lowest ribs articulate with single vertebrae. Thoracic discs grow thicker toward the lumbar spine, and this lower segment is more mobile as it approaches the thoracolumbar junction.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Most symptomatic thoracic herniations occur between T8 and T12, where the spine is more mobile.

intervertebral disk of eleventh thoracic.name: Intervertebral disc between T11 and T12
intervertebral disk of eleventh thoracic.desc: The fibrocartilage disc joining the bodies of T11 and T12, made of an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus. Unlike the discs above, it lies at a level where the ribs no longer cross the disc, because the lowest ribs articulate with single vertebrae. Thoracic discs grow thicker toward the lumbar spine, and this lower segment is more mobile as it approaches the thoracolumbar junction.
clinical: Thoracic disc herniations are rare and may compress the spinal cord, causing leg weakness and a sensory level, or a root, causing band-like chest wall pain.
Most symptomatic thoracic herniations occur between T8 and T12, where the spine is more mobile.

{S} first rib.name: First rib
{S} first rib.desc: The shortest, broadest and most curved rib, lying flat under the clavicle. Its head has a single facet for T1, and its costal cartilage joins the manubrium. On its upper surface the scalene tubercle receives anterior scalene, with a groove for the subclavian vein in front and for the subclavian artery and lower brachial plexus trunk behind. Middle scalene and serratus anterior also attach.
clinical: A first rib fracture signals high-energy trauma and should prompt a search for injury to the great vessels.
Narrowing between the first rib and clavicle or scalenes causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

{S} second rib.name: Second rib
{S} second rib.desc: A thinner, longer rib whose head articulates with T1 and T2 and whose costal cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle, the manubriosternal joint. A rough tuberosity on its outer surface gives origin to part of serratus anterior, and posterior scalene inserts on it. Because it lines up with the palpable sternal angle, it is the starting point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces.
clinical: Clinicians find the second rib at the sternal angle and count down to locate heart sounds and chest tube sites.
The second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is a classic site for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax.

{S} third rib.name: Third rib
{S} third rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 3 articulates with T2 and T3 and with the sternum through its costal cartilage, and pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3 to 5.
clinical: Intercostal nerve blocks are placed just below the rib to reach the nerve in the costal groove.
Rib fractures are painful and can make breathing shallow, risking pneumonia.

{S} fourth rib.name: Fourth rib
{S} fourth rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 4 is a true rib joined directly to the sternum by its costal cartilage, and pectoralis minor and serratus anterior attach to it. Its level corresponds roughly to the T4 dermatome at chest level.
clinical: The fourth to fifth intercostal space marks the top of the safe triangle for chest drains.
Multiple adjacent rib fractures broken in two places create a flail chest segment.

{S} fifth rib.name: Fifth rib
{S} fifth rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 5 articulates with T4 and T5 and joins the sternum as a true rib. Serratus anterior and external oblique interdigitate on its outer surface, and the fifth intercostal space below it is where the apex of the heart is usually felt.
clinical: The apex beat is normally palpable in the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
Chest tubes are usually inserted in the fifth intercostal space just in front of the mid-axillary line, above the sixth rib.

{S} sixth rib.name: Sixth rib
{S} sixth rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 6 joins the sternum through its costal cartilage near the xiphoid end of the sternal body. Serratus anterior and external oblique attach to its outer surface, and the diaphragm arises from the inner aspect of the lower costal cartilages, including the sixth.
clinical: Upper border of the sixth rib is the target for a standard chest drain so the needle avoids the neurovascular bundle below each rib.
Lower rib fractures should raise concern for injury to the liver or spleen.

{S} seventh rib.name: Seventh rib
{S} seventh rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 7 is the last true rib: its costal cartilage reaches the sternum directly, near the xiphisternal junction. Serratus anterior, external oblique and the diaphragm attach to it, and on the back the inferior angle of the scapula usually overlies it.
clinical: Fractures of ribs 7 to 10 can injure the liver on the right or the spleen on the left.
The seventh intercostal space is a common site for pleural fluid sampling posteriorly.

{S} eighth rib.name: Eighth rib
{S} eighth rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 8 is the first false rib: its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 7 rather than the sternum, helping form the costal margin. The diaphragm, external oblique, serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi attach to it.
clinical: Pleural taps are kept above about the ninth rib posteriorly to avoid the diaphragm and abdominal organs.
Slipping rib syndrome, a hypermobile false rib cartilage, can cause sharp lower chest pain.

{S} ninth rib.name: Ninth rib
{S} ninth rib.desc: A typical rib with a head carrying two demifacets, a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, an angle and a flat shaft whose lower inner border holds the costal groove for the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (top to bottom). Rib 9 is a false rib whose cartilage joins the one above to form the costal margin. The diaphragm, external oblique, serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi attach to it, and the lower ribs on each side shield the upper abdominal organs.
clinical: On the left, ribs 9 to 11 overlie the spleen, so fractures there can cause splenic rupture.
On the right, lower rib fractures can lacerate the liver.

{S} tenth rib.name: Tenth rib
{S} tenth rib.desc: The last false rib, whose head usually has a single facet for T10 alone. Its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 9, completing the costal margin, and the diaphragm, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis and latissimus dorsi attach to it. It overlies the spleen on the left and the liver on the right.
clinical: Left tenth rib fractures carry a risk of splenic injury.
The lowest point of the costal margin, at the tenth costal cartilage, marks the subcostal plane at about L3.

{S} eleventh rib.name: Eleventh rib
{S} eleventh rib.desc: A floating rib: its tip ends free in the abdominal wall muscles with no attachment to the sternum or other cartilages. Its head has a single facet for T11, and it has no tubercle joint with the transverse process. The diaphragm, internal and external obliques, latissimus dorsi and serratus posterior inferior attach to it, and it lies over the back of the kidney and, on the left, the spleen.
clinical: On the left, an eleventh rib fracture can injure the spleen.
Surgeons may work around or remove part of the eleventh or twelfth rib for flank access to the kidney.

{S} twelfth rib.name: Twelfth rib
{S} twelfth rib.desc: The shortest floating rib, sometimes very small, with a single head facet for T12 and no tubercle joint or angle. Quadratus lumborum, the diaphragm, latissimus dorsi, serratus posterior inferior and the abdominal wall muscles attach to it. It crosses the back of the kidney, and the pleural reflection dips below its medial part.
clinical: Because the pleura extends below the medial twelfth rib, flank kidney surgery can accidentally open the pleural cavity.
Tenderness at the costovertebral angle, between the twelfth rib and the spine, suggests kidney inflammation.

manubrium.name: Manubrium of sternum
manubrium.desc: The broad upper part of the sternum, lying at about T3 to T4. Its jugular notch sits between the sternoclavicular joints, where it articulates with both clavicles, and it joins the first costal cartilages and part of the second. It meets the sternal body at the sternal angle (manubriosternal joint). Sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major, sternohyoid and sternothyroid attach to it, and the left brachiocephalic vein and aortic arch branches lie just behind it.
clinical: The sternal angle, at the manubriosternal joint, marks the second rib, the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation.
Infection of the sternoclavicular joint can spread into the mediastinum behind the manubrium.

body of sternum.name: Body of sternum
body of sternum.desc: The long middle part of the sternum, formed from fused segments (sternebrae). Above it meets the manubrium at the sternal angle, below the xiphoid process, and its notched edges take the costal cartilages of ribs 2 (partly) to 7. Pectoralis major arises from its front and transversus thoracis from its back. Its spongy interior holds red bone marrow, and the heart lies directly behind its lower half.
clinical: Chest compressions in CPR are delivered over the lower half of the sternal body.
A median sternotomy, splitting the sternum lengthwise, is the standard approach for open-heart surgery.

xiphoid process.name: Xiphoid process
xiphoid process.desc: The small, variably shaped lowest part of the sternum, cartilaginous in young people and slowly ossifying in adulthood. It joins the sternal body at the xiphisternal joint, at about T9. The linea alba and rectus abdominis sheath attach to it, and fibers of the diaphragm arise from its back. It sits over the upper abdomen, near the left lobe of the liver and the heart's lower edge.
clinical: Hands placed too low in CPR can fracture the xiphoid and injure the liver.
It is the entry landmark for subxiphoid pericardiocentesis to drain fluid around the heart.

{S} clavicle.name: Clavicle (collarbone)
{S} clavicle.desc: An S-shaped long bone running horizontally across the base of the neck as a strut that holds the shoulder away from the trunk. Medially it forms the sternoclavicular joint with the manubrium and first costal cartilage, laterally the acromioclavicular joint with the acromion. SCM, trapezius, deltoid, pectoralis major and subclavius attach to it, and the coracoclavicular ligament anchors its underside. The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus pass beneath it.
clinical: It is the most commonly fractured bone, usually in the middle third; the medial fragment is pulled up by SCM and the arm drags the lateral part down.
It is the first bone to begin ossifying and its medial growth plate is among the last to close, in the mid-twenties.

{S} scapula.name: Scapula (shoulder blade)
{S} scapula.desc: A flat triangular bone on the back of the thorax over ribs 2 to 7. Its glenoid cavity articulates with the humeral head (shoulder joint) and its acromion with the clavicle. About 17 muscles attach: the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) in its fossae, deltoid and trapezius on the spine and acromion, serratus anterior, rhomboids and levator scapulae on its medial border, and biceps, triceps, coracobrachialis and pectoralis minor at the glenoid tubercles and coracoid process.
clinical: Injury to the long thoracic nerve paralyzes serratus anterior and causes a winged scapula.
Scapular fractures need high-energy trauma and often come with chest injuries.

{S} humerus.name: Humerus
{S} humerus.desc: The long bone of the arm. Its head articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula, and distally the trochlea meets the ulna and the capitulum meets the radius at the elbow. The greater tubercle takes supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor, the lesser tubercle subscapularis, the deltoid tuberosity the deltoid, and the medial and lateral epicondyles the forearm flexor and extensor origins. The axillary, radial and ulnar nerves lie directly on bone at the surgical neck, radial groove and medial epicondyle.
clinical: A midshaft fracture can injure the radial nerve in its groove, causing wrist drop.
Supracondylar fractures in children can damage the brachial artery and median nerve.

{S} radius.name: Radius
{S} radius.desc: The lateral (thumb-side) forearm bone. Its disc-shaped head turns against the capitulum of the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna, held by the annular ligament, while its wide distal end articulates with the scaphoid and lunate at the wrist and with the ulnar head. Biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity, and supinator, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and brachioradialis act on it, so it rotates around the ulna in pronation and supination.
clinical: A distal radius (Colles) fracture from a fall on an outstretched hand is the most common forearm fracture, giving a 'dinner fork' deformity.
In toddlers a sudden pull on the arm can slip the radial head out of the annular ligament (nursemaid's elbow).

{S} ulna.name: Ulna
{S} ulna.desc: The medial (little-finger side) forearm bone and the stable base of the elbow. Its olecranon and trochlear notch grip the humeral trochlea in a hinge joint, its radial notch holds the radial head, and its small distal head articulates with the radius, separated from the carpals by an articular disc. Triceps inserts on the olecranon and brachialis on the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity; flexor digitorum profundus, flexor carpi ulnaris, supinator and pronator quadratus also attach.
clinical: A Monteggia injury is a proximal ulna fracture with dislocation of the radial head.
An isolated shaft fracture from blocking a blow with the forearm is called a nightstick fracture.

interosseous membrane of {S} forearm.name: Interosseous membrane of the {S} forearm
interosseous membrane of {S} forearm.desc: A strong fibrous sheet stretched between the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna. Its main fibers run obliquely down and medially from radius to ulna, so force from the hand, which lands mostly on the radius, is passed to the ulna and on to the elbow. It separates the anterior and posterior compartments and gives origin to deep muscles such as flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus and the deep thumb extensors.
clinical: An Essex-Lopresti injury combines a radial head fracture, a torn interosseous membrane and disruption of the distal radioulnar joint.
The anterior interosseous nerve and artery run along its front surface.

{S} scaphoid.name: Scaphoid
{S} scaphoid.desc: The largest bone of the proximal carpal row, on the thumb side, shaped like a boat and bridging both rows. It articulates with the radius, lunate, capitate, trapezium and trapezoid, and forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. Its tubercle anchors the flexor retinaculum and abductor pollicis brevis. Most of its blood supply enters at the distal end from radial artery branches.
clinical: It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone; tenderness in the snuffbox after a fall needs treatment even if the first x-ray looks normal.
Waist fractures can cut off blood to the proximal pole, causing avascular necrosis and nonunion.

{S} lunate.name: Lunate
{S} lunate.desc: A moon-shaped bone in the middle of the proximal carpal row, between the scaphoid and triquetrum. It articulates with the radius above and the capitate (and sometimes the hamate) below, and is the keystone of wrist stability. Strong ligaments tie it to the scaphoid and triquetrum, and it sits just behind the carpal tunnel.
clinical: It is the most commonly dislocated carpal bone; a palmar dislocation can press on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
Kienbock disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate, causing chronic wrist pain.

{S} triquetral.name: Triquetrum (triquetral bone)
{S} triquetral.desc: A pyramid-shaped bone on the little-finger side of the proximal carpal row. It articulates with the lunate laterally, the hamate distally and the pisiform on its front surface. It is separated from the ulna by the triangular fibrocartilage complex, and the ulnar collateral and several dorsal wrist ligaments attach to it.
clinical: A small dorsal chip fracture of the triquetrum is the second most common carpal fracture.
Ulnar-sided wrist pain near it often comes from injury to the triangular fibrocartilage complex.

{S} pisiform.name: Pisiform
{S} pisiform.desc: A small pea-shaped sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, sitting on the palmar surface of the triquetrum. It gives origin to abductor digiti minimi and attachment to the flexor retinaculum, and continues to the hamate and fifth metacarpal through the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments. It forms the medial wall of Guyon's canal, through which the ulnar nerve and artery enter the hand.
clinical: It is easily felt at the base of the hypothenar eminence and is a landmark for the ulnar nerve.
Compression in Guyon's canal, for example in cyclists, causes ulnar nerve symptoms in the hand.

{S} trapezium.name: Trapezium
{S} trapezium.desc: The thumb-side bone of the distal carpal row. Its saddle-shaped distal surface forms the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb with the first metacarpal, allowing opposition, and it also articulates with the scaphoid, trapezoid and second metacarpal. Its tubercle and groove guide the flexor carpi radialis tendon and anchor the flexor retinaculum, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis.
clinical: Osteoarthritis of the thumb base (trapeziometacarpal joint) is very common and painful when pinching.
Severe cases may be treated by removing the trapezium (trapeziectomy).

{S} trapezoid.name: Trapezoid
{S} trapezoid.desc: A small wedge-shaped bone of the distal carpal row, between the trapezium and capitate. It articulates with the base of the second metacarpal distally, the scaphoid proximally and the trapezium and capitate on either side. Tight ligaments lock it to the second metacarpal, forming part of the rigid central pillar of the hand.
clinical: It is the least commonly fractured carpal bone.
Its tight joint with the second metacarpal explains why that carpometacarpal joint barely moves.

{S} capitate.name: Capitate
{S} capitate.desc: The largest carpal bone, in the center of the distal row. Its rounded head fits into the concavity formed by the scaphoid and lunate, and distally it articulates mainly with the third metacarpal, plus the second and fourth; the trapezoid and hamate sit on either side. Part of adductor pollicis arises from it, and wrist motion pivots around it.
clinical: It is the first carpal bone to ossify, in early infancy, which helps in estimating bone age.
Capitate fractures usually occur together with scaphoid fractures in high-energy wrist injuries.

{S} hamate.name: Hamate
{S} hamate.desc: A wedge-shaped bone on the little-finger side of the distal carpal row, recognized by its hook (hamulus) projecting into the palm. It articulates with the fourth and fifth metacarpals, the capitate, triquetrum and lunate. The hook anchors the flexor retinaculum, flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi, and forms the lateral wall of Guyon's canal.
clinical: Hook of hamate fractures happen in golf, baseball and racquet sports when the handle strikes the palm.
Such fractures can irritate the ulnar nerve and the flexor tendons of the little finger.

{S} first metacarpal bone.name: First metacarpal
{S} first metacarpal bone.desc: The shortest and thickest metacarpal, supporting the thumb. Its saddle-shaped base articulates with the trapezium in the highly mobile thumb carpometacarpal joint, and its head forms the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint. Abductor pollicis longus inserts on its base, opponens pollicis along its shaft, and the first dorsal interosseous partly arises from it. It sits more anteriorly and rotated about 90 degrees relative to the other metacarpals, which allows opposition.
clinical: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of its base, pulled apart by abductor pollicis longus.
A comminuted fracture of the base is called a Rolando fracture.

{S} second metacarpal bone.name: Second metacarpal
{S} second metacarpal bone.desc: Usually the longest metacarpal, supporting the index finger. Its notched base articulates with the trapezoid, trapezium, capitate and third metacarpal, locking it in place. Extensor carpi radialis longus inserts on the back of its base and flexor carpi radialis on the front, and interosseous muscles arise from its shaft.
clinical: Its carpometacarpal joint is nearly immobile, making it part of the stable central pillar of the hand.
Fractures of its neck are less forgiving of angulation than those of the fourth and fifth metacarpals.

{S} third metacarpal bone.name: Third metacarpal
{S} third metacarpal bone.desc: The metacarpal of the middle finger, distinguished by a styloid process on the back of its base. It articulates mainly with the capitate and with the second and fourth metacarpals. Extensor carpi radialis brevis inserts on its styloid process, the transverse head of adductor pollicis arises from its palmar shaft, and interossei attach along it.
clinical: With the second metacarpal it forms the fixed central axis of the hand.
A bony bump at its base on the back of the hand (carpal boss) can be mistaken for a ganglion cyst.

{S} fourth metacarpal bone.name: Fourth metacarpal
{S} fourth metacarpal bone.desc: The thin metacarpal of the ring finger. Its base articulates with the hamate and capitate and with the third and fifth metacarpals, allowing a little more motion than the central metacarpals. Dorsal and palmar interosseous muscles arise from its shaft.
clinical: Punching injuries often fracture the neck of the fourth or fifth metacarpal.
A noticeably short fourth metacarpal can be a sign of conditions such as Turner syndrome or pseudohypoparathyroidism.

{S} fifth metacarpal bone.name: Fifth metacarpal
{S} fifth metacarpal bone.desc: The metacarpal of the little finger. Its base articulates with the hamate and fourth metacarpal in a fairly mobile joint that lets the palm cup. Extensor carpi ulnaris inserts on the back of its base, opponens digiti minimi along its shaft, and flexor carpi ulnaris acts on it through the pisometacarpal ligament.
clinical: A 'boxer's fracture' is a fracture of its neck from punching with a closed fist.
Rotational deformity after fracture makes the little finger cross under the ring finger when making a fist.

distal phalanx of {S} index finger.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} index finger
distal phalanx of {S} index finger.desc: The fingertip bone of the index finger, ending in a flattened tuft that supports the nail bed and pulp. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on its palmar base, supplied for this finger by the median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), and the terminal extensor tendon inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: Mallet finger is loss of active fingertip extension when the terminal extensor tendon tears or pulls off a bone fragment.
Crush injuries commonly fracture the tuft and often come with a nail bed injury.

middle phalanx of {S} index finger.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} index finger
middle phalanx of {S} index finger.desc: The middle bone of the index finger, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum superficialis splits and inserts on the sides of its palmar shaft, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, while the central slip of the extensor mechanism inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: A torn central slip lets the finger buckle into a boutonniere deformity, bent at the middle joint and extended at the tip.
Volar plate injuries at its base are common in jammed-finger sports injuries.

proximal phalanx of {S} index finger.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} index finger
proximal phalanx of {S} index finger.desc: The longest bone of the index finger. Its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint with the metacarpal head, and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. The flexor tendons run along its palmar surface in a fibrous sheath, and the interossei and lumbricals act on it through the extensor expansion over its back.
clinical: Shaft fractures tend to angle toward the palm because of the pull of the interossei.
Any rotation after fracture makes the finger overlap its neighbor when making a fist.

distal phalanx of {S} middle finger.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} middle finger
distal phalanx of {S} middle finger.desc: The fingertip bone of the middle finger, ending in a flattened tuft that supports the nail bed and pulp. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on its palmar base, supplied for this finger by the median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), and the terminal extensor tendon inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: Mallet finger is loss of active fingertip extension when the terminal extensor tendon tears or pulls off a bone fragment.
Jersey finger is avulsion of the profundus tendon from its base, most often in the ring finger.

middle phalanx of {S} middle finger.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} middle finger
middle phalanx of {S} middle finger.desc: The middle bone of the middle finger, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum superficialis splits and inserts on the sides of its palmar shaft, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, while the central slip of the extensor mechanism inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: A torn central slip lets the finger buckle into a boutonniere deformity, bent at the middle joint and extended at the tip.
Volar plate injuries at its base are common in jammed-finger sports injuries.

proximal phalanx of {S} middle finger.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} middle finger
proximal phalanx of {S} middle finger.desc: The longest bone of the middle finger. Its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint with the metacarpal head, and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. The flexor tendons run along its palmar surface in a fibrous sheath, and the interossei and lumbricals act on it through the extensor expansion over its back.
clinical: Shaft fractures tend to angle toward the palm because of the pull of the interossei.
Any rotation after fracture makes the finger overlap its neighbor when making a fist.

distal phalanx of {S} ring finger.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} ring finger
distal phalanx of {S} ring finger.desc: The fingertip bone of the ring finger, ending in a flattened tuft that supports the nail bed and pulp. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on its palmar base, supplied for this finger by the ulnar nerve, and the terminal extensor tendon inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: Mallet finger is loss of active fingertip extension when the terminal extensor tendon tears or pulls off a bone fragment.
Jersey finger is avulsion of the profundus tendon from its base, most often in the ring finger.

middle phalanx of {S} ring finger.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} ring finger
middle phalanx of {S} ring finger.desc: The middle bone of the ring finger, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum superficialis splits and inserts on the sides of its palmar shaft, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, while the central slip of the extensor mechanism inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: A torn central slip lets the finger buckle into a boutonniere deformity, bent at the middle joint and extended at the tip.
Volar plate injuries at its base are common in jammed-finger sports injuries.

proximal phalanx of {S} ring finger.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} ring finger
proximal phalanx of {S} ring finger.desc: The longest bone of the ring finger. Its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint with the metacarpal head, and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. The flexor tendons run along its palmar surface in a fibrous sheath, and the interossei and lumbricals act on it through the extensor expansion over its back.
clinical: Shaft fractures tend to angle toward the palm because of the pull of the interossei.
Any rotation after fracture makes the finger overlap its neighbor when making a fist.

distal phalanx of {S} little finger.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} little finger
distal phalanx of {S} little finger.desc: The fingertip bone of the little finger, ending in a flattened tuft that supports the nail bed and pulp. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on its palmar base, supplied for this finger by the ulnar nerve, and the terminal extensor tendon inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: Mallet finger is loss of active fingertip extension when the terminal extensor tendon tears or pulls off a bone fragment.
Jersey finger is avulsion of the profundus tendon from its base, most often in the ring finger.

middle phalanx of {S} little finger.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} little finger
middle phalanx of {S} little finger.desc: The middle bone of the little finger, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum superficialis splits and inserts on the sides of its palmar shaft, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, while the central slip of the extensor mechanism inserts on its dorsal base.
clinical: A torn central slip lets the finger buckle into a boutonniere deformity, bent at the middle joint and extended at the tip.
Volar plate injuries at its base are common in jammed-finger sports injuries.

proximal phalanx of {S} little finger.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} little finger
proximal phalanx of {S} little finger.desc: The longest bone of the little finger. Its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint with the metacarpal head, and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. The flexor tendons run along its palmar surface in a fibrous sheath, and the interossei and lumbricals act on it through the extensor expansion over its back. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis insert on the ulnar side of its base.
clinical: Shaft fractures tend to angle toward the palm because of the pull of the interossei.
Any rotation after fracture makes the finger overlap its neighbor when making a fist.

distal phalanx of {S} thumb.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} thumb
distal phalanx of {S} thumb.desc: The tip bone of the thumb, which has only two phalanges. Its base forms the interphalangeal joint with the proximal phalanx; flexor pollicis longus inserts on its palmar base and extensor pollicis longus on its dorsal base. Its flattened tuft supports the thumbnail and the sensitive pulp used for pinch.
clinical: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy weakens flexor pollicis longus, so the patient cannot make a round 'OK' sign.
Crush injuries often fracture the tuft along with the nail bed.

proximal phalanx of {S} thumb.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} thumb
proximal phalanx of {S} thumb.desc: The first bone of the thumb, between the first metacarpal and the distal phalanx. Its base forms the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint, braced by strong collateral ligaments and two sesamoid bones. Abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis insert on the radial side of its base, adductor pollicis on the ulnar side, and extensor pollicis brevis on its dorsal base.
clinical: Skier's or gamekeeper's thumb is a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament at its base, sometimes with an avulsed bone fragment.
An untreated ulnar collateral ligament tear leaves a weak, unstable pinch.

{S} pelvic girdle.name: Hip bone (pelvic girdle)
{S} pelvic girdle.desc: Each half of the pelvic girdle is one hip bone formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse at the cup-shaped acetabulum in the mid-teens. It articulates with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint, with the other hip bone at the pubic symphysis and with the femoral head at the hip joint. The gluteal muscles and iliacus arise from the ilium, the abdominal wall attaches to the iliac crest, the hamstrings to the ischial tuberosity and the adductors to the pubis.
clinical: Pelvic ring fractures from high-energy trauma can cause life-threatening internal bleeding.
In teenage sprinters, sartorius or rectus femoris can pull off a piece of the anterior iliac spines (avulsion fracture).

sacrum.name: Sacrum
sacrum.desc: A triangular bone formed by five fused sacral vertebrae, wedged between the hip bones as the back of the pelvis. It articulates with L5 above at the sacral promontory, with the ilia at the sacroiliac joints and with the coccyx below. Paired foramina pass the rami of S1 to S4, and the sacral canal ends at the sacral hiatus. Gluteus maximus, piriformis, erector spinae and the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments attach to it.
clinical: The sacral hiatus is the entry point for caudal epidural injections.
Sacral insufficiency fractures cause low back pain in older adults with osteoporosis.

{S} femur.name: Femur (thigh bone)
{S} femur.desc: The longest and strongest bone in the body. Its head fits the acetabulum (hip joint) on a neck angled about 125 degrees to the shaft, and its distal condyles articulate with the tibia and patella (knee). Gluteus medius and minimus insert on the greater trochanter, iliopsoas on the lesser trochanter, and the adductors and vasti attach along the linea aspera. The gastrocnemius heads arise from just above the condyles.
clinical: Femoral neck fractures in older adults can tear the retinacular arteries from the medial circumflex femoral artery, causing avascular necrosis of the head.
A shaft fracture can lose over a liter of blood into the thigh.

{S} patella.name: Patella (kneecap)
{S} patella.desc: The largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee. Its back surface is covered by the thickest cartilage in the body and glides in the femoral trochlear groove (patellofemoral joint). The patellar ligament runs from its apex to the tibial tuberosity. It increases the quadriceps' lever arm and protects the front of the knee.
clinical: Lateral patellar dislocation is common in teenagers and often tears the medial patellofemoral ligament.
A bipartite patella, an unfused upper-outer fragment, is a normal variant that can mimic a fracture.

{S} tibia.name: Tibia (shinbone)
{S} tibia.desc: The large medial weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its flat condyles (tibial plateau) articulate with the femur at the knee, it joins the fibula above and below, and its distal end and medial malleolus form the roof and inner wall of the ankle joint with the talus. The patellar ligament inserts on the tibial tuberosity, sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the medial surface (pes anserinus), and tibialis anterior, popliteus, soleus and tibialis posterior also attach.
clinical: Its front edge lies just under the skin, so shaft fractures are often open and prone to compartment syndrome.
Osgood-Schlatter disease, pain at the tibial tuberosity, is common in active teens during growth spurts.

{S} fibula.name: Fibula
{S} fibula.desc: The slender lateral bone of the leg, carrying little body weight but anchoring muscles and stabilizing the ankle. Its head articulates with the lateral tibial condyle, and its distal end, the lateral malleolus, forms the outer wall of the ankle mortise around the talus. Biceps femoris and the lateral collateral ligament attach to its head; fibularis longus and brevis, the long toe extensors, soleus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior arise from its shaft.
clinical: The common fibular nerve wraps around its neck, so fractures or pressure there can cause foot drop.
Lateral malleolus fractures are the most common ankle fractures, usually from a twisting injury.

interosseous membrane of {S} leg.name: Interosseous membrane of the {S} leg
interosseous membrane of {S} leg.desc: A strong fibrous sheet joining the interosseous borders of the tibia and fibula. It separates the anterior compartment from the posterior compartment and gives origin to tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus in front and tibialis posterior behind. An opening near its top lets the anterior tibial vessels pass forward, and it continues below into the tibiofibular syndesmosis that binds the ankle.
clinical: A Maisonneuve injury tears the ankle syndesmosis and the membrane up to a fracture of the upper fibula.
High ankle sprains involve the syndesmosis continuous with its lower end.

{S} talus.name: Talus
{S} talus.desc: The ankle bone that links the leg to the foot. Its trochlea fits into the mortise formed by the tibia and fibula (talocrural joint), its underside sits on the calcaneus (subtalar joint), and its head articulates with the navicular. No muscles attach to it and most of its surface is cartilage, so its blood supply is limited and enters mainly through the neck. The trochlea is wider in front, making the ankle most stable in dorsiflexion.
clinical: Talar neck fractures can cut off blood to the body of the talus and cause avascular necrosis.
A fracture of its lateral process is called a snowboarder's fracture.

{S} calcaneus.name: Calcaneus (heel bone)
{S} calcaneus.desc: The largest tarsal bone, forming the heel. It supports the talus above at the subtalar joint and articulates with the cuboid in front. The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus inserts on its posterior tuberosity, and the plantar fascia, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi arise from it. Its sustentaculum tali shelves under the talus, with the flexor hallucis longus tendon gliding beneath.
clinical: Falls from a height can crush the calcaneus, and these fractures often come with lumbar spine fractures.
Plantar fasciitis causes sharp heel pain at the fascia's attachment, worst with the first steps in the morning.

navicular bone of {S} foot.name: Navicular bone of the {S} foot
navicular bone of {S} foot.desc: A boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the midfoot. It articulates with the head of the talus behind, the three cuneiforms in front and sometimes the cuboid laterally. Its tuberosity, felt on the inner foot, receives the main insertion of tibialis posterior, and the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament runs from the calcaneus to it, supporting the talar head and the medial arch.
clinical: Navicular stress fractures occur in sprinters and jumpers and heal slowly because the central third has poor blood flow.
An accessory navicular can cause painful bumps and weaken the tibialis posterior insertion.

{S} cuboid bone.name: Cuboid bone
{S} cuboid bone.desc: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the lateral side of the midfoot. It articulates with the calcaneus behind, the fourth and fifth metatarsals in front and the lateral cuneiform and sometimes the navicular medially. A groove on its plantar surface carries the fibularis longus tendon, and the long plantar ligament attaches to the ridge behind it. It forms part of the lateral longitudinal arch.
clinical: A 'nutcracker' fracture crushes the cuboid between the calcaneus and the metatarsals when the forefoot is forced outward.
Cuboid syndrome, a slight joint displacement, causes lateral foot pain in dancers and runners.

{S} medial cuneiform bone.name: Medial cuneiform bone
{S} medial cuneiform bone.desc: The largest cuneiform, on the inner side of the midfoot. It articulates with the navicular behind, the first metatarsal and side of the second metatarsal base in front, and the intermediate cuneiform laterally. Tibialis anterior and part of fibularis longus insert on it, and the Lisfranc ligament runs from it to the base of the second metatarsal.
clinical: Disruption of the Lisfranc ligament between it and the second metatarsal is a serious midfoot injury that is easily missed.
Bruising on the sole of the midfoot is a warning sign of a Lisfranc injury.

{S} intermediate cuneiform bone.name: Intermediate cuneiform bone
{S} intermediate cuneiform bone.desc: The smallest cuneiform, a wedge with its narrow edge pointing toward the sole, between the medial and lateral cuneiforms. It articulates with the navicular behind and the base of the second metatarsal in front. Because it is shorter than its neighbors, it creates a recess that locks the second metatarsal base in place like a keystone.
clinical: The recessed second metatarsal base is central to midfoot stability, so injuries here suggest a Lisfranc pattern.
Isolated fractures of the intermediate cuneiform are rare.

{S} lateral cuneiform bone.name: Lateral cuneiform bone
{S} lateral cuneiform bone.desc: The middle-sized cuneiform, between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid. It articulates with the navicular behind, the third metatarsal in front and the sides of the second and fourth metatarsal bases. Part of tibialis posterior inserts on it and part of flexor hallucis brevis arises from it. Its wedge shape helps form the transverse arch of the foot.
clinical: Cuneiform fractures usually occur with other midfoot injuries rather than alone.
The wedge-shaped cuneiforms make the transverse arch rigid enough to bear weight.

{S} first metatarsal bone.name: First metatarsal bone
{S} first metatarsal bone.desc: The shortest and thickest metatarsal, under the big toe. Its base articulates with the medial cuneiform, and its head bears much of the body's weight during push-off, resting on two sesamoid bones. Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus insert near its base, pulling from opposite sides.
clinical: In hallux valgus (a bunion) the first metatarsal drifts medially while the big toe angles toward the second toe.
Gout classically attacks the joint at its head, the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

{S} second metatarsal bone.name: Second metatarsal bone
{S} second metatarsal bone.desc: Usually the longest metatarsal. Its base is recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms and articulates with all three cuneiforms, locking the midfoot. The Lisfranc ligament ties its base to the medial cuneiform, and dorsal interosseous muscles arise from its shaft.
clinical: It is the most common site of a march (stress) fracture in runners and soldiers.
Freiberg disease, osteonecrosis of its head, affects adolescents, especially girls.

{S} third metatarsal bone.name: Third metatarsal bone
{S} third metatarsal bone.desc: The middle metatarsal, whose base articulates with the lateral cuneiform and the second and fourth metatarsals. Dorsal and plantar interosseous muscles arise from its shaft, and its head bears weight in the ball of the foot.
clinical: Stress fractures of the third metatarsal are common in runners, along with the second.
Pain between its head and the fourth may come from a Morton neuroma.

{S} fourth metatarsal bone.name: Fourth metatarsal bone
{S} fourth metatarsal bone.desc: A slender metatarsal whose base articulates with the cuboid and the lateral cuneiform. Interosseous muscles arise from its sides, and it forms part of the mobile lateral column of the foot.
clinical: A Morton neuroma, a thickened digital nerve, most often lies between the third and fourth metatarsal heads.
Its joint with the cuboid is more mobile than the medial tarsometatarsal joints.

{S} fifth metatarsal bone.name: Fifth metatarsal bone
{S} fifth metatarsal bone.desc: The metatarsal of the little toe, with a prominent tuberosity on the outer edge of its base that can be felt along the side of the foot. Its base articulates with the cuboid. Fibularis brevis inserts on the tuberosity and fibularis tertius on the dorsal base, while abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis act along it.
clinical: Ankle inversion can pull off the tuberosity (avulsion fracture) via fibularis brevis.
A Jones fracture, just beyond the tuberosity, heals poorly because of a watershed blood supply.

distal phalanx of {S} big toe.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} big toe
distal phalanx of {S} big toe.desc: The tip bone of the big toe, which has only two phalanges. Its base forms the interphalangeal joint with the proximal phalanx; flexor hallucis longus inserts on its plantar base and extensor hallucis longus on its dorsal base. Its broad tuft supports the toenail and the pad of the toe used in push-off.
clinical: Ingrown toenails most often affect the big toe, at the nail folds over this bone.
Crush injuries can cause a painful blood collection under the nail (subungual hematoma).

proximal phalanx of {S} big toe.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} big toe
proximal phalanx of {S} big toe.desc: The large first bone of the big toe. Its base forms the first metatarsophalangeal joint with the metatarsal head, and its head forms the interphalangeal joint. Flexor hallucis brevis inserts on both sides of its base through the two sesamoids, abductor hallucis on the medial side, adductor hallucis on the lateral side, and extensor hallucis brevis on its dorsal base.
clinical: Turf toe is a sprain of the plantar joint capsule at its base from forced bending upward.
In hallux valgus it angles toward the second toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.

distal phalanx of {S} second toe.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} second toe
distal phalanx of {S} second toe.desc: The tip bone of the second toe, a small bone with a tuft that supports the nail bed. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum longus inserts on its plantar base, and the extensor digitorum longus tendon reaches its dorsal base through the extensor expansion.
clinical: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at the joint just above this bone.
Stubbed-toe fractures of the small toes are usually treated by taping to the neighboring toe.

middle phalanx of {S} second toe.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} second toe
middle phalanx of {S} second toe.desc: The short middle bone of the second toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming both interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum brevis splits and inserts on the sides of its plantar surface, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, and the extensor expansion passes over its back.
clinical: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often in the second toe.
Tight, narrow shoes contribute to small-toe deformities and corns over these joints.

proximal phalanx of {S} second toe.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} second toe
proximal phalanx of {S} second toe.desc: The longest bone of the second toe. Its base forms the metatarsophalangeal joint with the metatarsal head and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. Lumbricals and interossei act on it through the extensor expansion. Two dorsal interossei insert on its sides, giving the second toe its own abductors in both directions.
clinical: Claw toe, extension at its base with flexion of the joints beyond, can signal nerve or muscle imbalance in the foot.
Small-toe proximal phalanx fractures usually heal well with buddy taping and a stiff shoe.

distal phalanx of {S} third toe.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} third toe
distal phalanx of {S} third toe.desc: The tip bone of the third toe, a small bone with a tuft that supports the nail bed. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum longus inserts on its plantar base, and the extensor digitorum longus tendon reaches its dorsal base through the extensor expansion.
clinical: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at the joint just above this bone.
Stubbed-toe fractures of the small toes are usually treated by taping to the neighboring toe.

middle phalanx of {S} third toe.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} third toe
middle phalanx of {S} third toe.desc: The short middle bone of the third toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming both interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum brevis splits and inserts on the sides of its plantar surface, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, and the extensor expansion passes over its back.
clinical: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often in the second toe.
Tight, narrow shoes contribute to small-toe deformities and corns over these joints.

proximal phalanx of {S} third toe.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} third toe
proximal phalanx of {S} third toe.desc: The longest bone of the third toe. Its base forms the metatarsophalangeal joint with the metatarsal head and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. Lumbricals and interossei act on it through the extensor expansion. A dorsal interosseous inserts on its lateral side and a plantar interosseous on its medial side.
clinical: Claw toe, extension at its base with flexion of the joints beyond, can signal nerve or muscle imbalance in the foot.
Small-toe proximal phalanx fractures usually heal well with buddy taping and a stiff shoe.

distal phalanx of {S} fourth toe.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} fourth toe
distal phalanx of {S} fourth toe.desc: The tip bone of the fourth toe, a small bone with a tuft that supports the nail bed. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum longus inserts on its plantar base, and the extensor digitorum longus tendon reaches its dorsal base through the extensor expansion.
clinical: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at the joint just above this bone.
Stubbed-toe fractures of the small toes are usually treated by taping to the neighboring toe.

middle phalanx of {S} fourth toe.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} fourth toe
middle phalanx of {S} fourth toe.desc: The short middle bone of the fourth toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming both interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum brevis splits and inserts on the sides of its plantar surface, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, and the extensor expansion passes over its back.
clinical: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often in the second toe.
Tight, narrow shoes contribute to small-toe deformities and corns over these joints.

proximal phalanx of {S} fourth toe.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} fourth toe
proximal phalanx of {S} fourth toe.desc: The longest bone of the fourth toe. Its base forms the metatarsophalangeal joint with the metatarsal head and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. Lumbricals and interossei act on it through the extensor expansion. A dorsal interosseous inserts on its lateral side and a plantar interosseous on its medial side.
clinical: Claw toe, extension at its base with flexion of the joints beyond, can signal nerve or muscle imbalance in the foot.
Small-toe proximal phalanx fractures usually heal well with buddy taping and a stiff shoe.

distal phalanx of {S} little toe.name: Distal phalanx of the {S} little toe
distal phalanx of {S} little toe.desc: The tip bone of the little toe, a small bone with a tuft that supports the nail bed. Its base forms the distal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx. Flexor digitorum longus inserts on its plantar base, and the extensor digitorum longus tendon reaches its dorsal base through the extensor expansion. In the little toe it is often fused with the middle phalanx.
clinical: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at the joint just above this bone.
Stubbed-toe fractures of the small toes are usually treated by taping to the neighboring toe.

middle phalanx of {S} little toe.name: Middle phalanx of the {S} little toe
middle phalanx of {S} little toe.desc: The short middle bone of the little toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges, forming both interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum brevis splits and inserts on the sides of its plantar surface, flexing the proximal interphalangeal joint, and the extensor expansion passes over its back. It is very small and often fused with the distal phalanx.
clinical: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often in the second toe.
Tight, narrow shoes contribute to small-toe deformities and corns over these joints.

proximal phalanx of {S} little toe.name: Proximal phalanx of the {S} little toe
