proximal phalanx of {S} little toe.desc: The longest bone of the little toe. Its base forms the metatarsophalangeal joint with the metatarsal head and its head forms the proximal interphalangeal joint. Lumbricals and interossei act on it through the extensor expansion. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis insert on the lateral side of its base, and a plantar interosseous on the medial side.
clinical: Claw toe, extension at its base with flexion of the joints beyond, can signal nerve or muscle imbalance in the foot.
Fractures of the little toe's proximal phalanx are common from striking furniture.

sesamoid bone of {S} foot.name: Sesamoid bones of the {S} foot (hallux sesamoids)
sesamoid bone of {S} foot.desc: Two small pea-shaped bones, medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular), embedded in the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis under the head of the first metatarsal. They articulate with grooves on the metatarsal head, take weight in the ball of the foot, protect the flexor hallucis longus tendon running between them and increase the leverage of the short flexor.
clinical: Sesamoiditis, inflammation from repeated loading, is common in dancers and runners.
A bipartite medial sesamoid is a normal variant that can be mistaken for a fracture.

{S} long plantar ligament.name: Long plantar ligament
{S} long plantar ligament.desc: The longest ligament of the sole. It runs from the plantar surface of the calcaneus, in front of its tuberosity, to the ridge of the cuboid, with superficial fibers continuing to the bases of the lateral metatarsals. It converts the cuboid's groove into a tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon and is a key passive support of the lateral longitudinal arch.
clinical: Together with the plantar fascia and short plantar ligament it resists flattening of the arch during standing.
It can be strained along with the plantar fascia in runners with lateral midfoot pain.

frontal bone.name: Frontal bone
frontal bone.desc: The bone of the forehead and the roofs of the orbits. It encloses the frontal sinuses, forms most of the anterior cranial fossa floor around the ethmoid, and meets the parietal bones at the coronal suture. It also articulates with the nasal, zygomatic, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and maxillary bones. The supraorbital notch or foramen transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels, and the frontal lobes rest on its inner surface.
clinical: Neurosurgeons open the frontal bone in frontal and bifrontal craniotomies to reach the frontal lobes and anterior skull base.
Frontal sinus fractures can involve its back wall and leak cerebrospinal fluid.

{S} parietal bone.name: Parietal bone
{S} parietal bone.desc: One of the paired bones forming the roof and upper sides of the skull. It meets its partner at the sagittal suture, the frontal bone at the coronal suture, the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture and the temporal bone at the squamous suture; its lower front corner helps form the pterion. Its inner surface is grooved by branches of the middle meningeal artery and, along the midline, by the superior sagittal sinus.
clinical: A fracture near the pterion can tear the middle meningeal artery, causing an epidural hematoma with a lucid interval.
Early fusion of the sagittal suture (craniosynostosis) produces a long, narrow skull.

occipital part of head.name: Occipital bone (back of the skull)
occipital part of head.desc: The bone forming the back and base of the skull around the foramen magnum, through which the brainstem continues as the spinal cord. Its occipital condyles articulate with the atlas, the hypoglossal canals carry CN XII, and it forms the back of the jugular foramen. Outside, the external occipital protuberance and nuchal lines anchor trapezius, semispinalis capitis and the ligamentum nuchae; inside, it cradles the cerebellum and occipital lobes and is grooved by the transverse sinuses.
clinical: In Chiari I malformation the cerebellar tonsils descend through the foramen magnum and may need posterior fossa decompression.
Basilar skull fractures through it can injure lower cranial nerves.

sphenoid bone.name: Sphenoid bone
sphenoid bone.desc: A butterfly-shaped bone that is the keystone of the skull base, touching every other cranial bone. Its body holds the sphenoid sinus and the sella turcica, which cradles the pituitary gland. The lesser wings carry the optic canals (CN II and ophthalmic artery); the superior orbital fissure passes CN III, IV, V1 and VI; and the greater wings hold the foramen rotundum (V2), ovale (V3) and spinosum (middle meningeal artery). The pterygoid plates anchor the pterygoid muscles.
clinical: Pituitary tumors are commonly removed through the nose and sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal surgery).
Meningiomas of the sphenoid wing can compress the optic nerve.

ethmoid.name: Ethmoid bone
ethmoid.desc: A light, box-like bone between the orbits at the center of the face and skull base. Its horizontal cribriform plate is perforated by olfactory nerve filaments and topped by the crista galli, where the falx cerebri attaches. Its perpendicular plate forms the upper nasal septum, and its lateral labyrinths hold the ethmoid air cells, the superior and middle nasal conchae and the paper-thin orbital plate (lamina papyracea).
clinical: A cribriform plate fracture can cause loss of smell and cerebrospinal fluid leaking from the nose.
Ethmoid sinusitis can spread through the lamina papyracea into the orbit, causing orbital cellulitis.

{S} temporal bone.name: Temporal bone
{S} temporal bone.desc: A complex bone of the side and base of the skull, made of squamous, petrous, mastoid and tympanic parts plus the styloid process. The dense petrous part houses the middle and inner ear and the internal acoustic meatus (CN VII and VIII); it also contains the carotid canal and helps form the jugular foramen. The mandibular fossa forms the jaw joint, the zygomatic process forms part of the cheek arch, and sternocleidomastoid inserts on the mastoid.
clinical: Temporal bone fractures can cause hearing loss, facial nerve palsy, bruising behind the ear (Battle sign) and blood behind the eardrum.
Mastoiditis is a spread of middle ear infection into its air cells.

{S} zygomatic bone.name: Zygomatic bone (cheekbone)
{S} zygomatic bone.desc: The cheekbone, forming the prominence of the cheek and parts of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit. Its frontal process meets the frontal bone, its maxillary border the maxilla, and its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch. Masseter arises from the arch, and zygomaticus major and minor arise from its surface.
clinical: A zygomaticomaxillary complex (tripod) fracture flattens the cheek and can numb the cheek through the infraorbital nerve.
Arch fractures can block mouth opening by impinging on the coronoid process.

{S} maxilla.name: Maxilla
{S} maxilla.desc: One of the paired bones forming the upper jaw. It makes up much of the orbit floor, the lateral nasal wall and the front three-quarters of the hard palate, and its alveolar process holds the upper teeth. It contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus, and the infraorbital foramen transmits the infraorbital nerve (V2). It articulates with the frontal, nasal, lacrimal, ethmoid, zygomatic, palatine, vomer and inferior concha bones and with its partner.
clinical: Maxillary sinusitis can feel like a toothache because upper molar roots lie close to the sinus floor.
An orbital floor blowout fracture can trap the inferior rectus, causing double vision on upward gaze.

upper jaw.name: Upper jaw
upper jaw.desc: The fixed upper part of the jaw apparatus, formed mainly by the two maxillae fused at the midline. Their alveolar processes carry the upper teeth, and their palatine processes, with the horizontal plates of the palatine bones, form the hard palate that separates the mouth from the nasal cavity. Unlike the mandible it does not move; chewing forces pass through bony buttresses up to the skull.
clinical: Le Fort fractures I, II and III describe classic patterns of upper jaw separation from the skull.
Cleft palate results from incomplete fusion of the palatal shelves during development.

{S} nasal bone.name: Nasal bone
{S} nasal bone.desc: One of two small oblong bones forming the bridge of the nose. It meets its partner in the midline and articulates with the frontal bone above, the frontal process of the maxilla laterally and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid behind. The nasal cartilages attach to its lower edge.
clinical: It is the most commonly fractured facial bone.
A septal hematoma after nasal trauma must be drained quickly to prevent cartilage death.

{S} lacrimal bone.name: Lacrimal bone
{S} lacrimal bone.desc: The smallest and most fragile facial bone, in the front of the medial wall of the orbit. With the frontal process of the maxilla it forms the lacrimal fossa, which holds the lacrimal sac, leading down into the nasolacrimal canal that drains tears into the nose. It articulates with the frontal bone, ethmoid, maxilla and inferior nasal concha.
clinical: Dacryocystorhinostomy creates a new tear drainage path through the lacrimal bone into the nose.
Its thinness makes the medial orbital wall vulnerable in blowout fractures.

{S} palatine bone.name: Palatine bone
{S} palatine bone.desc: An L-shaped bone at the back of the nasal cavity. Its horizontal plate forms the back of the hard palate, its perpendicular plate forms part of the lateral nasal wall, and a small orbital process reaches the orbit floor. It contributes to the pterygopalatine fossa, and the greater and lesser palatine foramina transmit the palatine nerves (V2) and vessels to the palate.
clinical: Cleft palate can involve its horizontal plates.
Dentists block the greater palatine nerve at its foramen to numb the back of the hard palate.

vomer.name: Vomer
vomer.desc: A thin, flat, unpaired bone forming the back and lower part of the nasal septum. It articulates with the sphenoid above, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid in front, the septal cartilage anteriorly and the maxillae and palatine bones below. Its free back edge separates the two posterior nasal openings (choanae).
clinical: A deviated nasal septum often involves the junction of the vomer with the septal cartilage.
Choanal atresia, blocked posterior nasal openings, involves the region of the vomer.

mandible.name: Mandible (lower jaw)
mandible.desc: The lower jaw and the only movable bone of the skull. Its horseshoe-shaped body holds the lower teeth, and each ramus ends in a condyle that forms the temporomandibular joint with the temporal bone and a coronoid process for temporalis. Masseter and medial pterygoid insert at the angle, lateral pterygoid at the condylar neck. The inferior alveolar nerve (V3) enters the mandibular foramen and exits the mental foramen as the mental nerve.
clinical: Because it is a ring with the skull, it often fractures in two places, commonly the condyle and the angle or body.
Dentists numb the lower teeth by blocking the inferior alveolar nerve near the mandibular foramen.

hyoid bone.name: Hyoid bone
hyoid bone.desc: A U-shaped bone in the front of the neck at about C3, unique in not articulating with any other bone. It has a body and paired greater and lesser horns, and hangs from the styloid processes by the stylohyoid ligaments. Suprahyoid muscles (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric, stylohyoid) and infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, omohyoid, thyrohyoid) attach to it, along with hyoglossus and the middle pharyngeal constrictor, so it anchors the tongue and moves the larynx during swallowing.
clinical: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck lump that moves on swallowing; surgery removes the middle of the hyoid body with it.
It is a palpable landmark just above the thyroid cartilage.

median thyrohyoid ligament.name: Median thyrohyoid ligament
median thyrohyoid ligament.desc: The thickened central part of the thyrohyoid membrane, running in the midline from the thyroid notch of the thyroid cartilage up to the back of the upper border of the hyoid body. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid, and the pre-epiglottic space filled with fat lies directly behind it, in front of the epiglottis.
clinical: Cancers of the epiglottis can spread forward into the pre-epiglottic space behind this ligament.
It lies in the midline between two easily felt landmarks, the hyoid and the thyroid notch.

{S} lateral thyrohyoid ligament.name: Lateral thyrohyoid ligament
{S} lateral thyrohyoid ligament.desc: A cord-like thickening of the back edge of the thyrohyoid membrane, running from the tip of the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage to the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid. It often contains a small nodule of cartilage, the triticeous cartilage. It helps suspend the larynx from the hyoid.
clinical: A calcified triticeous cartilage can be mistaken on x-ray for a swallowed foreign body or a calcified carotid plaque.
It lies close to the internal laryngeal nerve entering the larynx.

{S} thyrohyoid membrane.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
{S} thyrohyoid membrane.desc: A broad fibroelastic sheet connecting the upper border of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, thickened in the midline and at its back edges into the thyrohyoid ligaments. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery and vein pierce it on each side to supply the inside of the larynx above the vocal folds.
clinical: The internal laryngeal nerve can be numbed where it pierces the membrane for awake airway procedures.
An external laryngocele, an air-filled pouch, can bulge out through the membrane.

{S} stylohyoid ligament.name: Stylohyoid ligament
{S} stylohyoid ligament.desc: A fibrous cord running from the tip of the styloid process of the temporal bone to the lesser horn of the hyoid bone. It develops from the second pharyngeal arch, suspends the hyoid from the skull, and lies close to the internal and external carotid arteries and the tonsil.
clinical: In Eagle syndrome an elongated styloid process or calcified ligament causes throat pain, painful swallowing or carotid irritation.
It can partly ossify, appearing as a long bony spike on x-ray.

intervertebral disk.name: Intervertebral disc
intervertebral disk.desc: A fibrocartilage pad joining the bodies of adjacent vertebrae. Each disc has a tough outer ring of layered collagen (annulus fibrosus) around a gel-like, water-rich core (nucleus pulposus), with cartilage endplates above and below. The 23 discs absorb shock, spread load and allow movement, and together make up about a quarter of the column's length above the sacrum. There is no disc between the atlas and axis.
clinical: A herniated nucleus usually bulges posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest, and can compress a nerve root.
Discs lose water with age, which explains much of the height lost in later life.

intervertebral disk of axis.name: Intervertebral disc between C2 and C3
intervertebral disk of axis.desc: The highest intervertebral disc, joining the body of the axis to C3, since no disc lies between the atlas and axis. Like other discs it has an annulus fibrosus around a nucleus pulposus, flanked by uncovertebral joints. The C3 nerve root exits beside it.
clinical: Herniation at C2 to C3 is uncommon but can cause upper neck pain and C3 root symptoms.
The C2 to C3 level is a common site for congenital vertebral fusion, as in Klippel-Feil syndrome.

long head of {S} biceps brachii.name: Long head of the {S} biceps brachii
long head of {S} biceps brachii.desc: Arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; its tendon runs inside the shoulder joint capsule over the humeral head and down the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. It joins the short head to insert on the radial tuberosity and, via the bicipital aponeurosis, the forearm fascia. Flexes the elbow, is the strongest forearm supinator, and helps stabilise the humeral head. Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: Rupture of the long head tendon, usually in older adults, produces the bulging 'Popeye' deformity of the lower arm.
Bicipital tendinopathy causes anterior shoulder pain that worsens with resisted supination (Yergason test).

short head of {S} biceps brachii.name: Short head of the {S} biceps brachii
short head of {S} biceps brachii.desc: Arises from the tip of the coracoid process of the scapula with coracobrachialis and runs down the medial side of the arm. It merges with the long head to insert on the radial tuberosity and the bicipital aponeurosis. Flexes the elbow, supinates the forearm and weakly flexes and adducts the shoulder. Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: The coracoid origin is an important landmark in shoulder surgery; the 'conjoint tendon' of short head and coracobrachialis guards the brachial plexus medially.

acromial part of {S} deltoid.name: Acromial (middle) part of the {S} deltoid
acromial part of {S} deltoid.desc: The middle fibres arise from the lateral border of the acromion and descend to the deltoid tuberosity on the lateral humeral shaft. Multipennate and powerful, they abduct the arm from about 15 to 90 degrees after supraspinatus starts the movement. Axillary nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: Axillary nerve injury from shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture paralyses abduction and numbs the 'regimental badge' patch over the deltoid.

clavicular part of {S} deltoid.name: Clavicular (anterior) part of the {S} deltoid
clavicular part of {S} deltoid.desc: The anterior fibres arise from the lateral third of the clavicle and insert on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. They flex and medially rotate the arm and assist abduction. Bordered medially by the deltopectoral groove, which carries the cephalic vein. Axillary nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: The deltopectoral groove between this part and pectoralis major is the standard surgical approach to the front of the shoulder.

spinal part of {S} deltoid.name: Spinal (posterior) part of the {S} deltoid
spinal part of {S} deltoid.desc: The posterior fibres arise from the spine of the scapula and insert on the deltoid tuberosity. They extend and laterally rotate the arm and assist abduction and horizontal extension. Axillary nerve (C5-C6), which winds around the surgical neck of the humerus beneath it.
clinical: Intramuscular shoulder injections are given into the upper deltoid to avoid the axillary nerve running about 5 cm below the acromion.

{S} external oblique.name: External oblique
{S} external oblique.desc: The largest, most superficial flat abdominal muscle. Arises by fleshy slips from the outer surfaces of ribs 5-12 and runs inferomedially ('hands in pockets') to the linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior iliac crest; its lower free border forms the inguinal ligament. Compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and rotates it to the opposite side. Thoraco-abdominal nerves (T7-T11) and subcostal nerve (T12).
clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the superficial inguinal ring and the front wall of the inguinal canal, the site of inguinal hernias.

lateral head of {S} gastrocnemius.name: Lateral head of the {S} gastrocnemius
lateral head of {S} gastrocnemius.desc: Arises from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, sometimes containing a sesamoid bone (fabella). Joins the medial head and soleus to form the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, inserting on the calcaneus. Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee. Tibial nerve (S1-S2).
clinical: A fabella in the lateral head is a normal variant on knee X-rays and should not be mistaken for a loose body.

medial head of {S} gastrocnemius.name: Medial head of the {S} gastrocnemius
medial head of {S} gastrocnemius.desc: The larger head, arising from the posterior femur just above the medial condyle. It forms the inferomedial border of the popliteal fossa and joins the lateral head and soleus in the calcaneal tendon. Plantarflexes the ankle (push-off in walking and jumping) and flexes the knee. Tibial nerve (S1-S2).
clinical: 'Tennis leg' is a sudden tear of the medial head at its musculotendinous junction, felt as a kick in the back of the calf.

{S} gluteus maximus.name: Gluteus maximus
{S} gluteus maximus.desc: The largest and most superficial gluteal muscle. Arises from the posterior ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the dorsal sacrum and coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament. Most fibres insert into the iliotibial tract; deeper ones into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur. Extends and laterally rotates the hip, powering rising from a chair, climbing stairs and running. Inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2).
clinical: Weakness causes a backward-lurching 'gluteus maximus gait' to keep the centre of gravity behind the hip.
Intramuscular injections go in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve.

long head of {S} biceps femoris.name: Long head of the {S} biceps femoris
long head of {S} biceps femoris.desc: A true hamstring: arises from the ischial tuberosity with semitendinosus and crosses both hip and knee. Joins the short head to insert on the head of the fibula, forming the lateral border of the popliteal fossa. Extends the hip, flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed knee. Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5-S2).
clinical: It is the most commonly strained hamstring in sprinting athletes, usually at the proximal musculotendinous junction.

short head of {S} biceps femoris.name: Short head of the {S} biceps femoris
short head of {S} biceps femoris.desc: Arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and the lateral supracondylar line of the femur, so it crosses only the knee. Joins the long head to insert on the fibular head. Flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg. The only hamstring part supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5-S2).
clinical: Because it alone is innervated by the common fibular division, it helps localise sciatic versus fibular nerve injuries on EMG.

{S} semimembranosus.name: Semimembranosus
{S} semimembranosus.desc: A medial hamstring arising by a flat membranous tendon from the ischial tuberosity and lying deep to semitendinosus. Inserts mainly on the posterior medial tibial condyle, with expansions forming the oblique popliteal ligament. Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg. Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5-S2).
clinical: A Baker (popliteal) cyst usually arises from the bursa between semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius.

{S} semitendinosus.name: Semitendinosus
{S} semitendinosus.desc: A medial hamstring arising from the ischial tuberosity with the long head of biceps femoris; its long cord-like tendon begins mid-thigh. It inserts on the upper medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus with sartorius and gracilis. Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg. Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5-S2).
clinical: Its tendon, often with gracilis, is commonly harvested as a graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

abdominal part of {S} pectoralis major.name: Abdominal part of the {S} pectoralis major
abdominal part of {S} pectoralis major.desc: The small lowest slip, arising from the aponeurosis of the external oblique and the upper rectus sheath. Its fibres twist upward behind the others to insert on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove, forming the lower part of the anterior axillary fold. Helps adduct and extend the flexed arm and depress the shoulder. Medial pectoral nerve.
clinical: It contributes to the anterior axillary fold, a surface landmark for chest drain placement in the 'safe triangle'.

clavicular part of {S} pectoralis major.name: Clavicular part of the {S} pectoralis major
clavicular part of {S} pectoralis major.desc: Arises from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle and inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus. Flexes the extended arm to the horizontal and medially rotates and adducts it. Lateral pectoral nerve (C5-C7).
clinical: Testing arm flexion against resistance isolates this part; separation from the sternocostal part helps localise pectoral nerve injury.

sternocostal part of {S} pectoralis majo.name: Sternocostal part of the {S} pectoralis major
sternocostal part of {S} pectoralis majo.desc: The large main part, arising from the anterior sternum and the upper six costal cartilages and inserting on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove. Powerfully adducts and medially rotates the arm and extends it from a flexed position, as in climbing or push-ups. Medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C7-T1 mainly).
clinical: Pectoralis major tears occur during heavy bench pressing, with bruising and loss of the anterior axillary fold.
Congenital absence of the sternocostal head is seen in Poland syndrome.

{S} rectus femoris.name: Rectus femoris
{S} rectus femoris.desc: The only quadriceps head crossing the hip. Arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head) and a groove above the acetabulum (reflected head). Joins the vasti in the quadriceps tendon, which encloses the patella and continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Extends the knee and flexes the hip, as in kicking. Femoral nerve (L2-L4).
clinical: Avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine occurs in adolescent kicking athletes before the growth plate fuses.

{S} vastus intermedius.name: Vastus intermedius
{S} vastus intermedius.desc: The deepest quadriceps head, lying beneath rectus femoris on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft, from which it arises. It inserts into the deep part of the quadriceps tendon to the patella and, via the patellar ligament, the tibial tuberosity. Extends the knee. Femoral nerve (L2-L4). The small articularis genus beneath it lifts the suprapatellar bursa.
clinical: Being pressed against bone, it is the muscle most often involved in post-traumatic myositis ossificans after a 'dead leg' thigh contusion.

{S} vastus lateralis.name: Vastus lateralis
{S} vastus lateralis.desc: The largest quadriceps head. Arises from the greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line and lateral lip of the linea aspera, and inserts via the quadriceps tendon and lateral patellar retinaculum onto the patella and tibial tuberosity. Extends the knee. Femoral nerve (L2-L4).
clinical: It is a common site for intramuscular injections in infants and for muscle biopsy.

{S} vastus medialis.name: Vastus medialis
{S} vastus medialis.desc: Arises from the intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera; its lowest, nearly horizontal fibres (vastus medialis obliquus) insert on the medial border of the patella. Extends the knee and pulls the patella medially, resisting lateral patellar tracking. Femoral nerve (L2-L4).
clinical: Weakness or wasting of the obliquus fibres after knee injury predisposes to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar dislocation.

{S} sartorius.name: Sartorius
{S} sartorius.desc: The longest muscle in the body, a strap running obliquely from the anterior superior iliac spine across the thigh to the upper medial tibia (pes anserinus). It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal. Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee, as in sitting cross-legged. Femoral nerve (L2-L3).
clinical: Pes anserine bursitis causes pain over the upper medial tibia where sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert.

{S} soleus.name: Soleus
{S} soleus.desc: A broad flat muscle deep to gastrocnemius, arising from the posterior fibular head and upper fibula, the soleal line of the tibia and a tendinous arch between them. It joins gastrocnemius in the calcaneal tendon to the calcaneus. A postural plantarflexor rich in slow fibres; its contractions pump venous blood out of the leg (the 'calf muscle pump'). Tibial nerve (S1-S2).
clinical: The large venous sinuses within soleus are a common origin of deep vein thrombosis.

{S} sternocleidomastoid.name: Sternocleidomastoid
{S} sternocleidomastoid.desc: Arises by a sternal head from the manubrium and a clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process and lateral superior nuchal line. It divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles and covers the carotid sheath. Acting alone it tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side; together they flex the neck and assist breathing. Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioception from C2-C3.
clinical: Congenital muscular torticollis results from fibrosis of the SCM in infants, tilting the head to the affected side.

{S} tibialis anterior.name: Tibialis anterior
{S} tibialis anterior.desc: Arises from the lateral condyle and upper two-thirds of the lateral tibial surface and interosseous membrane. Its tendon passes under the extensor retinacula to the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal. Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot and supports the medial arch. Deep fibular nerve (L4-L5).
clinical: Paralysis from common fibular nerve injury causes foot drop with a high-stepping gait.
It is the main muscle affected in anterior compartment syndrome.

ascending part of {S} trapezius.name: Ascending (inferior) part of the {S} trapezius
ascending part of {S} trapezius.desc: The lower fibres arise from the spinous processes of T4-T12 and run upward to the medial end of the spine of the scapula. They depress and retract the scapula and, with the descending part and serratus anterior, rotate the glenoid upward for overhead reach. Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3-C4 proprioceptive fibres.
clinical: Weakness of the lower trapezius contributes to scapular dyskinesis and shoulder impingement in overhead athletes.

descending part of {S} trapezius.name: Descending (superior) part of the {S} trapezius
descending part of {S} trapezius.region: Back: back of neck and shoulder
descending part of {S} trapezius.desc: The upper fibres arise from the external occipital protuberance, medial superior nuchal line and ligamentum nuchae and insert on the lateral third of the clavicle. They elevate the scapula (shrugging) and rotate it upward, and help extend and tilt the head. Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
clinical: Injury to CN XI in the posterior triangle (e.g. during lymph node biopsy) causes a drooping shoulder and weak shrug.

transverse part of {S} trapezius.name: Transverse (middle) part of the {S} trapezius
transverse part of {S} trapezius.desc: The middle fibres arise from the spinous processes of C7-T3 and run horizontally to the medial acromion and upper border of the spine of the scapula. They retract the scapula, pulling the shoulders back. Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
clinical: Tested by resisted scapular retraction; weakness lets the scapula drift laterally and contributes to rounded-shoulder posture.

lateral head of {S} triceps brachii.name: Lateral head of the {S} triceps brachii
lateral head of {S} triceps brachii.desc: Arises from the posterior humerus above and lateral to the radial groove. Joins the long and medial heads in a common tendon to the olecranon of the ulna. Extends the elbow, especially against resistance. Radial nerve (C6-C8).
clinical: Mid-shaft humeral fractures can injure the radial nerve in the groove beneath this head, causing wrist drop while triceps is usually spared.

long head of {S} triceps brachii.name: Long head of the {S} triceps brachii
long head of {S} triceps brachii.desc: Arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, so it crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow. It inserts via the common triceps tendon on the olecranon. Extends the elbow and helps extend and adduct the arm. It separates the triangular and quadrangular spaces of the posterior shoulder. Radial nerve (C6-C8).
clinical: The quadrangular space, bounded laterally by this head, transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, which can be compressed there.

medial head of {S} triceps brachii.name: Medial head of the {S} triceps brachii
medial head of {S} triceps brachii.desc: The deepest head, arising from a wide area of the posterior humerus below the radial groove. It inserts on the olecranon with the other heads and is active in all elbow extension, even light movements. Radial nerve (C6-C8), plus a branch shared with anconeus.
clinical: The triceps reflex (C7) is tested by tapping the common tendon just above the olecranon.

{S} adductor brevis.name: Adductor brevis
{S} adductor brevis.desc: A short triangular adductor arising from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis, lying between adductor longus in front and adductor magnus behind. It inserts on the upper linea aspera and pectineal line of the femur. Adducts and helps flex the hip. Obturator nerve (L2-L4), whose anterior and posterior divisions pass in front of and behind it.
clinical: It is a landmark for obturator nerve blocks, which separate the two nerve divisions on either side of the muscle.

{S} adductor longus.name: Adductor longus
{S} adductor longus.desc: The most anterior adductor, arising by a rounded tendon from the body of the pubis below the pubic crest and fanning out to the middle third of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle. Adducts and flexes the hip. Anterior division of the obturator nerve (L2-L4).
clinical: It is the muscle most often strained in a 'groin pull' in footballers and hockey players.

{S} adductor magnus.name: Adductor magnus
{S} adductor magnus.desc: The largest adductor, with two parts. The adductor part arises from the ischiopubic ramus and inserts along the linea aspera; the hamstring part arises from the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the adductor tubercle of the femur. A gap between them, the adductor hiatus, lets the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa. Adducts the hip; the hamstring part also extends it. Obturator nerve and tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
clinical: The adductor hiatus is a common site of femoral artery atherosclerosis and occlusion.

{S} adductor minimus.name: Adductor minimus
{S} adductor minimus.desc: The upper, horizontal fibres of adductor magnus, often described as a separate muscle. Arises from the inferior pubic ramus and inserts on the upper linea aspera just below the quadratus femoris. Adducts and laterally rotates the hip. Obturator nerve (L3-L4).
clinical: It lies close to the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery, relevant in posterior hip surgery.

{S} extensor digitorum longus.name: Extensor digitorum longus
{S} extensor digitorum longus.desc: Arises from the lateral tibial condyle, upper three-quarters of the fibula and interosseous membrane, lateral to tibialis anterior. Its tendon splits into four under the extensor retinacula to the dorsal expansions of toes 2-5. Extends the lateral four toes and dorsiflexes and everts the foot. Deep fibular nerve (L5-S1).
clinical: Weak toe extension is an early sign of an L5 radiculopathy or deep fibular nerve injury.

{S} extensor hallucis longus.name: Extensor hallucis longus
{S} extensor hallucis longus.desc: Arises from the middle of the medial fibula and interosseous membrane, between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. Its tendon crosses the front of the ankle to the base of the distal phalanx of the big toe. Extends the big toe and helps dorsiflex the foot. Deep fibular nerve (L5).
clinical: Testing big toe extension strength is a classic check of the L5 nerve root.

{S} brachialis.name: Brachialis
{S} brachialis.desc: Lies deep to biceps, arising from the lower half of the anterior humerus and inserting on the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. It is the main flexor of the elbow in every forearm position, since it does not cross the radius. Mainly musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6), with a small lateral part from the radial nerve.
clinical: After elbow fractures or dislocations it is prone to myositis ossificans, which stiffens the joint.

{S} coracobrachialis.name: Coracobrachialis
{S} coracobrachialis.desc: Arises from the tip of the coracoid process with the short head of biceps and inserts on the medial humeral shaft around its middle. Flexes and adducts the arm and helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid. The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) supplies it and typically pierces it.
clinical: Hypertrophy or variant anatomy can compress the musculocutaneous nerve as it passes through the muscle.

lateral lumbar intertransversarius.name: Lateral lumbar intertransversarii
lateral lumbar intertransversarius.desc: Small paired slips running between the transverse processes of adjacent lumbar vertebrae, lateral to the medial set. They assist lateral bending of the lumbar spine and stabilise it. Supplied by ventral rami of the lumbar spinal nerves.
clinical: Like other short segmental muscles, they provide proprioceptive feedback; their dysfunction is thought to contribute to mechanical low back pain.

medial lumbar intertransversarius.name: Medial lumbar intertransversarii
medial lumbar intertransversarius.desc: Small slips connecting the accessory process of one lumbar vertebra to the mammillary process of the vertebra below. They help stabilise the lumbar segments and assist lateral bending. Supplied by dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves, which distinguishes them as true deep back muscles.
clinical: Their dorsal-ramus supply groups them with the deep back muscles targeted in segmental stabilisation exercises for back pain.

set of anterior cervical intertransversa.name: Anterior cervical intertransversarii
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.desc: Small slips connecting the anterior tubercles of adjacent cervical transverse processes. They assist lateral flexion of the neck and stabilise the vertebral column. Supplied by ventral rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: The vertebral artery and cervical nerve roots pass close to these muscles near the transverse foramina.

set of interspinales cervicis.name: Interspinales cervicis
set of interspinales cervicis.region: Neck: back of the cervical spine
set of interspinales cervicis.desc: Short paired muscles joining the bifid spinous processes of adjacent cervical vertebrae, from C2 to T1, on either side of the interspinous ligament. They assist extension of the neck and provide segmental proprioception. Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: They are split in the midline during posterior cervical surgery, such as laminectomy.

set of interspinales lumborum.name: Interspinales lumborum
set of interspinales lumborum.desc: Short paired muscles running between the spinous processes of adjacent lumbar vertebrae on either side of the interspinous ligament. They help extend the lumbar spine and act mainly as position sensors for spinal posture. Dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves.
clinical: They are encountered in posterior midline approaches to the lumbar spine for discectomy or fusion.

set of posterior cervical intertransvers.name: Posterior cervical intertransversarii
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.desc: Small slips between the posterior tubercles of adjacent cervical transverse processes. They assist lateral flexion and stabilise the neck. Their medial parts are supplied by dorsal rami and lateral parts by ventral rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: They lie close to the emerging cervical nerve roots, relevant in foraminal surgery.

thoracic rotator.name: Rotatores thoracis
thoracic rotator.desc: The deepest layer of the transversospinalis group: small muscles running from the transverse process of one thoracic vertebra to the lamina and spinous process base of the vertebra one or two levels above. Best developed in the thoracic region. They stabilise vertebrae and assist rotation and extension, acting largely as proprioceptive sensors. Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: Their density of muscle spindles suggests a role in sensing spinal position more than generating force.

{S} cervical rotator.name: Rotatores cervicis
{S} cervical rotator.desc: Small, variable deep muscles running from cervical transverse processes to the laminae of the vertebra above. They stabilise the cervical segments and assist rotation and extension. Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: They are among the deep stabilisers thought to be affected in chronic neck pain and after whiplash.

{S} lumbar rotator.name: Rotatores lumborum
{S} lumbar rotator.desc: Small deep muscles running from the mammillary processes of lumbar vertebrae to the laminae of the vertebra above. They stabilise lumbar segments and assist rotation and extension, with a mainly proprioceptive role. Dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves.
clinical: They lie directly on the laminae and facet joints, deep to multifidus, in posterior lumbar approaches.

{S} flexor digitorum longus.name: Flexor digitorum longus
{S} flexor digitorum longus.desc: Arises from the posterior tibia below the soleal line. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus, crosses the tendon of flexor hallucis longus in the sole and splits into four tendons to the distal phalanges of toes 2-5. Flexes the lateral four toes and helps plantarflex and invert the foot. Tibial nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Its tendon is used in transfer surgery to replace a failing tibialis posterior tendon in adult flatfoot.

{S} flexor hallucis longus.name: Flexor hallucis longus
{S} flexor hallucis longus.desc: Arises from the lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula and interosseous membrane. Its tendon grooves the back of the talus and the underside of the sustentaculum tali, then runs to the base of the distal phalanx of the big toe. Flexes the big toe, providing the final push-off in walking, and helps plantarflex the foot and support the medial arch. Tibial nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: FHL tendinitis, 'dancer's tendinitis', causes pain behind the medial ankle in ballet dancers working en pointe.

{S} plantaris.name: Plantaris
{S} plantaris.desc: A small muscle with a short belly arising from the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and a very long thin tendon running between gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus. A weak assistant of knee flexion and plantarflexion; absent in about 7-10% of people. Tibial nerve (S1-S2).
clinical: Its tendon is a popular graft for tendon reconstruction because losing it causes no functional deficit.

{S} popliteus.name: Popliteus
{S} popliteus.desc: A thin triangular muscle forming the floor of the lower popliteal fossa. Its tendon arises inside the knee joint capsule from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus; it inserts on the posterior tibia above the soleal line. It 'unlocks' the fully extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia, and pulls the lateral meniscus back during flexion. Tibial nerve (L4-S1).
clinical: Popliteus injury is part of posterolateral corner knee injuries, which cause instability if missed.

{S} tibialis posterior.name: Tibialis posterior
{S} tibialis posterior.desc: The deepest calf muscle, arising from the interosseous membrane and adjacent tibia and fibula. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the navicular tuberosity, with slips to the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases 2-4. The main inverter of the foot and key supporter of the medial longitudinal arch; also plantarflexes. Tibial nerve (L4-L5).
clinical: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flatfoot in adults, shown by the 'too many toes' sign.

{S} gemellus inferior.name: Inferior gemellus
{S} gemellus inferior.desc: A small muscle arising from the upper ischial tuberosity, running along the lower border of the obturator internus tendon and blending with it to insert on the medial greater trochanter. Laterally rotates the extended hip and abducts the flexed hip, and stabilises the femoral head. Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4-S1).
clinical: The deep rotators including the gemelli are divided or protected in the posterior approach to hip replacement.

{S} gemellus superior.name: Superior gemellus
{S} gemellus superior.desc: A small muscle arising from the outer surface of the ischial spine, running along the upper border of the obturator internus tendon and inserting with it on the medial greater trochanter. Laterally rotates the extended hip and abducts the flexed hip. Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S2).
clinical: Repairing the short external rotators after posterior hip replacement lowers the risk of dislocation.

{S} obturator externus.name: Obturator externus
{S} obturator externus.region: Lower limb: deep hip, medial thigh
{S} obturator externus.desc: A flat fan-shaped muscle covering the outer surface of the obturator membrane and the surrounding pubis and ischium. Its tendon passes behind the femoral neck to the trochanteric fossa. Laterally rotates the hip and stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum. Obturator nerve (L3-L4).
clinical: Its tendon runs close to the medial femoral circumflex artery, the main blood supply of the femoral head, which surgeons must protect.

{S} obturator internus.name: Obturator internus
{S} obturator internus.region: Lower limb: pelvic wall and deep gluteal region
{S} obturator internus.desc: Arises from the inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding pelvic bone, forming part of the lateral pelvic wall. Its tendon turns 90 degrees around the lesser sciatic notch, exits through the lesser sciatic foramen and inserts on the medial greater trochanter with the gemelli. Laterally rotates the extended hip and abducts the flexed hip. Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S2).
clinical: Its fascia forms the pudendal canal and gives origin to part of the levator ani, linking hip and pelvic floor anatomy.

{S} piriformis.name: Piriformis
{S} piriformis.desc: Arises from the anterior sacrum (S2-S4) and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen to insert on the upper border of the greater trochanter. It is the key landmark of the gluteal region: the superior gluteal vessels and nerve pass above it and the sciatic nerve usually emerges below it. Laterally rotates the extended hip and abducts the flexed hip. Nerve to piriformis (S1-S2).
clinical: In piriformis syndrome the sciatic nerve is irritated by the muscle, causing buttock pain and sciatica-like symptoms.
In some people part of the sciatic nerve passes through the muscle.

{S} quadratus femoris.name: Quadratus femoris
{S} quadratus femoris.desc: A flat quadrilateral muscle arising from the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity and inserting on the quadrate tubercle of the intertrochanteric crest. Laterally rotates the hip and stabilises the femoral head. Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4-S1). The sciatic nerve lies directly on its posterior surface.
clinical: Narrowing between the ischium and lesser trochanter can trap quadratus femoris (ischiofemoral impingement), causing deep buttock pain.

vertical intermediate part of longus col.name: Vertical intermediate part of longus colli
vertical intermediate part of longus col.desc: The central part of longus colli, running from the anterior bodies of C5-T3 up to the anterior bodies of C2-C4. It lies on the front of the vertebral column behind the pharynx and esophagus. Flexes the neck and stabilises the cervical spine. Ventral rami of C2-C6.
clinical: Longus colli is retracted laterally in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion; the sympathetic chain on its surface can be injured, causing Horner syndrome.

{S} longus capitis.name: Longus capitis
{S} longus capitis.desc: Arises from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3-C6 and ascends to the basilar part of the occipital bone. It lies in front of the upper cervical spine behind the pharynx. Flexes the head and upper neck. Ventral rami of C1-C3.
clinical: Calcific tendinitis of longus colli/capitis causes acute neck pain and painful swallowing and can mimic a retropharyngeal abscess.

spinalis.name: Spinalis
spinalis.desc: The most medial column of the erector spinae, running between spinous processes on either side of the midline. It has thoracic, cervical and capitis parts, of which the thoracic part is best developed. Extends the vertebral column. Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.
clinical: Erector spinae spasm is a common cause of acute mechanical back pain.

{S} iliocostalis cervicis.name: Iliocostalis cervicis
{S} iliocostalis cervicis.desc: The uppermost part of the lateral (iliocostalis) column of erector spinae. Arises from the angles of ribs 3-6 and inserts on the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4-C6. Extends and laterally flexes the neck. Dorsal rami of the cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: Strain of the cervical erector spinae is a frequent source of neck pain after whiplash.

{S} iliocostalis lumborum.name: Iliocostalis lumborum
{S} iliocostalis lumborum.desc: The lowest part of the lateral column of erector spinae. Arises from the iliac crest, sacrum and the common erector spinae tendon and inserts on the angles of the lower six to nine ribs and lumbar transverse processes. Extends and laterally flexes the lumbar spine and stabilises the lower ribs. Dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves.
clinical: It is the target of the erector spinae plane block, used for pain control after spine and chest surgery.

{S} iliocostalis thoracis.name: Iliocostalis thoracis
{S} iliocostalis thoracis.desc: The middle part of the lateral column of erector spinae. Arises from the upper borders of the angles of the lower six ribs and inserts on the angles of the upper six ribs and the transverse process of C7. Extends and laterally flexes the thoracic spine. Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: Its position over the rib angles makes it a landmark for paravertebral and erector spinae plane blocks.

{S} interspinalis thoracis.name: Interspinales thoracis
{S} interspinalis thoracis.desc: Small muscles between adjacent spinous processes in the thoracic region; they are usually present only at the upper (T1-T2) and lower (T11-T12) ends of the thoracic spine. They assist extension and give proprioceptive feedback. Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: They are frequently absent in the mid-thoracic region, a normal variant.

{S} longissimus capitis.name: Longissimus capitis
{S} longissimus capitis.desc: The uppermost part of the intermediate (longissimus) column of erector spinae. Arises from the transverse processes of T1-T5 and the articular processes of C4-C7, and inserts on the posterior margin of the mastoid process. Extends the head and turns it to the same side. Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: It lies deep to splenius capitis and is passed through in posterior approaches to the upper cervical spine.

{S} longissimus cervicis.name: Longissimus cervicis
{S} longissimus cervicis.desc: Part of the longissimus column, arising from the transverse processes of T1-T5 and inserting on the transverse processes of C2-C6. Extends and laterally flexes the neck. Dorsal rami of the cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: Tension in the posterior cervical extensors contributes to cervicogenic headache.

{S} longissimus thoracis.name: Longissimus thoracis
{S} longissimus thoracis.desc: The largest part of erector spinae, forming its intermediate column. Arises from the common tendon on the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spinous processes and inserts on the transverse processes of the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae and the lower ribs between tubercles and angles. Extends and laterally flexes the vertebral column. Dorsal rami of the thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves.
clinical: Paraspinal muscle spasm, often in longissimus, causes the loss of normal lumbar lordosis seen in acute back pain.

{S} semispinalis capitis.name: Semispinalis capitis
{S} semispinalis capitis.desc: A large muscle of the transversospinalis group forming much of the bulk at the back of the neck. Arises from the transverse processes of C7-T6 and the articular processes of C4-C6 and inserts on the occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines. Extends the head and helps turn it. Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves. The greater occipital nerve pierces it.
clinical: Compression of the greater occipital nerve where it pierces semispinalis capitis is a cause of occipital neuralgia.

{S} semispinalis cervicis.name: Semispinalis cervicis
{S} semispinalis cervicis.desc: A transversospinalis muscle arising from the transverse processes of T1-T6 and inserting on the spinous processes of C2-C5, mainly the large spine of C2. It extends the neck and rotates it to the opposite side, and is an important stabiliser of the cervical spine. Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: Preserving its C2 attachment during cervical laminoplasty reduces postoperative neck pain and loss of alignment.

{S} semispinalis thoracis.name: Semispinalis thoracis
{S} semispinalis thoracis.desc: A transversospinalis muscle arising from the transverse processes of T6-T10 and inserting on the spinous processes of the upper four thoracic and lower two cervical vertebrae, spanning about four to six segments. Extends the thoracic spine and rotates it to the opposite side. Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: It lies deep to the erector spinae and is stripped from the laminae in posterior thoracic spine surgery.

{S} spinalis thoracis.name: Spinalis thoracis
{S} spinalis thoracis.desc: The most medial erector spinae column in the thorax. Arises from the spinous processes of T11-L2 and inserts on the spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (about T1-T8). Extends the thoracic spine. Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: It is closely blended with semispinalis and can be hard to separate during dissection or surgery.

check ligament of {S} lateral rectus.name: Check ligament of the {S} lateral rectus
check ligament of {S} lateral rectus.desc: A triangular expansion of the fascial sheath of the lateral rectus that attaches to the lateral orbital tubercle of the zygomatic bone. It limits the action of the lateral rectus, preventing excessive abduction, and helps support the eyeball within the orbit. It blends with the suspensory ligament of the eye (Lockwood ligament).
clinical: Check ligaments help keep the globe stable; they are released or preserved during strabismus surgery depending on the correction needed.

check ligament of {S} medial rectus.name: Check ligament of the {S} medial rectus
check ligament of {S} medial rectus.desc: A triangular expansion of the fascial sheath of the medial rectus attaching to the lacrimal bone behind the posterior lacrimal crest. It limits adduction by the medial rectus and helps suspend the eyeball. It joins the lateral check ligament through the suspensory ligament (Lockwood ligament) below the globe.
clinical: Scarring of the orbital fascia after trauma or surgery can restrict eye movement and cause double vision.

inferior oblique part of longus colli.name: Inferior oblique part of longus colli
inferior oblique part of longus colli.desc: The lower lateral part of longus colli, running from the anterior bodies of T1-T3 up to the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C5-C6. Flexes the neck and helps bend it to the same side. Ventral rami of the lower cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: The cervical sympathetic chain lies on longus colli, so retraction during anterior neck surgery can cause Horner syndrome.

oblique head of {S} adductor hallucis.name: Oblique head of the {S} adductor hallucis
oblique head of {S} adductor hallucis.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, third layer
oblique head of {S} adductor hallucis.desc: The larger head of adductor hallucis, arising from the bases of metatarsals 2-4 and the sheath of the fibularis longus tendon. It runs obliquely to the lateral side of the base of the big toe's proximal phalanx and the lateral sesamoid. Adducts the big toe and helps maintain the transverse arch. Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Its unopposed pull contributes to the big toe deviation in hallux valgus (bunion), and it is often released during bunion surgery.

oblique head of {S} adductor pollicis.name: Oblique head of the {S} adductor pollicis
oblique head of {S} adductor pollicis.desc: Arises from the capitate and the bases of the second and third metacarpals and runs to the ulnar side of the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx, via the ulnar sesamoid. With the transverse head it adducts the thumb, giving power to pinch and grip. Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8-T1).
clinical: Ulnar nerve palsy weakens adductor pollicis, producing Froment sign: the thumb tip flexes to compensate when gripping paper.

superior oblique part of longus colli.name: Superior oblique part of longus colli
superior oblique part of longus colli.desc: The upper lateral part of longus colli, arising from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3-C5 and ascending to the anterior tubercle of the atlas (C1). Flexes the neck and helps rotate it. Ventral rami of the upper cervical spinal nerves.
clinical: Longus colli is a key stabiliser targeted in rehabilitation of chronic neck pain and after whiplash.

tendon of levator palpebrae superioris.name: Tendon (aponeurosis) of levator palpebrae superioris
tendon of levator palpebrae superioris.desc: The broad aponeurosis in which levator palpebrae superioris ends. It fans out across the upper eyelid, inserting into the skin of the lid and the anterior surface of the superior tarsal plate, with lateral and medial horns attaching to the orbital margins. It transmits the pull that raises the upper eyelid.
clinical: Stretching or detachment of this aponeurosis with age is the commonest cause of acquired drooping eyelid (aponeurotic ptosis), repaired surgically.

trochlea of {S} superior oblique.name: Trochlea of the {S} superior oblique
trochlea of {S} superior oblique.desc: A cartilaginous pulley attached to the trochlear fossa of the frontal bone at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The tendon of the superior oblique passes through it and turns sharply backward and laterally to the eyeball. This redirection lets the muscle depress, abduct and intort the eye.
clinical: Inflammation of the trochlea (trochleitis) causes pain at the inner upper orbit that worsens on looking up and in.

{S} common tendinous ring.name: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)
{S} common tendinous ring.desc: A fibrous ring at the back of the orbit surrounding the optic canal and the central part of the superior orbital fissure. The four rectus muscles arise from it. Through it pass the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery, plus the superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), the nasociliary nerve and the abducens nerve (CN VI); the trochlear, frontal and lacrimal nerves pass outside it.
clinical: Inflammation at the orbital apex can affect all structures through the ring together, causing combined eye movement paralysis and vision loss (orbital apex syndrome).

{S} inferior oblique.name: Inferior oblique
{S} inferior oblique.desc: The only extraocular muscle not arising at the orbital apex: it arises from the orbital surface of the maxilla near the nasolacrimal canal, passes under the eye and inserts on the posterolateral sclera. It extorts the eye and elevates it, most effectively when the eye is adducted. Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
clinical: Overaction of the inferior oblique causes the adducted eye to drift upward, a common finding in childhood strabismus.

{S} inferior rectus.name: Inferior rectus
{S} inferior rectus.desc: Arises from the common tendinous ring and runs forward along the orbital floor to insert on the inferior sclera. It depresses the eye, especially when abducted, and also extorts and adducts it. Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
clinical: In an orbital floor 'blowout' fracture the inferior rectus can be trapped, preventing upgaze and causing double vision.

{S} lateral rectus.name: Lateral rectus
{S} lateral rectus.desc: Arises from the common tendinous ring, spanning the superior orbital fissure, and inserts on the lateral sclera. It is the pure abductor of the eye. The only muscle supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI), giving the memory aid 'LR6 SO4, the rest 3'.
clinical: Abducens palsy, sometimes a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure, causes inward deviation and horizontal double vision.

{S} levator palpebrae superioris.name: Levator palpebrae superioris
{S} levator palpebrae superioris.desc: Arises from the lesser wing of the sphenoid above the optic canal and runs forward above superior rectus, ending in a broad aponeurosis in the upper eyelid. It raises the upper eyelid. Skeletal fibres are supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III); its deep smooth-muscle part (superior tarsal muscle) is sympathetic.
clinical: Complete ptosis suggests oculomotor nerve palsy, while mild ptosis with a small pupil suggests Horner syndrome affecting the superior tarsal muscle.

{S} medial rectus.name: Medial rectus
{S} medial rectus.desc: The largest extraocular muscle, arising from the common tendinous ring and running along the medial orbital wall to insert on the medial sclera. It is the pure adductor of the eye and is essential for convergence. Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
clinical: In internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (often multiple sclerosis), the medial rectus fails to adduct on lateral gaze.

{S} superior oblique.name: Superior oblique
{S} superior oblique.desc: Arises from the body of the sphenoid above the common tendinous ring and runs forward along the superomedial orbit; its tendon passes through the trochlea, turns back and inserts on the posterolateral sclera under superior rectus. It intorts the eye and depresses it, most effectively when adducted. Trochlear nerve (CN IV).
clinical: Trochlear palsy causes vertical double vision worse when looking down, such as reading or walking downstairs; patients tilt the head away from the affected side.

{S} superior rectus.name: Superior rectus
{S} superior rectus.desc: Arises from the upper part of the common tendinous ring and runs forward beneath levator palpebrae superioris to insert on the superior sclera. It elevates the eye, especially when abducted, and also intorts and adducts it. Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
clinical: The superior rectus and levator share a fascial connection, so eye elevation and lid lifting are coordinated.

{S} fibularis brevis.name: Fibularis (peroneus) brevis
{S} fibularis brevis.desc: Arises from the lower two-thirds of the lateral fibula, deep to fibularis longus. Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and inserts on the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal base. Everts the foot and weakly plantarflexes it, protecting against inversion sprains. Superficial fibular nerve (L5-S1).
clinical: An inversion injury can avulse its insertion, fracturing the base of the fifth metatarsal.

{S} fibularis longus.name: Fibularis (peroneus) longus
{S} fibularis longus.desc: Arises from the fibular head and upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula. Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, through a groove under the cuboid and across the sole to the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal. Everts and plantarflexes the foot and supports the transverse and lateral arches. Superficial fibular nerve (L5-S1).
clinical: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck within this muscle, where it is vulnerable to fracture or tight casts.

{S} fibularis tertius.name: Fibularis (peroneus) tertius
{S} fibularis tertius.desc: A small, variably present muscle that is part of extensor digitorum longus, arising from the lower anterior fibula. Its tendon inserts on the dorsum of the base of the fifth metatarsal. Dorsiflexes and everts the foot. Deep fibular nerve (L5-S1).
clinical: It is absent in a minority of people, a normal variation of no clinical consequence.

{S} fifth costal cartilage.name: Fifth costal cartilage
{S} fifth costal cartilage.desc: The bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the fifth rib forward to the sternum. It articulates medially with the side of the sternal body at a synovial sternocostal joint. Gives origin to part of pectoralis major and attachment to the internal intercostal and transversus thoracis muscles. Its flexibility lets the chest wall expand during breathing.
clinical: The fifth intercostal space just below it, in the midaxillary line, marks the upper limit of the safe triangle for chest drains.

{S} first costal cartilage.name: First costal cartilage
{S} first costal cartilage.desc: The short, broad cartilage joining the first rib to the manubrium of the sternum just below the clavicle, through a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) that allows little movement. It gives attachment to the costoclavicular ligament and the subclavius muscle. It tends to ossify early in adulthood.
clinical: Ossification of the first costal cartilage is common with age and can look like a nodule on a chest X-ray.

abductor digiti minimi of {S} foot.name: Abductor digiti minimi of the {S} foot
abductor digiti minimi of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, first layer
abductor digiti minimi of {S} foot.desc: Lies along the lateral border of the sole. Arises from the medial and lateral processes of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis and inserts on the lateral base of the little toe's proximal phalanx. Abducts and flexes the little toe and supports the lateral arch. Lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Entrapment of the nerve to abductor digiti minimi (Baxter nerve) is an underrecognised cause of chronic heel pain.

first lumbrical of {S} foot.name: First lumbrical of the {S} foot
first lumbrical of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, second layer
first lumbrical of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the medial side of the flexor digitorum longus tendon to the second toe and inserts on the medial side of the extensor expansion of the second toe. It flexes the toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends it at the interphalangeal joints, keeping the toe flat during push-off. Medial plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Lumbrical weakness lets toes buckle into claw or hammer toe deformities, as in peripheral neuropathy.

first plantar interosseous of {S} foot.name: First plantar interosseous of the {S} foot
first plantar interosseous of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, fourth layer
first plantar interosseous of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the medial side of the third metatarsal and inserts on the medial base of the third toe's proximal phalanx and its extensor expansion. It adducts the third toe toward the second-toe axis and helps flex the metatarsophalangeal joint. Lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Wasting of the small foot muscles, seen as guttering between the metatarsals, suggests a neuropathy or S1-S2 nerve root lesion.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of {S} foot.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of the {S} foot
flexor digiti minimi brevis of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, third layer
flexor digiti minimi brevis of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the base of the fifth metatarsal and the sheath of the fibularis longus tendon and inserts on the lateral base of the little toe's proximal phalanx. Flexes the little toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint. Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: It lies near the fifth metatarsal base, a frequent site of fractures after ankle inversion injuries.

fourth lumbrical of {S} foot.name: Fourth lumbrical of the {S} foot
fourth lumbrical of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, second layer
fourth lumbrical of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the adjacent sides of the flexor digitorum longus tendons to the fourth and fifth toes and inserts on the medial extensor expansion of the fifth toe. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints of the little toe. Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Imbalance between lumbricals and long toe flexors underlies claw toes in diabetic neuropathy.

lateral head of {S} flexor hallucis brev.name: Lateral head of the {S} flexor hallucis brevis
lateral head of {S} flexor hallucis brev.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, third layer
lateral head of {S} flexor hallucis brev.desc: Arises from the plantar surface of the cuboid and lateral cuneiform and inserts, with adductor hallucis, on the lateral side of the base of the big toe's proximal phalanx; its tendon contains the lateral sesamoid. Flexes the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint. Medial plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: The sesamoid within this tendon can fracture or become inflamed (sesamoiditis) in runners and dancers.

medial head of {S} flexor hallucis brevi.name: Medial head of the {S} flexor hallucis brevis
medial head of {S} flexor hallucis brevi.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, third layer
medial head of {S} flexor hallucis brevi.desc: Arises from the cuboid and lateral cuneiform with the lateral head and inserts, blending with abductor hallucis, on the medial side of the base of the big toe's proximal phalanx; its tendon contains the medial sesamoid. Flexes the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint and supports the medial arch. Medial plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: The medial sesamoid bears much of the load at push-off and is the more commonly injured of the two; a two-part (bipartite) sesamoid can mimic a fracture.

opponens digiti minimi of {S} foot.name: Opponens digiti minimi of the {S} foot
opponens digiti minimi of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, third layer
opponens digiti minimi of {S} foot.desc: A small, inconstant slip often regarded as part of flexor digiti minimi brevis. It arises from the long plantar ligament and fibularis longus sheath and inserts along the lateral shaft of the fifth metatarsal. It draws the fifth metatarsal slightly toward the sole. Lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Unlike its namesake in the hand, it produces no true opposition and is frequently absent.

second lumbrical of {S} foot.name: Second lumbrical of the {S} foot
second lumbrical of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, second layer
second lumbrical of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the adjacent sides of the flexor digitorum longus tendons to the second and third toes and inserts on the medial extensor expansion of the third toe. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints. Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: The interdigital nerve between the third and fourth toes, near the lumbricals, is the usual site of a Morton neuroma.

second plantar interosseous of {S} foot.name: Second plantar interosseous of the {S} foot
second plantar interosseous of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, fourth layer
second plantar interosseous of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the medial side of the fourth metatarsal and inserts on the medial base of the fourth toe's proximal phalanx and its extensor expansion. It adducts the fourth toe toward the second-toe axis and helps flex the metatarsophalangeal joint. Lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Testing toe adduction and abduction helps assess lateral plantar nerve and S2 function.

third lumbrical of {S} foot.name: Third lumbrical of the {S} foot
third lumbrical of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of foot, second layer
third lumbrical of {S} foot.desc: Arises from the adjacent sides of the flexor digitorum longus tendons to the third and fourth toes and inserts on the medial extensor expansion of the fourth toe. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints. Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Loss of lumbrical function causes toe clawing, which raises pressure under the metatarsal heads and can lead to ulcers in diabetes.

third plantar interosseous of {S} foot.name: Third plantar interosseous of the {S} foot
third plantar interosseous of {S} foot.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
third plantar interosseous of {S} foot.desc: Small unipennate muscle arising from the medial side of the fifth metatarsal and inserting on the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe and its extensor expansion. It adducts the fifth toe toward the axis of the second toe and helps flex the metatarsophalangeal joint while extending the interphalangeal joints. Supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Weakness of the intrinsic foot muscles, as in diabetic neuropathy, contributes to claw toe deformity.
Plantar interossei ADduct (PAD) and dorsal interossei ABduct (DAB) the toes.

transverse head of {S} adductor hallucis.name: Transverse head of the {S} adductor hallucis
transverse head of {S} adductor hallucis.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
transverse head of {S} adductor hallucis.desc: Thin, transverse band in the fourth layer of the sole, arising from the plantar metatarsophalangeal ligaments of the third to fifth toes and the deep transverse metatarsal ligament. It joins the oblique head to insert on the lateral sesamoid and lateral base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe. It adducts the hallux and helps hold the metatarsal heads together; supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
clinical: A tight adductor hallucis is one of the soft tissue forces that drives hallux valgus (bunion) deformity and is often released surgically.

{S} abductor hallucis.name: Abductor hallucis
{S} abductor hallucis.region: Lower limb: medial sole of the foot
{S} abductor hallucis.desc: Superficial muscle along the medial border of the sole. It arises from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, the flexor retinaculum and the plantar aponeurosis, and inserts with the medial head of flexor hallucis brevis on the medial base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe. It abducts and flexes the hallux and supports the medial longitudinal arch. Supplied by the medial plantar nerve (S1-S2).
clinical: The tibial nerve and its plantar branches can be compressed beneath its fascial origin (tarsal tunnel syndrome).
Its muscle belly is a common flap used to cover defects of the heel and medial foot.

{S} extensor hallucis brevis.name: Extensor hallucis brevis
{S} extensor hallucis brevis.region: Lower limb: dorsum of the foot
{S} extensor hallucis brevis.desc: The medial slip of the extensor digitorum brevis, often described as a separate muscle. It arises from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus and inserts on the dorsal base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, extending the hallux at the metatarsophalangeal joint. Supplied by the lateral terminal branch of the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve.
clinical: Its tendon crosses the dorsalis pedis artery, a landmark when feeling for the dorsalis pedis pulse.
Atrophy over the lateral dorsum of the foot can signal a deep fibular nerve or L5 problem.

{S} flexor accessorius.name: Flexor accessorius (quadratus plantae)
{S} flexor accessorius.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
{S} flexor accessorius.desc: Second-layer muscle of the sole with two heads arising from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus. It inserts on the lateral margin of the flexor digitorum longus tendon, correcting the oblique pull of that tendon so the lateral four toes flex in a straight line. Supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (S2-S3).
clinical: Accessory or enlarged heads can rarely compress nerves in the tarsal tunnel.

{S} flexor digitorum brevis.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
{S} flexor digitorum brevis.region: Lower limb: sole of the foot
{S} flexor digitorum brevis.desc: Superficial muscle in the center of the sole, lying just deep to the plantar aponeurosis. It arises from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and the plantar aponeurosis and splits into four tendons that insert on the middle phalanges of the lateral four toes. It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and helps support the longitudinal arch. Supplied by the medial plantar nerve.
clinical: Its origin is next to the plantar fascia attachment, so it is involved in plantar heel pain and plantar fasciitis.
Its tendons split to let the flexor digitorum longus tendons pass, like the hand's FDS.

{S} abductor pollicis longus.name: Abductor pollicis longus
{S} abductor pollicis longus.desc: Deep posterior forearm muscle arising from the posterior surfaces of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane. Its tendon crosses superficial to the radial wrist extensors and runs in the first extensor compartment with extensor pollicis brevis to insert on the base of the first metacarpal. It abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint and helps radially deviate the wrist. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve (C7-C8).
clinical: De Quervain tenosynovitis inflames the APL and EPB tendons in the first dorsal compartment; Finkelstein's test reproduces the pain.
Its tendon forms the lateral (radial) border of the anatomical snuffbox.

{S} anconeus.name: Anconeus
{S} anconeus.desc: Small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow, arising from the posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus and inserting on the lateral olecranon and upper posterior ulna. It assists triceps in extending the elbow, stabilizes the joint and may abduct the ulna during pronation. Supplied by a branch of the radial nerve to the medial head of triceps.
clinical: The interval between anconeus and extensor carpi ulnaris (Kocher approach) is a classic surgical route to the radial head.

{S} brachioradialis.name: Brachioradialis
{S} brachioradialis.desc: Superficial muscle forming the lateral border of the cubital fossa and the fleshy lateral forearm. It arises from the upper lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the lateral side of the distal radius just above the styloid process. It flexes the elbow most strongly with the forearm in mid-pronation. Although it is a flexor, it lies in the posterior compartment and is supplied by the radial nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: The brachioradialis reflex tests the C6 root.
The superficial branch of the radial nerve and the radial artery run under its cover in the forearm.

{S} extensor carpi radialis brevis.name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
{S} extensor carpi radialis brevis.desc: Superficial extensor arising from the lateral epicondyle by the common extensor origin. Its tendon runs in the second extensor compartment with ECRL and inserts on the base of the third metacarpal. It extends the wrist and helps radially deviate it, and fires to stabilize the wrist during gripping. Supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve.
clinical: Degeneration of the ECRB origin is the main lesion in lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).

{S} extensor carpi radialis longus.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
{S} extensor carpi radialis longus.desc: Muscle arising from the lower lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, just below brachioradialis. Its tendon passes through the second extensor compartment and inserts on the base of the second metacarpal. It extends and radially deviates the wrist and weakly flexes the elbow. Supplied directly by the radial nerve before it divides (C6-C7).
clinical: It is spared in posterior interosseous nerve palsy, so the wrist still extends but drifts radially.
Its tendon is a common donor in tendon transfer surgery.

{S} extensor carpi ulnaris.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
