{S} extensor carpi ulnaris.desc: Superficial extensor arising from the lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin) and the posterior border of the ulna. Its tendon runs in the sixth extensor compartment in a groove beside the ulnar styloid and inserts on the base of the fifth metacarpal. It extends and ulnarly deviates the wrist. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve (C7-C8).
clinical: ECU tendon subluxation or tendinitis causes ulnar-sided wrist pain, common in tennis and golf.

{S} extensor digiti minimi.name: Extensor digiti minimi
{S} extensor digiti minimi.desc: Slender muscle that splits from the ulnar side of extensor digitorum at the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle. Its tendon runs in the fifth extensor compartment over the distal radioulnar joint and joins the extensor expansion of the little finger. It extends the little finger. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: Rupture of the EDM tendon over an arthritic distal ulna (Vaughan-Jackson lesion) is an early sign in rheumatoid arthritis.

{S} extensor digitorum.name: Extensor digitorum
{S} extensor digitorum.desc: Main finger extensor of the superficial posterior forearm, arising from the lateral epicondyle by the common extensor tendon. It forms four tendons that pass through the fourth extensor compartment, are linked on the back of the hand by juncturae tendinum, and insert via extensor expansions on the middle and distal phalanges of the index to little fingers. It extends the fingers and helps extend the wrist. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve (C7-C8).
clinical: Injury to the extensor mechanism at the distal phalanx causes mallet finger; at the middle phalanx it can cause a boutonniere deformity.

{S} extensor indicis.name: Extensor indicis
{S} extensor indicis.desc: Deep posterior forearm muscle arising from the distal posterior ulna and interosseous membrane. Its tendon runs through the fourth extensor compartment, deep and ulnar to the extensor digitorum tendon of the index finger, and joins the index extensor expansion. It allows independent extension of the index finger, as in pointing. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: Because the index has two extensors, extensor indicis is a favorite donor for transfer to repair a ruptured extensor pollicis longus.

{S} extensor pollicis longus.name: Extensor pollicis longus
{S} extensor pollicis longus.desc: Deep posterior forearm muscle arising from the middle posterior ulna and interosseous membrane. Its tendon hooks around Lister's tubercle of the radius in the third extensor compartment and inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. It extends all joints of the thumb and helps retroposition it. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve (C7-C8).
clinical: The EPL tendon can rupture weeks after an undisplaced distal radius fracture, often from rubbing at Lister's tubercle.
It forms the medial (ulnar) border of the anatomical snuffbox.

{S} supinator.name: Supinator
{S} supinator.desc: Deep muscle that wraps around the upper radius. It arises from the lateral epicondyle, the radial collateral and annular ligaments, and the supinator crest of the ulna, and inserts on the lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of the proximal third of the radius. It supinates the forearm, especially when the elbow is extended. Supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve, which passes between its two layers and emerges as the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: The fibrous arcade of Frohse at its upper edge is the usual site of posterior interosseous nerve compression, causing finger drop without sensory loss.

humeral head of {S} flexor carpi ulnaris.name: Humeral head of the {S} flexor carpi ulnaris
humeral head of {S} flexor carpi ulnaris.desc: The upper of the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, arising from the medial epicondyle of the humerus by the common flexor tendon. It joins the ulnar head through a fibrous arch (Osborne's ligament) under which the ulnar nerve enters the forearm. Together the heads insert on the pisiform, hook of hamate and base of the fifth metacarpal, flexing and ulnarly deviating the wrist. Supplied by the ulnar nerve.
clinical: The aponeurotic arch between the two FCU heads is a common site of ulnar nerve compression in cubital tunnel syndrome.

ulnar head of {S} flexor carpi ulnaris.name: Ulnar head of the {S} flexor carpi ulnaris
ulnar head of {S} flexor carpi ulnaris.desc: The lower head of flexor carpi ulnaris, arising from the medial margin of the olecranon and the upper two-thirds of the posterior border of the ulna by an aponeurosis. It unites with the humeral head over the ulnar nerve, and the muscle inserts via the pisiform onto the hook of hamate and fifth metacarpal. It flexes and ulnarly deviates the wrist. Supplied by the ulnar nerve (C7-C8, T1).
clinical: Its tendon is the landmark for finding the ulnar artery and nerve just radial to it at the wrist.

humeral head of {S} pronator teres.name: Humeral head of the {S} pronator teres
humeral head of {S} pronator teres.desc: The larger, superficial head of pronator teres, arising from the medial epicondyle and medial supracondylar ridge of the humerus. It joins the ulnar head and the muscle inserts on the middle of the lateral surface of the radius (pronator tuberosity). It pronates the forearm and helps flex the elbow. It forms the medial border of the cubital fossa. Supplied by the median nerve (C6-C7).
clinical: The median nerve usually passes between the humeral and ulnar heads, where it can be compressed (pronator syndrome).

ulnar head of {S} pronator teres.name: Ulnar head of the {S} pronator teres
ulnar head of {S} pronator teres.desc: The small, deep head of pronator teres, arising from the medial side of the coronoid process of the ulna. It joins the humeral head to insert on the pronator tuberosity of the radius, and helps pronate the forearm. The median nerve typically runs between the two heads, and the ulnar artery passes deep to this head. Supplied by the median nerve.
clinical: This head is sometimes absent; a thickened deep head can compress the median nerve in pronator syndrome.

{S} flexor carpi radialis.name: Flexor carpi radialis
{S} flexor carpi radialis.desc: Superficial forearm flexor arising from the medial epicondyle by the common flexor tendon. Its tendon passes through its own groove in the trapezium, outside the main carpal tunnel, to insert on the bases of the second and third metacarpals. It flexes and radially deviates the wrist. Supplied by the median nerve (C6-C7).
clinical: The radial artery pulse is felt just lateral to the FCR tendon at the wrist.
The FCR sheath is the standard surgical approach to distal radius fractures (volar Henry approach).

{S} flexor digitorum profundus.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
{S} flexor digitorum profundus.desc: Deep forearm flexor arising from the anterior and medial ulna and interosseous membrane. Its four tendons pass through the carpal tunnel, perforate the FDS tendons in the fingers and insert on the bases of the distal phalanges. It is the only muscle that flexes the distal interphalangeal joints. Dual nerve supply: the lateral part (index, middle) by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, the medial part (ring, little) by the ulnar nerve.
clinical: An avulsed FDP tendon from the distal phalanx, often of the ring finger in a grab, is called jersey finger.
The lumbricals arise from its tendons in the palm.

{S} flexor digitorum superficialis.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
{S} flexor digitorum superficialis.desc: Intermediate-layer forearm flexor with a humero-ulnar head (medial epicondyle and coronoid process) and a radial head (anterior oblique line of the radius). Its four tendons pass through the carpal tunnel and split at the proximal phalanx to insert on the sides of the middle phalanges. It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and assists at the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist. Supplied by the median nerve (C7-T1).
clinical: Testing PIP flexion while holding the other fingers straight isolates FDS function.

{S} flexor pollicis longus.name: Flexor pollicis longus
{S} flexor pollicis longus.desc: Deep forearm flexor arising from the anterior radius and interosseous membrane. Its tendon runs through the radial side of the carpal tunnel, between the two sesamoids of the thumb, and inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. It flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint, the only muscle that does so. Supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C7-C8).
clinical: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy weakens FPL and index FDP, so the patient cannot make an OK sign and instead pinches with straight fingertips.

{S} palmaris longus.name: Palmaris longus
{S} palmaris longus.desc: Small superficial flexor arising from the medial epicondyle. Its long slender tendon runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum and blends into the palmar aponeurosis. It weakly flexes the wrist and tenses the palmar fascia. Supplied by the median nerve. It is absent in about 15 percent of people on one or both sides.
clinical: Because it is expendable, its tendon is a common graft for tendon and ligament reconstructions.
The median nerve lies just deep and slightly radial to its tendon at the wrist.

{S} pronator quadratus.name: Pronator quadratus
{S} pronator quadratus.desc: Flat quadrilateral muscle lying deepest in the distal anterior forearm. It arises from the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna and inserts on the anterior distal radius. It is the main pronator of the forearm and holds the distal radius and ulna together. Supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
clinical: It is lifted off the radius during plate fixation of distal radius fractures and covers the plate afterward.

{S} fourth costal cartilage.name: Fourth costal cartilage
{S} fourth costal cartilage.desc: Bar of hyaline cartilage joining the anterior end of the fourth rib to the side of the sternal body at the fourth sternocostal joint. It adds elasticity to the chest wall so the ribs can rise and fall during breathing. Internal intercostal and transversus thoracis muscles attach near it, and pectoralis major covers it anteriorly.
clinical: Inflammation at the costochondral or sternocostal joints (costochondritis) is a common cause of benign chest wall pain in teenagers.

{S} gluteus medius.name: Gluteus medius
{S} gluteus medius.desc: Fan-shaped muscle on the outer ilium, partly covered by gluteus maximus. It arises from the external surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines and inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It abducts and medially rotates the hip and, most importantly, holds the pelvis level when the opposite foot is off the ground. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1).
clinical: Weakness or superior gluteal nerve injury causes a positive Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the opposite side during single-leg stance.
Its tendon is a common site of tendinopathy causing lateral hip pain.

{S} gluteus minimus.name: Gluteus minimus
{S} gluteus minimus.desc: The smallest and deepest gluteal muscle, lying beneath gluteus medius. It arises from the external ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines and inserts on the anterior surface of the greater trochanter. It abducts and medially rotates the hip and works with gluteus medius to keep the pelvis level during walking. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1).
clinical: Tears of the gluteus minimus and medius tendons are sometimes called the rotator cuff tears of the hip.

{S} tensor fasciae latae.name: Tensor fasciae latae
{S} tensor fasciae latae.desc: Small muscle at the front of the lateral hip, arising from the anterior iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine. It inserts into the iliotibial tract, which runs down to Gerdy's tubercle on the lateral tibia. It flexes, abducts and medially rotates the hip and helps stabilize the extended knee. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1).
clinical: Tightness of the TFL and iliotibial band is linked to lateral knee pain in runners (iliotibial band syndrome).
The interval between TFL and sartorius is used in the anterior approach to hip replacement.

{S} gracilis.name: Gracilis
{S} gracilis.desc: Long, strap-like muscle that is the most superficial of the medial thigh adductors. It arises from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts on the upper medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus, with sartorius and semitendinosus. It adducts the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the leg. Supplied by the obturator nerve (L2-L3).
clinical: Its tendon is commonly harvested for ACL reconstruction, and the whole muscle is a workhorse free flap in reconstructive surgery.
Pes anserine bursitis causes pain just below the medial knee.

abductor digiti minimi of {S} hand.name: Abductor digiti minimi of the {S} hand
abductor digiti minimi of {S} hand.desc: The most superficial and medial hypothenar muscle. It arises from the pisiform and the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and inserts on the ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. It abducts the little finger and helps flex its metacarpophalangeal joint. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8-T1).
clinical: Persistent abduction of the little finger from weak third palmar interosseous with unopposed extensor digiti minimi is Wartenberg's sign of ulnar nerve palsy.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of {S} hand.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of the {S} hand
flexor digiti minimi brevis of {S} hand.desc: Hypothenar muscle lying lateral to abductor digiti minimi. It arises from the hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum and inserts on the ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. It flexes the metacarpophalangeal joint of the little finger. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve passes between it and abductor digiti minimi, so hook of hamate fractures can injure the nerve.

opponens digiti minimi of {S} hand.name: Opponens digiti minimi of the {S} hand
opponens digiti minimi of {S} hand.desc: The deepest hypothenar muscle. It arises from the hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum and inserts along the medial border of the fifth metacarpal. It rotates the fifth metacarpal forward and laterally, cupping the palm and bringing the little finger toward the thumb. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Hypothenar wasting with an intact thenar eminence points to an ulnar rather than median nerve lesion.

set of dorsal interossei of {S} hand.name: Dorsal interossei of the {S} hand
set of dorsal interossei of {S} hand.desc: Four bipennate muscles, each arising from the adjacent sides of two metacarpals. They insert on the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of the index, middle (both sides) and ring fingers. They abduct the fingers away from the axis of the middle finger, and help flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8-T1).
clinical: Wasting of the first dorsal interosseous, seen as a hollow between thumb and index, is an early sign of ulnar nerve or T1 root damage.
Remember DAB: dorsal ABduct.

set of lumbricals of {S} hand.name: Lumbricals of the {S} hand
set of lumbricals of {S} hand.region: Upper limb: palm of the hand
set of lumbricals of {S} hand.desc: Four small worm-like muscles that arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus in the palm. Each passes on the radial side of its finger to insert on the extensor expansion. They flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. Lumbricals 1 and 2 are supplied by the median nerve; 3 and 4 by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Loss of lumbrical function in ulnar nerve injury produces the claw hand of the ring and little fingers.
Their unusual origin from a moving tendon makes them important sensors of finger position.

set of palmar interossei of {S} hand.name: Palmar interossei of the {S} hand
set of palmar interossei of {S} hand.desc: Small unipennate muscles, each arising from one metacarpal (the second, fourth and fifth, plus a variable thumb slip). They insert on the proximal phalanx and extensor expansion of the same finger. They adduct the fingers toward the middle finger and help flex the metacarpophalangeal and extend the interphalangeal joints. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Inability to grip a card between straightened fingers tests the palmar interossei and the ulnar nerve.
Remember PAD: palmar ADduct.

superficial head of {S} flexor pollicis.name: Superficial head of the {S} flexor pollicis brevis
superficial head of {S} flexor pollicis.desc: The larger head of flexor pollicis brevis, arising from the flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium. It inserts with the deep head on the radial sesamoid and radial base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. It flexes the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint. Usually supplied by the recurrent (thenar) branch of the median nerve.
clinical: The superficial head often has dual median and ulnar supply, which is why thumb flexion can survive a median nerve injury.

transverse head of {S} adductor pollicis.name: Transverse head of the {S} adductor pollicis
transverse head of {S} adductor pollicis.region: Upper limb: deep palm, thumb web
transverse head of {S} adductor pollicis.desc: Fan-shaped head arising from the palmar ridge of the shaft of the third metacarpal. It converges with the oblique head to insert on the ulnar sesamoid and ulnar base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. It adducts the thumb toward the palm, powering key pinch. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Froment's sign: with ulnar palsy, adductor pollicis is weak, so the patient flexes the thumb tip with FPL to pinch a sheet of paper.

{S} abductor pollicis brevis.name: Abductor pollicis brevis
{S} abductor pollicis brevis.desc: The most superficial thenar muscle. It arises from the flexor retinaculum and the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium, and inserts on the radial base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. It abducts the thumb, lifting it away from the palm at a right angle. Supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8-T1).
clinical: Weakness and wasting of APB is the classic motor sign of carpal tunnel syndrome.

{S} extensor pollicis brevis.name: Extensor pollicis brevis
{S} extensor pollicis brevis.desc: Deep posterior forearm muscle arising from the posterior radius and interosseous membrane, distal to abductor pollicis longus. Its tendon runs with APL in the first extensor compartment and inserts on the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. It extends the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: Together with APL it forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox, where scaphoid fracture tenderness is checked.
It is inflamed in de Quervain tenosynovitis.

{S} flexor pollicis brevis.name: Flexor pollicis brevis
{S} flexor pollicis brevis.desc: Thenar muscle with a superficial head from the flexor retinaculum and trapezium and a deep head from the trapezoid and capitate. It inserts on the radial sesamoid and base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. It flexes the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint and helps opposition. The superficial head is usually supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve and the deep head by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Its variable dual innervation explains why thenar function varies after median or ulnar nerve injury.

{S} opponens pollicis.name: Opponens pollicis
{S} opponens pollicis.desc: Thenar muscle lying deep to abductor pollicis brevis. It arises from the flexor retinaculum and tubercle of the trapezium and inserts along the whole radial border of the first metacarpal. It rotates and flexes the first metacarpal so the thumb pad can meet the fingertips, the movement of opposition that makes precise grip possible. Supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
clinical: Loss of opposition after median nerve injury at the wrist leaves the thumb lying flat beside the fingers (ape hand).

{S} digastric.name: Digastric
{S} digastric.desc: Two-bellied suprahyoid muscle. The posterior belly arises from the mastoid notch of the temporal bone; the anterior belly from the digastric fossa of the mandible. The bellies meet at an intermediate tendon held to the hyoid by a fibrous sling. It elevates the hyoid and helps open the jaw. The anterior belly is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (CN V3), the posterior belly by the facial nerve (CN VII).
clinical: Its bellies outline the submandibular and carotid triangles, key surgical landmarks in the neck.
The double nerve supply reflects its origin from two pharyngeal arches.

{S} geniohyoid.name: Geniohyoid
{S} geniohyoid.region: Head and neck: floor of the mouth
{S} geniohyoid.desc: Short narrow muscle lying above mylohyoid, beside the midline. It arises from the inferior mental spine on the inner mandible and inserts on the front of the hyoid body. It pulls the hyoid forward and up, widening the pharynx in swallowing, and helps depress the mandible. Supplied by C1 fibers carried with the hypoglossal nerve.
clinical: Forward pull on the hyoid by geniohyoid and genioglossus helps keep the upper airway open during sleep.

{S} mylohyoid.name: Mylohyoid
{S} mylohyoid.region: Head and neck: floor of the mouth
{S} mylohyoid.desc: Flat sheet that forms the muscular floor of the mouth. It arises from the mylohyoid line on the inner mandible and inserts on a midline raphe and the hyoid body. It raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid during swallowing and speech and helps depress the jaw. Supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (CN V3).
clinical: Dental infections from teeth whose roots lie below the mylohyoid line spread into the submandibular space, as in Ludwig angina.

{S} omohyoid.name: Omohyoid
{S} omohyoid.desc: Two-bellied infrahyoid strap muscle. The inferior belly arises from the upper border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch, and an intermediate tendon is bound to the clavicle by a fascial sling deep to sternocleidomastoid. The superior belly inserts on the lower border of the hyoid. It depresses and steadies the hyoid. Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3).
clinical: The omohyoid crosses the internal jugular vein and is a landmark in neck dissection.
It divides the posterior triangle into occipital and subclavian triangles.

{S} sternohyoid.name: Sternohyoid
{S} sternohyoid.desc: Thin strap muscle on the front of the neck. It arises from the back of the manubrium and medial clavicle and inserts on the lower border of the hyoid body. It depresses the hyoid after swallowing and speech. Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3).
clinical: Strap muscles are separated in the midline to reach the thyroid gland and trachea during thyroidectomy and tracheostomy.

{S} stylohyoid.name: Stylohyoid
{S} stylohyoid.desc: Slender suprahyoid muscle running with the posterior belly of digastric. It arises from the styloid process of the temporal bone and inserts on the hyoid at the junction of body and greater horn, splitting around the digastric tendon. It pulls the hyoid up and back during swallowing. Supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
clinical: A long styloid process or calcified stylohyoid ligament (Eagle syndrome) can cause throat and neck pain on swallowing.

{S} thyrohyoid.name: Thyrohyoid
{S} thyrohyoid.desc: Short infrahyoid muscle continuing upward from sternothyroid. It arises from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and inserts on the greater horn and body of the hyoid. It depresses the hyoid or, with the hyoid fixed, raises the larynx during swallowing. Supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve.
clinical: Its laryngeal elevation helps close the airway during swallowing; weakness raises aspiration risk.

{S} iliacus.name: Iliacus
{S} iliacus.desc: Fan-shaped muscle filling the iliac fossa on the inner surface of the ilium. It also arises from the iliac crest, sacral ala and front of the sacroiliac joint, then joins the psoas major tendon to insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur as iliopsoas. It is a powerful hip flexor and stabilizes the hip. Supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L3).
clinical: Bleeding into the iliacus, for example in hemophilia or on anticoagulants, can compress the femoral nerve and cause thigh weakness and numbness.

{S} sternothyroid.name: Sternothyroid
{S} sternothyroid.desc: Infrahyoid strap muscle lying deep to sternohyoid. It arises from the back of the manubrium and first costal cartilage and inserts on the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage. It pulls the larynx down after swallowing or voice production. Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3).
clinical: It lies directly on the thyroid lobes, so a large goiter stretches it and it is often divided to remove one.

external intercostal muscle.name: External intercostal muscle
external intercostal muscle.desc: Outermost of the three intercostal layers in each space. Fibers run down and forward from the lower border of one rib to the upper border of the rib below, like hands in front pockets. They extend from the tubercles of the ribs to the costochondral junctions, where they become the external intercostal membrane. They raise the ribs in inspiration and stiffen the chest wall. Supplied by the intercostal nerves (T1-T11).
clinical: Accessory breathing effort recruits the intercostals; visible retractions between ribs are a sign of respiratory distress.

innermost intercostal muscle.name: Innermost intercostal muscle
innermost intercostal muscle.desc: Deepest intercostal layer, with fibers running in the same direction as the internal intercostals. It is best developed in the lateral parts of the lower spaces. The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run between it and the internal intercostal, sheltered in the costal groove. It is thought to act with the internal intercostals in forced expiration. Supplied by the intercostal nerves.
clinical: Chest drains and needles are passed just above the upper border of a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle in the costal groove of the rib above.

internal intercostal muscle.name: Internal intercostal muscle
internal intercostal muscle.desc: Middle intercostal layer, with fibers running down and backward at right angles to the external intercostals. It extends from the sternum to the rib angles, where it becomes the internal intercostal membrane. The interosseous part depresses the ribs in forced expiration, while the parasternal part between the costal cartilages helps raise the ribs in inspiration. Supplied by the intercostal nerves.
clinical: Intercostal nerve blocks numb the space for pain control after rib fractures or chest surgery.

set of {S} levatores costarum breves.name: Short levatores costarum of the {S} side
set of {S} levatores costarum breves.desc: Small muscles on the back of the thorax. Each arises from the tip of a transverse process from C7 to T11 and passes down and laterally to insert on the outer surface of the rib immediately below, between its tubercle and angle. They elevate the ribs and may help extend, laterally bend and rotate the spine. Supplied by the dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.
clinical: They are rarely injured alone but can contribute to posterior rib pain when strained.

set of {S} levatores costarum longi.name: Long levatores costarum of the {S} side
set of {S} levatores costarum longi.desc: Longer slips of the levatores costarum found in the lower thoracic region. Each arises from a thoracic transverse process, skips one rib, and inserts on the second rib below near its angle. Like the short set, they elevate the ribs and assist lateral bending and rotation of the trunk. Supplied by the dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
clinical: Being segmentally innervated by dorsal rami, they are part of the deep back muscle group rather than true intercostals.

{S} transversus thoracis.name: Transversus thoracis
{S} transversus thoracis.desc: Thin muscle on the inner surface of the front chest wall. It arises from the back of the lower sternum and xiphoid process and fans upward and laterally to insert on the inner surfaces of costal cartilages 2 to 6. It weakly depresses the ribs during expiration. Supplied by intercostal nerves. The internal thoracic artery runs between it and the costal cartilages.
clinical: It lies in the plane used for parasternal nerve blocks after heart surgery through a sternotomy.

{S} levator scapulae.name: Levator scapulae
{S} levator scapulae.region: Neck: posterior triangle and upper back
{S} levator scapulae.desc: Strap-like muscle at the side and back of the neck. It arises from the transverse processes of C1 to C4 and inserts on the medial border of the scapula from the superior angle to the root of the spine. It elevates the scapula, rotates it to tilt the glenoid down, and bends the neck to the same side. Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and C3-C4 cervical nerves.
clinical: Spasm of levator scapulae is a classic cause of a stiff neck that hurts when turning the head.

{S} pectineus.name: Pectineus
{S} pectineus.region: Lower limb: medial thigh, femoral triangle
{S} pectineus.desc: Flat quadrangular muscle in the floor of the femoral triangle. It arises from the pecten (pectineal line) of the superior pubic ramus and inserts on the pectineal line of the femur below the lesser trochanter. It adducts and flexes the hip. Usually supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L3), sometimes with a branch of the obturator nerve.
clinical: Its double nerve supply reflects that it sits at the border of the anterior and medial thigh compartments.
It is a common site of groin strain in athletes.

{S} pectoralis minor.name: Pectoralis minor
{S} pectoralis minor.desc: Thin triangular muscle lying deep to pectoralis major. It arises from the outer surfaces of ribs 3 to 5 near their costal cartilages and inserts on the coracoid process of the scapula. It draws the scapula forward and down and helps raise the ribs in forced inspiration. Supplied by the medial pectoral nerve (C8-T1). It divides the axillary artery into three parts.
clinical: A tight pectoralis minor can compress the brachial plexus and axillary vessels beneath it (a form of thoracic outlet syndrome).

{S} coccygeus.name: Coccygeus
{S} coccygeus.desc: Triangular muscle forming the back of the pelvic floor, lying on the deep surface of the sacrospinous ligament. It arises from the ischial spine and inserts on the lateral borders of the lower sacrum and coccyx. It supports the pelvic organs and pulls the coccyx forward after defecation. Supplied by branches of the anterior rami of S4-S5.
clinical: It is largely fused with the sacrospinous ligament, which is used as an anchor in surgical repair of pelvic organ prolapse.

{S} iliococcygeus.name: Iliococcygeus
{S} iliococcygeus.desc: Thin posterior part of levator ani. It arises from the ischial spine and the tendinous arch over obturator internus fascia and inserts into the anococcygeal body and coccyx. It forms a supportive hammock for the pelvic organs and rises against increases in abdominal pressure, as when coughing. Supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3-S4) and the pudendal nerve.
clinical: Pelvic floor weakness can lead to urinary incontinence and prolapse of pelvic organs.

{S} pubococcygeus.name: Pubococcygeus
{S} pubococcygeus.desc: Main middle part of levator ani. It arises from the back of the body of the pubis and the front of the tendinous arch, and runs back to the anococcygeal body and coccyx. It supports the pelvic organs and helps control continence of urine and stool. Supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3-S4) and the pudendal nerve.
clinical: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) strengthens pubococcygeus to treat stress urinary incontinence.

{S} puborectalis.name: Puborectalis
{S} puborectalis.desc: Thick U-shaped part of levator ani arising from the back of the pubis on each side. The two sides join behind the anorectal junction to form a sling that pulls it forward, creating the anorectal angle. It is a key muscle of fecal continence and relaxes to allow defecation. Supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3-S4) and the pudendal nerve.
clinical: Failure of puborectalis to relax during straining (dyssynergic defecation) is a common cause of chronic constipation.

{S} platysma.name: Platysma
{S} platysma.desc: Broad thin sheet of muscle in the superficial fascia of the neck. It arises from the fascia over the upper pectoralis major and deltoid and runs up over the clavicle to the lower border of the mandible, the skin of the lower face and the corner of the mouth. It tenses the neck skin and draws the corners of the mouth down. Supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
clinical: Neck wounds that cut through the platysma are classed as penetrating and need careful assessment of deeper structures.
Platysma bands become visible with age and are targeted in neck-lift surgery.

{S} psoas major.name: Psoas major
{S} psoas major.desc: Long muscle beside the lumbar spine. It arises from the sides of the T12 to L5 vertebral bodies, their intervertebral discs and the lumbar transverse processes, then passes under the inguinal ligament to join iliacus and insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur. It flexes the hip and bends the lumbar spine. Supplied by anterior rami of L1-L3; the lumbar plexus forms within the muscle.
clinical: Pain on hip extension (psoas sign) suggests irritation by a retrocecal appendicitis or psoas abscess.
Infection from the spine can track down its sheath to present as a groin swelling.

{S} rhomboid major.name: Rhomboid major
{S} rhomboid major.region: Back: upper back between the scapulae
{S} rhomboid major.desc: Flat muscle deep to trapezius. It arises from the spinous processes of T2 to T5 and inserts on the medial border of the scapula below the root of the spine down to the inferior angle. It retracts the scapula, rotates it to tilt the glenoid down, and holds it against the chest wall. Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5).
clinical: Dorsal scapular nerve injury weakens the rhomboids and causes mild winging of the medial scapular border.

{S} rhomboid minor.name: Rhomboid minor
{S} rhomboid minor.region: Back: upper back between the scapulae
{S} rhomboid minor.desc: Small band just above rhomboid major and deep to trapezius. It arises from the lower ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 and T1 and inserts on the medial border of the scapula at the root of the spine. It retracts and stabilizes the scapula and helps rotate it downward. Supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5).
clinical: Testing scapular retraction (pressing the hands back on the hips) assesses the rhomboids and C5 root.

{S} infraspinatus muscle.name: Infraspinatus
{S} infraspinatus muscle.desc: Thick triangular rotator cuff muscle filling the infraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula. Its tendon passes behind the shoulder joint to insert on the middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in the glenoid. Supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: Suprascapular nerve compression at the spinoglenoid notch, for example by a ganglion cyst, weakens infraspinatus alone and is seen in volleyball players.

{S} subscapularis.name: Subscapularis
{S} subscapularis.desc: Large triangular rotator cuff muscle filling the subscapular fossa on the front of the scapula. Its tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint to insert on the lesser tubercle of the humerus. It is the main medial rotator of the arm and stops the humeral head sliding forward. Supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5-C6).
clinical: Subscapularis tears are tested with the lift-off and belly-press tests.
It is the only rotator cuff muscle on the front of the scapula.

{S} supraspinatus.name: Supraspinatus
{S} supraspinatus.desc: Rotator cuff muscle in the supraspinous fossa above the spine of the scapula. Its tendon runs under the acromion and coracoacromial arch to insert on the superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus. It starts abduction of the arm and holds the humeral head in the glenoid. Supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: It is the most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon and the classic site of shoulder impingement under the acromion.
The empty can test checks its strength.

{S} scalenus anterior.name: Scalenus anterior
{S} scalenus anterior.desc: Neck muscle lying deep to sternocleidomastoid. It arises from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6 and inserts on the scalene tubercle of the first rib. It raises the first rib in forced inspiration and bends the neck forward and to the same side. Supplied by anterior rami of C4-C6. The phrenic nerve runs down on its front surface, and the subclavian vein passes in front of it while the subclavian artery passes behind.
clinical: The gap between scalenus anterior and medius (scalene triangle) is a site of thoracic outlet syndrome, compressing the brachial plexus and subclavian artery.

{S} scalenus medius.name: Scalenus medius
{S} scalenus medius.desc: The largest scalene muscle. It arises from the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2 to C7 and inserts on the upper surface of the first rib behind the subclavian groove. It raises the first rib and bends the neck to the same side. Supplied by anterior rami of C3-C8. The brachial plexus roots and subclavian artery pass between it and scalenus anterior, and the long thoracic and dorsal scapular nerves pierce it.
clinical: Hypertrophy or fibrous bands of scalenus medius can entrap the long thoracic nerve, causing winged scapula.

{S} scalenus posterior.name: Scalenus posterior
{S} scalenus posterior.desc: The smallest and deepest scalene muscle. It arises from the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4 to C6 and inserts on the outer surface of the second rib. It raises the second rib during forced inspiration and bends the neck to the same side. Supplied by anterior rami of C6-C8.
clinical: Scalene muscles become active accessory muscles of breathing in conditions like asthma and COPD.

{S} second costal cartilage.name: Second costal cartilage
{S} second costal cartilage.desc: Hyaline cartilage joining the second rib to the sternum at the sternal angle, where it articulates with both the manubrium and the sternal body through a joint with two synovial cavities. Its level marks the start of rib counting on the chest. Pectoralis major and the internal intercostals attach near it.
clinical: The sternal angle and second costal cartilage are the landmark used to count ribs and find the second intercostal space for chest needle decompression.

{S} third costal cartilage.name: Third costal cartilage
{S} third costal cartilage.desc: Hyaline cartilage linking the third rib to the side of the sternal body at the third sternocostal joint. It gives the upper chest wall its spring during breathing. Pectoralis minor arises from the third rib near this cartilage, and pectoralis major and transversus thoracis attach in the area.
clinical: Tietze syndrome causes painful swelling of the upper costal cartilages, most often the second and third.

{S} sixth costal cartilage.name: Sixth costal cartilage
{S} sixth costal cartilage.desc: Hyaline cartilage connecting the sixth rib to the lower sternal body near the xiphisternal junction. It is longer than the upper cartilages and slopes upward to reach the sternum. The diaphragm and transversus abdominis attach to the inner surfaces of the lower cartilages, and rectus abdominis inserts on cartilages 5 to 7.
clinical: Costal cartilages can calcify with age and may be mistaken for lung nodules on X-ray.

{S} seventh costal cartilage.name: Seventh costal cartilage
{S} seventh costal cartilage.desc: The longest true-rib cartilage, joining the seventh rib to the sternum at the xiphisternal junction. The eighth to tenth cartilages connect to it, forming the costal margin. Rectus abdominis inserts on it, and the diaphragm and transversus abdominis arise from its inner surface.
clinical: Hypermobile lower costal cartilages can slip and pinch intercostal nerves, causing slipping rib syndrome.

{S} serratus anterior.name: Serratus anterior
{S} serratus anterior.desc: Broad sheet on the side of the chest with saw-tooth slips arising from the outer surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs. It wraps around the chest to insert on the costal surface of the medial border of the scapula. It protracts the scapula, holds it against the chest wall and rotates it upward so the arm can be raised above the head. Supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7).
clinical: Injury to the long thoracic nerve, for example during axillary surgery, causes winging of the scapula when pushing against a wall.

{S} serratus posterior inferior.name: Serratus posterior inferior
{S} serratus posterior inferior.desc: Thin muscle deep to latissimus dorsi. It arises from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 and the thoracolumbar fascia and inserts on the lower borders of ribs 9 to 12 near their angles. It pulls the lower ribs down and back, and may act more as a proprioceptive structure than a strong mover. Supplied by anterior rami of T9-T12.
clinical: Its exact respiratory role is debated; it is mainly a landmark during back dissections.

{S} serratus posterior superior.name: Serratus posterior superior
{S} serratus posterior superior.desc: Thin muscle deep to the rhomboids. It arises from the lower ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 to T3 and inserts on the upper borders of ribs 2 to 5 lateral to their angles. It is thought to raise the upper ribs, though it may serve mainly proprioception. Supplied by the intercostal nerves T2-T5.
clinical: It has been proposed as a source of trigger point pain between the shoulder blades.

{S} splenius capitis.name: Splenius capitis
{S} splenius capitis.desc: Broad strap muscle on the back of the neck deep to trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. It arises from the lower ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 to T3 or T4 and inserts on the mastoid process and lateral superior nuchal line. Together the two sides extend the head; one side turns and tilts the head to the same side. Supplied by dorsal rami of the middle cervical nerves.
clinical: It is commonly strained in whiplash injuries.

{S} splenius cervicis.name: Splenius cervicis
{S} splenius cervicis.desc: Narrow muscle lying just below and lateral to splenius capitis. It arises from the spinous processes of T3 to T6 and inserts on the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1 to C3. It extends the neck and rotates and bends it to the same side. Supplied by dorsal rami of the lower cervical nerves.
clinical: It can contribute to neck pain and stiffness in cervical strain.

{S} subclavius.name: Subclavius
{S} subclavius.desc: Small cylindrical muscle beneath the clavicle. It arises from the junction of the first rib and its costal cartilage and inserts in a groove on the underside of the middle third of the clavicle. It anchors and depresses the clavicle, stabilizing the sternoclavicular joint. Supplied by the nerve to subclavius (C5-C6) from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.
clinical: It cushions the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus from bone fragments in clavicle fractures.

{S} obliquus capitis inferior.name: Obliquus capitis inferior
{S} obliquus capitis inferior.desc: The largest suboccipital muscle and the only one that does not attach to the skull. It arises from the spinous process of the axis (C2) and inserts on the transverse process of the atlas (C1). It rotates the atlas and head to the same side. It forms the lower border of the suboccipital triangle. Supplied by the suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C1).
clinical: The greater occipital nerve hooks around its lower border, where it can be irritated, causing occipital neuralgia.

{S} obliquus capitis superior.name: Obliquus capitis superior
{S} obliquus capitis superior.desc: Small suboccipital muscle arising from the transverse process of the atlas (C1) and inserting on the occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines. It extends the head and bends it to the same side. It forms the lateral border of the suboccipital triangle. Supplied by the suboccipital nerve (C1).
clinical: Suboccipital muscles are rich in muscle spindles and help sense head position; tension here is linked to tension-type and cervicogenic headache.

{S} rectus capitis anterior.name: Rectus capitis anterior
{S} rectus capitis anterior.desc: Short muscle in front of the atlanto-occipital joint, deep to longus capitis. It arises from the front of the lateral mass of the atlas (C1) and inserts on the basilar part of the occipital bone just in front of the foramen magnum. It flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint. Supplied by anterior rami of C1-C2.
clinical: Together with longus capitis it helps stabilize the craniovertebral junction, which is approached through the mouth or nose in some skull base surgeries.

{S} rectus capitis lateralis.name: Rectus capitis lateralis
{S} rectus capitis lateralis.desc: Short muscle arising from the upper surface of the transverse process of the atlas (C1) and inserting on the jugular process of the occipital bone. It bends the head to the same side and steadies it. It lies just behind the internal jugular vein as the vein leaves the jugular foramen. Supplied by anterior rami of C1-C2.
clinical: It is a surgical landmark for the jugular foramen and the lower cranial nerves in skull base approaches.

{S} rectus capitis posterior major.name: Rectus capitis posterior major
{S} rectus capitis posterior major.desc: Suboccipital muscle arising from the spinous process of the axis (C2) and inserting on the lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone. It extends the head and rotates it to the same side. It forms the upper medial border of the suboccipital triangle, which contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve. Supplied by the suboccipital nerve (C1).
clinical: The suboccipital triangle it borders is the key landmark for exposing the vertebral artery on the atlas in posterior skull base surgery.

{S} rectus capitis posterior minor.name: Rectus capitis posterior minor
{S} rectus capitis posterior minor.desc: Small suboccipital muscle arising from the posterior tubercle of the atlas (C1) and inserting on the medial part of the inferior nuchal line. It extends the head. Fibrous connections (the myodural bridge) link it to the dura mater through the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane. Supplied by the suboccipital nerve (C1).
clinical: The myodural bridge may help keep the dura from folding during head movement and has been studied in cervicogenic headache.

fascia lata of {S} thigh.name: Fascia lata of the {S} thigh
fascia lata of {S} thigh.region: Lower limb: deep fascia of the thigh
fascia lata of {S} thigh.desc: Strong deep fascia that wraps the whole thigh like a stocking. It attaches above to the inguinal ligament, pubis, iliac crest, sacrum and ischial tuberosity, and below to the bony landmarks around the knee. Laterally it thickens into the iliotibial tract. Intermuscular septa from it divide the thigh into anterior, medial and posterior compartments, and the saphenous opening lets the great saphenous vein pass through.
clinical: Strips of fascia lata are used as graft material, for example to repair the dura or hernias.
Swelling within its tight compartments can cause compartment syndrome of the thigh.

flexor retinaculum of {S} wrist.name: Flexor retinaculum of the {S} wrist
flexor retinaculum of {S} wrist.desc: Thick fibrous band (transverse carpal ligament) arching across the front of the carpal bones. It attaches to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally and to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially, converting the carpal arch into the carpal tunnel. The median nerve and nine flexor tendons pass beneath it. The thenar and hypothenar muscles arise partly from it.
clinical: Dividing it in carpal tunnel release relieves pressure on the median nerve.
The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to it in Guyon's canal.

intermediate tendon.name: Intermediate tendon
intermediate tendon.desc: A tendon that links two bellies of one muscle, as in the digastric and omohyoid muscles of the neck. The digastric intermediate tendon is held to the hyoid bone by a fibrous sling and passes through stylohyoid, while the omohyoid intermediate tendon is bound to the clavicle by a fascial sling beneath sternocleidomastoid. The sling lets a two-bellied muscle pull around a corner.
clinical: The digastric intermediate tendon and the hypoglossal nerve nearby are landmarks in submandibular surgery.

{S} calcaneal tendon.name: Calcaneal tendon (Achilles tendon)
{S} calcaneal tendon.region: Lower limb: back of the ankle
{S} calcaneal tendon.desc: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed by the joining of the gastrocnemius and soleus tendons in the lower calf. It twists as it descends and inserts on the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneus, with a bursa in front of it. It transmits the force of the calf muscles to plantarflex the foot for walking, running and jumping.
clinical: Rupture usually occurs 2-6 cm above the insertion; a positive Thompson test (no plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed) confirms it.
Tapping it elicits the ankle reflex, which tests the S1 root.

{S} teres major.name: Teres major
{S} teres major.desc: Thick rounded muscle arising from the dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula. It passes forward to insert on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus, alongside latissimus dorsi. It adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm. Supplied by the lower subscapular nerve (C5-C7). Its lower border marks where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery.
clinical: It bounds the quadrangular and triangular spaces, through which the axillary and radial nerves pass.

{S} teres minor.name: Teres minor
{S} teres minor.desc: Narrow rotator cuff muscle arising from the upper two-thirds of the lateral border of the scapula. Its tendon inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus. It laterally rotates the arm and helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid. Supplied by the axillary nerve (C5-C6).
clinical: Axillary nerve injury from shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture weakens teres minor and deltoid and numbs the regimental badge area.

uvular muscle.name: Musculus uvulae
uvular muscle.desc: Paired small muscle inside the uvula, often treated as one. It arises from the posterior nasal spine and the palatine aponeurosis and runs back into the mucosa of the uvula. It shortens and lifts the uvula and thickens the back of the soft palate, helping seal the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech. Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X).
clinical: With a vagus nerve lesion the uvula deviates away from the weak side, toward the intact side.

{S} genioglossus.name: Genioglossus
{S} genioglossus.desc: Fan-shaped extrinsic tongue muscle forming most of the tongue's bulk. It arises from the superior mental spine on the inner mandible and fans into the whole length of the tongue, with lowest fibers reaching the hyoid. It protrudes the tongue and depresses its center. Supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
clinical: With a hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates toward the weak side.
Loss of genioglossus tone in sleep lets the tongue fall back, contributing to obstructive sleep apnea.

{S} hyoglossus.name: Hyoglossus
{S} hyoglossus.desc: Thin quadrilateral extrinsic tongue muscle arising from the body and greater horn of the hyoid and passing up into the side of the tongue. It depresses and retracts the tongue. The lingual nerve, submandibular duct and hypoglossal nerve run on its outer surface, while the lingual artery passes deep to it. Supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
clinical: It is a key landmark in submandibular surgery because it separates the hypoglossal nerve from the lingual artery.

{S} levator veli palatini.name: Levator veli palatini
{S} levator veli palatini.desc: Cylindrical muscle arising from the petrous part of the temporal bone and the cartilage of the auditory (Eustachian) tube. It descends into the soft palate to join its partner in the palatine aponeurosis. It elevates the soft palate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech. Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X).
clinical: In cleft palate the levator fibers insert abnormally, and repairing this sling is central to good speech after surgery.

{S} pterygomandibular raphe.name: Pterygomandibular raphe
{S} pterygomandibular raphe.region: Head and neck: side of the oral cavity
{S} pterygomandibular raphe.desc: Tendinous band running from the hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate down to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. Buccinator attaches to its front edge and the superior pharyngeal constrictor to its back edge, linking the cheek and pharyngeal walls. It shows as a fold of mucosa inside the mouth behind the last molar.
clinical: It is the main landmark for giving an inferior alveolar nerve block in dentistry.

{S} tensor veli palatini.name: Tensor veli palatini
{S} tensor veli palatini.desc: Thin triangular muscle arising from the scaphoid fossa of the sphenoid, the spine of the sphenoid and the auditory tube cartilage. Its tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus and spreads into the palatine aponeurosis. It tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube during swallowing and yawning to equalize middle ear pressure. Supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid (CN V3).
clinical: Poor tensor function in cleft palate impairs auditory tube opening, so these children often get middle ear effusions.

{S} amygdala.name: Amygdala
{S} amygdala.desc: Almond-shaped cluster of nuclei deep to the uncus, just anterior to the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle and the hippocampal head. Its basolateral group receives cortical and thalamic sensory input; the central nucleus projects to the hypothalamus and brainstem to drive fear and autonomic responses. Major outputs run in the stria terminalis and the ventral amygdalofugal pathway. It tags stimuli with emotional value and strengthens emotional memories.
clinical: Bilateral amygdala damage (e.g. Urbach-Wiethe disease) impairs fear recognition; Kluver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral anterior temporal lesions.
The amygdala is a common seizure focus in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, often producing a rising epigastric sensation or fear as an aura.

{S} caudate nucleus.name: Caudate nucleus
{S} caudate nucleus.region: Brain: basal ganglia, wall of lateral ventricle
{S} caudate nucleus.desc: C-shaped nucleus of the dorsal striatum with a head bulging into the lateral wall of the frontal horn, a body along the body of the lateral ventricle, and a tail curving into the roof of the temporal horn. The anterior limb of the internal capsule separates it from the lentiform nucleus. It receives cortical (largely prefrontal) and nigral dopaminergic input and projects to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, helping with goal-directed behaviour, eye movements and cognitive loops.
clinical: Caudate head atrophy in Huntington disease enlarges the frontal horns, giving a box-car ventricle appearance on MRI.
Because the caudate forms the ventricular wall, caudate hemorrhage often ruptures into the lateral ventricle.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.desc: Lies in the posterior cranial fossa beneath the tentorium cerebelli, behind the pons and medulla and roofing the fourth ventricle. A midline vermis and two hemispheres divide into anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes. It connects to the brainstem by superior (mainly output), middle (pontine input) and inferior (spinal and olivary input) peduncles. Its deep nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) carry its output, which coordinates timing, accuracy and balance; each hemisphere controls the same side of the body.
clinical: Hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor; midline vermis lesions cause truncal ataxia and wide-based gait.
Cerebellar hemorrhage or infarct with swelling can compress the brainstem and fourth ventricle, and may need urgent suboccipital decompression.

{S} cingulate gyrus.name: Cingulate gyrus
{S} cingulate gyrus.region: Brain: medial surface of cerebral hemisphere
{S} cingulate gyrus.desc: Arches over the corpus callosum on the medial hemisphere surface, separated from it by the callosal sulcus and bounded above by the cingulate sulcus. It continues behind the splenium through the isthmus into the parahippocampal gyrus, forming much of the limbic lobe. The anterior cingulate handles conflict monitoring, motivation and pain affect; the posterior cingulate is a hub of the default mode network. The cingulum bundle runs within it.
clinical: Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation pushes the cingulate gyrus under the falx and can compress the anterior cerebral artery.
Bilateral anterior cingulate damage can cause akinetic mutism, a profound loss of drive to move or speak.

corpus callosum.name: Corpus callosum
corpus callosum.desc: The largest commissure, about 200 million axons connecting matching cortical areas of the two hemispheres. From front to back it has a rostrum, genu, body (trunk) and splenium; it forms the roof of the lateral ventricles, with the septum pellucidum and fornix hanging beneath it. The genu links prefrontal cortex (forceps minor) and the splenium links occipital and temporal cortex (forceps major).
clinical: Corpus callosotomy is a surgical option for drop attacks in severe epilepsy; splitting it produces disconnection signs on testing.
Splenial lesions can cause alexia without agraphia when combined with left visual cortex damage.

commissure of fornix of forebrain.name: Commissure of the fornix
commissure of fornix of forebrain.region: Brain: under the splenium of corpus callosum
commissure of fornix of forebrain.desc: Also called the hippocampal commissure or psalterium: a thin sheet of fibres crossing between the two crura of the fornix, just beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. It carries fibres linking the left and right hippocampal formations, so memory-related activity can be shared between the two temporal lobes. It is much smaller in humans than in many other mammals.
clinical: It lies in the roof of the lateral ventricle atria, close to approaches used for tumours of the posterior third ventricle and pineal region.

{S} fornix of forebrain.name: Fornix
{S} fornix of forebrain.region: Brain: under corpus callosum, medial ventricle wall
{S} fornix of forebrain.desc: Main efferent tract of the hippocampus. Fimbria fibres leave the hippocampus, form the crus that arches under the splenium, join the opposite side as the body beneath the corpus callosum, then split into columns that pass in front of the interventricular foramina and behind the anterior commissure. Most fibres end in the mammillary body, with others reaching the septal nuclei and anterior thalamus, forming part of the Papez circuit for memory.
clinical: Bilateral fornix injury, for example during colloid cyst surgery near the foramen of Monro, can cause severe anterograde amnesia.
The fornix columns form the anterior border of the interventricular foramen, a key landmark in endoscopic third ventricle surgery.

orbital gyrus.name: Orbital gyri
orbital gyrus.region: Brain: inferior (orbital) surface of frontal lobe
orbital gyrus.desc: Gyri on the undersurface of the frontal lobe, resting on the orbital plates above the orbits, arranged around an H-shaped orbital sulcus into anterior, posterior, medial and lateral orbital gyri; the gyrus rectus lies medially beside the olfactory tract. Together they form orbitofrontal cortex, which links with the amygdala, hypothalamus and striatum to judge reward value, guide decisions and control social behaviour.
clinical: Orbitofrontal damage, often from contusion on the rough orbital roof after head injury, causes disinhibition and poor social judgment.
Olfactory groove meningiomas compress this region and may present with personality change and loss of smell.

{S} inferior frontal gyrus.name: Inferior frontal gyrus
{S} inferior frontal gyrus.desc: Lowest of the three horizontal gyri on the lateral frontal lobe, below the inferior frontal sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Rami of the lateral sulcus divide it into pars orbitalis, pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, pars triangularis and pars opercularis form Broca area (Brodmann 44 and 45), essential for speech production and grammar. It is supplied by superior division branches of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: A dominant-hemisphere lesion here causes Broca (expressive) aphasia: effortful, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
Surgeons map this area with awake stimulation before resecting nearby tumours to protect speech.

{S} middle frontal gyrus.name: Middle frontal gyrus
{S} middle frontal gyrus.desc: Lies between the superior and inferior frontal sulci on the lateral frontal lobe, running forward from the precentral sulcus. Its posterior part contains the frontal eye field (around Brodmann 8), which drives voluntary saccades to the opposite side; more anteriorly it forms dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann 46 and 9), central to working memory, planning and attention. Supplied mainly by the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: An acute frontal eye field lesion causes gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion; a seizure focus here drives the eyes away.
The middle frontal gyrus is a common landmark for transcortical approaches to the lateral ventricle.

{S} superior frontal gyrus.name: Superior frontal gyrus
{S} superior frontal gyrus.region: Brain: dorsal and medial frontal lobe
{S} superior frontal gyrus.desc: Uppermost frontal gyrus, running from the frontal pole back to the precentral sulcus above the superior frontal sulcus and continuing onto the medial surface. Its posterior medial part holds the supplementary motor area (medial Brodmann 6), which plans and initiates movement sequences; anteriorly it contributes to prefrontal cognition. Medially it is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, laterally by the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: Resection of the supplementary motor area can cause a temporary SMA syndrome of contralateral weakness and mutism that usually recovers over weeks.
Parasagittal meningiomas often press on this gyrus.

{S} globus pallidus.name: Globus pallidus
{S} globus pallidus.region: Brain: basal ganglia, medial to putamen
{S} globus pallidus.desc: Pale, wedge-shaped nucleus forming the medial part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen and lateral to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The external segment (GPe) is part of the indirect pathway; the internal segment (GPi) is a major basal ganglia output, sending inhibitory GABAergic fibres through the ansa and lenticular fasciculus to the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus. It is supplied by lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal branches.
clinical: GPi is a standard deep brain stimulation target for dystonia and Parkinson disease.
Bilateral pallidal injury is classic after carbon monoxide poisoning and shows as symmetric T2 bright lesions.

{S} hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
{S} hippocampus.region: Brain: medial temporal lobe, floor of temporal horn
{S} hippocampus.desc: Curved ridge of archicortex in the floor and medial wall of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, with a head (pes), body and tail that sweeps up under the splenium. Its subfields CA1 to CA4 with the dentate gyrus form the trisynaptic circuit fed by entorhinal cortex. Output leaves through the alveus, fimbria and fornix. It encodes new declarative memories and spatial maps. Supplied by hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral and anterior choroidal arteries.
clinical: Hippocampal sclerosis, with loss of CA1 neurons, is the commonest cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy and can be treated by resection.
CA1 is very sensitive to hypoxia; bilateral injury causes severe anterograde amnesia.

hypothalamus.name: Hypothalamus
hypothalamus.region: Brain: diencephalon, floor and walls of third ventricle
hypothalamus.desc: Forms the floor and lower lateral walls of the third ventricle, below the hypothalamic sulcus, from the lamina terminalis back to the mammillary bodies, with the optic chiasm in front and the infundibulum descending to the pituitary. Its nuclei control temperature, hunger, thirst, water balance, circadian rhythm and autonomic output, and regulate the pituitary through releasing hormones in the portal system and vasopressin-secreting axons to the posterior lobe.
clinical: Damage to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei or the stalk can cause central diabetes insipidus.
Craniopharyngiomas and hypothalamic hamartomas arise here; hamartomas can cause gelastic (laughing) seizures.

intermediate hypothalamic region.name: Intermediate (tuberal) hypothalamic region
intermediate hypothalamic region.region: Brain: middle hypothalamus, above the tuber cinereum
intermediate hypothalamic region.desc: The middle zone of the hypothalamus, lying above the tuber cinereum and median eminence, between the anterior (supraoptic) and posterior (mammillary) regions. It contains the ventromedial, dorsomedial and arcuate nuclei. The arcuate nucleus senses leptin and other signals to regulate appetite and releases dopamine and releasing hormones into the hypophyseal portal vessels; the ventromedial nucleus contributes to satiety and energy balance.
clinical: Tumours or surgery affecting this region can cause hypothalamic obesity, with uncontrolled appetite that is hard to treat.

mammillary body.name: Mammillary bodies
mammillary body.desc: Paired round swellings on the underside of the posterior hypothalamus, in front of the posterior perforated substance and between the cerebral peduncles. Each contains medial and lateral mammillary nuclei. They receive the fornix from the hippocampus and send the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, a key link in the Papez memory circuit; the mammillotegmental tract reaches the midbrain.
clinical: Mammillary body atrophy is characteristic of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency, with marked memory loss and confabulation.

{S} insula.name: Insula
{S} insula.region: Brain: deep in the lateral sulcus
{S} insula.desc: Cortex buried at the floor of the lateral (Sylvian) fissure, hidden by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula and outlined by the circular sulcus. A central sulcus divides it into short anterior and long posterior gyri; its limen joins the anterior perforated substance. It processes taste, visceral and pain sensation, interoception and autonomic control. The M2 segments of the middle cerebral artery run over its surface, and the extreme capsule, claustrum and external capsule lie deep to it.
clinical: Loss of the insular ribbon on CT is an early sign of middle cerebral artery infarction.
Insular gliomas are surgically demanding because of the overlying MCA branches and lenticulostriate arteries nearby.

medulla oblongata.name: Medulla oblongata
medulla oblongata.region: Brainstem: lowest part, above foramen magnum
medulla oblongata.desc: Lowest part of the brainstem, from the pontomedullary junction to just above the first cervical nerve rootlets at the foramen magnum. Its front shows the pyramids (corticospinal tracts, which mostly cross at the pyramidal decussation) and the olives; its back forms the lower floor of the fourth ventricle. It holds nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII, the nucleus ambiguus, solitary nucleus and respiratory and cardiovascular centres. Supplied by vertebral, anterior spinal and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.
clinical: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from vertebral or PICA occlusion causes vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and crossed pain loss.
Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla and can stop breathing.

brachium of {S} inferior colliculus.name: Brachium of the {S} inferior colliculus
brachium of {S} inferior colliculus.desc: A band of fibres running forward and upward from the inferior colliculus along the side of the midbrain to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus. It is a link in the ascending auditory pathway, carrying signals that have already been processed in the cochlear nuclei, superior olive, lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus on their way to auditory cortex.
clinical: Because auditory pathways are bilateral above the cochlear nuclei, a unilateral brachium lesion rarely causes deafness in one ear.

brachium of {S} superior colliculus.name: Brachium of the {S} superior colliculus
brachium of {S} superior colliculus.desc: Fibre band passing between the lateral geniculate body and superior colliculus, along the side of the midbrain. It carries optic tract fibres that bypass the geniculate to reach the superior colliculus and pretectal area, plus cortical fibres. This route supports visual orienting, reflex eye and head turning, and, through pretectal relays, the pupillary light reflex.
clinical: Pretectal fibres near this route explain why some optic tract lesions affect the pupil response, while lesions of the geniculate radiations spare it.

midbrain.name: Midbrain
midbrain.desc: Shortest brainstem segment, passing through the tentorial notch between the pons and diencephalon. Front to back it has the cerebral peduncles (crura carrying corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres), the tegmentum (red nucleus, substantia nigra, oculomotor and trochlear nuclei, reticular formation) and the tectum (superior and inferior colliculi) around the cerebral aqueduct. It controls eye movement, pupillary reflexes, arousal and motor modulation. Supplied by posterior cerebral, superior cerebellar and basilar perforating arteries.
clinical: Weber syndrome, from a ventral midbrain stroke, causes an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome from pineal tumours causes upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation.

peduncle of midbrain.name: Cerebral peduncle
peduncle of midbrain.desc: Each half of the midbrain in front of the cerebral aqueduct, made of the crus cerebri in front, the substantia nigra, and the tegmentum behind it. The crus carries descending fibres from the internal capsule: frontopontine fibres medially, corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the middle, and parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibres laterally. The two peduncles border the interpeduncular fossa, where the oculomotor nerves emerge.
clinical: In uncal herniation the opposite peduncle can be pushed against the tentorium (Kernohan notch), causing weakness on the same side as the mass, a false localising sign.

{S} inferior colliculus.name: Inferior colliculus
{S} inferior colliculus.desc: Lower pair of rounded swellings on the back of the midbrain, just above the trochlear nerve exit. It is the main auditory relay of the midbrain: it receives the lateral lemniscus from both ears and sends fibres through its brachium to the medial geniculate body. It integrates sound timing and intensity cues for localisation and contributes to startle and orienting reflexes.
clinical: Tectal plate gliomas in this region often present with hydrocephalus because they narrow the cerebral aqueduct.

{S} superior colliculus.name: Superior colliculus
{S} superior colliculus.desc: Upper pair of rounded swellings on the back of the midbrain, below the pineal gland. Its layered structure receives retinal, visual cortical, auditory and somatosensory input and builds a map of space; deep layers drive saccades and head turning through the tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts. The nearby pretectal area handles the pupillary light reflex.
clinical: Compression of the dorsal midbrain here, as by a pineal tumour, causes Parinaud syndrome with impaired upward gaze.

{S} precentral gyrus.name: Precentral gyrus
{S} precentral gyrus.desc: Strip of cortex in front of the central sulcus, the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4). Its giant Betz cells and other layer V neurons send corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres that control the opposite side of the body. The motor homunculus maps face and hand low on the lateral surface (MCA territory) and the leg on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule (ACA territory). The hand knob is a reliable MRI landmark.
clinical: Strokes or tumours here cause contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs; the pattern shows which part of the homunculus is hit.
Jacksonian seizures start here and march along the homunculus, for example from hand to face.

{S} occipital lobe.name: Occipital lobe
{S} occipital lobe.desc: Back of each hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus medially and an imaginary line to the preoccipital notch laterally, resting on the tentorium cerebelli. The calcarine sulcus on its medial surface holds primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex), with the cuneus above and lingual gyrus below; the macula maps to the occipital pole. Surrounding association cortex analyses form, colour and motion. Supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery.
clinical: Occipital infarction causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing because the pole may also receive MCA supply.
Bilateral occipital damage can cause cortical blindness, sometimes with denial of blindness (Anton syndrome).

inferior branch of {S} oculomotor nerve.name: Inferior branch of the {S} oculomotor nerve
inferior branch of {S} oculomotor nerve.desc: Larger of the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve, formed in the cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure and entering the orbit through the common tendinous ring. It supplies the medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique, and carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion for the pupil sphincter and ciliary muscle.
clinical: Isolated inferior division lesions are rare; they weaken adduction and depression and may give a dilated pupil.

superior branch of {S} oculomotor nerve.name: Superior branch of the {S} oculomotor nerve
superior branch of {S} oculomotor nerve.desc: Smaller division of the oculomotor nerve, entering the orbit through the common tendinous ring and running up lateral to the optic nerve. It supplies the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris, raising the eye and the upper eyelid.
clinical: A lesion causes ptosis and weak upgaze; the pupil is spared because its fibres travel in the inferior division.

communicating branch of {S} nasociliary.name: Communicating branch of the {S} nasociliary nerve with the {S} ciliary ganglion
communicating branch of {S} nasociliary.desc: Sensory root of the ciliary ganglion: a slender branch from the nasociliary nerve that enters the ganglion and passes through it without synapsing. Its fibres continue in the short ciliary nerves to carry sensation from the cornea, iris and ciliary body back to the ophthalmic nerve.
clinical: These fibres form part of the sensory (afferent) limb of the corneal reflex.

{S} anterior ethmoidal nerve.name: Anterior ethmoidal nerve
{S} anterior ethmoidal nerve.region: Orbit, anterior cranial fossa and nasal cavity
{S} anterior ethmoidal nerve.desc: Branch of the nasociliary nerve that leaves the medial orbit through the anterior ethmoidal foramen with its artery, briefly crosses the anterior cranial fossa beside the cribriform plate, then descends into the nasal cavity. It supplies the anterior ethmoidal air cells, the front of the nasal septum and lateral wall, and its external nasal branch supplies skin of the nose down to the tip.
clinical: Vesicles on the tip of the nose in shingles (Hutchinson sign) indicate nasociliary involvement and a higher risk of eye disease.

{S} frontal nerve.name: Frontal nerve
{S} frontal nerve.desc: Largest branch of the ophthalmic nerve. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring, then runs forward between the levator palpebrae superioris and the orbital roof periosteum. It divides into the supra-orbital and supratrochlear nerves, which carry sensation from the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid and frontal sinus.
clinical: Supraorbital and supratrochlear nerve blocks numb the forehead for laceration repair and are sometimes used in headache treatment.

{S} lacrimal nerve.name: Lacrimal nerve
{S} lacrimal nerve.desc: Smallest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure above the common tendinous ring and running along the upper border of the lateral rectus to the lacrimal gland. It supplies sensation to the gland, conjunctiva and lateral upper eyelid. It also picks up postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the zygomatic nerve, ultimately from the pterygopalatine ganglion, to drive tear secretion.
clinical: Lesions of the facial nerve proximal to the geniculate ganglion reduce tearing because these secretomotor fibres originate with the facial nerve.

{S} long ciliary nerve.name: Long ciliary nerves
{S} long ciliary nerve.desc: Usually two or three branches of the nasociliary nerve that run alongside the optic nerve and pierce the sclera to travel forward between the sclera and choroid. They carry sensation from the cornea, iris and ciliary body and convey postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion to the dilator pupillae muscle.
clinical: Interruption of the sympathetic pathway anywhere along its course to these fibres causes Horner syndrome with a small pupil.

{S} nasociliary nerve.name: Nasociliary nerve
{S} nasociliary nerve.desc: Branch of the ophthalmic nerve that enters the orbit inside the common tendinous ring, crosses above the optic nerve with the ophthalmic artery, and runs along the medial wall. It gives the sensory root to the ciliary ganglion, long ciliary nerves, the posterior and anterior ethmoidal nerves, and ends as the infratrochlear nerve. It carries sensation from the eyeball, cornea, ethmoid sinuses, nasal cavity and skin of the nose.
clinical: Corneal sensation travels largely in this nerve, so its testing with the corneal reflex checks the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

{S} ophthalmic nerve.name: Ophthalmic nerve
{S} ophthalmic nerve.desc: First and smallest division of the trigeminal nerve, purely sensory. It leaves the trigeminal ganglion, runs forward in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the trochlear nerve, and divides into the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves that pass through the superior orbital fissure. It supplies the eyeball, cornea, upper eyelid, forehead and scalp to the vertex, the dorsum of the nose, and parts of the nasal cavity, sinuses and dura.
clinical: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is shingles in this division and needs urgent eye assessment.
