Cavernous sinus lesions can affect V1 together with cranial nerves III, IV and VI.

{S} posterior ethmoidal nerve.name: Posterior ethmoidal nerve
{S} posterior ethmoidal nerve.desc: Small branch of the nasociliary nerve that leaves the orbit through the posterior ethmoidal foramen. It supplies the mucosa of the posterior ethmoidal air cells and the sphenoid sinus. It is inconstant and absent in some people.
clinical: The posterior ethmoidal foramen lies close to the optic canal, so it is a landmark for protecting the optic nerve during orbital surgery.

{S} supra-orbital nerve.name: Supra-orbital nerve
{S} supra-orbital nerve.desc: Larger terminal branch of the frontal nerve. It leaves the orbit through the supra-orbital notch or foramen at the upper orbital rim, about in line with the pupil, and divides into medial and lateral branches. It supplies the upper eyelid, conjunctiva, frontal sinus and skin of the forehead and scalp back to near the vertex.
clinical: Pressing on the supra-orbital notch is a standard painful stimulus when assessing consciousness in head-injured patients.

optic chiasm.name: Optic chiasm
optic chiasm.region: Brain: suprasellar region, front of third ventricle
optic chiasm.desc: X-shaped junction where the two optic nerves meet above the diaphragma sellae and pituitary, in front of the infundibulum and below the floor of the third ventricle. Fibres from the nasal half of each retina, carrying the temporal visual fields, cross here; temporal retinal fibres stay on the same side. The internal carotid arteries lie lateral to it and the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries above.
clinical: Pituitary macroadenomas press upward on the chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia.
Anterior communicating artery aneurysms and craniopharyngiomas can also compress the chiasm.

{S} optic nerve.name: Optic nerve
{S} optic nerve.desc: About 1.2 million retinal ganglion cell axons forming a tract of the central nervous system, wrapped in all three meningeal layers. It runs from the optic disc through the orbit inside the cone of extraocular muscles, through the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery, to the optic chiasm. The central retinal artery and vein enter it behind the globe. It carries all visual input from one eye.
clinical: Because the subarachnoid space surrounds it, raised intracranial pressure causes papilloedema.
Optic neuritis, often linked to multiple sclerosis, causes painful vision loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect.

{S} optic tract.name: Optic tract
{S} optic tract.region: Brain: wraps around the cerebral peduncle
{S} optic tract.desc: Continuation of the visual pathway from the optic chiasm, sweeping back around the cerebral peduncle to end mostly in the lateral geniculate body. Each tract carries fibres from the temporal retina of the same eye and the nasal retina of the opposite eye, so it represents the opposite visual field. A smaller share goes to the pretectal area and superior colliculus for reflexes. It is supplied mainly by the anterior choroidal artery.
clinical: A tract lesion causes an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with a relative afferent pupillary defect in the opposite eye.

{S} parahippocampal gyrus.name: Parahippocampal gyrus
{S} parahippocampal gyrus.desc: Gyrus on the inferomedial temporal lobe between the hippocampal sulcus and the collateral sulcus, continuous behind with the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus. Its front hooks back as the uncus. The anterior part forms entorhinal cortex, the main gateway between neocortex and hippocampus through the perforant path; the posterior part (parahippocampal place area) helps recognise scenes and places.
clinical: The uncus is the part that herniates over the tentorial edge in uncal herniation, compressing the oculomotor nerve and causing a dilated pupil.
Entorhinal cortex is among the first regions to show tangles in Alzheimer disease.

{S} angular gyrus.name: Angular gyrus
{S} angular gyrus.desc: Part of the inferior parietal lobule that arches around the upturned end of the superior temporal sulcus, behind the supramarginal gyrus (roughly Brodmann area 39). It is a heteromodal hub joining visual, auditory and somatosensory information, important for reading, writing, calculation, semantic processing and spatial attention. Supplied by the angular branch of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: A dominant angular gyrus lesion can cause Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion.
Damage here can also cause alexia with agraphia.

{S} superior parietal lobule.name: Superior parietal lobule
{S} superior parietal lobule.desc: Area of parietal cortex above the intraparietal sulcus and behind the postcentral sulcus, continuous medially with the precuneus (Brodmann 5 and 7). It integrates touch and joint position with vision to build a body schema and guide reaching and grasping in space. It is supplied mainly by the anterior cerebral artery medially and the middle cerebral artery laterally.
clinical: Lesions can cause optic ataxia, inaccurate reaching under visual guidance, and contribute to Balint syndrome when bilateral.

{S} supramarginal gyrus.name: Supramarginal gyrus
{S} supramarginal gyrus.desc: Front part of the inferior parietal lobule, curving around the upturned end of the lateral sulcus (roughly Brodmann area 40). In the dominant hemisphere it joins Wernicke and Broca areas via the arcuate fasciculus beneath it and supports phonological working memory; it also contributes to praxis and touch interpretation. Supplied by parietal branches of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: Lesions here or the underlying arcuate fasciculus can cause conduction aphasia, with poor repetition despite fluent speech and good comprehension.
Dominant inferior parietal damage can cause ideomotor apraxia.

pons.name: Pons
pons.desc: Middle segment of the brainstem, resting on the clivus in front and forming the upper floor of the fourth ventricle behind. Its basilar part holds descending corticospinal fibres and pontine nuclei whose crossing fibres form the middle cerebellar peduncles. The tegmentum contains nuclei of cranial nerves V to VIII, the medial longitudinal fasciculus, paramedian pontine reticular formation and ascending lemnisci. Supplied by pontine perforators of the basilar artery.
clinical: Basilar thrombosis or a large ventral pontine infarct can cause locked-in syndrome, with consciousness and vertical eye movements preserved.
Rapid correction of low sodium can cause osmotic demyelination of the central pons.

{S} putamen.name: Putamen
{S} putamen.region: Brain: basal ganglia, lateral lentiform nucleus
{S} putamen.desc: Outer part of the lentiform nucleus, lateral to the globus pallidus and separated from the claustrum and insula by the external capsule. With the caudate it forms the dorsal striatum, linked to it by grey bridges across the internal capsule. It receives motor and sensory cortex and nigral dopamine input and projects to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra within the motor loop. Supplied by lateral lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: The putamen is the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, from rupture of lenticulostriate arteries.
Dopamine loss in the putamen underlies the motor signs of Parkinson disease.

{S} postcentral gyrus.name: Postcentral gyrus
{S} postcentral gyrus.desc: Strip of cortex behind the central sulcus, the primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2). It receives touch, vibration, joint position, pain and temperature from the opposite body via the ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial thalamic nuclei. A sensory homunculus mirrors the motor map, with face and hand laterally and the leg on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule.
clinical: Lesions cause contralateral loss of fine touch, position sense and two-point discrimination, with astereognosis.
Seizures starting here produce a spreading tingling (sensory Jacksonian march).

spinal cord.name: Spinal cord
spinal cord.region: Vertebral canal: foramen magnum to about L1-L2
spinal cord.desc: Continuation of the medulla from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris, usually ending at the L1-L2 disc in adults, with cervical and lumbar enlargements for the limbs. Central grey matter (dorsal, ventral and in the thoracic and upper lumbar cord lateral horns) is surrounded by white columns carrying ascending tracts (dorsal columns, spinothalamic, spinocerebellar) and descending tracts (corticospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal). Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves arise from it. Supplied by one anterior and two posterior spinal arteries plus radicular feeders.
clinical: Brown-Sequard syndrome from hemisection causes same-side weakness and position-sense loss with opposite-side pain and temperature loss.
Lumbar puncture is done below L2, usually at L3-L4 or L4-L5, to avoid the cord.

anterior part of {S} superior temporal g.name: Anterior part of the {S} superior temporal gyrus
anterior part of {S} superior temporal g.desc: Front portion of the superior temporal gyrus, lying below the lateral sulcus toward the temporal pole. It belongs to the auditory association and ventral language streams, helping recognise sounds and voices and combine words into meaning. The transverse temporal (Heschl) gyri forming primary auditory cortex lie on the upper surface of the gyrus within the lateral sulcus, around its middle.
clinical: Anterior temporal lobectomy for epilepsy removes part of this region; on the dominant side language mapping or limited resection reduces naming problems.

posterior part of {S} superior temporal.name: Posterior part of the {S} superior temporal gyrus
posterior part of {S} superior temporal.desc: Back portion of the superior temporal gyrus, including the planum temporale. In the dominant hemisphere it contains Wernicke area (posterior Brodmann 22), essential for understanding spoken language, and connects to Broca area through the arcuate fasciculus. It is supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: A dominant lesion causes Wernicke aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension, often without weakness.
Awake mapping is used to protect this region during tumour surgery.

{S} fusiform gyrus.name: Fusiform gyrus
{S} fusiform gyrus.region: Brain: inferior temporal and occipital surface
{S} fusiform gyrus.desc: Long spindle-shaped gyrus on the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes, between the collateral sulcus medially and the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally. It belongs to the ventral visual stream: the fusiform face area recognises faces, and in the dominant hemisphere the visual word form area recognises written words. Supplied mostly by the posterior cerebral artery.
clinical: Bilateral or right fusiform damage can cause prosopagnosia, the inability to recognise familiar faces.
Left-sided damage can cause pure alexia.

{S} inferior temporal gyrus.name: Inferior temporal gyrus
{S} inferior temporal gyrus.region: Brain: lateral and inferior temporal lobe
{S} inferior temporal gyrus.desc: Lowest gyrus on the lateral temporal surface, below the inferior temporal sulcus, curving onto the underside of the lobe beside the fusiform gyrus. It is high-level visual association cortex in the ventral "what" stream, recognising objects and their meaning. It is supplied by temporal branches of the middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
clinical: The inferior temporal gyrus is often used as a corridor for reaching the temporal horn or medial temporal structures while sparing the superior gyrus language areas.

{S} middle temporal gyrus.name: Middle temporal gyrus
{S} middle temporal gyrus.desc: Gyrus between the superior and inferior temporal sulci on the lateral temporal lobe. It supports semantic memory and word meaning, especially in the dominant hemisphere, and its posterior part near the occipital lobe includes the motion-sensitive visual area MT/V5. Supplied by temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery.
clinical: Lesions near the occipitotemporal junction can cause akinetopsia, difficulty perceiving motion.
The middle temporal gyrus is a common entry point for transcortical approaches to the temporal horn.

{S} lateral geniculate body.name: Lateral geniculate body
{S} lateral geniculate body.desc: Small swelling under the back of the thalamus (pulvinar) where most optic tract fibres end. It has six layers: layers 1, 4 and 6 receive the opposite eye and layers 2, 3 and 5 the same eye; layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular (motion) and 3 to 6 parvocellular (detail and colour). It projects via the optic radiations to primary visual cortex. Supplied by the anterior choroidal and posterior choroidal arteries.
clinical: Lesions cause a contralateral homonymous field defect; anterior and lateral choroidal infarcts produce distinctive wedge or sector patterns.

{S} medial geniculate body.name: Medial geniculate body
{S} medial geniculate body.desc: Rounded swelling under the pulvinar, medial to the lateral geniculate body. It is the thalamic relay of the auditory pathway, receiving the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projecting through the acoustic radiation in the sublentiform part of the internal capsule to primary auditory cortex in the transverse temporal gyri.
clinical: Because hearing reaches both hemispheres, a one-sided medial geniculate lesion rarely causes deafness but can impair sound localisation.

{S} thalamus.name: Thalamus
{S} thalamus.region: Brain: diencephalon, lateral wall of third ventricle
{S} thalamus.desc: Paired egg-shaped mass of grey matter forming the lateral walls of the third ventricle, often joined by the interthalamic adhesion, with the posterior limb of the internal capsule lateral to it. The internal medullary lamina divides it into anterior, medial and lateral groups, including VPL and VPM (body and face sensation), VL and VA (motor loops), the pulvinar and geniculate bodies. It relays and gates nearly all input to cortex and supports arousal. Supplied by thalamoperforating, thalamogeniculate and choroidal branches.
clinical: Thalamic stroke can cause contralateral sensory loss and later a burning central pain (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome).
The ventral intermediate nucleus is a deep brain stimulation target for essential tremor.

{S} infratrochlear nerve.name: Infratrochlear nerve
{S} infratrochlear nerve.region: Orbit: medial angle of the eye
{S} infratrochlear nerve.desc: Terminal branch of the nasociliary nerve that runs along the medial orbital wall below the trochlea of the superior oblique tendon. It supplies skin of the medial eyelids and side of the upper nose, the conjunctiva near the medial angle, the lacrimal sac and the caruncle. It is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve, not the trochlear nerve.
clinical: An infratrochlear nerve block helps anaesthetise the medial eyelid and lacrimal sac for minor procedures.

{S} supratrochlear nerve.name: Supratrochlear nerve
{S} supratrochlear nerve.desc: Smaller terminal branch of the frontal nerve, passing above the trochlea at the medial end of the orbital rim, medial to the supra-orbital nerve. It supplies skin of the medial upper eyelid, conjunctiva and lower central forehead. It belongs to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, not the trochlear nerve.
clinical: It is blocked with the supra-orbital nerve to anaesthetise the forehead for wound repair.

{S} trochlear nerve.name: Trochlear nerve
{S} trochlear nerve.desc: Thinnest cranial nerve and the only one to leave the back of the brainstem, emerging below the inferior colliculus after crossing in the superior medullary velum, so each nucleus supplies the opposite eye. It wraps around the midbrain, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring, and supplies the superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye and intorts it.
clinical: Palsy causes vertical double vision worse looking down, as on stairs or reading, and patients tilt the head away from the affected side.
Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to head trauma.

cerebral aqueduct.name: Cerebral aqueduct
cerebral aqueduct.desc: Narrow channel, about 1.5 cm long, through the midbrain between the tectum behind and the tegmentum in front, connecting the third ventricle to the fourth. It is surrounded by periaqueductal grey matter, which modulates pain and defensive behaviour. It contains no choroid plexus and is the narrowest point of the ventricular system.
clinical: Aqueductal stenosis, congenital or from a tectal tumour, causes obstructive hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth.
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy bypasses the blockage.

fourth ventricle.name: Fourth ventricle
fourth ventricle.desc: Tent-shaped cavity behind the pons and upper medulla and in front of the cerebellum. Its diamond-shaped floor (rhomboid fossa) carries the facial colliculus, hypoglossal and vagal trigones and the area postrema; its roof is the superior and inferior medullary vela with choroid plexus. It receives CSF from the aqueduct and drains to the subarachnoid space through the median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka), and below into the central canal.
clinical: Medulloblastoma and ependymoma in children often fill the fourth ventricle and cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
Dandy-Walker malformation enlarges the fourth ventricle into a posterior fossa cyst.

third ventricle.name: Third ventricle
third ventricle.desc: Narrow midline slit between the two thalami and hypothalami. Its roof is a thin layer with choroid plexus under the fornix; its floor holds the optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies; the lamina terminalis and anterior commissure form its front wall. It connects to each lateral ventricle through an interventricular foramen (Monro) and to the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct. Optic, infundibular, suprapineal and pineal recesses project from it.
clinical: A colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro can block both lateral ventricles and cause sudden hydrocephalus.
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy perforates its floor between the infundibulum and mammillary bodies.

wall of ventricle.name: Wall of the ventricle
wall of ventricle.desc: The lining walls of the brain ventricles, covered by ependyma, a single layer of ciliated cells that help move cerebrospinal fluid. The walls are formed by surrounding structures such as the caudate nucleus, thalamus, corpus callosum, septum pellucidum and fornix. A subventricular zone beside the lateral ventricles keeps a small population of neural stem cells in adults.
clinical: Periventricular white matter next to these walls is a classic site for multiple sclerosis plaques, which often lie perpendicular to the ventricles.
Ventriculitis after infection shows as enhancement of the ventricular walls on MRI.

{S} lateral ventricle.name: Lateral ventricle
{S} lateral ventricle.desc: Largest CSF cavity, C-shaped, inside each hemisphere. It has a frontal horn (bounded by the corpus callosum, septum pellucidum and caudate head), a body, an atrium (trigone) where most choroid plexus sits, an occipital horn and a temporal horn whose floor holds the hippocampus. It drains into the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen of Monro.
clinical: An external ventricular drain is placed into the frontal horn through Kocher point to measure pressure and drain CSF.
Asymmetric or enlarged ventricles on CT can signal hydrocephalus or mass effect.

anterior commissure.name: Anterior commissure
anterior commissure.region: Brain: front wall of third ventricle
anterior commissure.desc: Compact bundle of crossing fibres in the lamina terminalis, in front of the fornix columns. Its smaller anterior part links olfactory structures and its larger posterior part links the anterior and inferior temporal lobes, including the amygdalae. Together with the posterior commissure it defines the AC-PC line, the reference plane for stereotactic coordinates.
clinical: The AC-PC line and midcommissural point are used to plan deep brain stimulation targets in stereotactic surgery.

choroid plexus of cerebral hemisphere.name: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle
choroid plexus of cerebral hemisphere.desc: Fringe of vascular tissue covered by choroid epithelium, running along the choroid fissure from the interventricular foramen through the body and atrium into the temporal horn, where it forms a large tuft (glomus) at the atrium. Along with plexuses in the third and fourth ventricles it produces most cerebrospinal fluid, about 500 mL a day. Supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.
clinical: The glomus often calcifies with age and is a normal symmetric finding on CT.
Choroid plexus papillomas, mostly in young children, can cause hydrocephalus by overproducing CSF.

decussation.name: Decussation
decussation.desc: A decussation is a point where nerve fibres cross the midline to the other side of the central nervous system. Key examples are the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla (corticospinal fibres), the sensory decussation of internal arcuate fibres forming the medial lemniscus, the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles in the midbrain, and the optic chiasm. They explain why each hemisphere controls and feels the opposite side of the body.
clinical: Knowing where each pathway crosses lets clinicians localise lesions, as in crossed brainstem syndromes with face signs on one side and body signs on the other.

anterior chamber of {S} eyeball.name: Anterior chamber of the {S} eyeball
anterior chamber of {S} eyeball.desc: Fluid-filled space between the back of the cornea and the front of the iris and lens, communicating with the posterior chamber through the pupil. It contains aqueous humour made by the ciliary processes, which drains at the iridocorneal angle through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm. The balance of production and drainage sets intraocular pressure.
clinical: Narrowing of the iridocorneal angle can cause acute angle-closure glaucoma, an emergency with a painful red eye and rising pressure.
Blood layering here after trauma is a hyphema.

branch of ciliary ganglion.name: Branch of the ciliary ganglion (short ciliary nerve)
branch of ciliary ganglion.desc: The branches of the ciliary ganglion are the short ciliary nerves, about 6 to 10, which pierce the sclera around the optic nerve. They carry postganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle for pupil constriction and accommodation, plus sensory fibres from the eyeball and some sympathetic fibres that pass through the ganglion without synapsing.
clinical: Damage to these nerves or the ganglion causes a tonic (Adie) pupil that reacts poorly to light but slowly to near effort.

optic part of {S} retina.name: Optic part of the {S} retina
optic part of {S} retina.region: Eye: inner layer of posterior eyeball
optic part of {S} retina.desc: The light-sensitive part of the retina, lining the back of the eyeball from the optic disc to the ora serrata. It has ten layers, including rods and cones, bipolar cells and ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve. Centrally the macula and its fovea provide sharp central and colour vision. Its outer layers rely on the choroid; its inner layers are supplied by the central retinal artery.
clinical: Retinal detachment separates it from the pigment epithelium and causes flashes, floaters and a curtain of vision loss.
The optic disc is a blind spot because it has no photoreceptors.

suspensory ligament of {S} lens.name: Suspensory ligament of the {S} lens
suspensory ligament of {S} lens.desc: Ring of fine zonular fibres running from the ciliary body to the equator of the lens capsule. When the ciliary muscle relaxes the fibres are taut and the lens flattens for distance vision; when the muscle contracts during near focus the fibres slacken and the elastic lens rounds up, increasing its power (accommodation).
clinical: Weak zonules, as in Marfan syndrome, let the lens dislocate (ectopia lentis), usually upward and outward.

tarsal plate of {S} upper eyelid.name: Tarsal plate of the {S} upper eyelid
tarsal plate of {S} upper eyelid.desc: Dense plate of connective tissue that stiffens the upper eyelid, about 10 mm tall at its middle. It attaches to the orbital rim by the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments. The levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis inserts on its front and the superior tarsal (Muller) muscle, which is sympathetically supplied, on its upper edge. Meibomian glands run vertically inside it and secrete the oily layer of the tear film.
clinical: Blocked Meibomian glands cause a chalazion, a painless lump in the eyelid.
Loss of sympathetic tone to the superior tarsal muscle gives the mild ptosis of Horner syndrome.

{S} choroid.name: Choroid
{S} choroid.desc: Thin, darkly pigmented vascular layer between the sclera and the retina, running from the optic disc forward to the ciliary body. Its dense capillary bed (choriocapillaris) nourishes the outer retina, including the photoreceptors, and its pigment absorbs stray light. It is supplied mainly by the short posterior ciliary arteries from the ophthalmic artery.
clinical: Choroidal melanoma is the commonest primary eye tumour in adults.
Choroiditis or choroidal neovascularisation can threaten central vision.

{S} ciliary ganglion.name: Ciliary ganglion
{S} ciliary ganglion.region: Orbit: lateral to the optic nerve
{S} ciliary ganglion.desc: Small parasympathetic ganglion near the orbital apex, between the optic nerve and lateral rectus. Preganglionic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus arrive via the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve and synapse here; postganglionic fibres leave in the short ciliary nerves to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Sensory fibres from the nasociliary nerve and sympathetic fibres pass through without synapsing.
clinical: Damage to the ganglion, often after a viral illness, causes Adie tonic pupil, a dilated pupil with slow, sustained constriction.

{S} cornea.name: Cornea
{S} cornea.desc: Clear, curved front window of the eye, continuous with the sclera at the limbus. It has five classic layers: epithelium, Bowman layer, collagen stroma, Descemet membrane and endothelium, which pumps fluid out to keep it clear. It has no blood vessels and provides about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power. It is one of the most densely innervated tissues, via ciliary nerves from the ophthalmic nerve.
clinical: Corneal abrasions are very painful and show up with fluorescein dye under blue light.
Endothelial failure causes corneal swelling and cloudiness, a reason for corneal transplantation.

{S} corona ciliaris.name: Corona ciliaris
{S} corona ciliaris.desc: Front, folded part of the ciliary body, forming a ring of about 70 radiating ciliary processes just behind the iris. These processes secrete aqueous humour into the posterior chamber and anchor many zonular fibres of the suspensory ligament of the lens. Behind it the smooth pars plana extends back to the ora serrata.
clinical: Some glaucoma treatments reduce aqueous production by targeting the ciliary processes, either with drugs or with laser cyclophotocoagulation.

{S} iris.name: Iris
{S} iris.region: Eye: in front of the lens
{S} iris.desc: Pigmented, contractile disc between the cornea and lens, with the pupil at its centre, dividing the anterior and posterior chambers. Its sphincter pupillae, supplied by parasympathetic fibres from the ciliary ganglion, constricts the pupil; its radial dilator pupillae, supplied by sympathetic fibres, widens it. Pigment in its stroma and posterior epithelium gives eye colour.
clinical: A fixed dilated pupil in a drowsy patient can signal oculomotor nerve compression from uncal herniation.
Iritis causes a painful red eye with a small pupil and light sensitivity.

{S} lacrimal canaliculus.name: Lacrimal canaliculus
{S} lacrimal canaliculus.desc: Small tear-draining channels, one in each eyelid, starting at the lacrimal punctum at the medial lid margin. Each runs about 2 mm vertically then about 8 mm horizontally, and the upper and lower canaliculi usually join a common canaliculus that enters the lacrimal sac. Blinking pumps tears through them.
clinical: Lacerations near the medial lid can cut a canaliculus and need repair with a stent to prevent a watery eye.

{S} lacrimal gland.name: Lacrimal gland
{S} lacrimal gland.desc: Almond-sized gland in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone, at the upper outer part of the orbit, divided by the levator aponeurosis into orbital and palpebral lobes. Its ducts open into the upper outer conjunctival fornix. It makes the watery part of tears; secretion is driven by parasympathetic fibres from the facial nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion, reaching it with the lacrimal nerve.
clinical: Dry eye occurs when the gland is damaged, for example in Sjogren syndrome.
Enlargement can come from inflammation, sarcoidosis or tumours, and may push the eye down and inward.

{S} lacrimal lake.name: Lacrimal lake
{S} lacrimal lake.desc: Small triangular space at the medial angle of the eye, between the medial ends of the eyelids, where tears collect around the caruncle before draining through the lacrimal puncta into the canaliculi.
clinical: If the eyelids turn outward (ectropion), the puncta no longer dip into the lacrimal lake and tears spill onto the cheek.

{S} lacrimal sac.name: Lacrimal sac
{S} lacrimal sac.desc: Upper dilated end of the tear-drainage system, lying in the lacrimal fossa between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests, behind the medial palpebral ligament. It receives the canaliculi and continues downward as the nasolacrimal duct. Orbicularis oculi fibres around it help pump tears with each blink.
clinical: Infection of a blocked sac (dacryocystitis) causes a painful swelling below the medial corner of the eye.
Dacryocystorhinostomy creates a new opening from the sac into the nose.

{S} lens.name: Lens
{S} lens.desc: Clear, biconvex structure behind the iris and in front of the vitreous, held by the suspensory ligament from the ciliary body. It is made of tightly packed fibre cells inside an elastic capsule and has no blood vessels or nerves. By changing shape it fine-tunes focus for near and far vision (accommodation), adding to the cornea's fixed power.
clinical: Clouding of the lens is a cataract, treated by removing it and implanting an artificial lens.
Loss of lens elasticity with age (presbyopia) causes difficulty with near vision.

{S} lower eyelid.name: Lower eyelid
{S} lower eyelid.desc: Mobile fold of skin and muscle below the eye. From front to back it has skin, orbicularis oculi, the inferior tarsal plate with Meibomian glands, the capsulopalpebral fascia (lower lid retractors) and conjunctiva. The lower lacrimal punctum sits on its medial margin. Orbicularis oculi, supplied by the facial nerve, closes it; sensation is mainly from the infraorbital nerve.
clinical: Facial nerve palsy causes the lower lid to sag outward (ectropion) and the eye to water and dry out.
Laxity with age can also cause the lid margin to turn inward (entropion) so lashes rub the cornea.

{S} nasolacrimal duct.name: Nasolacrimal duct
{S} nasolacrimal duct.region: Face: between orbit and nasal cavity
{S} nasolacrimal duct.desc: Membranous channel about 12 mm long running down from the lacrimal sac through a bony canal formed by the maxilla, lacrimal bone and inferior nasal concha. It opens into the inferior meatus of the nose under the inferior concha, where a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner) partly guards it. It carries tears into the nose.
clinical: Congenital blockage at the valve of Hasner causes a watery, sticky eye in infants and usually resolves on its own.
This route explains why the nose runs when you cry.

{S} sclera.name: Sclera
{S} sclera.desc: Tough, white outer coat of the eyeball made of dense collagen, continuous with the cornea at the limbus and with the dural sheath of the optic nerve at the back, where it forms the sieve-like lamina cribrosa. The six extraocular muscles insert on it. It protects the eye and keeps its shape against intraocular pressure.
clinical: Scleritis is a deep, severe eye pain often linked to autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis.
A blue-tinted sclera can occur in osteogenesis imperfecta.

{S} vitreous body.name: Vitreous body
{S} vitreous body.desc: Clear gel filling the space between the lens and the retina, about four-fifths of the eye's volume. It is mostly water held in a framework of collagen and hyaluronan, firmly attached at the vitreous base near the ora serrata and around the optic disc. It keeps the eye's shape and transmits light to the retina.
clinical: With age the gel liquefies and can pull away from the retina (posterior vitreous detachment), causing floaters and sometimes a retinal tear.
Vitrectomy removes the gel to treat bleeding or detachment.

habenula.name: Habenula
habenula.region: Brain: epithalamus, beside the pineal stalk
habenula.desc: Small paired nuclei (medial and lateral) in the epithalamus at the back of the third ventricle roof, joined by the habenular commissure just above the pineal stalk. It receives input through the stria medullaris from the septal area, basal forebrain and pallidum, and sends the fasciculus retroflexus to the interpeduncular nucleus and midbrain monoamine centres. The lateral habenula signals disappointment or missing reward by suppressing dopamine neurons.
clinical: Overactive lateral habenula signalling is linked to depression, and the habenula is being studied as a deep brain stimulation target.
Calcification of the habenular commissure is a common normal finding on CT.

{S} internal capsule.name: Internal capsule
{S} internal capsule.region: Brain: between thalamus/caudate and lentiform nucleus
{S} internal capsule.desc: V-shaped band of white matter on horizontal section. The anterior limb lies between the caudate head and lentiform nucleus (frontopontine and thalamocortical fibres); the genu carries corticobulbar fibres; the posterior limb, between thalamus and lentiform nucleus, carries corticospinal fibres to arm then leg, and thalamocortical sensory fibres. Retrolentiform and sublentiform parts carry the optic and acoustic radiations. Supplied by lenticulostriate arteries, the anterior choroidal artery and recurrent artery of Heubner.
clinical: A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb can cause pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg.
Hemorrhage into the internal capsule from the putamen or thalamus causes dense contralateral weakness.

lamina terminalis.name: Lamina terminalis
lamina terminalis.region: Brain: front wall of the third ventricle
lamina terminalis.desc: Thin sheet of grey matter and pia stretching from the optic chiasm up to the anterior commissure and rostrum of the corpus callosum, forming the front wall of the third ventricle. It marks the rostral end of the embryonic neural tube. It contains the organum vasculosum, a circumventricular organ with leaky capillaries that senses blood composition and helps regulate thirst and fever.
clinical: Opening the lamina terminalis during aneurysm surgery is sometimes done to drain CSF and relax the brain.
It is a route for reaching lesions in the anterior third ventricle.

posterior commissure.name: Posterior commissure
posterior commissure.desc: Bundle of crossing fibres in the back wall of the third ventricle, just above the opening of the cerebral aqueduct and below the pineal gland. It carries fibres from the pretectal nuclei to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, making the light reflex consensual, and fibres serving vertical gaze, including from the interstitial nucleus of Cajal. With the anterior commissure it defines the AC-PC line used in stereotactic surgery.
clinical: Lesions near the posterior commissure, such as pineal tumours, cause upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation in Parinaud syndrome.

septum of telencephalon.name: Septum of the telencephalon
septum of telencephalon.desc: Midline region between the lateral ventricles below the corpus callosum. It includes the thin septum pellucidum, a double membrane separating the frontal horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles, and the septal area (septal nuclei) below it near the lamina terminalis. The septal nuclei connect with the hippocampus through the fornix, with the habenula through the stria medullaris, and contribute to hippocampal theta rhythm, reward and emotion.
clinical: A cavum septum pellucidum, a fluid gap between its two layers, is a common normal variant.
Absence of the septum pellucidum can occur with septo-optic dysplasia.

{S} stria medullaris of thalamus.name: Stria medullaris of the thalamus
{S} stria medullaris of thalamus.desc: Fibre bundle running along the upper medial edge of the thalamus, at the attachment of the third ventricle roof (tela choroidea). It carries fibres from the septal nuclei, lateral hypothalamus and globus pallidus back to the habenula, where some cross in the habenular commissure.
clinical: It is a landmark seen through the third ventricle roof during endoscopic and transcallosal approaches.

stria terminalis.name: Stria terminalis
stria terminalis.region: Brain: groove between caudate and thalamus
stria terminalis.desc: Slender fibre bundle, the main dorsal output of the amygdala. It arches with the tail of the caudate nucleus along the roof of the temporal horn and floor of the body of the lateral ventricle, running in the groove between caudate and thalamus with the thalamostriate vein, to reach the hypothalamus and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis near the anterior commissure. It links emotional processing to hormonal and autonomic responses.
clinical: The thalamostriate vein in the same groove is a key landmark at the foramen of Monro during ventricular surgery.
The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis is studied for its role in sustained anxiety.

{S} stria terminalis.name: Stria terminalis
{S} stria terminalis.region: Brain: groove between caudate and thalamus
{S} stria terminalis.desc: One-sided segment of the stria terminalis, the main dorsal output bundle of the amygdala. It follows the curve of the caudate tail along the lateral ventricle, running in the groove between the caudate and thalamus beside the thalamostriate vein, to reach the hypothalamus and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis. It carries amygdala signals that trigger hormonal and autonomic stress responses.
clinical: The thalamostriate vein in this groove marks the route to the foramen of Monro in transventricular surgery.

subarachnoid incisure.name: Subarachnoid incisure
subarachnoid incisure.desc: A segment of the subarachnoid space as modelled in BodyParts3D, marking a notch-like recess where cerebrospinal fluid lies between the arachnoid and pia mater around the brain surface. The subarachnoid space carries CSF and the major cerebral arteries and veins, and widens into cisterns at the base of the brain.
clinical: Blood in the subarachnoid space, most often from a ruptured aneurysm, causes a sudden worst-ever headache and needs urgent CT and vascular imaging.

subcortex of {S} cerebral hemisphere.name: Subcortex of the {S} cerebral hemisphere
subcortex of {S} cerebral hemisphere.region: Brain: deep to the cerebral cortex
subcortex of {S} cerebral hemisphere.desc: Everything beneath the cortex of one hemisphere: the white matter (association, commissural and projection fibres such as the corona radiata and internal capsule) and the deep grey nuclei, including the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus), claustrum and amygdala. It connects cortical areas to each other and to the thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord.
clinical: Small vessel disease damages subcortical white matter and causes slowed thinking and gait problems, seen as bright patches on T2 MRI.
Subcortical strokes can cause dense weakness while sparing language and other cortical functions.

inferior lingular bronchial tree.name: Inferior lingular bronchial tree
inferior lingular bronchial tree.desc: The inferior lingular segmental bronchus (B5 of the left lung) and all its branches. It arises from the lingular bronchus, a division of the left upper lobe bronchus, and ventilates the lower part of the lingula, which sits against the heart and corresponds to the right middle lobe's medial segment.
clinical: Lingular pneumonia blurs the left heart border on a frontal chest X-ray (silhouette sign).

lateral segmental bronchial tree.name: Lateral segmental bronchial tree
lateral segmental bronchial tree.desc: The lateral segmental bronchus of the right middle lobe (B4) and its branches. It arises from the middle lobe bronchus, which leaves the front of the bronchus intermedius, and ventilates the lateral part of the middle lobe.
clinical: The long, narrow middle lobe bronchus drains poorly, which predisposes to recurrent middle lobe collapse and infection (middle lobe syndrome).

medial segmental bronchial tree.name: Medial segmental bronchial tree
medial segmental bronchial tree.desc: The medial segmental bronchus of the right middle lobe (B5) and its branches, ventilating the medial part of the middle lobe that rests against the right side of the heart.
clinical: Consolidation here blurs the right heart border on a frontal chest X-ray.

superior lingular bronchial tree.name: Superior lingular bronchial tree
superior lingular bronchial tree.desc: The superior lingular segmental bronchus (B4 of the left lung) and its branches. It arises from the lingular bronchus of the left upper lobe and ventilates the upper part of the lingula, the left lung's equivalent of the right middle lobe.
clinical: The lingula can be removed on its own (lingulectomy) for localised disease, sparing the rest of the upper lobe.

{S} anterior basal segmental bronchial t.name: Anterior basal segmental bronchial tree
{S} anterior basal segmental bronchial t.desc: Anterior basal segmental bronchus (B8) of the lower lobe and its branches, ventilating the front part of the lung base above the diaphragm. On the left it commonly shares a stem with the medial basal bronchus as the anteromedial basal bronchus (B7+8).
clinical: Basal segments are common sites for aspiration in upright patients, especially on the right where the bronchial path is more vertical.

{S} anterior segmental bronchial tree.name: Anterior segmental bronchial tree
{S} anterior segmental bronchial tree.desc: Anterior segmental bronchus (B3) of the upper lobe and its branches, ventilating the front part of the upper lobe. On the right it arises from the right upper lobe bronchus; on the left from the upper division of the left upper lobe bronchus.
clinical: Segmental anatomy guides bronchoscopy and segmentectomy, which removes only the diseased segment along its bronchus and artery.

{S} apical segmental bronchial tree.name: Apical segmental bronchial tree
{S} apical segmental bronchial tree.desc: Apical segmental bronchus (B1) of the upper lobe and its branches, ventilating the lung apex that rises into the root of the neck. On the right it arises from the upper lobe bronchus; on the left it usually shares a common apicoposterior stem (B1+2) with the posterior segmental bronchus.
clinical: Reactivated tuberculosis favours the apical and posterior upper lobe segments.
Apical (Pancoast) tumours can invade the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain, causing arm pain and Horner syndrome.

{S} lateral basal segmental bronchial tr.name: Lateral basal segmental bronchial tree
{S} lateral basal segmental bronchial tr.desc: Lateral basal segmental bronchus (B9) of the lower lobe and its branches. It arises from the basal trunk of the lower lobe bronchus, usually sharing a short stem with the posterior basal bronchus, and ventilates the lateral part of the lung base near the costodiaphragmatic recess.
clinical: Basal segment disease can blunt the costophrenic angle on X-ray and be confused with a small effusion.

{S} main bronchus.name: Main bronchus
{S} main bronchus.desc: Each main (primary) bronchus begins at the tracheal bifurcation (carina) at about the T4-T5 level and enters the lung hilum. The right is shorter, wider and more vertical, gives off the upper lobe bronchus early, and continues as the bronchus intermedius. The left is longer, passes under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus and descending aorta, and divides into upper and lower lobe bronchi. C-shaped cartilage rings and smooth muscle keep it open.
clinical: Inhaled foreign bodies most often lodge in the right main bronchus because it is wider and more vertical.
Bronchoscopy inspects the main bronchi for tumours, bleeding and blockage.

{S} medial basal segmental bronchial tre.name: Medial basal segmental bronchial tree
{S} medial basal segmental bronchial tre.desc: Medial basal segmental bronchus (B7) of the lower lobe and its branches, ventilating the medial lung base beside the heart and the inferior vena cava. It is distinct on the right; on the left it commonly shares a stem with the anterior basal bronchus (anteromedial basal, B7+8).
clinical: Medial basal consolidation can hide behind the heart on a frontal chest X-ray, so a lateral view helps.

{S} posterior basal segmental bronchial.name: Posterior basal segmental bronchial tree
{S} posterior basal segmental bronchial.desc: Posterior basal segmental bronchus (B10) of the lower lobe and its branches, the continuation of the basal trunk. It ventilates the lowest, most posterior part of the lung, which fills the deep posterior costodiaphragmatic recess beside the spine.
clinical: Aspiration while upright often ends in the right posterior basal segment because it is the most dependent area.

{S} posterior segmental bronchial tree.name: Posterior segmental bronchial tree
{S} posterior segmental bronchial tree.desc: Posterior segmental bronchus (B2) of the upper lobe and its branches, ventilating the back of the upper lobe. On the right it arises from the upper lobe bronchus; on the left it usually joins the apical bronchus in a common apicoposterior stem (B1+2).
clinical: Aspiration while lying on the back or side commonly reaches the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
It is also a favoured site of reactivated tuberculosis.

{S} superior segmental bronchial tree.name: Superior segmental bronchial tree
{S} superior segmental bronchial tree.desc: Superior segmental bronchus (B6) of the lower lobe and its branches, the first branch from the back of the lower lobe bronchus. It ventilates the top of the lower lobe, which lies against the back of the chest at about the level of the scapula.
clinical: Because it points backward, it is a common site of aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess in patients lying on their back.

diaphragm.name: Diaphragm
diaphragm.desc: Dome-shaped muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen. It arises from the xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs, and the lumbar vertebrae by the right and left crura and arcuate ligaments, and inserts into a central tendon. Openings pass the inferior vena cava (T8), oesophagus (T10) and aorta (T12). It is the main muscle of breathing, flattening to draw air in. Supplied by the phrenic nerves (C3-C5).
clinical: Phrenic nerve injury paralyses one half of the diaphragm, which rises on X-ray and moves paradoxically on sniff testing.
A hiatal hernia lets part of the stomach slide through the oesophageal opening.

cricoid cartilage.name: Cricoid cartilage
cricoid cartilage.desc: The only complete cartilage ring of the airway, shaped like a signet ring with a narrow anterior arch and a tall posterior lamina, at the level of C6. It articulates with the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage and with the arytenoid cartilages on its upper lamina. The trachea hangs from its lower border by the cricotracheal ligament, and the pharynx becomes the oesophagus behind it.
clinical: In infants the cricoid ring is the narrowest part of the airway, so swelling here, as in croup, narrows breathing quickly.
It is a key landmark for emergency cricothyroidotomy just above it.

cricothyroid ligament.name: Cricothyroid ligament
cricothyroid ligament.desc: Elastic membrane joining the cricoid arch to the lower border of the thyroid cartilage. Its thick midline part, the median cricothyroid ligament, can be felt as a soft gap below the thyroid prominence; its lateral parts continue upward as the conus elasticus to the vocal ligaments.
clinical: Emergency cricothyroidotomy cuts through the median cricothyroid ligament to secure an airway when intubation fails.

extrinsic ligament of larynx.name: Extrinsic ligament of the larynx
extrinsic ligament of larynx.desc: Ligaments and membranes that join the larynx to neighbouring structures: the thyrohyoid membrane and its median and lateral thyrohyoid ligaments to the hyoid bone, the hyoepiglottic ligament from the epiglottis to the hyoid, and the cricotracheal ligament to the first tracheal ring. They suspend the larynx so it rises and falls with the hyoid during swallowing.
clinical: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane, a site for a nerve block before awake intubation.

oblique part of {S} cricothyroid.name: Oblique part of the {S} cricothyroid
oblique part of {S} cricothyroid.desc: Posterior part of the cricothyroid muscle, running from the side of the cricoid arch backward and upward to the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage. With the straight part it tilts the thyroid cartilage forward relative to the cricoid, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds. Supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Injury to the external laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery weakens this muscle, causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue.

straight part of {S} cricothyroid.name: Straight part of the {S} cricothyroid
straight part of {S} cricothyroid.desc: Anterior part of the cricothyroid muscle, running from the front of the cricoid arch almost vertically upward to the lower border of the thyroid lamina. It is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle on the outside of the larynx, and it raises pitch by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward and stretching the vocal folds. Supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
clinical: The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels, which is why surgeons ligate them carefully near the gland.

thyro-epiglottic ligament.name: Thyro-epiglottic ligament
thyro-epiglottic ligament.desc: Ligament attaching the narrow stalk (petiolus) of the epiglottic cartilage to the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage just below the thyroid notch. It anchors the epiglottis while letting its free upper part tilt back over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
clinical: Tumours of the epiglottis can spread forward into the pre-epiglottic space around this attachment, which affects surgical planning.

thyroid cartilage.name: Thyroid cartilage
thyroid cartilage.desc: Largest laryngeal cartilage, formed by two quadrilateral laminae fused in front at the laryngeal prominence with the superior thyroid notch above it. Its superior horns attach to the hyoid via the thyrohyoid membrane and its inferior horns articulate with the cricoid. The oblique line on each lamina gives attachment to sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor; the vocal ligaments attach inside the angle.
clinical: The laryngeal prominence and cricothyroid gap are palpated to find the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy.
Fractures from blunt neck trauma can threaten the airway.

transverse arytenoid.name: Transverse arytenoid
transverse arytenoid.desc: Unpaired muscle stretching across the backs of the two arytenoid cartilages, deep to the oblique arytenoids. It draws the arytenoids together, closing the posterior (intercartilaginous) part of the glottis. It is the only unpaired intrinsic laryngeal muscle and receives supply from both recurrent laryngeal nerves.
clinical: Along with other adductors it helps protect the airway during swallowing and coughing.

{S} aryepiglotticus.name: Aryepiglotticus
{S} aryepiglotticus.desc: Thin continuation of the oblique arytenoid muscle running from the apex of the arytenoid cartilage within the aryepiglottic fold to the side of the epiglottis. It helps narrow the laryngeal inlet and pull the epiglottis back during swallowing. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Short or tight aryepiglottic folds contribute to laryngomalacia, the commonest cause of noisy breathing in infants.

{S} arytenoid cartilage.name: Arytenoid cartilage
{S} arytenoid cartilage.desc: Small pyramid-shaped cartilage sitting on the upper border of the cricoid lamina. Its vocal process points forward and anchors the vocal ligament; its muscular process points sideways for the crico-arytenoid muscles; the corniculate cartilage caps its apex. Rotating and sliding at the crico-arytenoid joint, it opens and closes the vocal folds.
clinical: Arytenoid dislocation from intubation trauma can cause hoarseness that mimics nerve palsy.
Rheumatoid arthritis can stiffen the crico-arytenoid joint.

{S} conus elasticus.name: Conus elasticus
{S} conus elasticus.desc: Cone-shaped elastic membrane, the lateral part of the cricothyroid membrane, rising from the upper border of the cricoid arch to its free upper edge, which thickens as the vocal ligament between the thyroid angle and the arytenoid vocal process. It forms the wall of the subglottic space below the vocal folds.
clinical: Subglottic stenosis, often after long intubation, narrows the airway at the level of the conus elasticus and cricoid.

{S} corniculate cartilage.name: Corniculate cartilage
{S} corniculate cartilage.desc: Small horn-shaped nodule of elastic cartilage sitting on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage, within the back of the aryepiglottic fold. It makes the corniculate tubercle seen on laryngoscopy and stiffens the fold at the rear of the laryngeal inlet.
clinical: The corniculate tubercles are landmarks at the back of the glottis that help guide tube placement during intubation.

{S} cuneiform cartilage.name: Cuneiform cartilage
{S} cuneiform cartilage.desc: Small rod of elastic cartilage embedded in each aryepiglottic fold, in front of the corniculate cartilage. It produces the cuneiform tubercle on laryngoscopy and helps stiffen the fold, supporting the margin of the laryngeal inlet.
clinical: The cuneiform tubercles are visible landmarks at the edge of the inlet during laryngoscopy.

{S} lateral crico-arytenoid.name: Lateral crico-arytenoid
{S} lateral crico-arytenoid.desc: Intrinsic muscle running from the upper border of the cricoid arch backward to the muscular process of the arytenoid. It rotates the arytenoid so the vocal processes swing inward, adducting the vocal folds for voice and airway closure. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury weakens this adductor and the others, leaving a breathy, weak voice and risk of aspiration.

{S} oblique arytenoid.name: Oblique arytenoid
{S} oblique arytenoid.desc: Paired muscle bands that cross in an X on the back of the arytenoids, superficial to the transverse arytenoid, each running from the muscular process of one arytenoid to the apex of the other. Some fibres continue as the aryepiglotticus. They pull the arytenoids together and narrow the laryngeal inlet. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: With the aryepiglotticus they act like a sphincter around the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

{S} posterior crico-arytenoid.name: Posterior crico-arytenoid
{S} posterior crico-arytenoid.desc: Fan-shaped muscle from the back of the cricoid lamina to the muscular process of the arytenoid. It rotates the arytenoid so the vocal processes swing outward, and is the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds to open the airway. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyses both posterior crico-arytenoids, leaving the folds near the midline and causing dangerous stridor.

{S} thyro-arytenoid.name: Thyro-arytenoid
{S} thyro-arytenoid.desc: Broad muscle lateral to the vocal fold, running from the inner surface of the thyroid angle back to the anterolateral surface of the arytenoid. Its medial, deepest part forms the vocalis. It pulls the arytenoids forward, shortening and relaxing the vocal folds, and helps close the glottis. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Botulinum toxin injected into this muscle is a standard treatment for adductor spasmodic dysphonia.

{S} vocal ligament.name: Vocal ligament
{S} vocal ligament.desc: Thickened free upper edge of the conus elasticus, stretched from the inner surface of the thyroid angle back to the vocal process of the arytenoid. Covered by mucosa and the vocalis muscle, it forms the core of the vocal fold. The gap between the two vocal folds is the rima glottidis, the narrowest part of the adult larynx.
clinical: Vocal fold nodules form on the mucosa over the ligament from voice overuse and cause hoarseness.
Laryngeal cancer at the vocal folds causes early hoarseness, so it is often caught early.

{S} vocalis.name: Vocalis
{S} vocalis.desc: Medial, deepest fibres of the thyro-arytenoid muscle, lying just lateral to and along the vocal ligament from the thyroid angle to the vocal process. It fine-tunes tension along parts of the vocal fold, adjusting pitch and voice quality. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
clinical: Atrophy of the vocalis with age (presbylaryngis) leaves the folds bowed and the voice weak and breathy.

pharyngeal raphe.name: Pharyngeal raphe
pharyngeal raphe.desc: Midline tendinous seam on the back of the pharynx, running from the pharyngeal tubercle on the base of the skull down to the oesophagus. The left and right pharyngeal constrictor muscles insert into it, so it anchors the muscular tube in the midline.
clinical: Just above the cricopharyngeus, a weak area of the back wall (Killian dehiscence) is where a Zenker diverticulum forms.

subdivision of pharynx.name: Subdivision of the pharynx
subdivision of pharynx.desc: The pharynx is divided into three parts: the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity (with the adenoid and openings of the auditory tubes), the oropharynx behind the mouth (with the palatine tonsils and back of the tongue), and the laryngopharynx behind the larynx, which leads into the oesophagus at C6. Together they form a shared passage for air and food.
clinical: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma can block the auditory tube and present with one-sided middle ear fluid in an adult.
Obstructive sleep apnoea comes from collapse of the oropharynx during sleep.

{S} inferior pharyngeal constrictor.name: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor
{S} inferior pharyngeal constrictor.desc: Thickest pharyngeal constrictor, with a thyropharyngeus part from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and a cricopharyngeus part from the side of the cricoid. Thyropharyngeal fibres fan back to the pharyngeal raphe; cricopharyngeal fibres form a horizontal sling that acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter, staying closed at rest and relaxing to let food pass. Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus), with the cricopharyngeus also receiving recurrent laryngeal fibres.
clinical: A Zenker diverticulum bulges through the weak gap between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus, causing regurgitation of old food and bad breath.

{S} middle pharyngeal constrictor.name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor
{S} middle pharyngeal constrictor.desc: Fan-shaped muscle arising from the greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament, spreading back to insert into the pharyngeal raphe. It overlaps the superior constrictor and is overlapped by the inferior. It narrows the pharynx to push a swallowed bolus down. Supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus.
clinical: Weakness of the constrictors after stroke or neuromuscular disease leaves food pooling in the pharynx and raises the risk of aspiration.

{S} palatopharyngeus.name: Palatopharyngeus
{S} palatopharyngeus.region: Head and neck: soft palate and pharynx
{S} palatopharyngeus.desc: Longitudinal muscle running from the palatine aponeurosis and hard palate down in the palatopharyngeal arch, behind the palatine tonsil, to the thyroid cartilage and the side wall of the pharynx. It raises the pharynx and larynx and draws the palatopharyngeal arches together during swallowing. Supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.
clinical: The palatopharyngeal arch forms the back border of the tonsil bed, so it is a landmark during tonsillectomy.

{S} salpingopharyngeus.name: Salpingopharyngeus
{S} salpingopharyngeus.desc: Slender longitudinal muscle from the cartilage of the auditory (Eustachian) tube near its pharyngeal opening, running down in the salpingopharyngeal fold to blend with palatopharyngeus. It raises the pharynx during swallowing and may help open the auditory tube. Supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.
clinical: The fold it creates borders the pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmuller), a common origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

{S} stylopharyngeus.name: Stylopharyngeus
{S} stylopharyngeus.desc: Long thin muscle from the medial base of the styloid process, passing down between the superior and middle constrictors to blend with the pharyngeal wall and the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage. It lifts and widens the pharynx during swallowing and speech. It is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which winds around it.
clinical: Testing gag and swallow helps assess the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is often damaged with the vagus in jugular foramen lesions.

{S} superior pharyngeal constrictor.name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor
{S} superior pharyngeal constrictor.desc: Thin muscle arising from the pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, mylohyoid line of the mandible and side of the tongue, curving back to the pharyngeal raphe and pharyngeal tubercle. Its upper border leaves a gap closed by the pharyngobasilar fascia. It narrows the upper pharynx and helps seal off the nasopharynx during swallowing. Supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.
clinical: The palatine tonsil lies on this muscle, so bleeding after tonsillectomy comes from vessels in the tonsil bed beside it.

trachea.name: Trachea
trachea.region: Neck and superior mediastinum: C6 to T4-T5
trachea.desc: Airway tube about 10 to 12 cm long, from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to the carina at about the sternal angle (T4-T5), where it splits into the main bronchi. Sixteen to 20 C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open, closed behind by the trachealis muscle next to the oesophagus. In the neck the thyroid isthmus crosses rings 2 to 4; in the chest the aortic arch and brachiocephalic artery lie in front and to the left. It is lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium.
clinical: Tracheostomy is placed through the upper rings, below the cricoid, for long-term ventilation.
A widened or deviated trachea on X-ray can signal tension pneumothorax, a goitre or a mass.

septal nasal cartilage.name: Septal nasal cartilage
septal nasal cartilage.desc: Quadrangular plate of hyaline cartilage forming the front of the nasal septum. It joins the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid behind and above, the vomer and maxillary crest below, and supports the nasal dorsum and lateral cartilages in front. It divides the nasal cavity into left and right passages.
clinical: A deviated septum can block one side of the nose and is corrected by septoplasty.
An untreated septal haematoma after trauma can kill the cartilage and cause a saddle-nose deformity.

{S} inferior nasal concha.name: Inferior nasal concha
{S} inferior nasal concha.region: Face: lateral wall of nasal cavity
{S} inferior nasal concha.desc: Separate curved bone projecting from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, the largest of the three conchae, covered by thick, highly vascular mucosa. It articulates with the maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid and palatine bones. The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath it. It warms and humidifies inhaled air and directs airflow.
clinical: Swelling of the inferior turbinates from allergy or infection is a common cause of nasal blockage and can be reduced surgically.

{S} lateral nasal cartilage.name: Lateral nasal cartilage
{S} lateral nasal cartilage.desc: Triangular cartilage forming the side wall of the middle third of the nose, joined above to the nasal bone and maxilla and medially to the septal cartilage. Its lower edge overlaps the major alar cartilage at the scroll. The angle between it and the septum forms the internal nasal valve.
clinical: The internal nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway, and its collapse causes blockage that may be treated with spreader grafts.

{S} major alar cartilage.name: Major alar cartilage
{S} major alar cartilage.desc: U-shaped cartilage that shapes the tip and nostril of the nose. Its medial crus runs in the columella beside the other side's, and its lateral crus curves around the nostril. Together the two cartilages define the shape and support of the nasal tip and keep the nostrils open.
clinical: Weak lateral crura can collapse inward when breathing in (external valve collapse).
Reshaping these cartilages is the main step in nasal tip surgery.

appendix.name: Vermiform appendix
appendix.desc: A narrow, blind-ended tube about 6 to 10 cm long arising from the posteromedial cecum, where the three taeniae coli converge, roughly 2 cm below the ileocecal junction. Its position varies (retrocecal most often, then pelvic). Its wall is packed with lymphoid follicles (gut-associated lymphoid tissue), and it is supplied by the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery.
clinical: Appendicitis classically starts as periumbilical pain (visceral, T10) that shifts to McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
Following the taeniae coli down to their meeting point is how surgeons find the base of the appendix.

mesoappendix.name: Mesoappendix
mesoappendix.desc: A small triangular fold of peritoneum that suspends the appendix from the lower end of the mesentery of the small intestine, behind the terminal ileum. Between its two layers it carries the appendicular artery and vein and lymphatics to the appendix.
clinical: The appendicular artery is an end artery, so inflammation and swelling can thrombose it, causing gangrene and perforation of the appendix.
During appendectomy the mesoappendix is divided and the appendicular artery ligated before the appendix is removed.

ascending colon.name: Ascending colon
ascending colon.desc: The part of the large intestine running upward from the cecum along the right side of the abdomen to the right colic (hepatic) flexure under the liver. It is secondarily retroperitoneal, lying on the posterior abdominal wall in front of the right kidney. Supplied by the ileocolic and right colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery, it absorbs water and electrolytes from liquid chyme.
clinical: Right-sided colon cancers often present with iron-deficiency anemia from occult bleeding rather than obstruction, because the stool here is still liquid.
Its fixed retroperitoneal position makes it mobilizable along the avascular white line of Toldt during right hemicolectomy.

descending colon.name: Descending colon
descending colon.desc: The part of the large intestine running down the left side of the abdomen from the left colic (splenic) flexure to the sigmoid colon at the pelvic brim. It is secondarily retroperitoneal, lying in front of the left kidney and posterior abdominal wall muscles. It is supplied by the left colic artery from the inferior mesenteric artery and stores and moves increasingly solid stool.
clinical: Left-sided tumors tend to cause obstruction and changes in bowel habit because the lumen is narrower and the stool firmer.
Diverticular disease most often affects the descending and sigmoid colon.

ileocecal junction.name: Ileocecal junction
ileocecal junction.desc: The point where the terminal ileum opens into the medial side of the cecum through the ileocecal orifice, guarded by the ileocecal valve (lips formed by an invagination of the ileum). It slows the passage of ileal contents into the colon and limits reflux of colonic contents and bacteria back into the small intestine.
clinical: It is a common site for Crohn's disease, intussusception in children and impacted foreign bodies or gallstones (gallstone ileus).
A competent ileocecal valve in colonic obstruction creates a closed loop, raising the risk of cecal perforation.

taenia libera.name: Taenia libera
taenia libera.desc: One of the three taeniae coli, the flattened ribbons formed by the gathered outer longitudinal muscle of the colon. The taenia libera is the free band, not attached to any mesentery or omentum; on the transverse colon it runs along the inferior surface. The taeniae are shorter than the colon itself, which bunches the wall into haustra.
clinical: The three taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, a key surgical landmark.
Taeniae coli are absent on the rectum, where the longitudinal muscle spreads out into a continuous coat.

taenia mesocolica.name: Taenia mesocolica
taenia mesocolica.desc: One of the three taeniae coli of the large intestine. It lies where the transverse mesocolon attaches to the transverse colon, and on the ascending and descending colon it runs along the posteromedial surface facing the posterior abdominal wall. Like the other taeniae, it is a concentrated band of outer longitudinal smooth muscle.
clinical: Taeniae and haustra help distinguish large bowel from small bowel on imaging and at surgery.
Following any taenia toward the cecum leads to the base of the appendix.

taenia omentalis.name: Taenia omentalis
taenia omentalis.desc: One of the three taeniae coli. On the transverse colon it is where the greater omentum attaches, and on the ascending and descending colon it runs along the posterolateral surface. It is a thickened band of the colon's outer longitudinal smooth muscle that shortens the colon into haustral sacculations.
clinical: The omental taenia is the line along which surgeons separate the greater omentum from the transverse colon to enter the lesser sac.
Fatty tags called appendices epiploicae hang along the taeniae and can twist, causing epiploic appendagitis.

transverse colon.name: Transverse colon
transverse colon.desc: The longest and most mobile part of the large intestine, crossing the abdomen from the right colic (hepatic) flexure to the left colic (splenic) flexure. It hangs on the transverse mesocolon, often sagging toward the pelvis, with the greater omentum attached to its anterior surface. It is supplied mainly by the middle colic artery (superior mesenteric) with a contribution from the left colic artery near the splenic flexure.
clinical: The splenic flexure is a watershed zone between superior and inferior mesenteric territories and is vulnerable to ischemic colitis.
Toxic megacolon, a dangerous dilation in severe colitis, typically shows on X-ray as a widened transverse colon.

transverse mesocolon.name: Transverse mesocolon
transverse mesocolon.desc: The broad peritoneal fold that suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall, attaching along the anterior border of the pancreas. It divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments and carries the middle colic vessels, lymphatics and autonomic nerves to the transverse colon.
clinical: Surgeons pass through a window in the transverse mesocolon for retrocolic gastrojejunostomy and to reach the lesser sac.
Pancreatic inflammation can spread into the transverse mesocolon because of its attachment along the pancreas.

duodenum.name: Duodenum
duodenum.region: Abdomen: upper, around the head of the pancreas
duodenum.desc: The first and shortest part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, forming a C-shaped curve around the head of the pancreas in four parts: superior, descending, horizontal and ascending, ending at the duodenojejunal flexure. Except for its first few centimeters it is retroperitoneal. The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open at the major duodenal papilla in the descending part, where bile and enzymes neutralize and digest chyme.
clinical: Most peptic ulcers occur in the first part of the duodenum; a posterior ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed massively.
The horizontal part crosses between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery and can be compressed there (SMA syndrome).

esophagus.name: Esophagus
esophagus.desc: A muscular tube about 25 cm long carrying food from the pharynx (at C6) to the stomach (at about T11). It descends behind the trachea and left atrium, passes through the diaphragm at T10, and joins the stomach at the gastroesophageal junction. Its upper third is skeletal muscle, its lower third smooth muscle, and peristalsis plus upper and lower sphincters move each bolus and limit reflux.
clinical: Chronic acid reflux can change the lower lining to intestinal-type columnar epithelium (Barrett esophagus), a precancerous change.
In portal hypertension, veins at the lower esophagus enlarge into varices that can bleed catastrophically.

cystic duct.name: Cystic duct
cystic duct.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, hepatic hilum
cystic duct.desc: A short duct, about 3 to 4 cm long, running from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct, forming the common bile duct. Its lining has spiral mucosal folds (the spiral valve of Heister). Bile passes through it into the gallbladder for storage and back out when the gallbladder contracts after a fatty meal.
clinical: A gallstone stuck in the cystic duct causes biliary colic and, if it persists, acute cholecystitis.
The cystic duct, common hepatic duct and liver edge form the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle, which surgeons clear before clipping anything in cholecystectomy.

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, under the liver
gallbladder.desc: A pear-shaped sac lying in a fossa on the visceral surface of the liver between segments IV and V, with a fundus, body and neck. It stores and concentrates bile made by the liver and contracts in response to cholecystokinin, sending bile through the cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum. It is supplied by the cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery.
clinical: Murphy's sign, catching the breath on deep inspiration under right subcostal pressure, suggests acute cholecystitis.
Gallbladder pain often refers to the right shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve when the diaphragm is irritated.

distal part of ileum.name: Distal part of ileum (terminal ileum)
distal part of ileum.region: Abdomen: right iliac fossa and lower pelvis
distal part of ileum.desc: The last stretch of the small intestine, ending at the ileocecal junction with the cecum. Its wall has prominent Peyer's patches (aggregated lymphoid follicles), and it is the main site where vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor and bile salts are absorbed. It is supplied by ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery and the ileocolic artery.
clinical: Crohn's disease most often involves the terminal ileum, which can cause B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption.
Removal of the terminal ileum requires lifelong B12 replacement by injection.

distal part of jejunum.name: Distal part of jejunum
distal part of jejunum.desc: The lower segment of the jejunum, merging gradually with the proximal ileum without a sharp boundary. Compared with the ileum, the jejunum has a thicker wall, wider lumen, taller circular folds (plicae circulares), longer vasa recta and fewer arterial arcades in its mesentery. It continues the absorption of sugars, amino acids and fats, supplied by jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
clinical: Surgeons tell jejunum from ileum by feel and by the mesenteric vessels: long vasa recta and few arcades mean jejunum.
Jejunal loops are commonly used for reconstructions such as Roux-en-Y limbs.

middle part of ileum.name: Middle part of ileum
middle part of ileum.desc: The middle stretch of the ileum, the final three-fifths of the mobile small intestine. Its loops tend to lie in the lower abdomen and pelvis. It has a thinner wall and lower circular folds than the jejunum, more fat in its mesentery, multiple arterial arcades with short vasa recta, and increasing lymphoid tissue. It absorbs remaining nutrients and water, supplied by ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
clinical: A Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the embryonic vitelline duct, sits on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, typically about 60 cm from the ileocecal junction.
Ileal loops in the pelvis can adhere after surgery and cause small bowel obstruction.

middle part of jejunum.name: Middle part of jejunum
middle part of jejunum.desc: The middle stretch of the jejunum, which makes up roughly the first two-fifths of the mobile small intestine and lies mostly in the left upper abdomen. It has a deep red color, thick wall, tall closely packed circular folds and long finger-like villi that give it a huge absorptive surface. It is supplied by jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery and drained to the superior mesenteric vein.
clinical: Celiac disease flattens the villi of the proximal small intestine, reducing absorption of iron, folate and fats.
Acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus classically spares the first part of the jejunum but threatens much of the rest of the small bowel.

proximal part of ileum.name: Proximal part of ileum
proximal part of ileum.desc: The first part of the ileum, continuing directly from the jejunum with no visible line between them. From here on the wall gets thinner, the circular folds lower and sparser, and the mesentery fattier with more arterial arcades and shorter vasa recta. It absorbs nutrients and water and is supplied by ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
clinical: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions or hernias commonly involves loops of the ileum.
The junction between jejunum and ileum is gradual, so surgeons describe positions in centimeters from the duodenojejunal flexure or ileocecal valve.

proximal part of jejunum.name: Proximal part of jejunum
proximal part of jejunum.desc: The first part of the jejunum, beginning at the duodenojejunal flexure, which is held up by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz). From here the small intestine is intraperitoneal and hangs on the mesentery. Its tall circular folds and dense villi make it a major site of absorption of iron, folate, sugars, amino acids and fats, supplied by jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
clinical: The ligament of Treitz separates upper from lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
Feeding tubes (jejunostomy) are placed into the proximal jejunum when the stomach cannot be used.

caudate lobe of liver.name: Caudate lobe of liver
caudate lobe of liver.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, posterior liver
caudate lobe of liver.desc: A small lobe on the posterior (visceral) surface of the liver, wrapped around the front of the inferior vena cava, between the IVC groove and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum.
