It corresponds to Couinaud segment I. It receives blood from both the right and left portal veins and hepatic arteries and drains through its own short hepatic veins directly into the IVC.
clinical: In Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein blockage) the caudate lobe often enlarges because its separate veins still drain into the IVC.
Its position against the IVC makes caudate lobe resection technically demanding.

hepatovenous segment ii.name: Hepatic segment II
hepatovenous segment ii.region: Abdomen: left upper quadrant, left lateral liver
hepatovenous segment ii.desc: The superior part of the left lateral section of the liver (Couinaud segment II), lying to the left of the falciform ligament and fissure for the ligamentum venosum. It is supplied by a branch of the left portal vein and left hepatic artery, drains bile to the left hepatic duct and drains blood through the left hepatic vein. It touches the diaphragm and lies over the stomach.
clinical: Segments II and III together form the left lateral section, the part most often taken in living donor transplantation for a child.
Couinaud segments matter because each can be removed separately along its own vascular and biliary pedicle.

hepatovenous segment iii.name: Hepatic segment III
hepatovenous segment iii.region: Abdomen: left upper quadrant, left lateral liver
hepatovenous segment iii.desc: The inferior part of the left lateral section of the liver (Couinaud segment III), to the left of the falciform ligament and ligamentum teres. It is supplied by a branch of the left portal vein and left hepatic artery, drains bile to the left hepatic duct and drains blood into the left hepatic vein. Its anterior edge forms part of the liver's sharp inferior border.
clinical: The segment III duct, reached at the base of the ligamentum teres, can be used for biliary bypass when the hilum is blocked by tumor.
Together with segment II it is the left lateral section, used in pediatric split-liver transplants.

hepatovenous segment iv.name: Hepatic segment IV
hepatovenous segment iv.desc: The medial section of the left lobe in the functional (Couinaud) scheme, lying between the middle hepatic vein and the falciform ligament and fissure for the ligamentum teres. It is often split into IVa above and IVb below; IVb includes the quadrate lobe next to the gallbladder. It is supplied by the left portal vein and left hepatic artery and drains to the middle and left hepatic veins.
clinical: Gallbladder cancer commonly invades segments IVb and V, which are removed with it in radical cholecystectomy.
The middle hepatic vein separating segment IV from the right liver defines the plane of a right or left hemihepatectomy.

hepatovenous segment ix.name: Hepatic segment IX (paracaval caudate)
hepatovenous segment ix.region: Abdomen: posterior liver, beside the IVC
hepatovenous segment ix.desc: A subdivision proposed by Couinaud for the right, paracaval portion of the caudate lobe, lying directly in front of and to the right of the inferior vena cava near the hepatic vein confluence. Like the rest of the caudate region, it drains through short veins directly into the IVC. Many surgeons simply count it as part of segment I.
clinical: Its tight relation to the IVC and hepatic vein confluence makes tumors here among the hardest to resect.
Segment naming varies between classifications, so imaging reports usually state which scheme they use.

hepatovenous segment v.name: Hepatic segment V
hepatovenous segment v.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, anterior right liver
hepatovenous segment v.desc: The inferior part of the right anterior section of the liver (Couinaud segment V), lying to the right of the gallbladder bed and middle hepatic vein. It is supplied by the anterior branch of the right portal vein and right hepatic artery, drains bile through the right anterior duct and drains blood mainly into the middle hepatic vein.
clinical: Segment V is resected along with IVb in radical surgery for gallbladder cancer.
Liver biopsies taken through the right lower intercostal space often sample segments V or VI.

hepatovenous segment vi.name: Hepatic segment VI
hepatovenous segment vi.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, posterolateral right liver
hepatovenous segment vi.desc: The inferior part of the right posterior section of the liver (Couinaud segment VI), lying low and lateral, next to the right kidney and hepatic flexure of the colon. It is supplied by the posterior branch of the right portal vein and right hepatic artery, drains bile through the right posterior duct and drains blood into the right hepatic vein.
clinical: The right kidney presses on segment VI, creating the renal impression on the liver's visceral surface.
Its lateral position makes it a common target for percutaneous liver biopsy.

hepatovenous segment vii.name: Hepatic segment VII
hepatovenous segment vii.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, posterosuperior right liver
hepatovenous segment vii.desc: The superior part of the right posterior section of the liver (Couinaud segment VII), tucked high and posterior beneath the right dome of the diaphragm. It is supplied by the posterior branch of the right portal vein and right hepatic artery, drains bile through the right posterior duct and drains blood into the right hepatic vein near its entry to the IVC.
clinical: Lesions in segments VII and VIII sit under the diaphragm and can be hard to reach by biopsy or laparoscopic surgery.
Liver abscesses commonly form in the right lobe, including segment VII, and can irritate the diaphragm and right lung base.

hepatovenous segment viii.name: Hepatic segment VIII
hepatovenous segment viii.region: Abdomen: right upper quadrant, anterosuperior right liver
hepatovenous segment viii.desc: The superior part of the right anterior section of the liver (Couinaud segment VIII), lying under the diaphragm between the middle and right hepatic veins. It is supplied by the anterior branch of the right portal vein and right hepatic artery, drains bile through the right anterior duct and drains blood into the middle and right hepatic veins.
clinical: Its high position near the hepatic vein confluence makes segment VIII resection technically challenging.
Ultrasound of segment VIII often needs an intercostal window because the ribs and lung shadow it.

{S} duct of caudate lobe of liver.name: Duct of caudate lobe
{S} duct of caudate lobe of liver.desc: A small bile duct draining the caudate lobe (segment I). The caudate lobe usually has several such ducts that empty into the right or left hepatic duct near the hilum, and this one joins the left hepatic duct system. It carries bile made in the caudate lobe toward the common hepatic duct.
clinical: Hilar bile duct cancers (Klatskin tumors) often involve the caudate ducts, so the caudate lobe is commonly removed with the tumor.
Injury to small caudate ducts during liver surgery can cause postoperative bile leaks.

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.desc: A long, soft retroperitoneal gland lying across the posterior abdominal wall behind the stomach at about L1 to L2, divided into head (in the duodenal C-loop), uncinate process, neck, body and tail (reaching the splenic hilum). Its exocrine acini secrete digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum, and its islets of Langerhans secrete insulin, glucagon and somatostatin into the blood. It is supplied by the splenic and pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
clinical: Acute pancreatitis, most often caused by gallstones or alcohol, gives severe epigastric pain radiating to the back.
Cancer of the pancreatic head can block the common bile duct, causing painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).

pancreatic duct.name: Main pancreatic duct
pancreatic duct.desc: The duct of Wirsung, running the length of the pancreas from tail to head and collecting enzyme-rich juice from smaller ducts along the way. In the head it usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi. An accessory duct (of Santorini) often drains the upper head at the minor papilla.
clinical: A dilated main pancreatic duct on imaging can signal obstruction by stones, chronic pancreatitis or a tumor.
Pancreas divisum, a failed fusion of the dorsal and ventral ducts, is the most common pancreatic developmental variant.

pancreatic duct tree.name: Pancreatic duct system
pancreatic duct tree.desc: The branching network of ducts that carries pancreatic juice from the acini to the duodenum: intercalated ducts lead to intralobular and interlobular ducts, which feed the main pancreatic duct and the accessory pancreatic duct. Duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes stomach acid in the duodenum.
clinical: In cystic fibrosis, thick secretions plug the pancreatic ducts, leading to exocrine insufficiency and fat malabsorption.
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) images and treats the duct system through the duodenal papilla.

parenchyma of pancreas.name: Pancreatic parenchyma
parenchyma of pancreas.desc: The functional tissue of the pancreas. About 98 percent is exocrine acini, grape-like clusters of cells secreting digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen, lipase and amylase; scattered among them are about a million islets of Langerhans, containing beta cells (insulin), alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin) and PP cells.
clinical: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of beta cells removes insulin production.
Premature activation of trypsin inside the parenchyma lets the pancreas digest itself in acute pancreatitis.

rectum.name: Rectum
rectum.region: Pelvis: posterior, in front of the sacrum
rectum.desc: The final part of the large intestine, about 12 to 15 cm long, running from the sigmoid colon at about S3 down along the curve of the sacrum to the anorectal junction, where it passes through the pelvic floor to become the anal canal. It lacks taeniae and haustra and stores feces until defecation. It is supplied by the superior rectal artery (inferior mesenteric) plus middle and inferior rectal arteries.
clinical: Rectal cancer is staged with MRI and treated by surgery that removes the rectum with its surrounding mesorectum (total mesorectal excision).
The digital rectal exam lets a clinician feel the lower rectum for masses or blood.

{S} sublingual gland.name: Sublingual gland
{S} sublingual gland.desc: The smallest of the three major paired salivary glands, an almond-shaped gland lying under the mucosa of the floor of the mouth, above the mylohyoid muscle and beside the genioglossus. It drains through many small ducts (of Rivinus) on the sublingual fold, sometimes also via a major duct joining the submandibular duct. Its secretion is mostly mucous, and its parasympathetic supply comes from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion.
clinical: A blocked sublingual duct can form a ranula, a bluish cyst in the floor of the mouth.
The lingual nerve and submandibular duct run close to the gland and are at risk when it is removed.

{S} submandibular gland.name: Submandibular gland
{S} submandibular gland.desc: A walnut-sized salivary gland in the submandibular triangle below the mandible, wrapping around the posterior edge of the mylohyoid muscle into superficial and deep parts. Its duct (Wharton's duct) runs forward in the floor of the mouth to open at the sublingual caruncle beside the frenulum of the tongue. It makes about two-thirds of resting saliva, mixed serous and mucous, under parasympathetic control from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani.
clinical: About 80 percent of salivary stones form in the submandibular gland, causing painful swelling at mealtimes.
In surgery here the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve, the lingual nerve and the hypoglossal nerve must be protected.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.region: Abdomen: left upper quadrant and epigastrium
stomach.desc: A J-shaped muscular sac between the esophagus and duodenum, divided into cardia, fundus, body, antrum and pylorus, with lesser and greater curvatures. Its glands secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (parietal cells), pepsinogen (chief cells) and gastrin (G cells in the antrum). It stores food, churns it into chyme, starts protein digestion and releases it through the pyloric sphincter. It is supplied by branches of the celiac trunk.
clinical: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use are the two main causes of gastric ulcers.
Loss of parietal cells in autoimmune gastritis removes intrinsic factor, causing pernicious anemia from B12 deficiency.

tongue.name: Tongue
tongue.desc: A muscular organ forming the floor of the mouth, with an oral part (anterior two-thirds) and pharyngeal part (posterior third) divided by the V-shaped sulcus terminalis. Intrinsic muscles change its shape and extrinsic muscles move it; all are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) except palatoglossus (vagus). Touch on the front two-thirds is via the lingual nerve (V3) and taste via the chorda tympani (VII); the back third uses the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) for both.
clinical: A hypoglossal nerve lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate toward the weak side.
Squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue most often arises on its lateral border.

anterior inferior tributary of {S} hepat.name: Anterior inferior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
anterior inferior tributary of {S} hepat.desc: The bile duct draining the anteroinferior part of the right liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment V. It joins the anterior superior (segment VIII) duct to form the right anterior sectoral duct, which unites with the right posterior duct to form the right hepatic duct. It runs alongside the matching branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery.
clinical: Variations in where the right sectoral ducts join are common and matter in living donor liver surgery.
Segmental ducts can be injured during cholecystectomy because segment V lies right next to the gallbladder bed.

anterior superior tributary of {S} hepat.name: Anterior superior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
anterior superior tributary of {S} hepat.desc: The bile duct draining the anterosuperior part of the right liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment VIII. It joins the anterior inferior (segment V) duct to form the right anterior sectoral duct, which then unites with the right posterior sectoral duct as the right hepatic duct. It travels with segmental branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery.
clinical: Each segmental duct travels with its portal and arterial branch in a Glissonian sheath, which lets surgeons clamp a whole segment's pedicle at once.
Biliary dilation limited to one segment on imaging points to a blockage at that segment's duct.

caudate lobe tributary of {S} hepatic bi.name: Caudate lobe tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
caudate lobe tributary of {S} hepatic bi.desc: A small bile duct draining part of the caudate lobe (segment I) into the hepatic duct system near the hilum. The caudate lobe is unusual because it sends bile into both the right and left hepatic ducts; this branch carries its bile into one of them, close to the hepatic duct confluence.
clinical: Because caudate ducts join right at the confluence, hilar cholangiocarcinoma often spreads into them, and the caudate lobe is resected with the tumor.
Leaks from small caudate ducts are a recognized complication after major liver resection.

common hepatic duct.name: Common hepatic duct
common hepatic duct.region: Abdomen: hepatic hilum and hepatoduodenal ligament
common hepatic duct.desc: The duct formed at the porta hepatis by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts, about 3 cm long. It runs down in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament), to the right of the hepatic artery and in front of the portal vein, until the cystic duct joins it to form the common bile duct. It carries all bile leaving the liver.
clinical: It forms the medial border of the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle; mistaking the bile duct for the cystic duct is the classic cause of injury in cholecystectomy.
Obstruction here causes jaundice with dilated intrahepatic ducts but a normal-sized gallbladder.

lateral inferior tributary of {S} hepati.name: Lateral inferior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
lateral inferior tributary of {S} hepati.desc: The bile duct draining the inferior part of the left lateral section of the liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment III. It joins the lateral superior (segment II) duct, usually near the umbilical fissure, and the combined duct receives the segment IV ducts to form the left hepatic duct. It runs with segment III branches of the left portal vein and left hepatic artery.
clinical: The segment III duct can be reached at the base of the round ligament for a bypass (hepaticojejunostomy) when the hilum is blocked.
Its position in the left lateral section makes it relevant in pediatric split-liver transplantation.

lateral superior tributary of {S} hepati.name: Lateral superior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
lateral superior tributary of {S} hepati.desc: The bile duct draining the superior part of the left lateral section of the liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment II. It unites with the segment III duct and then with the segment IV ducts to form the left hepatic duct, running with the segment II branches of the left portal vein and left hepatic artery.
clinical: In a left lateral sectionectomy for a living donor, the segment II and III ducts are divided together as the graft's bile duct.
Isolated dilation of a segmental duct on scans points to a stone or stricture at that branch.

medial inferior tributary of {S} hepatic.name: Medial inferior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
medial inferior tributary of {S} hepatic.region: Abdomen: central liver, medial left section
medial inferior tributary of {S} hepatic.desc: The bile duct draining the lower part of the medial section of the left liver, corresponding to segment IVb (which includes the quadrate lobe near the gallbladder). It joins the segment IVa duct and the left lateral ducts to form the left hepatic duct near the hilum.
clinical: Segment IV ducts often join the left hepatic duct close to the confluence, so they can be involved early by hilar tumors.
Segment IVb is removed in radical surgery for gallbladder cancer, and its duct must be ligated.

medial superior tributary of {S} hepatic.name: Medial superior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
medial superior tributary of {S} hepatic.region: Abdomen: central liver, medial left section
medial superior tributary of {S} hepatic.desc: The bile duct draining the upper part of the medial section of the left liver, corresponding to segment IVa, which lies under the diaphragm between the middle hepatic vein and the falciform ligament. It joins the segment IVb duct and the left lateral ducts to form the left hepatic duct.
clinical: Variant drainage of segment IV ducts into the right system is a known pitfall when splitting the liver for transplantation.
Segmental biliary anatomy is mapped with MRCP before complex liver surgery.

posterior inferior tributary of {S} hepa.name: Posterior inferior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
posterior inferior tributary of {S} hepa.desc: The bile duct draining the posteroinferior part of the right liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment VI. It joins the segment VII duct to form the right posterior sectoral duct, which typically hooks over the right anterior portal vein before joining the right anterior duct to form the right hepatic duct.
clinical: The right posterior duct often drains anomalously into the left hepatic duct, a variant surgeons must find before donor or major hepatectomy.
Percutaneous biliary drains are often placed into right lobe ducts such as this one through the right flank.

posterior superior tributary of {S} hepa.name: Posterior superior tributary of the {S} hepatic biliary tree
posterior superior tributary of {S} hepa.desc: The bile duct draining the posterosuperior part of the right liver, corresponding to Couinaud segment VII, high under the diaphragm. It joins the segment VI duct to form the right posterior sectoral duct, which unites with the right anterior duct as the right hepatic duct, travelling beside segmental portal and arterial branches.
clinical: Variations in right posterior duct drainage are present in a sizable minority of people and are checked on imaging before liver surgery.
Strictures of high segmental ducts can cause recurrent cholangitis in the drained segment.

{S} hepatic duct.name: Hepatic duct
{S} hepatic duct.desc: One of the two main bile ducts leaving the liver at the porta hepatis. The right hepatic duct is short and formed by the right anterior and right posterior sectoral ducts; the left hepatic duct is longer, runs horizontally under segment IV, and collects bile from segments II, III and IV. The two join to form the common hepatic duct.
clinical: Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor) arises at or near the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts.
The longer extrahepatic course of the left hepatic duct makes it the preferred site for surgical bypass of a blocked hilum.

mesentery of small intestine.name: Mesentery of small intestine
mesentery of small intestine.desc: A fan-shaped double fold of peritoneum suspending the jejunum and ileum from the posterior abdominal wall. Its root is only about 15 cm long, running obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (left of L2) to the right sacroiliac joint, while its intestinal border spans about 6 meters of bowel. It carries the superior mesenteric vessels, their jejunal and ileal branches, lymph nodes, lymphatics (lacteals) and autonomic nerves.
clinical: A twist of the small bowel around its mesentery (volvulus) cuts off blood supply and is a surgical emergency, especially with malrotation in infants.
Its root crosses the duodenum, aorta, IVC and right ureter, linking these structures surgically.

gingiva of lower jaw.name: Mandibular gingiva
gingiva of lower jaw.desc: The gum of the lower jaw: firm, keratinized mucosa tightly bound to the alveolar process of the mandible and wrapping the necks of the lower teeth, with a free margin forming a shallow sulcus around each tooth. Its buccal side is innervated by the buccal and mental nerves and its lingual side by the lingual nerve, all branches of the mandibular nerve (V3).
clinical: Gingivitis from plaque causes red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing; untreated it can progress to periodontitis and tooth loss.
Lower gum numbness after a dental anesthetic block reflects anesthesia of mandibular nerve branches.

subdivision of mouth.name: Oral cavity
subdivision of mouth.desc: The space of the mouth, divided into the vestibule (between the lips and cheeks and the teeth and gums) and the oral cavity proper (inside the dental arches). Its roof is the hard and soft palate, its floor is the mylohyoid muscle with the tongue resting on it, and it opens back into the oropharynx through the oropharyngeal isthmus. It begins digestion by chewing, mixing food with saliva and shaping it for swallowing.
clinical: Medication tablets placed under the tongue absorb quickly through the thin mucosa of the oral floor into the bloodstream.
Persistent white or red patches in the mouth (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) can be precancerous and are biopsied.

{S} lower central secondary incisor toot.name: Lower central incisor (permanent)
{S} lower central secondary incisor toot.desc: The permanent incisor nearest the midline of the lower jaw, the smallest and narrowest tooth in the mouth, with a chisel-shaped crown for cutting and a single root. It usually erupts at about 6 to 7 years and sits in the alveolar process of the mandible. It is innervated by the incisive branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
clinical: Lower incisors are usually among the first permanent teeth to erupt, often around the same time as the first molars.
Tartar builds up fastest behind the lower incisors because the submandibular and sublingual ducts open just below them.

{S} lower first secondary molar tooth.name: Lower first molar (permanent)
{S} lower first secondary molar tooth.desc: A large grinding tooth of the lower jaw with a five-cusped crown and two roots, mesial and distal. It is the first permanent tooth to erupt, at about 6 years (the six-year molar), behind the baby teeth. It is innervated by the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), and its roots lie above the mandibular canal.
clinical: The lower first molar is the permanent tooth most often affected by decay, partly because it erupts so early.
Dental sealants are applied to its grooves soon after eruption to prevent cavities.

{S} lower first secondary premolar tooth.name: Lower first premolar (permanent)
{S} lower first secondary premolar tooth.desc: The premolar just behind the lower canine, with a single root and a crown that has a large buccal cusp and a small lingual cusp, giving it a canine-like look. It erupts at about 10 to 12 years. It is innervated by the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), and the mental foramen typically lies below the roots of the lower premolars.
clinical: The mental nerve exits the mandible near the premolar roots and can be injured during extraction or implant surgery, numbing the lower lip and chin.
Premolars are the teeth most often removed to make space in orthodontic treatment.

{S} lower lateral secondary incisor toot.name: Lower lateral incisor (permanent)
{S} lower lateral secondary incisor toot.desc: The permanent incisor just lateral to the lower central incisor, slightly wider, with a chisel-shaped crown and a single root. It erupts at about 7 to 8 years. It is innervated by the incisive branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3) and supported by the alveolar bone of the anterior mandible.
clinical: Crowding of the lower incisors is one of the most common reasons for orthodontic treatment in teenagers.
Thin bone over the lower incisor roots makes them prone to gum recession.

{S} lower second secondary molar tooth.name: Lower second molar (permanent)
{S} lower second secondary molar tooth.desc: The grinding tooth behind the lower first molar, usually with four cusps and two roots, mesial and distal. It erupts at about 11 to 13 years (the twelve-year molar). It is innervated by the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), and its roots lie close to the mandibular canal and the lingual nerve on the inner side of the jaw.
clinical: Its grooves are prone to decay soon after eruption, so sealants are often placed on it too.
Its roots can lie close to the inferior alveolar canal, a consideration during extraction or root canal treatment.

{S} lower second secondary premolar toot.name: Lower second premolar (permanent)
{S} lower second secondary premolar toot.desc: The premolar just in front of the lower first molar, with a single root and a crown that usually has one buccal and one or two lingual cusps. It erupts at about 11 to 12 years, replacing the second baby molar. It is innervated by the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), and the mental foramen often lies near its root apex.
clinical: It is one of the teeth most often congenitally missing, after the third molars.
Anesthetic injected at the mental foramen near this tooth numbs the lower lip and chin on that side.

{S} lower secondary canine tooth.name: Lower canine (permanent)
{S} lower secondary canine tooth.desc: The pointed tooth at the corner of the lower dental arch, with a single long root, sitting between the lateral incisor and first premolar. It erupts at about 9 to 10 years and helps grip and tear food and guide the jaw in side-to-side movements. It is innervated by the incisive branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
clinical: Its long root makes it one of the most stable teeth, often among the last kept in old age.
Canine guidance, where the canines touch first in sideways chewing, protects the back teeth from heavy side forces.

{S} upper central secondary incisor toot.name: Upper central incisor (permanent)
{S} upper central secondary incisor toot.desc: The large front tooth beside the midline of the upper jaw, the widest incisor, with a broad chisel-shaped crown and a single conical root set in the alveolar process of the maxilla. It erupts at about 7 to 8 years and cuts food. It is innervated by the anterior superior alveolar nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) via the infraorbital nerve.
clinical: Upper central incisors are the permanent teeth most often injured in falls and sports; a knocked-out tooth has the best chance if replanted within minutes.
A gap between them (midline diastema) can be normal or caused by a low-attached frenum of the upper lip.

{S} upper first secondary molar tooth.name: Upper first molar (permanent)
{S} upper first secondary molar tooth.desc: A large grinding tooth of the upper jaw with four main cusps (often plus a small Carabelli cusp) and three roots: two buccal and one palatal. It erupts at about 6 years. It is innervated by the posterior superior alveolar nerve (V2), with a variable contribution from the middle superior alveolar nerve, and its roots lie just below the floor of the maxillary sinus.
clinical: Infection at its root tips can spread into the maxillary sinus, causing one-sided sinusitis.
Extracting an upper molar can open a channel between mouth and sinus (oroantral fistula).

{S} upper first secondary premolar tooth.name: Upper first premolar (permanent)
{S} upper first secondary premolar tooth.desc: The premolar just behind the upper canine, with two cusps (buccal and palatal) and usually two roots, one buccal and one palatal. It erupts at about 10 to 11 years. It is innervated by the middle superior alveolar nerve when present, otherwise by the anterior or posterior superior alveolar nerves, all branches of the maxillary nerve (V2).
clinical: It is the upper tooth most often extracted for orthodontic space.
Its two thin roots make root canal treatment more complex than in single-rooted teeth.

{S} upper lateral secondary incisor toot.name: Upper lateral incisor (permanent)
{S} upper lateral secondary incisor toot.desc: The incisor just lateral to the upper central incisor, smaller and more rounded, with a single root. It erupts at about 8 to 9 years. It is innervated by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2) and sits in the part of the maxilla that develops from the premaxilla.
clinical: It is commonly small and peg-shaped or congenitally missing.
Cleft lip and alveolus typically occur near the upper lateral incisor, where the premaxilla meets the rest of the maxilla.

{S} upper second secondary molar tooth.name: Upper second molar (permanent)
{S} upper second secondary molar tooth.desc: The grinding tooth behind the upper first molar, usually with four cusps (the distopalatal often small) and three roots that may be closer together or fused. It erupts at about 12 to 13 years. It is innervated by the posterior superior alveolar nerve (V2), and its roots lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
clinical: The parotid duct opens into the cheek opposite the upper second molar, a landmark used in examining the mouth.
Like the first molar, root infections here can spread to the maxillary sinus.

{S} upper second secondary premolar toot.name: Upper second premolar (permanent)
{S} upper second secondary premolar toot.desc: The premolar just in front of the upper first molar, with two nearly equal cusps (buccal and palatal) and usually a single root. It erupts at about 10 to 12 years, replacing the second baby molar. It is innervated by the middle superior alveolar nerve when present, otherwise by the posterior or anterior superior alveolar nerves (V2), and its root may lie near the maxillary sinus.
clinical: It is one of the teeth most often congenitally missing.
Its root tip can sit close to the maxillary sinus floor, so extraction occasionally opens the sinus.

{S} upper secondary canine tooth.name: Upper canine (permanent)
{S} upper secondary canine tooth.desc: The pointed tooth at the corner of the upper dental arch, with the longest root of any tooth, reaching up near the side of the nasal cavity. It erupts at about 11 to 12 years, among the last front teeth. It grips and tears food and guides side-to-side jaw movements, and it is innervated by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).
clinical: After the wisdom teeth, the upper canine is the tooth most often impacted, usually on the palatal side, and may need surgical exposure.
Its root forms a ridge on the front of the maxilla (canine eminence), a landmark for facial surgery.

urinary bladder.name: Urinary bladder
urinary bladder.region: Pelvis: anterior, behind the pubic symphysis
urinary bladder.desc: A hollow muscular organ in the anterior pelvis that stores urine. Its wall is the detrusor smooth muscle, lined by stretchy transitional epithelium (urothelium). The two ureters enter obliquely at the back and the urethra leaves from the neck; these three openings mark the smooth trigone. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) contract the detrusor for voiding, while sympathetic fibers relax it during filling.
clinical: As it fills it rises above the pubic symphysis, so an over-full bladder can be felt and drained through the lower abdominal wall (suprapubic catheter).
Spinal cord injury above the sacral segments can cause a spastic bladder that empties reflexively without voluntary control.

{S} kidney.name: Kidney
{S} kidney.desc: A bean-shaped retroperitoneal organ lying against the posterior abdominal wall from about T12 to L3, the right slightly lower because of the liver. Each contains about a million nephrons that filter blood, reabsorb water and solutes, and excrete waste as urine through the renal pelvis into the ureter. It also secretes renin and erythropoietin and activates vitamin D. Its renal artery branches directly from the aorta.
clinical: Kidney stones cause colicky flank pain radiating to the groin as they pass down the ureter.
Renal artery narrowing reduces kidney perfusion, triggering renin release and hypertension.

{S} ureter.name: Ureter
{S} ureter.desc: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by peristalsis. It runs down on the psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, then curves forward to enter the back of the bladder obliquely, which forms a one-way valve. Small branches of the renal artery, aorta, iliac and vesical arteries supply it along its course.
clinical: Stones lodge at three narrow points: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the entry into the bladder.
The ureter is at risk of injury during pelvic and colorectal surgery, where it lies close to major vessels.

{S} adrenal gland.name: Adrenal gland (suprarenal gland)
{S} adrenal gland.region: Abdomen: retroperitoneal, on top of the kidney
{S} adrenal gland.desc: A small endocrine gland capping the upper pole of each kidney, the right pyramidal and the left crescent-shaped. Its outer cortex has three zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol) and reticularis (adrenal androgens). Its inner medulla is modified sympathetic tissue releasing epinephrine and norepinephrine. It has a rich arterial supply from three sources, but a single adrenal vein: the right drains into the IVC and the left into the left renal vein.
clinical: A pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the medulla, causes episodes of severe hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
Adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) causes fatigue, low blood pressure and darkened skin, and an adrenal crisis is life-threatening.

pineal body.name: Pineal gland
pineal body.desc: A small pinecone-shaped gland of the epithalamus projecting backward from the roof of the third ventricle, above the superior colliculi of the midbrain. Its pinealocytes secrete melatonin at night, controlled by light signals relayed from the retina through the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus and a sympathetic pathway via the superior cervical ganglion. It helps set circadian rhythm.
clinical: A pineal tumor can press on the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud syndrome: impaired upward gaze) and block the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.
The pineal often calcifies with age, making it a visible midline marker on CT.

pituitary gland.name: Pituitary gland (hypophysis)
pituitary gland.region: Skull base: sella turcica of the sphenoid
pituitary gland.desc: A pea-sized endocrine gland in the sella turcica, hanging from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum, beneath the optic chiasm and between the cavernous sinuses. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), controlled by hypothalamic releasing hormones via the portal vessels, secretes growth hormone, TSH, ACTH and others. The posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) made by hypothalamic neurons.
clinical: A pituitary adenoma growing upward compresses the optic chiasm, classically causing bitemporal hemianopia (loss of both outer visual fields).
Neurosurgeons usually reach pituitary tumors through the nose and sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal surgery).

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.region: Abdomen: left upper quadrant, under ribs 9 to 11
spleen.desc: The largest lymphoid organ, lying in the left upper quadrant behind the stomach, under the diaphragm along ribs 9 to 11. Its red pulp filters blood and removes old or damaged red cells, and its white pulp is lymphoid tissue that mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens. It is supplied by the splenic artery from the celiac trunk, and its splenic vein feeds the portal vein.
clinical: The spleen is the most commonly injured abdominal organ in blunt trauma, and rupture can cause life-threatening internal bleeding.
After splenectomy, vaccination is needed against encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus because overwhelming infection becomes a risk.

{S} lobe of thymus.name: Lobe of thymus
{S} lobe of thymus.desc: One of the two lobes of the thymus, a lymphoid organ lying behind the sternum in the anterior superior mediastinum, in front of the great vessels and pericardium. In the cortex, immature T cells from the bone marrow mature, and in the medulla, cells that react to the body's own tissues are eliminated. It is largest relative to body size in childhood and is gradually replaced by fat from the teenage years on.
clinical: Thymomas, tumors of the thymus, are linked to myasthenia gravis, and removing the thymus can improve the disease.
Children born without a thymus (DiGeorge syndrome) have severe T cell deficiency.

{S} lung.name: Lung
{S} lung.desc: The lungs fill most of the chest on either side of the heart, wrapped in pleura and resting on the diaphragm. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two plus the lingula, leaving room for the heart. Air reaches millions of alveoli through the bronchial tree, where oxygen crosses into pulmonary capillaries and carbon dioxide leaves.
clinical: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space that lets part of a lung collapse; tension pneumothorax is an emergency.
Inhaled objects more often lodge in the right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter and more vertical.
